Why must we also connect philosophy with the development of the natural sciences?

Because the development of philosophy in a materialist direction depends on the progress made by scientific knowledge of nature and on the extent to which science discovers nature’s objective laws.

The history of human knowledge in every age, as well as the reality of our own civilization, confirms that scientific knowledge of nature forms part of the foundation of every major advance in the different branches of knowledge—especially philosophy, with its attempt to understand the universe, nature, and society.

This point also has a social foundation.

Human knowledge of nature is directly connected with the material world outside us. It is therefore necessarily connected with material and social activity.

Indeed, the history of human civilizations shows in practical terms that this connection has always existed.

Human material needs have continually driven people, through the process of producing what they need, to discover the laws of nature and use those laws in production.

At the same time, the development of society’s material production and the development of the natural sciences have continually influenced one another.

The point can be put simply.

Just as the development of material production helps determine the development of human consciousness, of which philosophy is one of the highest forms, the development of the natural sciences also helps determine the forms that this consciousness takes.

8

The discussion so far has shown that the particular historical setting is what determines the forms taken by the materialist tendencies39 in the Arab-Islamic philosophical heritage. What, then, shaped this historical setting?

Two main factors stand out.

First, there was the nature of the feudal mode of production in Arab-Islamic society during the Abbasid period. It existed alongside the remains of a declining slave system, a growing commercial sector, and relatively advanced craft industries.

Second, the natural sciences flourished during this period, especially in the fourth century AH, or the tenth century CE.

These two main factors help explain why the materialist tendencies in this philosophical heritage did not take one fixed form. Instead, they moved back and forth between metaphysical and dialectical forms, at a level suited to the historical conditions of the time.

There were two reasons for this movement. On the one hand, the philosophers themselves often shifted between different positions. On the other, metaphysical and dialectical tendencies were also mixed together within the natural sciences of the period.

The dialectical form appears most clearly when texts from this heritage discuss motion, time, and space, especially their relationship to matter.40

This is one example of how philosophical ideas developed alongside the natural sciences. Studies of motion in nature, in particular, had made noticeable progress by this period. That progress found its way into philosophy partly because the philosophers themselves were often active in both fields. They combined philosophical thought with theoretical and experimental work on nature.

We can see the same movement between early metaphysical forms of materialism and early dialectical forms in Ibn Sīnā’s treatment of the relationship between the universal and the particular. He discusses this both as a question about existence in nature and as a question of logic.

For Ibn Sīnā, the relationship can take three forms:

  1. The universal, or essence, can exist within the particular thing. This is the position we later find in Hegel. Aristotle’s view also appears in this form, and it contains the idea of immanence.

  2. The universal can exist before individual things exist. This is the Platonic idealist position.

  3. The universal can exist after individual things exist. This is the materialist position.

All three tendencies appeared in medieval scholastic philosophy: the Aristotelian, the Platonic, and the materialist.

It is worth noting here that materialist tendencies appeared in both Arab-Islamic philosophy and European scholastic philosophy before the rise of the mechanistic materialists.

So on this question we can see Ibn Sīnā moving between three positions: a metaphysical position, a purely idealist position, and a materialist position that contains, to some extent, a dialectical element. In the last of these, the universal gains its existence from the existence of particular things.

9

We said that the historical setting of a philosophical heritage is shaped mainly by the two factors just discussed. But these are not the only factors. To claim that they were would itself go against our scientific method.

We therefore have to consider other influences when defining the historical setting of any philosophical heritage. The Arab-Islamic heritage is no exception. In fact, we will see that these other influences played such a strong role in it that they became part of its historical character.

Some of these factors belong to the objective forces that guide the development and history of philosophy. Two are especially important.

First: the relationship between internal and external conditions

Every society has its own internal conditions: national, regional, and local. But it also exists within wider conditions beyond itself: international conditions, continental conditions, and the conditions of a larger region containing several societies that may resemble one another in important ways.

The relationship between these internal and external conditions, and the forms of social consciousness that grow out of it, necessarily affects the direction and form of philosophical development.

This means that philosophy does not develop only because of conditions inside one particular society. It is also influenced by conditions outside it.

This external factor is very important if we want to study an intellectual heritage—and especially a philosophical heritage—in a scientific and genuinely comprehensive way.

It is also important because it helps us reject a claim often found in bourgeois histories of philosophy: the idea of “closed civilizations” or “closed cultures.”

According to this view, a civilization or culture develops entirely within the local conditions of one people, nation, or region, without being influenced by other civilizations and without influencing them in return. We find versions of this idea in thinkers such as Spengler and Toynbee.

But this claim lacks historical support.

History does not give us examples of civilizations or cultures that were completely closed in this way. Could the idea really be applied to Chinese civilization? To Indian civilization? To Arab civilization?

A culture can certainly be relatively closed for a limited period. But at other stages it may be influenced by other cultures, may influence them, or may do both at once.

Arab culture is a clear example. It absorbed influences from several major civilizations and cultures, including Indian, Persian, and Greek culture. It later influenced European civilization and culture, and in modern times it came under European influence in return.

The same basic pattern can be found in the history of other civilizations and cultures.

We may even question whether it is always correct to speak of separate “civilizations” in the plural.

Humanity has, in one sense, a shared civilization. Its many elements were created by different peoples, nations, and human groups across the different stages of history. They developed through interaction that was sometimes continuous and sometimes interrupted.

The history of human civilization therefore rests on a dialectical unity between the achievements of different peoples. All peoples pass through broadly similar stages of history in different parts of the world, but each passes through them in its own particular way.

If we do speak of several distinct civilizations, their differences must still be understood within this larger dialectical unity.

For this reason, we can see a kind of horizontal interaction running through their histories. A later civilization does not simply erase or cancel the civilization that came before it. On the contrary, it carries parts of it forward.

It does this by entering into contact with the earlier civilization, adapting some of its elements to its own conditions, developing others further, and abandoning still others as new and more advanced elements appear.

The general course of human civilization therefore continues to move forward. It does so despite its many twists and turns, and even despite periods of interruption. Those interruptions themselves become part of the larger movement.

If we look specifically at the history of philosophy across the world’s different cultures and civilizations, the same point becomes even clearer.

Even if we accepted the idea of a “closed” civilization or culture, we would still have to admit that philosophy has never developed through internal conditions alone. External conditions have always played a part as well.

But there is an important objective law that we must keep in mind here.

External influences can only take effect through internal conditions. They have to become part of those internal conditions rather than remaining separate from them. Otherwise, their influence will be artificial, superficial, or temporary.

There is another objective law that also matters when we study the relationship between cultures, and especially between philosophical traditions.

The degree of outside influence depends partly on how similar the social and intellectual conditions are in the two countries concerned—the country influencing and the country being influenced.

The closer their conditions are, the stronger the influence is likely to be. But we must look at the right kinds of similarities: the level of scientific development, class relations, and relations of production.

Second: the relative independence of philosophy

To understand the historical setting properly, we also have to take account of another factor: philosophy has a certain relative independence.

This independence appears in several ways. The one that concerns us here is simple.

Every new generation enters a world in which material and social relationships already exist. Those relationships were formed before that generation appeared and independently of its wishes.

The same is true of ideas.

Every generation also inherits a body of ideologies and intellectual traditions that developed before it. It receives a certain amount of intellectual material created by earlier generations, independently of what the new generation itself wants or does.

These inherited ideas cannot simply be treated as products of the material conditions that exist in the new generation’s own present. They came from the past.

But once they enter new conditions, they begin to change.

Put another way, no genuinely new idea or way of looking at the world can develop without inheriting older intellectual material and transforming it in a new way to match changes in material conditions.

This is the spirit behind Lenin’s discussion of the three sources of Marxism. He argued that Marxism did not arise outside the main course of human intellectual development. On the contrary, it answered questions that humanity had already been asking throughout earlier ages.

This idea also expresses the Marxist position toward national and global cultural heritage.

The aim is to preserve that heritage, but not simply because it is heritage.

The aim is to discover within it those elements of human thought that are shared across different peoples and generations, and then to follow those elements through their continuing development and change.

This development takes place through a double process: first, changes in society; and second, the changes in human consciousness that necessarily follow from them.

Seen in this light, we can clearly see how empty the attempts are of certain sections of the Arab intelligentsia41 who call for the Arab cultural heritage to be discarded, or for all engagement with it to end.42

This nihilist position is the direct opposite of the Salafi call to “modernize” the heritage in the sense discussed earlier.

The Salafi position treats past and present as if they were essentially the same. The nihilist position treats them as complete opposites.

The first wants to make the present subordinate to the past. In doing so, it alienates modern Arab society and modern Arab thought from their own age and from the revolutionary changes taking place within it.

The second wants to cut the present off from the past. In doing so, it alienates modern Arab society and modern Arab thought from their own history and from the roots that confirm their genuine place within that history.43

So although these two positions appear to be opposites, they meet on common ground.

Both uproot Arab society and Arab thought from the present itself.

One uproots them from historical authenticity. The other uproots them from modern life.

Both are therefore forms of separation from the present, because the present exists through a dialectical unity between historical roots and contemporary life. It is the unity of the relationship between past, present, and future.

Once one side of this unity is torn away, the unity itself loses its meaning. The present can no longer remain fully present in the historical and dialectical sense.

This is why the call to abandon all engagement with the heritage—whatever its ideological starting point—rests on assumptions that are rejected by the actual logic of social and historical reality. And in questions of this kind, that reality is the final test of whether an idea, theory, or assumption is sound.

10

After these methodological explanations, we can now move to a critical historical survey of the different positions taken toward the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage in general, and toward its philosophical part in particular, both in the past and in the present.

This survey is itself methodologically necessary.

It will allow us to compare these different positions with the theoretical and ideological principles we have already set out. We can then see where they agree with those principles and where they depart from them, and we can ask what lies behind each agreement or disagreement.

In the end, this should also allow us to give a brief answer, here in the introduction, to a question that has been with us since the idea for this book first arose and remained with us throughout the years of research that produced it:

Why do we need another work on the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage, and especially its philosophical heritage, after so much has already been written about it from the end of the Middle Ages to the second half of the twentieth century?

Our survey of the different positions taken toward this heritage—across both older and modern works—showed us how to answer that question.

We found that many of these positions, despite the very different periods they came from, the different societies in which they appeared, and the different bodies of knowledge and standards they used to judge the heritage, remained fundamentally one-sided.

We mentioned this at the beginning of the introduction. We now need to examine the matter in much greater detail and show why we believe that one-sidedness dominates the overwhelming majority of these positions.

This will not be a simple list of authors and books.

That kind of approach is very far from our method, because it comes too close to a purely subjective treatment. Still, some listing may occasionally be unavoidable while we analyze the different positions and group them into broader currents.

The people who have written histories, interpretations, and studies of the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage come from very different backgrounds.

They belong to different periods, societies, and ideological traditions. They come from different countries, and the knowledge they bring to the heritage also varies greatly.

Some are ancient, others modern. Some are progressive, others conservative. Some are materialists, others idealists. Some are Salafis, others nihilists. Some are Arab, some Eastern, and some Western. Among them are historians, theologians, social researchers, and philosophers.

These identities overlap in complicated ways. We therefore cannot use a simple classification that separates each one from the others.

We need a classification that reflects the overlap itself.

For this reason, we will use two different but overlapping forms of classification.

The first is methodological. It is based on the different ways scholars have viewed the heritage and the different intellectual methods they have used to deal with it.

The second is descriptive. It divides researchers into three broad groups:

  1. Ancient Arab and Eastern writers, from the Middle Ages through the later period up to the eighteenth century.

  2. Modern Arab and Eastern writers, from the nineteenth century to our own time in the twentieth century.

  3. Other researchers from different national backgrounds, especially Orientalists.

The first, methodological classification cuts across all three groups in the second classification.

Every researcher within those groups can be placed, broadly speaking, within one of the following four intellectual approaches.

First: treating the history of thought as a history of ideas alone

The first approach treats the history of thought, especially philosophy, as nothing more than a history of ideas or the product of “personal” thought.

It connects ideas only to the individuals who produced them, without asking how either those ideas or those individuals were related to the conditions of their age or to the society in which they lived and thought.

It therefore ignores the historical character of social relations and ignores the interaction between intellectual life and the economic, social, political, and historical relationships around it.

Those who have used this method to discuss the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage—across all three groups in our descriptive classification—have usually done little more than present a chronological account of the names and ideas of Arab-Islamic thinkers and philosophers.

Their explanations remain detached from the interaction between those thinkers and the societies and periods in which they lived.

There is, however, one kind of relationship to which these historians and researchers often pay close attention: the influence of one thinker on another.

They look at the influence of earlier thinkers on later ones, or at the influence of thinkers outside the Arab-Islamic tradition—Greek, Persian, or Indian—on individual Arab-Islamic thinkers.

In other words, they reduce historical relationships to relationships between individuals and to personal intellectual influence.

It is as if every thinker existed in a world of his own, separate from social reality, and as if intellectual influence passed directly between these isolated worlds without being shaped by social relations.

This way of thinking is clearly idealist.

Second: treating cultural influence as a simple mechanical transfer

The second approach sees the exchange between cultures in purely mechanical terms.

It assumes that once the culture of one people reaches another people, by whatever means, it can simply take control of their thinking, erase the distinctive features of their own culture, and replace them with the characteristics of the incoming culture.

Many studies of Arab-Islamic philosophy have taken this view.

This is especially true of some European Orientalists who claimed that Arab-Islamic philosophy was Arab or Islamic only in the sense that it was an Arabic copy of Greek philosophy,44 which the Arabs and Muslims simply adopted in its various “Pythagorean,” Platonic, Aristotelian, and Neoplatonic forms.

Some modern Arab researchers followed a similar approach.

One of them, for example, claimed that the Islamic spirit had been unable to understand the spirit of Greek philosophy, and that none of the Muslims who studied Greek philosophy possessed a genuinely philosophical spirit. Otherwise, he argued, they would have absorbed Greek philosophy fully, moved on to real intellectual creation, and produced a new philosophy of their own.45

There is an obvious difference between these two claims.

The first gives the philosophical work of the Arabs and Muslims a purely Greek character.

The second goes further and denies it even that much, because it denies that Arab-Islamic thinkers possessed a true philosophical spirit at all.

But despite this difference, both claims rest on the same simplified, mechanical way of thinking about the relationship between the thought of one people and the thought of another.

The first sees only the external form of the questions discussed by Arab-Islamic philosophy. It fails to understand that this form belonged to philosophy more generally during the historical period extending into the Middle Ages.

The second assumes that the only proof of a true philosophical spirit would have been for Arab-Islamic philosophers to discuss exactly the same questions as Greek philosophy. When it does not find those same questions reproduced in exactly the same way, it denies that Arab-Islamic thought was philosophical at all.

But the relationship between two intellectual or philosophical traditions belonging to two different societies is much more complicated than this.

It is part of the relationship between internal and external forms of social consciousness, and that relationship follows its own laws and its own dialectical movement.

The first basic feature of these laws is that they are objective. They do not depend simply on individual choice or intention.

The second is that ideas coming from outside can only become active and influential within a society by passing through its own internal relationships.

In other words, outside ideas can only become effective through the questions that already form part of the social fabric of that society—questions shaped by its own circumstances, its material relations of production, and its particular history.

Because these researchers did not approach Arab-Islamic philosophy in this way, they were unable to understand the inner dialectic of Arab thought in general, and Arab philosophical thought in particular.

They failed, first, to understand its relationship with Islam as thought, belief, and social system.

Second, they failed to understand its relationship with the questions facing Arab-Islamic society itself. These questions formed an extremely complicated web in which social and political issues were intertwined with religious, doctrinal, and legal ones.

And because they failed to understand this, they were also unable to understand the relationship between what was purely internal to Arab thought and what came from outside, whether through Greek thought in the West or Persian and Indian thought in the East.

This simplified mechanical view allowed them to deny the philosophical originality of Arab-Islamic thought.

Had they understood both sides of the problem—the inner logic of Arab thought and the way it interacted with thought coming from outside—they would have seen the heart of the matter more easily.

Greek philosophy could only have had its well-known historical influence on Arab-Islamic philosophy by being absorbed, transformed, and reshaped through the internal workings of Arab-Islamic thought itself.

Through this process, Greek philosophy became part of an Arab-Islamic reality and acquired a new life that was different from its purely Greek form.46

Third: explaining cultural differences in racial terms

The third approach explains differences between national cultures through race.

This is the worst of the approaches we are discussing.

It is not only a form of idealist thinking. It also grows out of a colonial and fascist ideology that places peoples in a hierarchy based on a “theory of race” that science rejected long ago.

A number of researchers have approached the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage in this racial way. They include Orientalists, Arabs, and other Eastern writers.

Some still approach it in this spirit today, consciously in some cases and unconsciously in others.47

Fourth: the historical approach

The fourth approach is to study the heritage historically.

The people who use this approach differ greatly in their methods, but they share one basic principle: they look for the relationship between inherited intellectual works and the historical conditions in which those works were produced.

Their differences come from the different ways they understand this relationship and from how deeply they trace it.

Some deal only with secondary or surface-level historical connections. Others try to reach the more fundamental ones.

Researchers who read the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage, especially its philosophical heritage, through historical questions in this general sense all belong somewhere along this line.

Among them are also those whose work goes beyond a general historical approach and adopts a specifically scientific method based on the principles of historical materialism.

These, then, are four intellectual approaches that have shaped many attempts, in different periods, to understand what medieval Arab-Islamic thinkers produced in fields such as theology, jurisprudence, law, philosophy, the natural and mathematical sciences, literature, and others.

We do not claim that these four approaches are the only ones that have shaped such studies. There are countless other ways in which people have approached this heritage.

But we can say that the first three, despite their differences in style, all grow out of one general intellectual method: an ahistorical method.

What ultimately unites them is the idealist position.

From that same position come other ways of looking at intellectual production, and from it also comes the broader ahistorical method that provides the general framework for approaches of this kind.

11

We have used the methodological classification as the main basis for our survey of how historians and researchers have approached our intellectual heritage.

But this does not mean that we can dispense with the descriptive classification. That second classification helps us place each position within its own historical, intellectual, and ideological setting.

As we have already said, it divides historians and researchers into three broad groups: ancient writers; modern Arab and Eastern writers; and Orientalists and other Western researchers.

We can now examine the positions found within each group.

A — The Ancient Writers

To understand how ancient Arab and Eastern writers approached this heritage, we have to go far back in time—back to a period when the heritage had not yet become heritage at all.

It was still the living present.

It was still being born and continually renewed. It was growing and changing. People devoted themselves to it, argued over it, and developed their own specialties within it. It raised problems for them, and they in turn raised new problems within it.

Different positions toward it already existed at that stage, before it had become a heritage inherited from the past.

Once it did become a heritage, new positions continued to appear in both East and West. They still appear today, and they will continue to appear in the future.

During the period when this body of thought was first developing, it moved through several stages: from purely Islamic theological forms, to theological-rational forms in Muʿtazilite kalām, then to its first philosophical form with al-Kindī, and finally to mature forms of philosophy that became independent in content from theological thought, beginning with al-Fārābī.

At every stage, this developing intellectual tradition provoked debate and was itself provoked by debate. It entered into conflicts and became the target of conflict.

It was always “partisan” in one sense or another, and it was always challenged by opposing forms of partisanship.

In every period it became the subject of disagreement and controversy. These intellectual and ideological struggles reflected, to different degrees, the social and political struggles taking place at each stage in the history of Arab-Islamic society.

The question of divine decree and human freedom was the first major issue that Arab-Islamic thought approached in a rational and explicitly “partisan” way—that is, from a defined intellectual position and with a political starting point, namely opposition to Umayyad rule.

As this question became one of the central intellectual issues debated between the first and second centuries AH, beginning around the middle of the seventh century, supporters and opponents entered into an increasingly intense struggle.

Those who opposed the rejection of predestination used religious authority to intimidate the other side.

Al-Muṣʿab al-Zubayrī, for example, reports Mālik ibn Anas (96–179 AH / 714–795 CE) as saying:

“I dislike discussion in religion. The people of our city have always disliked it and forbidden it, such as discussion of Jahm’s views, divine decree, and similar matters...”48

The opponents of human freedom went even further. They used religion to distort the position they were attacking by calling its supporters the Qadariyya, even though that name would seem more logically suited to those who believed the opposite—that human acts were determined.

The purpose was to apply to the supporters of free choice a saying attributed to the Prophet:

“The Qadariyya are the Magians of this community.”

The Muʿtazilites rejected the label. They argued:

“The term Qadariyya applies to those who say that divine decree, both good and evil, comes from God.”49

And that was not their own position.

The Muʿtazilites then developed the rational tendency further and gave it stronger theoretical foundations, drawing on philosophical influences from several sources.

Their movement marked a turning point in Arab-Islamic thought in two important areas.

The first concerned knowledge.

The Muʿtazilites broke with the idea that knowledge could have only one source, namely divine revelation. They added reason as another source of knowledge, even in questions of religious belief.

The second concerned human freedom and responsibility.

They built their understanding of divine justice on the idea that human beings are free and therefore responsible for their own actions. In doing so, they rejected absolute determinism.

Opposition soon developed against both sides of this position.

Religion was again used as a tool to restrain Muʿtazilite rationalism and to block its possible development toward a philosophical form of thought more independent of theology.

During the period when Muʿtazilism was at its height, this opposition was represented by three main currents: the Salafi current, the Hanbali current, and the Ashʿarī current.50

All three shared one basic feature: hostility toward the relatively progressive elements in Muʿtazilite thought.

• By the middle of the ninth century CE, the conservative currents had combined their efforts to remove Muʿtazilite thought almost completely from active intellectual life.

What happened afterward is remarkable.

The disappearance of the Muʿtazilites from the intellectual scene was followed by the almost complete disappearance of their original writings from Arab-Islamic libraries.

As a result, later generations were left with Muʿtazilite ideas mainly as their opponents had presented them: scattered, shortened, and removed from their original context.

Later readers were therefore denied the chance to encounter Muʿtazilite thought in the complete form in which the Muʿtazilites themselves had written it.

Only a very small number of their original works eventually reached us.

These included al-Intiṣār by Abū al-Ḥasan al-Khayyāṭ, along with several manuscripts discovered in Yemen by an Egyptian scholarly mission in relatively recent years. Some volumes of one of these works, al-Mughnī by the Muʿtazilite judge ʿAbd al-Jabbār, were later published in Egypt.51

It is clear to us now that this hostility would not have reached the point of almost erasing the Muʿtazilite heritage if its real target had not been the strong tendency toward intellectual freedom that ran through that heritage.

The campaign against Muʿtazilite thought continued into later periods and eventually took the form of hostility toward other kinds of thought based on reason, including the natural sciences, philosophy, and mathematics.

• Al-Masʿūdī describes how conservative Sunnis viewed Muʿtazilite thought under the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil.

He writes that although al-Mutawakkil was “one of the most unjust caliphs,” the Sunni scholars praised him and overlooked his actions because he had ended the miḥna—by which al-Masʿūdī means the period in which Muʿtazilite doctrine had official power. He adds that many hadith scholars claimed to have seen al-Mutawakkil in dreams in which they were told that God had forgiven him.52

Al-Suyūṭī gives us a similar example from the jurists and hadith scholars.

He tells us that during al-Mutawakkil’s reign, Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shayba sat in the Ruṣāfa Mosque while his brother sat in the Manṣūr Mosque, and both encouraged the people to pray for al-Mutawakkil and praise him.53

But opposition went much further than praise for al-Mutawakkil.

Muʿtazilite thought was attacked, distorted, and sometimes deliberately misrepresented.

Al-Isfarāyīnī, for example, gave a remarkable interpretation of Muʿtazilite texts on divine justice.

The Muʿtazilites had argued that human power is limited by the power of God.54

Al-Isfarāyīnī, one of the major Ashʿarī writers, interpreted their position in an extraordinary way.

Because the Muʿtazilites held that human beings create their own acts, he claimed that their view meant:

“Every one of them—even the gnat, the mosquito, the bee, the ant, and the worm—is a creator, creating its own acts. God is not the creator of their acts and has no power over any of them. Indeed, He has no power over anything done by all the animals. They therefore establish countless creators (...) and in doing so prepare the way for dualism.”55

This interpretation ignores the fact that when Muʿtazilite texts speak of “God’s servants” in this context, they mean human beings.

It also ignores the fact that the Muʿtazilites could hardly be accused of dualism. They defended the absolute unity of God so strongly that they fought bitter intellectual battles against dualists, as well as against those who gave God human-like qualities or a bodily form.

• Ibn Khaldūn may have been the only major ancient writer who, despite his own Ashʿarī allegiance, understood the importance of the historical conditions that made Muʿtazilite thought so attractive to many people of its time.

He recognized that the Muʿtazilite period was also a period of scientific development.

In his view, this historical reality helped philosophy spread and made people increasingly interested in it. It also created the conditions in which the Muʿtazilites could introduce what he called their “innovation”—a word that reflects his own Ashʿarī standpoint.

The Muʿtazilites used philosophy in their arguments, Ibn Khaldūn explains, and this made it difficult for their opponents to refute them because their arguments rested on philosophical foundations.

He then says that this was precisely why Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī took on the task of defending Sunni doctrine through rational arguments—in other words, by using the Muʿtazilites’ own weapon.

Later Ashʿarī thinkers followed the same path. They introduced logic into their discussions and eventually philosophy as well, while still keeping the questions of kalām separate from the questions of philosophy.

Ibn Khaldūn points in particular to the works of al-Ghazālī and “Imam Ibn al-Khaṭīb” as models of this approach.

He criticizes later theologians for confusing the two methods: the method of Sunni kalām and the method of the philosophers.56

Whatever Ibn Khaldūn himself intended, his discussion amounts to an indirect admission that the Muʿtazilites were the first to make the relationship between kalām and philosophy a historical reality.

Among the ancient Arab-Islamic thinkers, Ibn Khaldūn stands out for his sharp historical sense.

It gave his interpretation of events a more scientific character and allowed him to look beyond surface appearances, even though he remained an opponent of the Muʿtazilites because of his Ashʿarī commitments.

In fact, it is fair to say that his allegiance did not prevent him from seeing the deeper connection between the development of the sciences and the development of philosophical thought.

He understood that this connection helped explain the success of the Muʿtazilites. He also understood that the same historical conditions later allowed Ashʿarī kalām to become one of the two major successors to Muʿtazilite theology.

The other successor was philosophy itself.

The struggle had originally been between two main intellectual currents.

The first, represented by the Muʿtazilites, was trying to free itself from its theological ties, although it never fully succeeded.

The second insisted that thought must remain tied to theology. The Ashʿarī school eventually became the most advanced form of this second current because it was less isolated from the wider intellectual development of its time.

The historical forces behind this conflict were too powerful for the suppression of Muʿtazilite thought to end the conflict itself.

Those forces followed objective laws. They did not depend on personal wishes or deliberate decisions.

So even though Muʿtazilite thought was removed by force, the struggle did not disappear.

Instead, it moved into a higher form.

After the Muʿtazilites themselves vanished from the scene, the conflict developed along two major paths that remained in tension with one another until what we call the modern period.

The first path was philosophy: what we call Arab-Islamic philosophy.

The second was Ashʿarī kalām.

This new division marked a qualitative change in the form of the struggle.

The earlier conflict had been between pure theology and a form of theology that had become rationalized.

The new conflict was between a rationalized theology, represented by Ashʿarism, and a form of rational thought in Arab-Islamic philosophy that was pushing strongly toward independence from its theological origins.

Al-Ghazālī became the clearest representative of one side of this new struggle: the side that historical circumstances had forced to rationalize Islamic theology.

From al-Ghazālī onward, we can see more clearly how ancient writers positioned themselves toward philosophical thought.

By this point, philosophy had become the fullest expression of the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage. It had also entered into a dialectical interaction with major scientific achievements in physics, chemistry, astronomy, mathematics, and geography.

The effects of this interaction appeared in what we call the materialist tendencies.

Yet the dominant attitude toward philosophy among these writers came to follow the path of al-Ghazālī himself.

He turned the weapon of religious and intellectual intimidation against philosophy and the philosophers, and his approach went on to shape, to a great extent, the one-sided ways in which later Ashʿarī theologians and other historians viewed this heritage.

There are perhaps two major exceptions among the great Ashʿarī thinkers: al-Shahrastānī, the famous historian of philosophy, and Ibn Khaldūn.

Al-Shahrastānī was a model of a historian who remained faithful to historical evidence even while retaining his Ashʿarī commitments in matters of personal belief.

His theological position shaped his opinions, but not his historical investigation.

Ibn Khaldūn, as we have already said, stands out for a way of understanding history that often moves in a scientific direction. For this reason, he is much less often trapped by a one-sided view.

Hostility toward philosophy, however, began long before al-Ghazālī.

It even appeared before the time of Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī himself.

The difference is that the earlier hostility usually came from a vague sense that philosophy posed some kind of “danger” to Islamic belief—or, more fundamentally, to the ideology of political power—without any clear understanding of what that danger actually was.

It was driven first by conservatism itself, and second by the encouragement of political rulers and those who defended their ideology.

But from the third century AH, or the ninth century CE, philosophical knowledge became an organic part of the wider intellectual world.

From that point on, hostility toward philosophy increasingly came from a more explicit awareness of the danger that new philosophical trends posed to the dominant ideology.

These were trends that took philosophical truth itself as the basis for understanding the world.

This more conscious and informed kind of opposition is what we find in the Ashʿarī current and in its greatest representative, al-Ghazālī.57

By the last third of the third century AH, hostility toward philosophy was becoming increasingly severe.

Book copyists were even forced to swear that they would not copy philosophical works.

One result was that some abandoned their profession altogether.58

The date of this episode places it around the rise of the Ashʿarī current.

And the fact that book copyists abandoned their trade after being forbidden to copy philosophical works tells us something else: philosophical books must have been so widely read that banning their reproduction seriously damaged the copyists’ livelihood.

Among the ancient writers, then, one-sided views of the philosophy of this period appeared in several forms.

Most of them shared a common intellectual approach dominated by supernaturalism, subjectivism, and a static, metaphysical way of thinking.

□ One of the first places we see this approach is in the explanations earlier writers gave for the translation movement that brought philosophical and scientific works into Arabic and became especially active under al-Maʾmūn. A famous explanation came from Ibn al-Nadīm (d. 385 AH/995 CE). He tells us that al-Maʾmūn saw Aristotle in a dream and asked him a number of questions. When al-Maʾmūn awoke, he ordered Aristotle’s books to be translated. He wrote to the Byzantine emperor asking permission to select from the ancient books of learning preserved in Byzantine lands. The emperor at first refused, but eventually agreed. Al-Maʾmūn then sent a group that included al-Ḥajjāj ibn Maṭar, Ibn al-Biṭrīq, Salm, the head of the House of Wisdom, and others. They selected the books they wanted from those they found and brought them back. Al-Maʾmūn then ordered them to translate the books, and they did.59

So this is how a historical movement of enormous importance to the development of Arab-Islamic thought was explained: through a supernatural and purely personal way of thinking, and with remarkable simplicity and naivety.

What is more surprising is that later Arab-Islamic historians repeated Ibn al-Nadīm’s explanation without questioning it, almost as though it were self-evidently true. It therefore stopped being the explanation of one individual and became part of a wider way of understanding major historical events.

This way of thinking prevented those historians from seeing an important fact. The connection between Arab-Islamic thought and the ancient sciences—that is, philosophy together with logic, natural science, mathematics, and medicine—had begun before the time of al-Maʾmūn. It did not have to wait for the caliph to have his “historic” dream.

It did not have to wait because the course of history itself had already created the social pressures, intellectual exchanges, and cultural needs that gradually established this connection during the first two Islamic centuries. Aristotle could hardly have had the “honour” of appearing in al-Maʾmūn’s dream if he had not already been present in the intellectual world of the Abbasid caliphs who came before al-Maʾmūn.

And Aristotle would receive far greater attention than anything suggested by this dream, especially from al-Maʾmūn himself. Al-Maʾmūn really did play a major role in developing the connection with ancient learning. But he did so in response to the real conditions of his society and his time, not because of an accidental dream, a passing coincidence, or his own personal will.

□ We see the same general approach in another form when writers discuss whether the “Arab mind” was naturally capable of philosophical knowledge. Here a racial way of thinking begins to appear.

The judge Ṣāʿid al-Andalusī (d. 463 AH/1070 CE) used this kind of reasoning when he discussed the sciences among the Arabs. He wrote:

“As for philosophy, God Almighty granted them no share of it, nor did He shape their natural disposition to take an interest in it. I know of no one of Arab stock who became famous for it except Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī and Abū Muḥammad al-Ḥasan al-Hamdānī.”60

It is clear that Ṣāʿid’s generalization was not limited to pre-Islamic Arabia, even though the surrounding discussion in his book might initially suggest that it was. His judgment reaches all the way to the periods of al-Kindī and al-Hamdānī. In other words, he treats it as a judgment about Arabs as a human race in every age of their history, rather than about a particular society living under particular conditions at a particular stage of history.

We will see this racial way of thinking appear again in discussions of Arab-Islamic philosophy, both among earlier writers other than Ṣāʿid and among modern Arab researchers and Orientalists.61

For the author of Ṭabaqāt al-Umam, then, Arabs were a “race” that was not naturally or instinctively suited to receiving philosophy, or to acquiring this kind of higher knowledge.

His exceptions—al-Kindī and al-Hamdānī—only serve to confirm the rule he believed he had found.

At the same time, however, Ṣāʿid did not divide the philosophers of this intellectual heritage according to their original ethnic ancestry. We can see this first from the distinction just discussed, and second from the praise and admiration he gives al-Fārābī elsewhere in the book, even though he regarded al-Fārābī as being of non-Arab origin.

Dividing the philosophers of this heritage according to their different ethnic origins does more than introduce a racial view that cannot be accepted scientifically. It also breaks apart the unity of the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage.

That heritage cannot be broken up along racial lines.

Its unity rests on two foundations that are historically and objectively bound together: its Arab character and its Islamic character.

The heritage is Arab as a whole, whatever the ethnic origins of the people who produced it. It is Arab not simply because Arabic was its language. Its linguistic structure was also bound up with its intellectual, social, and political structure. At the same time, it was connected with philological, anthropological, and psychological structures.

Its Islamic character was equally bound up with this whole formation, in both its existence and its development. The Islamic character of the heritage cannot be separated from its Arab character.

For all these reasons, it is wrong to look at the people who created this heritage and say that one was Arab while another was not. In cultural and intellectual terms, they all belonged to the Arab tradition, and they all belonged to the Islamic intellectual world as well.

This broad category also includes non-Muslims who helped create the heritage in any of the ways known to history—for example, by translating Greek, Persian, and Indian cultures and philosophies.

□ Al-Shahrastānī himself fell into another kind of unrealistic and unscientific way of looking at this heritage.

Speaking of the “later philosophers of Islam,” he writes that:

“They all followed the method of Aristotle in everything he taught and in the views peculiar to him, except for a few points where they may have preferred the opinion of Plato or the earlier philosophers. Since Ibn Sīnā’s method is regarded by the group as more precise, and his investigation of realities as more penetrating, I chose to present his method from his books (...) and passed over the methods of the others. The whole prize of the hunt is there.”62

To be fair to al-Shahrastānī as a scholar, we should not begin simply by criticizing the weakness in his approach that appears in this passage. Before explaining that criticism, we must recognize the major contribution al-Shahrastānī made to the history of philosophy.63

His book al-Milal wa-l-Niḥal (Religions and Sects)64 marked something close to a whole new stage in the development of the history of philosophy as a field of study. He set out to write a history of world philosophy as it was known up to his own time.

He also seems to have had a good knowledge of the sources he used. He presented the philosophies of the Greeks, Persians, Indians, and Arabs in a connected sequence while preserving the distinctive features of each.

The work was especially important because al-Shahrastānī tried to draw a line between religion and philosophy.

This probably did not come only from something distinctive in his own education. More importantly, it came from the principle he adopted in his method of research. At that stage of history, this principle was itself highly progressive.

At the beginning of the second part of his book, he writes:

“Chapter One: the followers of opinions and sects among the Sabians, the philosophers, the views of the Arabs in the Age of Ignorance, and the views of the Indians. These stand in direct opposition to the followers of religions, as we have said. They rely on sound natural disposition, complete reason, and a clear mind.”65

In this passage, al-Shahrastānī does more than distinguish religion from philosophy. He also states, quite objectively, that philosophers rely on “sound natural disposition, complete reason, and a clear mind.”

This does not contradict the dismissive language he later uses about philosophers whom he classifies as eternalists, naturalists, and metaphysicians. He was still approaching philosophy as a Muslim committed to the Ashʿarite school.

But it is important enough that he separated religion from philosophy and acknowledged that philosophy rests on principles he could not simply deny.

Al-Shahrastānī made another important contribution as well. He tried to distinguish philosophies from one another according to broad intellectual currents, rather than merely according to the personal opinions and ideas of individual thinkers.

This was one of his greatest contributions to the development of the history of philosophy.

He divided philosophers into:

A — Materialists or naturalists. He said that they relied on the world known through the senses, and he called them naturalist eternalists.

B — Metaphysical philosophers. He said that they accepted sensory reality and also affirmed what can be known by reason, but rejected religious laws, revealed law, and Islam. According to him, they regarded religious laws as arrangements made for the general welfare of society. Legal limits and rulings, and the categories of permitted and forbidden, were human conventions. The founders of religions, in their view, were men of practical wisdom.66

In another classification, which he called his comprehensive scheme, al-Shahrastānī wrote:

“Among people are those who accept neither what is known through the senses nor what is known through reason. These are the Sophists. Some accept what is known through the senses but not what is known through reason. These are the naturalists. Some accept both the sensory and the rational but do not accept legal limits and rulings. These are the eternalist philosophers. Some accept the sensory, the rational, and legal limits and rulings, but do not accept revealed law and Islam. These are the Sabians. Some accept all of these, together with a revealed law and a form of Islam, but do not accept the revealed law of our Prophet Muḥammad. These are the Magians, Jews, and Christians. And some accept all of these. These are the Muslims.”67

In this attempt by al-Shahrastānī, we can also see an early step toward distinguishing materialist philosophers from idealist philosophers.

There is another important distinction in al-Milal wa-l-Niḥal. Al-Shahrastānī sees philosophy as an arena of conflict between these two groups: the materialists and the idealists.

This was another very important principle to appear at that stage in the writing of the history of philosophy. It meant that this historian was trying to identify the source and driving force behind the development of philosophy itself.

All these principles give al-Shahrastānī’s history of philosophy great importance. Its value lies not only in the material it contains, but also in the fact that it established important principles of research that later philosophers developed further in their own works.

Yet all these major strengths do not prevent us from finding a weakness in al-Shahrastānī’s approach when he discusses the philosophers of the Arab-Islamic heritage.

His claim that they all followed Aristotle in everything Aristotle taught and in everything distinctive to his philosophy, apart from a few points where they may have preferred Plato or other earlier philosophers, is contrary both to the historical evidence and to any scientific understanding of how different cultures and philosophies interact.

As for the evidence itself, a close study of these philosophers reveals many ways in which they departed from Aristotle, even though they never made a complete break with the Aristotelian tradition. It also shows that their creative differences from Aristotle affected the foundations of their theories in important ways, especially in relation to the theory of emanation.

In the present book, we will repeatedly try to show where the philosophers of our heritage differed from Aristotle and from other earlier philosophers.

Even if we accepted the view that the work of these philosophers was limited to commenting on and interpreting classical texts, a closer look at those commentaries and interpretations would still reveal their distinctive value.

Commentary and interpretation could become independent acts of creative thought. At times they produced genuinely new ideas, from which the first seeds of new theories emerged and the foundations of an independent philosophy began to take shape.

As for the interaction between different cultures, we have already pointed out earlier in this introduction that an outside culture can influence another culture only through the internal factors already operating within the receiving society. In other words, the influence passes through the particular conditions in which that culture exists.

Those conditions may be economic, social, political, or intellectual. Underlying them is the particular kind of relations of production that exists in that society and the historical form those relations take.

This is a general objective law.

It therefore makes no sense to suppose that Arab-Islamic philosophers living in the Middle Ages, in a society dominated by its own particular form of feudal relations of production, would think in exactly the same way as Aristotle, whose philosophy reflected the conditions of the ancient world and its particular slaveholding society.

Of course, we have no right to expect al-Shahrastānī, living when he did, to have known this law, much less to have applied it.

But given the remarkable qualities he showed as a historian of philosophy, we can reasonably expect him to have noticed what the philosophers of the Arab-Islamic tradition developed independently of Aristotle and the other “earlier philosophers.”

We can also expect him to have seen, for example, what distinguished al-Kindī and al-Fārābī from Ibn Sīnā.

He should not simply have presented Ibn Sīnā’s method and ignored “the methods of the others” on the grounds that “the whole prize of the hunt is there.” That proverb proves neither a philosophical point nor even a historical one.

We have spent time on this criticism of al-Shahrastānī because his approach reflects a widespread way in which earlier writers dealt with the Arab-Islamic philosophical heritage.68 We find many examples of it among them, just as we also find it frequently in the work of modern Orientalists and Arab researchers.

□ There is another model of how earlier writers understood—or perhaps misunderstood—the heritage.

A traditionalist current arose that wanted to cut even the thin thread the Ashʿarite school had left as a formal connection between the rational method of logic and philosophy on the one hand and the traditionalist method on the other.

Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ (d. 643 AH) was at first the most extreme of the later jurists who represented this current.

He became famous for a legal ruling in which he declared the study of logic and philosophy forbidden.69

Logic was forbidden because, as he put it, “logic is the gateway to philosophy, and the gateway to evil is itself evil.”

Philosophy, meanwhile, was evil itself. It was:

“the foundation of foolishness and dissolution, the source of confusion and error, and the cause of deviation and heresy (...) As for using the terminology of logic in questions of religious law, this is among the reprehensible and repulsive innovations and the newly introduced deviations. Religious law—praise be to God—has no need whatsoever for logic. As for what the logician claims about the usefulness of definition70 and demonstration, God has spared every sound mind any need for them...”71

In his campaign against logic and philosophy, Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ even attacked Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī himself.

He objected to what al-Ghazālī wrote at the beginning of the introduction to al-Mustaṣfā. Speaking about logic, though without naming it directly, al-Ghazālī said:

“It is the introduction to all the sciences, and anyone who has not mastered it”—meaning this logical introduction—“cannot be trusted in any of his knowledge.”72

Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ included this among his criticisms of al-Ghazālī in a statement on:

“important matters for which al-Ghazālī was criticized in his writings, and irregularities in his work that neither the scholars of his own school nor others approved.”73

Al-Ghazālī’s remarks about logic were one of these “important matters.”

□ After Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, the banner of this traditionalist current was taken up by “Shaykh al-Islām” Taqī al-Dīn Aḥmad ibn al-ʿAbbās, better known as Ibn Taymiyya (661–729 AH).

For scholars of the intellectual heritage, Ibn Taymiyya’s name is closely associated with the two-front struggle he fought.

On one front, from his Hanbali position,74 he opposed the Ashʿarite school and the theological schools more generally.75

On the other, he opposed Aristotelian logic and philosophy.

The basic principle behind Ibn Taymiyya’s method appears in the title The Agreement of Clear Reason with Authentic Revelation.76 The idea is that everything reliably transmitted in the Islamic texts must necessarily agree with reason.

For Ibn Taymiyya, then, there can be no real conflict between reason and revealed law.

If a conflict appears, the transmitted text must be unreliable. But if a genuine conflict remains even though the text is authentic, then the text—not reason—must be the final authority.

He built his arguments on both fronts around this principle.

Ibn Taymiyya did not, however, take an absolutely negative position toward logic. Unlike Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, he did not simply forbid people from studying it.

Instead, in a number of his works,77 he examined the foundations of Aristotelian logic and the ways it had been applied in the arguments of Muslim theologians from different schools.

Here too, his criticism returns to the same basic principle.

For Ibn Taymiyya, the logic of the Aristotelians conflicted with authentic Islamic texts. In his system, this necessarily meant that it also conflicted with sound reason.

His overall criticism of Aristotelian logic and of the Muslim theologians who used it centers on two main questions: definition and syllogism.

This form of logic was concerned with organizing the ways in which two kinds of knowledge could be reached: knowledge of concepts and knowledge of judgments.

It made definition the route to knowledge of concepts, and syllogism the route to knowledge of judgments.

Ibn Taymiyya rejects both claims. He denies that Aristotelian definition is the necessary route to the first kind of knowledge, and that Aristotelian syllogism is the necessary route to the second.

He therefore also rejects the Aristotelians’ claim that concepts can be reached only through definition and judgments only through syllogism.

As he puts it:

“All these claims are false, both in what they deny and in what they affirm. Not everything they reject in the methods of others is false, and not everything they affirm in their own methods is true in the way they claim.”78

The most important arguments Ibn Taymiyya uses against Aristotelian definition are connected with his view of the relation between essence and existence—or, more plainly, between the universal and the particular.

He draws a sharp line between essence—the universal or general—and existence outside the mind.

For him, essence exists only in the mind. Outside the mind, only particulars exist: the individual, concrete instances of an essence.

Abstract essences therefore have no independent existence outside the mind, as they do in Plato’s theory of Forms. Nor do they exist alongside individual things in the way they do for Aristotle and the Muslim Aristotelians.79

Ibn Taymiyya thus breaks the real connection between the universal and the particular. The first exists only in the mind; the second exists only in the external world.

This is the basis of his objection to the Aristotelian idea of logical definition.

For the Aristotelians, a true definition is made up of the essential qualities of the thing being defined. Those essential qualities form part of the thing’s essence.

In Ibn Taymiyya’s view, however, this would mean that the essences of things—their true realities—must themselves exist outside the mind.

It would also mean, first, that this external existence was different from their existence in the mind, and second, that it was different from the concrete existence of the individual things in which those essences appeared.

Ibn Taymiyya describes these supposed consequences as separating an essence from its existence—by which he means its existence in the mind.80

All this means that the source of his objection is his opposition to what he sees as the consequences of believing in fixed, abstract essences.

One possible consequence is the existence of eternal essences in a world above nature, as in Plato’s Forms. This would mean accepting a plurality of eternal realities.

The other is the idea of an eternal essence of matter—prime matter—that exists potentially before becoming actual through form. This, in turn, leads to the claim that the material world is eternal, as implied by Aristotle’s theory of matter and form in his “first philosophy.”

Both conclusions conflict with Islamic doctrine: the first with the unity of God, and the second with the belief that the world was created in time.

Ibn Taymiyya’s criticism of Aristotelian logical definition is therefore religious in its basis. It follows from his principle that clear reason must agree with authentic revelation.

It is not a purely logical criticism. In other words, it does not begin by examining the idea of definition simply as a problem within logic.

We should nevertheless recognize that Ibn Taymiyya’s criticism of the distinction made by Peripatetic logicians between essential and accidental qualities in definitions81 has a positive side and comes closer to reality.

It leads him to reject fixed essences understood in an idealist and metaphysical sense.

But his criticism still rests mainly on his decision to break the real connection between an essence and its concrete instances in the external world, because he confines the existence of essence to the mind.

The second main target of Ibn Taymiyya’s criticism of Aristotelian logic is the syllogism.

Here he goes into considerable detail. Some of his arguments concern the propositions used to build a demonstration, while others concern the methods of logical inference themselves.

When discussing propositions, Ibn Taymiyya makes a major effort to establish the certainty of particular propositions based on experience and of reports transmitted through many independent chains.

His aim is to establish the certainty of ḥadīth in the Islamic sense and thereby support his basic principle: the agreement of clear reason with authentic revelation.

He criticizes philosophers for refusing to recognize widely transmitted reports as a source of certain knowledge. In his view, they restrict certain knowledge to theoretical propositions—that is, propositions produced through rational logical syllogism.82

He also rejects the philosophers’ claim that certain knowledge is produced by rational logical demonstration and that the propositions produced by such demonstration must be universal.

Here again, his criticism follows from his belief that universals exist only in the mind and that only individual, concrete things exist outside it.

If that is true, then logical demonstration cannot give us knowledge of anything that actually exists in the external world.

As he writes:

“What perfection does the soul gain simply by conceiving these general and universal things if it does not conceive the particular, concrete beings that actually exist? And what knowledge of the Lord of the worlds can there be in this, when the soul can reach perfection only by knowing Him and worshipping Him with love and submission?”83

The source of Ibn Taymiyya’s criticism here is the belief that God is a specific, individual reality rather than a universal.

A universal implies a plurality of individual instances, and this would conflict with the doctrine of divine unity.

Ibn Taymiyya therefore concludes that universal knowledge cannot be certain and that logical demonstration does not provide real knowledge.84

The error in all these equations, however, lies in the foundation on which Ibn Taymiyya builds them.

He denies that essences, or universals, exist in the external world within particular things.

In other words, the basic weakness in all these arguments is that he has no scientific solution to the problem of how the universal and the particular—the general and the specific—are related in reality.

This is why Ibn Taymiyya continues trying to prove that the universal premises used in Aristotelian logical demonstration are neither truly universal nor truly certain.85

Yet after all the effort he puts into rejecting reliance on universal propositions, he is not troubled by contradicting himself in two other statements.

The first concerns religious questions. Here he says:

“In matters known through the sayings of the prophets, the need for a universal proposition becomes clear. One example of such a universal proposition is the saying of the Messenger, peace be upon him, that every intoxicant is forbidden.”86

In another statement, he writes:

“Grasping the universal is one of the most distinctive qualities of reason, by which it differs from the senses. The senses know only a particular thing, while reason understands it universally and without restriction.”87

But even this recognition of universal propositions is connected with a strongly sensory and empirical position.

In his reply to the logicians, Ibn Taymiyya argues that particular items of knowledge—knowledge gained through the senses—are the only realities that actually exist in the particular things of the external world.

From this he concludes that universals are of no real use because they exist only in the mind.

His final conclusion is that the knowledge produced by logical demonstration is not knowledge of what actually exists. It is knowledge only of something purely mental, with no reality outside the mind.88

As for Ibn Taymiyya’s criticism of the methods of Aristotelian logical inference, it is built in general on the same foundations as his criticism of Aristotelian definition in the formation of concepts and his criticism of the propositions that make up—and are produced by—demonstration in the Aristotelian theory of judgments.

In fact, many Muslim theologians and scholars of legal theory took a similar position toward Aristotelian logic because of their position on the problem of definition.

They feared the consequences that might follow for Islamic metaphysics if they accepted a theory of definition based on fixed essences. We saw this clearly in our discussion of Ibn Taymiyya’s position.

□ After Ibn Taymiyya, two currents appeared among the traditionalists.

One continued in his general direction.

The other followed the Ashʿarite line, opposing philosophy and philosophers with the weapons of philosophy itself.

Within the first current, some returned to Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ’s method of simply forbidding logic and philosophy. Among them were Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya (d. 751 AH),89 al-Ṣanʿānī (d. 840 AH),90 and al-Suyūṭī (d. 911 AH).91

The second current—the Ashʿarite one—eventually included later thinkers who practiced philosophical reasoning quite freely.

Some modern researchers have described their method by saying that they:

“became deeply immersed in philosophical books, until the subject matter of the two sciences—kalām and philosophy—became confused for them and they treated the two as one. Questions of kalām became mixed with questions of philosophy until the two disciplines could no longer be clearly distinguished, as happened with al-Bayḍāwī (d. 691 AH/1286 CE) in al-Ṭawāliʿ and ʿAḍud al-Dīn al-Ījī (d. 750 AH/1355 CE) in al-Mawāqif.”92

The general pattern in how earlier writers approached the philosophical heritage after Ibn Taymiyya, well beyond the sixteenth century, was shaped by these two currents, despite some very important exceptions.

The Ashʿarite current, however, generally kept its dominant position in intellectual activity in this field.

Most of the major later commentators on theological and philosophical works, and most historians of philosophy, were Ashʿarites, from Ibn Khaldūn to Ṭāshkubrīzāda (d. 963 AH/1550 CE).93

Among the important exceptions were the later Shiʿi philosophers, above all Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī, better known as Mullā Ṣadrā or Ṣadr al-Mutaʾallihīn (980–1050 AH/1573–1640 CE).94

They are exceptions in two senses.

First, these Shiʿi philosophers approached philosophical thought from outside both of the currents discussed above—the Hanbali and the Ashʿarite—at least in terms of their formal school affiliation.

Second, their approach to philosophy had a strong internal consistency.

This was possible because they developed its metaphysical categories and concepts in ways that matched Shiʿi concepts, especially those concerning prophecy and the Imamate.

For this reason, Shiʿi philosophical activity in the later period of the classical tradition was not only intellectually fertile. It also developed features of its own.

Perhaps the most striking of these was the close internal connection between the philosophical outlook and the religious spirit of the school.

This led some Eastern and Orientalist researchers95 to see Shiʿi philosophy as having a mystical character.

But what appears to be mystical in it comes, in our view, from the deep absorption of Shiʿi thought in the doctrine of the infallibility of the Imams.

That devotion, together with the tragic historical conditions faced by the Shiʿi movement at different stages of its history, gave Shiʿi philosophical thought an unusually strong emotional intensity. This is what gave it the character that sometimes brings it close to mysticism.

Here we mean the Twelver Imami Shiʿa in particular, rather than the Ismailis or other Shiʿi groups.

Most of the critical discussion so far has focused on earlier writers who worked directly in intellectual fields such as logic, theology, philosophy, or legal theory.

We have discussed historians only when a particular historian also took part in historical theory or the philosophy of history, as in the cases of Ibn Khaldūn and al-Shahrastānī.

We therefore need to stop briefly and look at the attitudes of earlier Arab-Islamic historians themselves. Their surviving works recorded many features of medieval Arab-Islamic society during the period in which this intellectual heritage was produced.

We should note, however, that most of these historical works are general histories of events, individuals, or countries.

Works devoted specifically to the history of intellectual life in general, or to one particular intellectual phenomenon, are relatively rare.

There is also a lack of works devoted specifically to the history of philosophy as a discipline in the sense in which we understand it today.

Al-Shahrastānī may have been almost alone in laying the foundations for a history of philosophy at the level possible in his own age, just as Ibn Khaldūn, in the Muqaddima, was almost alone in laying the foundations for a social science of history at the level possible in his.

But this does not mean that the historians of Arab-Islamic society ignored intellectual life, including philosophy.

In fact, some of their works come close to specialized histories of particular fields of thought.

Examples include the books known as works of biography and “classes”: classes of philosophers, physicians, poets, scholars of ḥadīth—that is, transmitters of reports about the Prophet—and others.96

There were also books on religious sects and schools.

These are, in fact, historical records of an important part of intellectual life because they present the intellectual and theoretical principles behind the differences and disputes between the various sects and schools, including theological, legal-theoretical, and philosophical schools.

And even general historical works contain, to different degrees and with different levels of quality, records of intellectual events, movements, and developments, biographies of thinkers, and sometimes discussions of one field or another within Arab-Islamic thought.

Taken together, these historical writings therefore allow us to identify the ways in which Arab-Islamic historians approached the intellectual heritage that concerns us here.

● What stands out most clearly to the modern scientific researcher is that one approach dominates the way these historians looked at the heritage—that is, at the movement of intellectual life they were describing in their historical works.

It is a quantitative and fragmentary approach, something that can be seen as a historical form of what we would now call empiricism.

In the writings of these historians, intellectual events, movements, and currents appear as piles of separate episodes.

Events, periods, places, people, and situations accumulate one after another, but the internal relationships that connect them and turn them into broader historical patterns remain unseen.

The same is true of the external relationships through which these events and movements affect one another and are themselves affected.

Nor do these historians see how a gradual accumulation of quantitative changes can produce a qualitative transformation.

Their attention usually remains fixed on the outward course of each separate event, or on some side angle chosen by the historian that never reaches the deeper line running through the origin, development, and transformation of the larger historical process.

That side angle is often the reign of a caliph, the term of a governor, the rule of an emir, the command of a military leader, or a particular year marked by war, famine, or fitna.

Very often what they call fitna was actually a social revolt with deep causes that lay outside the way these historians understood the event.

They describe the war, the famine, or the fitna without discussing its deeper social causes.

This way of looking at intellectual activity naturally reflects the way these historians looked at the historical process in its more basic field: social life itself.

For historical reasons, they were unable to see realistically how social history develops or to identify the basic forces that decisively shape its direction in a particular society.

They were therefore also unable to see, first, the essential connection between intellectual activity and social activity and, second, the internal relationships between intellectual events and movements themselves.

● But this historical limitation does not explain every position taken by these historians.

It is true that a scientific understanding of historical development had not yet become possible in their age.

But in some cases that explanation is not enough.

We must also take account of personal motives, as well as objective class and ideological forces that shaped their positions.

We should not ignore the fact that many of them wrote history—whether political history or intellectual history—from the standpoint of the ruling power.

Some did so out of self-interest, some out of fear, some because they had absorbed the officially favoured ideology, and some simply because of their own class position.97

One especially clear example is the attitude of earlier historians toward one of the most important historical crises faced by the Abbasid caliphate.

We mean the mass peasant uprising that spread across large sections of the peoples of the Arab-Islamic empire in Azerbaijan, northwestern Iran, and eastern Armenia at the beginning of the third Islamic century, during the reigns of al-Maʾmūn and al-Muʿtaṣim.

The uprising was led by Bābak al-Khurramī between 816 and 838 CE. It therefore became known as the Bābak revolt and remained active for twenty years, from 202 to 222 AH.

It so happens that the major Arabic historical sources for this period of Arab-Islamic society were written by historians who lived in the third and fourth Islamic centuries. Some of these historians lived through the Bābakī revolt themselves. Others wrote about the period while the events were still fresh. Yet in their major works, we find either silence about the revolt or a distorted picture of it—of its events, its aims, its ideology, and its social principles.

These distortions helped bury the revolt’s real character and obscure its radical social and intellectual dimensions. They came partly from the bias of these early historians, who sided with the caliphate, local rulers, and great feudal landowners—the very forces targeted by the revolt. In some cases, their own class background also shaped their views. And beyond this, they lacked the historical tools needed to uncover the social roots of this peasant uprising.

For one reason or another, most of them accepted the two-part historical deception spread by the authorities, their officials, and their allies, all of whom were threatened by the revolt’s aims.
