The revolt was presented, first, as an uprising against Islam and an expression of hostility toward the Arabs; and second, as a movement whose principles would destroy the moral order of society.

In general, these historians viewed the revolt from the standpoint of political authority and feudal ideology, though this bias took different forms in different writers.

Take al-Balādhurī, Abū al-ʿAbbās Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā (d. 279 AH/892 CE). He may well have witnessed the Bābakī revolt in his youth, or at least felt the intensity of a crisis that deeply troubled the caliphal court. Yet in his Conquests of the Lands, he virtually ignores it and gives it no direct treatment. The intellectual side of the movement appears only in a passing reference, where he calls Bābak, the leader of the revolt, “the unbelieving Khurramite.”98

In doing so, he follows the same path as other writers who repeated accusations against the rebels without examining them, helping stir hostility toward them among Muslim populations throughout the Abbasid realm.

This position is hardly surprising when we remember al-Balādhurī’s close ties to the Abbasid caliphs99 and what is known of his habit of “seeking the company of men of rank and power.”100 Perhaps by remaining silent about the revolt and its social principles, he was keeping to himself an opinion that differed from the official one. He may have preferred silence rather than risk angering the very people whose favor he sought. Otherwise, it is difficult to explain why he said so little.

To his credit, however, al-Balādhurī gives us detailed reports about the way land was granted and controlled in the regions affected by the Khurramite revolt. He also describes the oppression suffered by the people of those areas, especially the peasants, at the hands of landholders, as well as the heavy taxes imposed by the caliphate and the harshness of its tax collectors.101 In this way, he provides us with evidence that helps reveal the social conditions that made the revolt inevitable.

Al-Yaʿqūbī, Aḥmad ibn Abī Yaʿqūb (d. after 284 AH), takes a somewhat different position in his well-known History.102

The difference appears in two ways. First, he does not ignore the revolt, though he gives few details. Second, in the little he says about its ideology, he partly joins those who attack it, accusing the Bābakī rebels of plundering settlements, travelers, and pilgrims.103

Even so, al-Yaʿqūbī and al-Balādhurī, together with al-Ṭabarī,104 Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn Jarīr (224–310 AH), and al-Masʿūdī,105 Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn (d. 346 AH), did less than most of the historians discussed here to distort the real character of this peasant mass revolt.

With Ibn al-Nadīm,106 Abū al-Faraj Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq al-Warrāq (d. 385 AH/995 CE), the picture begins to grow darker. Myth and fact become increasingly tangled, until the myths themselves turn into “facts” in the works of the generation after Ibn al-Nadīm, then in those of later modern Arab researchers and Orientalists.

This continued until a contemporary Arab scholar107 confronted this whole obscuring tradition. He belongs to a new generation of researchers who are courageously opening the way toward studying our history and intellectual heritage through a scientific view of social history—historical materialism—and of the development of human thought within it.

This introduction cannot examine every position taken by the early writers toward the intellectual heritage we are studying. But the general survey above has shown the main trends in those positions and provided examples that reveal the intellectual and ideological assumptions behind them.

12

B — The Approaches of Modern Scholars

In the opening pages of this introduction, we placed the modern Arab return to its older heritage within the historical setting in which it began to take shape more than a century ago.

At that time, the return to the heritage was the intellectual expression of the changes that announced the beginning of the movement later called the “Arab Renaissance,” or Nahda. We traced this concern with the heritage back to the same forces that first produced the Nahda in its early, shallow form.

Later, a new form of the movement emerged from deeper popular currents within Arab society and from a broader social horizon. Its content changed. What had begun as a reformist “renaissance,” tied to the ambitions of leading Arab elites and to their indirect attempts to compromise with Western imperial ambitions, developed into a national liberation movement.

As the Arab movement changed, the idea of “returning to the heritage” changed with it.

At first, this return had the same renaissance character as the reformist Arab movement itself. In this form, it was close to romanticism. It looked back to the past simply because it was the past. It was driven by an emotional attachment to the past for its own sake and by a tendency to praise everything inherited from it without distinction or examination.

Earlier, we described this phenomenon through two qualities that seem contradictory: its content was reactionary, but its motives were progressive.

Its content was reactionary because it glorified the past without qualification. Its motives were progressive because it helped awaken national feeling and contributed to the revival of an Arab “identity” in the face of a double challenge: Turkish racialist Turanism on one side, and Western imperialism on the other, already preparing to divide the inheritance of the “sick man.”

At this stage, the movement back to the heritage took on the character suggested by the name commonly given to it: the “revival of the heritage.”

Literature—and especially poetry—was the first form this “revival” took.

But in reality, this was less a revival of the heritage than a draining away of what life still remained in it. Writers imitated its language, styles, images, and themes, but much of the living substance that had originally given those forms meaning was missing.108

A new form of this “revival” then appeared. It was more useful and much closer to a real revival: the publication of old works in literature, criticism, poetry, history, law, and religious doctrine through the new technology of mechanical printing, which began spreading during the nineteenth century in countries such as Egypt, Lebanon, and Syria.109

At first, however, these publishing efforts were largely unsystematic.

For one thing, books were usually chosen simply because the work or its author was famous. There was no broader principle guiding what should be published.

For another, publishers generally did not compare different manuscript copies of the same work in order to establish the most accurate text and date it properly, as Orientalist scholars were doing when they published works from the Arab-Islamic heritage.110

There were probably several reasons for this weakness. Publishers often did not know the methods of scholarly manuscript editing. Many old manuscripts had also disappeared from Arab libraries because of repeated invasions and wars over many centuries. Another factor was the presence of Orientalists in Arab countries during and after the Crusades and their acquisition of a large share of the surviving manuscript heritage.

Even during this first stage of the return to the heritage, however, an important new movement appeared in the final third of the nineteenth century. It was new in its outlook and had a deep influence across the Muslim East: the school of Jamāl al-Dīn al-Afghānī (d. 1897) and his student Shaykh Muḥammad ʿAbduh (d. 1905).

Their approach to the heritage went beyond the almost romantic attitude that had dominated the period.

The Afghānī-ʿAbduh school approached the heritage with a degree of criticism. Al-Afghānī believed that the countries of the East needed to resist Western colonial ambitions with a form of thought freed from rigid and unquestioning reverence for the past.

The present, he believed, required a new understanding of inherited ideas—one that could help Eastern societies confront the growing danger of colonial domination.

From this starting point, al-Afghānī urged these societies to abandon inherited ideas and customs when they followed them blindly. He condemned the passivity and absolute fatalism that reached them under the name of divine decree and destiny.

This was the basis of his well-known attack on Sufis “who turn belief in divine decree and destiny into an excuse for sitting idle instead of earning a living.” He judged that people who understood trust in God as nothing more than passive dependence deserved to be humiliated and that society should be cleansed of their harmful influence, because their ideas did not agree with religion.111

Muḥammad ʿAbduh, who represented the Arab-Egyptian wing of this school, worked from the same basic principle in his social and intellectual call to reinterpret the heritage of Islam—both doctrine and law—and the heritage of Muslim theologians and philosophers in the light of a modern world very different from the medieval one.

In this spirit, he wrote:

“Whoever follows the path of independent reasoning, does not rely on imitation in matters of belief, and is not protected from error may indeed make mistakes. But his error is accepted by God so long as the aim of his effort and the purpose of his careful examination are to reach the truth and arrive at certainty.”112

The same outlook also kept Muḥammad ʿAbduh from following the traditionalist path of hostility toward the rationalist tradition represented by the Muʿtazila and the philosophers. Nor did he declare someone an unbeliever simply for believing in the eternity of the world.113

He did not accept Sufism either, except when it took the form of “moral discipline guided by rational discipline.”114

Nor did he side with reactionaries who said women should be denied education. He found it astonishing that people should be left trapped in ignorance and even encouraged to remain there.115

He also rejected the inherited claim of strict jurists that Islam forbids sculpture and painting,116 and so on.

Even so, although the Afghānī-ʿAbduh school helped crack the wall of absolute reverence surrounding the heritage, it did not develop a method for studying that heritage that fundamentally broke with the older methods. It remained tied to the same ideological foundations on which those methods rested.

The first stage of the return to the heritage came to an end only when the movement itself began to take shape within the forces we analyzed at the beginning of this introduction.

By this we mean the growing transformations within the Arab national liberation movement: both its progressive content and the increasing maturity of the class and ideological struggles taking place inside the liberation movement itself.

In this new stage, the way people looked at the heritage began to acquire a progressive content on one level while becoming part of ideological struggle on another.

This change cannot be separated from the development of the Arab national liberation movement. But neither can it be separated from the growth of scientific knowledge among Arab researchers, their exposure to academic methods used in Western universities and Orientalist scholarship, and their growing familiarity with modern intellectual and philosophical currents emerging in developed capitalist societies.

For many, however, this opening toward outside knowledge remained one-sided. For some, it never went beyond a liberal outlook.

If we want to move beyond general statements and identify the different positions taken by modern Arab researchers toward our intellectual heritage, we need to return briefly to the earlier classification we used for the main ways of studying it. These modern positions have not completely broken with those older approaches.

Let us recall them briefly, so that we can build directly on them without treating the list as exhaustive:

  1. An approach that treats the history of thought as a history of individual thinkers and their personal ideas.
  2. A mechanical approach to the exchange between different cultures.
  3. An approach that explains differences between human cultures on racial grounds.
  4. The historical approach.

Before going further, however, we should warn against turning these categories into rigid boxes.

In reality, there are no sealed boundaries between one approach and another. We therefore have no right to place a particular researcher in one “box” or another and then pass a single, absolute judgment on him.

That kind of rigid judgment would itself violate the method we are using.

The habit of treating the development of human thought in a given society as a sequence of individual thinkers, or as a sequence of their ideas, is widespread in modern histories of Arab-Islamic philosophy.

It is especially common in books prepared for teaching the subject in final-year secondary schools or universities.

In this way, such books help reinforce an idealist way of thinking among generations of school and university students.

One example is a book used by philosophy students preparing for the Lebanese secondary-school certificate, titled Great Figures of Arab Philosophy.117

The book shows both sides of this tendency. On the one hand, it presents the history of Arab philosophy as the history of its “great figures.” The title itself is enough to show this. On the other hand, it presents that history as a history of the ideas held by those individuals.

We find an example in the following passage:

“The Qadarites: Maʿbad al-Juhanī.

“The first person who became known for saying that man has free choice and is not compelled was Maʿbad ibn Khālid al-Juhanī. It is said that he took this idea from a Christian in Iraq who had converted to Islam and later returned to Christianity. Maʿbad’s student, close companion, and successor Ghaylān ibn Marwān al-Dimashqī then took it from him. Ghaylān spread and popularized the idea, argued for it, and defended it vigorously. He later added other views of his own on questions that had become widely debated. His ideas then formed a school, and his followers became a sect known as the Qadarites, whose teaching rested on three main views.”118

This is how the Qadarite movement appears: one man has an idea; another man receives it from him and adds further ideas of his own; these ideas then form a school; and the Qadarites become “his followers.”

What disappears from view is the fact that the Qadarite movement was a historical movement, one that arose as an almost direct reflection of a social and political struggle within a society ruled by an absolute hereditary monarchy that justified itself in the name of divine decree and destiny.119

The authors of the book do not consider this, even though the historical sources themselves do not identify the beginning of the Qadarite movement with anything like the rigid certainty found in the passage just quoted.120

Only an idealist way of thinking can accept such an explanation for the origin of intellectual—or any other—historical phenomena.

The Qadarites also appear here in another way: Maʿbad al-Juhanī supposedly received the idea from a Christian, and so on. In other words, the idea appears as something purely religious, passed from one individual to another, from Christianity into Islam, until it became an Islamic religious issue.

We therefore find two approaches overlapping here.

First, intellectual history is treated as a history of personal ideas isolated from the history of the society in which the people holding those ideas lived.

Second, it is treated as the history of religious ideas with no connection to the earthly problems of human beings.

Both approaches come from an idealist and ahistorical method.

The habit of looking at this heritage only from its religious side, cut off from its human and social roots, is also widespread among modern Arab scholars. It is found even among contemporary writers living in the final decades of the twentieth century.

Consider, for example, what they write about the origins of kalām, philosophy, or Sufism.

How, according to them, did these intellectual traditions—which form some of the central parts of our heritage—come into being?

Their answers are almost all the same, or variations on the same theme.

They generally agree that kalām began as debate over religious doctrine. In the days of the Prophet and his Companions, they say, these debates remained within the religious texts and their obvious meanings. Later, the debates went beyond this and became “the defense of religious beliefs through rational arguments”121 in response to “foreign influences.”122

Some writers define these foreign influences as “a continuing campaign of attack against the new religion and its doctrines,” or as “philosophical attacks coming from different religions, different philosophical beliefs, and various Eastern schools that existed in the lands the Muslims conquered.”123

On this point, they are largely in agreement.

They differ more when discussing internal influences.

One writer argues that “the whole of Islamic life is nothing more than an interpretation of the Qurʾān: from studying the Qurʾān’s practical laws came jurisprudence; from studying it as a book dealing with metaphysics came kalām; from studying it as a book concerned with the afterlife came asceticism, Sufism, and ethics; from studying it as a book of government came political science; and from studying its language came the linguistic sciences,” and so on.124

Others identify the following internal factors:

  1. “The Qurʾān discussed the main sects and religions that existed in the time of the Prophet Muḥammad—peace be upon him—and answered them and refuted their claims.”125
  2. “When the Muslims had finished their conquests, settled down, and become prosperous, their minds began to philosophize about religion. Religious disagreements arose, and they began to examine them and try to reconcile their different aspects. This seems to be a general feature of all the religions we know...”126
  3. The disputes centered on the caliphate after the Prophet.
  4. The ambiguous Qurʾānic verses and disagreements over how to interpret them.127

To explain the rise of kalām in this way—as modern Arab researchers do in almost all its main outlines, however much their wording or details differ—is to take the question outside history.

The one apparent link with history is their reference to the struggle over the caliphate and its role in the rise of Islamic sects, each of which needed theological arguments to support its position.

That struggle was certainly historical.

But its real historical content was very different from what these writers usually describe.

They treat the caliphate mainly as a religious office. The struggle over it therefore becomes a legal or, in modern terms, “constitutional” disagreement: a dispute over which authority Islamic law had designated to choose the caliph after the Prophet.

The disagreement, on this view, is theoretical and legal. Nothing more.

When some of these writers occasionally call it “political,” their idea of politics remains very shallow. It usually goes no further than the personal ambitions of the individuals competing for the caliphate.

Some go even further and remove even this limited idea of politics from the historical struggle.

One contemporary researcher, for example, finds no “clear conflict” even in the struggle that ended with the killing of the third Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUthmān. Instead, he sees only “a great preparation for a coming intellectual movement in which debate would intensify...

“There was no major disagreement. The third caliph stood by the Qurʾān and followed the practice of the great Prophet. The Messenger of God died pleased with ʿUthmān, and the two great elders died pleased with ʿUthmān. Even this learned guide of the community, its scholar—indeed the man most devoted to truth,” meaning ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, “was also pleased with the third caliph. What, then, was there to disagree about?”128

When the “historical” relation between the rise of kalām and the struggle over the caliphate is treated in this way, through such a metaphysical style of thinking, history itself almost disappears.

Aḥmad Amīn is nearly alone in understanding this relationship historically in a way that comes somewhat closer to the reality of the problem.

He argues that the struggle over the caliphate was political, much like struggles between political parties in our own time, even though parties then did not take the same modern organizational form.

Instead, he writes:

“They took on a strongly religious character. Every political party became a religious sect, and those who fought one another politically also fought one another religiously. Instead of the party being given a political name expressing the political principle it supported, it was given a name expressing a religious doctrine: Shīʿa, Khārijites, Murjiʾa...”

The same applies, he says, to familiar theological questions such as whether a Muslim who committed a major sin was an unbeliever or still a believer:

“It seems that the discussion was not purely theological. Its origin lay in the judgments political parties made about one another...”129

But Aḥmad Amīn does not take this sound historical insight far enough.

He does not reach the deeper core of the issue: the social content of the political groupings involved in the conflict.

Because of his bourgeois intellectual and ideological method, we have already seen him explain the Muslims’ “philosophizing about religion” after they had “finished the conquest and settled down” as simply one example of “a general feature of all the religions we know.”

He does not place it within the particular history of that stage of Muslim society—that is, within a political struggle that had a definite social content.

So he retreats from the historical reasoning he had briefly approached when discussing religious-political sects and finally returns the rise of kalām to a purely religious starting point separated from its specific historical conditions.

The bourgeois analyses of the rise of kalām found in these modern studies are not capable of revealing the full dimensions of the problem.

Those dimensions reach back to the social conditions in which Islam first appeared in Mecca. At that time, there was already an embryonic social conflict, though it still took a tribal form.

When the struggle over the caliphate erupted after the Prophet’s death, that earlier conflict now appeared in a religious form. Under the new conditions, it found the forces that allowed it to grow and expand into a social and political struggle far beyond the place and time in which it had first emerged before Islam.

These social and political dimensions did not become fully visible until the caliphate of the third Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUthmān, and especially in the period immediately after his death.

His killing was connected with the first uprising of its kind in Arab history after Islam, because this uprising openly raised mass demands centered on a clearly defined social and political issue. It had stripped away—or almost stripped away—even its religious form.

This uprising reflected a major development among broad sections of the new society in the newly founded provincial centers.

The killing of Caliph ʿUthmān brought problems that had been developing beneath the surface sharply into the open. They became violent and bloody. Their social and political dimensions appeared with new force, especially after the Umayyad party took hold of them, even though it had itself been one of the direct forces that helped provoke them.

These conflicts inevitably had to find expression in forms of thought that, for historical reasons, took an Islamic religious form.

Out of these intense social problems emerged competing intellectual currents. At first, ideas accumulated unevenly and without any clear system. At the same time, they interacted with several streams of non-Arab culture.

Eventually, this gradual accumulation reached the point where it changed in quality and became a more organized field of knowledge.

Muʿtazilite kalām was this new form.130

The same problem appears when modern scholars discuss the Arab-Islamic philosophical heritage. Even contemporary researchers still often use the same approach they use when explaining the origins of kalām.

□ Philosophy in this heritage is described as “Islamic philosophy.”

For many of these scholars, it is Islamic not in a historical sense—not because it arose within a society whose medieval history was closely tied to Islam and whose political and social system developed under the Islamic caliphate—but in a religious sense: Islamic doctrine and Islamic law.

The historian and philosophical thinker Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq built his analysis of the heritage on this understanding. He used the same meaning when he called the philosophical heritage “Islamic” in the title of his work on its history.131

This is why, in his view, Islamic philosophy includes Islamic legal theory, or uṣūl al-fiqh. His reason is that most of the questions discussed in legal theory are, he argues, much like the questions discussed in the study of the foundations of religious doctrine—that is, in kalām.132

ʿAbd al-Rāziq does not place Islamic kalām outside “Islamic philosophy.” Instead, he sees the discussions of kalām and legal theory as basic elements in the structure of that philosophy.

For this reason, he even calls al-Shāfiʿī (d. 204 AH/819 CE), the founder of the Sunni legal school named after him, a philosopher.

His reason is that al-Shāfiʿī “developed a method for deriving legal judgments”133 based on

“the direction of the scientific mind, which is not concerned merely with individual details and branches. His thinking was the thinking of someone who did not focus on isolated questions and disagreements, but sought to organize detailed arguments under general principles that brought them together. That is philosophical reasoning.”134

A contemporary Ashʿarite scholar follows a similar path and calls al-Shāfiʿī “Islam’s greatest philosopher of legal principles.”135

But this scholar goes further and limits the whole philosophical heritage to the work of Muslim theologians and scholars of legal theory.

The philosophy of al-Kindī, al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, Ibn Rushd, and others “who are called the philosophers of Islam,” he argues, is not “authentic Islamic philosophy.” Instead, it is “Greek in both its general principles and its details, a mixture of Aristotelianism, Platonism, and Neoplatonism.”136

Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq does not go that far.

He strongly emphasizes the Islamic character of the philosophical heritage, ties this character to Islamic doctrine and law, and sees this connection as the basis of the originality of “Islamic philosophy.”

Even so, he does not deny the originality of philosophical activity outside theology and legal theory.

He does not take the completely dismissive position adopted by al-Nashshār.

Instead, he places the philosophers and the scholars of theology and legal theory within a single connected intellectual tradition.

By “Islamic philosophy,” then, ʿAbd al-Rāziq means all intellectual work produced within “Islamic” thought that contains elements of philosophical reasoning, including rational methods of inference and the organization of detailed arguments under broader principles.

He goes further still.

ʿAbd al-Rāziq defends the originality of the Muslim philosophers—figures such as al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, and Ibn Rushd, whom al-Nashshār describes as imitators of earlier masters.

He also rejects the racial theories used by some Western scholars when discussing these philosophers, especially attempts to divide thought into a “Semitic mind” and an “Aryan mind.”

He writes:

“By the twentieth century, the idea of bringing Semitism and Aryanism into judgments about Islamic philosophy had almost disappeared, as the theory of Semitism and Aryanism itself weakened and lost much of its scientific support.”137

There are also two points where ʿAbd al-Rāziq moves beyond his own traditionalist method and comes close to a historical one.

The first is that he is willing to use the term “philosophers of Islam” even for philosophers who were not Muslims, and to call their philosophy “Islamic”:

“Those who practiced philosophy under Islam, Muslims and non-Muslims alike, are called the philosophers of Islam, and their philosophy is called Islamic philosophy in the conventional sense...”138

The second is that he supports the name “Islamic philosophy” partly because the people who practiced this philosophy themselves used that name.139

From this he reaches an important conclusion:

“For all these reasons, we believe that we should call the philosophy we are discussing by the name its own people gave it: ‘Islamic philosophy,’ meaning that it arose in the lands of Islam and under the rule of the Islamic state, regardless of the religion or language of those who produced it.”140

On these two points, and especially in this final explanation, ʿAbd al-Rāziq moves beyond his original method toward another one that comes close, as we have said, to a historical approach.

But this shift remains limited because the heart of his argument is still not historical.

At its core, his analysis rests on two ideas.

First, he ties “Islamic philosophy” to Islamic doctrine and law.

Second, he has a particular view of the relationship between religion and the heritage of the “philosophers of Islam.”

For him, this relationship is based on reconciliation between religion and philosophy and on the idea that religion and philosophy share “one truth and one goal.”141

This is the heart of the issue not only for ʿAbd al-Rāziq, but for other modern thinkers whose understanding of the heritage rests on a bourgeois ideological position that also shapes their views of contemporary questions more generally.

Their insistence that the Arab-Islamic philosophical heritage as a whole had a religious and “reconciliatory” character, and their insistence that all its philosophers accepted a “unity of truth and unity of purpose” between religion and philosophy, does not mainly come from a failure to study the texts deeply enough or to recognize their historical setting.

Its deeper source is an intellectual outlook that can see the heritage only from its religious and metaphysical side because it follows—sometimes consciously, sometimes unconsciously—the dominant ideological structure of bourgeois thought.

One aim of this book is to challenge the “myth” that this heritage was essentially based on reconciliation between religion and philosophy.

It will also try to remove the surface appearance that has led people to imagine that the “philosophers of Islam,” or at least the major ones among them, accepted the idea that religion and philosophy share “one truth and one goal.”

□ Ibrāhīm Madkūr also tried to move beyond both the traditionalist method and the Western Orientalist method toward what he called a “historical method.”

He noticed the weaknesses in existing studies of the heritage of “Islamic philosophy” and the mistaken assumptions on which many of those studies were based.

He therefore concluded that researchers needed to rely on “the historical method” if they wanted to correct these weaknesses and challenge those assumptions.142

This is a valuable proposal from a major scholar in the field of modern philosophical studies, and it deserves to be treated positively.

That remains true even if we set aside Madkūr’s unconvincing attempt to excuse the assumptions of Western researchers.

He argues that these assumptions arose “mostly because they were formed before a complete study had been made, and because they were not drawn directly from Islamic thought in its original sources, but were instead suggested by a distorted picture found in the Latin manuscripts then in circulation.”

He also writes that “some historians of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries discussed Muslim intellectual life without knowing the language, or without having enough Arabic sources available to them.”143

In reality, Western scholars, including Orientalists, did not reach their conclusions simply because they were “ignorant” of the original sources or lacked knowledge of Arabic.

The original sources of the heritage have often been more available to them than to us.

And the many Western scholars who know Arabic are no less proficient in it than many contemporary Arab researchers themselves.

Dr. Madkūr must know this very well.

So, leaving aside this “explanation,” which does not change the historical reality, we can still view his call for a “historical method” positively.

But what exactly does Madkūr mean by this method?

He says that Islamic thought should be

“presented in itself and studied realistically in light of the foreign ideas that reached the Muslims and on the basis of the questions and discussions produced within the Islamic environment itself. It should be known directly through those who created it and expressed it, so that it can be understood as it truly was and properly grasped. Its stages of development should then be followed: its origin, growth, completion, and maturity, and the extent of its influence on later generations and schools should be shown.”144

He also says that the researcher should try, as far as possible, to enter into the life of the people of the past.

Ideas should not be studied in isolation from one another.

The philosopher being studied should be placed properly within his environment.

The researcher should understand the philosopher’s formation and how it was connected to the ideas of his time.

His views should not be separated from other connected areas of Islamic culture.

Historical periods should not be divided by artificial boundaries.

And history should not be turned into a set of hypotheses with no connection to reality.145

These are the main outlines of Madkūr’s “historical method,” scattered throughout the introduction to his book.

If we bring them together and treat them as a single whole, they provide a sound basis for historical research into the heritage.

At the same time, we can already see signs that Madkūr’s idea of “historical method” is mainly concerned with the internal history of ideas and thinkers themselves. It sometimes seems closer to historical editing of texts and to intellectual biography than to a history of the wider society in which those ideas arose.

For the moment, however, we will not base our judgment on these hints. It would be too early.

Looking only at the method as he presents it in theory, we have to view it positively and consider it a new attempt to produce a modern understanding of the heritage.

That is true at the formal and theoretical level.

But whether its intellectual and ideological starting point is sound can only be decided by looking at how the method is actually applied.

Madkūr gives the book we are discussing the slogan “A Method and Its Application.” In the introduction, he promises that applying the method will confirm and clarify it.146

When he discusses the relationship between Islamic and Greek philosophy, he rejects theories claiming that Islamic philosophy was simply a copy of Aristotle, as Renan argued, or of Neoplatonism, as Duhem claimed.

In arguing against these views, he points out that Muslim philosophers lived in an environment and under conditions different from those of other philosophers, and that it is a mistake to ignore the effect of those conditions on their ideas and theories.

He writes:

“The Islamic world was therefore able to form a philosophy of its own, one that developed in harmony with its religious and social foundations...”147

All of this suggests that we are about to see a serious practical application to match the serious theoretical proposal.

But we run into the problem from the very first step.

Madkūr begins his practical application by discussing the “theory of happiness and union” and its relation to Islamic Sufism. He then examines Islamic Sufism itself and, after that, al-Fārābī’s Sufism.148

Sufism may be one of the best possible tests of a historical method.

Its historical character can only be uncovered by someone who takes the scientific core of that method seriously, rather than stopping at a formal version of history concerned only with “the internal history of the thinker and his thought.”

Sufism is certainly subjective in one sense: it is an inner experience lived by the individual Sufi.

But in reality, it is also a social phenomenon because it expresses an indirect response to a particular social reality.

This is why Sufism takes different forms and develops different features under different kinds of social relations, political conditions, and systems of power.

Studying Sufism in any particular society is therefore a demanding test. The facts themselves reveal how strong or weak a research method is, and they also reveal its intellectual and ideological character.

This is exactly what we find when Madkūr applies his “historical” method to Sufism.

From the first step, as we have said, the method disappoints us.

In his analysis, Sufism is reduced to individual experience and never opens out onto historical reality, except for the personal “history” of the individual having the experience.

And when it does look beyond that individual, it finds only other individual “experiences.”

Al-Fārābī, the first subject to which Madkūr applies his method, is presented as a Sufi who represents “the earliest form of Sufi ideas among the philosophers of Islam.”

Madkūr divides the influences on al-Fārābī’s Sufism into two kinds: internal and external.

The internal influence is that al-Fārābī “lived a life of asceticism and austerity and preferred solitude and seclusion.”

But what is the source of that?

The first external influence is “the environment in which Abū Naṣr lived.”

At this point, we expect something new. We expect Madkūr to show us the social environment of al-Fārābī’s time and explain how that environment contributed to his Sufism.

But we soon discover that by “environment” he means only the many Sufi ideas circulating in the Islamic world during al-Fārābī’s lifetime.149

And the only “historical” explanation he offers for those ideas is that they came from “Indian, Persian, African, or Christian origins.”150

The second external influence on al-Fārābī’s Sufism is that he lived at the same time as major Sufis who believed in divine indwelling, such as al-Junayd, al-Shiblī, and al-Ḥallāj.151

The third is that al-Fārābī’s theory of happiness was taken from Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics.152153

The fourth is that he was influenced by Plotinus’s theory of “ecstasy.”154155

After listing these “external” influences, Madkūr reaches the following conclusion:

“We can therefore see that al-Fārābī’s theory of happiness arose from several factors and different circumstances. It owes as much to al-Fārābī’s own inclinations and dispositions as it does to his environment and to the Muslim thinkers around him.”156

This conclusion, together with everything that comes before it, shows us what Madkūr really means by “environment,” “social conditions,” and “surroundings” when he uses these terms in the main outline of his “historical” method.

In the end, the method we were told was historical turns out not to be historical at all.

We have spent this much time on Madkūr’s “historical” method because it represents a trend in contemporary studies of the heritage that has emerged more recently, after the traditionalist method came under growing pressure to change its old ways.

New approaches began to appear that borrowed the forms and language of scientific method, which in our own time has been gaining ground across many areas of research and thought.

But the older traditionalist method still has a powerful influence, even in its older forms.

Let us therefore look at some other examples of approaches that continue to appear in new books and in widely read Arab journals.

□ In one modern traditionalist work, we find a discussion of the relationship between Arab-Islamic culture and the other cultures it came into contact with and absorbed.

The relationship is described in the following way:

● During the time of ʿUmar, the Arabs conquered a number of different kingdoms and came into contact with very different cultures: Egypt, with the remains of Alexandria, then a center of learning; Persia and Iraq, both rich in different religious and philosophical movements such as Nestorianism, Mazdakism, and Manichaeism; and Syria, where the Sabians and other followers of ancient religions lived...

This meant that a great body of knowledge was now within reach of the Arabs, if they wished to draw from it.

But at first, we are told, the Muslims rejected these cultures and turned away from them, apart from a few rare exceptions. They were proud of their religion and unwilling to become students of peoples who had become their subjects. They did not seriously turn toward those cultures until changing circumstances brought them down from their former position of dominance.157

There is more than one problem here from the standpoint of scientific method.

Before we even reach the question of method, there is a historical problem.

The claim that the Arabs “rejected” these cultures and “turned away from them except in a few rare cases,” and that they “did not turn toward them until changing circumstances brought them down from their position of dominance,” is contradicted by the historical evidence itself.

The historical sources give us no shortage of evidence to the contrary.158

Even the works of Muslim historians and researchers, both older and modern, tell a different story.

They describe in great detail—sometimes even exaggerating—the many religious and philosophical ideas that entered from outside.

These ideas did not merely become part of Arab-Islamic culture. They also entered into the very disputes and conflicts that helped form some of the central structures of that culture.

Where rejection did occur, it was not a rejection of foreign cultures simply because they were foreign, or because they belonged to peoples who had “become subjects” of the Arabs, supposedly because the Arabs were too “proud of their religion” to become students of such “subjects.”

Nor did “the Arabs” as a whole, as one people or nation, reject these cultures in the way Ghurāba’s account seems to suggest.

Rejection came from particular groups, particular schools, or particular movements. It was one expression of wider social, intellectual, and ideological struggles.

Some ideas were rejected and others accepted.

Every act of rejection stood beside an act of acceptance.

But neither rejection nor acceptance was ever based simply on whether an idea was foreign. Ideas were accepted or rejected because they agreed or disagreed with the intellectual and ideological positions of the people considering them.

That is the first point.

The second is that it is historically wrong to say that the Arabs did not seriously engage with foreign cultures until “changing circumstances brought them down from their position of dominance.”

The historical record shows that interaction with these cultures had already begun in the early Umayyad period.159

It then became a powerful current during part of the early Abbasid period, when Arab political dominance was at one of its highest points.

That is the historical problem.

The methodological problem is that Ghurāba’s account contains two approaches that scientific method rejects.

The first is a racially arrogant view of non-Arab peoples and their cultures.

This appears in the language of “tribal pride toward other peoples” and in the description of those peoples as “subjects.” Both expressions carry traces of an ideology of despotic domination and of class and racial superiority.

The second problem is the way cultural exchange is treated as something simple and mechanical on the one hand, and as a matter of personal choice on the other.

Once the Arabs had this “great body of knowledge” within reach, was the whole matter really just a question of what they personally wanted?

If they had “wanted” to draw from it, they could have done so—but they supposedly “did not want” to, and therefore did not?

Can a researcher writing in the second third of the twentieth century really imagine that the relationship between cultures works in such a simple, mechanical, and voluntary way?

The form taken by the relationship between one culture and another is not decided by personal wishes.

It is determined by objective reality—above all, by how close or how different the social relations reflected in the two cultures are.

Cultural interaction develops on this basis.

And this process of interaction is what produces the particular relationship between the two cultures.

The result is always a new stage in the development of both cultures.

But the decisive factor in shaping that new development is the internal dynamics of the culture doing the receiving, not the culture coming from outside.

This process of interaction has three main features.

First, it is complex, not simple.

Second, it is dialectical, not mechanical.

Third, it is objective, not subjective.

Acceptance and rejection are therefore not, at the deepest level, simple acts of accepting or rejecting something by conscious choice.

They are not voluntary acts of selection.

At their core, they are the result of ideas being absorbed and transformed from within.

Ultimately, they are the result of a complex, objective, dialectical process.

□ On the relationship between religion and philosophy, another book appeared after Ghurāba’s. Its title, The Story of the Conflict Between Religion and Philosophy,160 seems at first to promise a new view of that relationship.

One might expect it to reach the underlying basis of the long-running conflict between religion and philosophy.

But the author describes the different forms this conflict took across the histories of Christianity and Islam, in Europe and in the East, from a secondary angle that remains far from the heart of the problem.

The main feature of his approach is the idea of reconciliation.

He begins from the unity of “truth,” which in the end means the truth of faith. Philosophical truth is therefore assumed to agree necessarily with religious truth.

From this traditionalist starting point, the history of the conflict between religion and philosophy can appear only as a series of different attempts to “reconcile” the two, with the form of reconciliation changing according to the religion, philosophy, and historical period involved.

Muslim philosophers, on this view, had to believe that religion and philosophy had the same aim and dealt with the same subjects.

They therefore had to make the attempt that supposedly gave Arab philosophy its distinctive character: the attempt to reconcile religion and philosophy.161

But how do modern traditionalists understand this attempt?

The author of The Story of the Conflict Between Religion and Philosophy gives us a clear example.

Ibn Rushd, he says,

“reconciles religion and philosophy by interpreting religious verses in a way that makes their meaning agree with Aristotle (...) In other words, Ibn Rushd made religion submit to philosophy.”162

Ibn Rushd, he adds,

“was no less enthusiastic than Saint Thomas in supporting the ideal that reason and faith are in harmony.”163

He also says that Ibn Rushd tried to answer al-Ghazālī on the questions for which al-Ghazālī had declared the philosophers unbelievers, but that “reconciliation escaped him in this attempt.”164

These statements contain three elements.

Taken together or separately, they produce a confused picture of “reconciliation.” But at the same time, they reveal that what the Muslim philosophers were actually trying to do was something other than reconciliation.

The first contradiction is between making religion submit to philosophy165 and being “enthusiastic for the ideal that reason and faith are in harmony.”

If religion is made to submit to philosophy, then there is no such “harmony.” Otherwise, why would one need to submit to the other?

The appeal to the interpretation of religious verses does not solve the problem.

In the history of Arab-Islamic thought, interpretation was often used by sects, schools, and intellectual movements as a way of hiding conclusions they did not dare state openly—especially their awareness that their own ideas conflicted with the apparent meaning of religious texts.

Different schools held different ideas, principles, and ideologies, and so they also developed different standards and methods of interpretation.

There was no single standard, no single method, and no universal rule governing interpretation.

The standard was often subjective or specific to a particular school.

Each legal, theological, doctrinal, or philosophical school might establish its own rules for how interpretation should be carried out.

Among extremist sects and philosophical schools in particular, interpretation was often a way to avoid openly confronting a conflict between their own ideas and the content of religious texts.

It was never, by itself, proof that their ideas were in “harmony” with those texts.

The second contradiction appears in the claim that Ibn Rushd tried to answer al-Ghazālī on the questions for which he had condemned the philosophers, but that “reconciliation escaped him.”

If making religion submit to philosophy really agreed with the supposed “harmony” between reason and faith, Ibn Rushd should have had little difficulty succeeding in this attempt.

But “reconciliation escaped him” because he could not in fact create a “harmony” that had no basis either in his philosophical system or in his ideological starting point.

Third, making religion submit to philosophy and reconciling religion with philosophy cannot be placed on the same level.

They mean different things.

Submission means committing oneself to one side—in this case, philosophy—rather than the other, religion.

Reconciliation means committing oneself to both sides, religion and philosophy.

So if Ibn Rushd and the earlier “philosophers of Islam” really did make religion submit to philosophy—and this is in fact what they tried to do—then the “reconciliatory” character that modern traditionalist historians of philosophy, together with most Orientalists, have attached to Arab-Islamic philosophy is an illusion.

Modern Arab writers impose this character on the philosophy from particular social positions, just as many Orientalists do so from particular political positions.

The effect is to turn attention away from the real conflict between faith-based knowledge and rational knowledge, and away from the materialist tendencies contained in many of the conclusions reached by the “philosophers of Islam.”

□ The same starting point also lies behind the subjective or “ahistorical” explanations that modern traditionalists, and some other thinkers, give for the persecution of Muslim philosophers and philosophy.

For example, the author of The Story of the Conflict Between Religion and Philosophy also explains this persecution in terms of political and personal causes. The personal causes, he says, include “the envy scholars feel toward those among them who excel—that is, the philosophers; their resentment at seeing others become famous and widely known; their unease at the appearance of new ideas they are not used to; their attachment to old views they grew up with and came to believe were true (...) and, finally, the nature of religious belief itself. Faith often leads to dogmatism, and dogmatism cannot easily coexist with complete freedom of thought or with a willingness to accept whatever conclusions research and reflection may uncover.”166

As for the political causes, we might expect the author to come closer here to the real logic of the problem. But that hope soon disappears, because he takes the argument in the opposite direction. By political causes, he means that rulers follow public opinion, accommodate the feelings of different groups, and adapt themselves to the outlook of the masses. Religious leaders, he says, may do the same in order to gain a good reputation among the people.167

But looking at the political causes in this way turns the real logic of the problem upside down.

The problem has another logic: the logic of social and historical reality. When those rulers persecuted philosophy and philosophers, they were not simply following public opinion. They were acting in line with their own ideology as rulers in control of an autocratic, feudal system. Because of their position, they persecuted any form of thought that they believed might develop in a direction connected with the ideology of “public opinion” or “the masses”—even if this connection existed objectively and the philosophers themselves were not directly aware of it.

Persecution, then, was part of the normal pattern of rule under those caliphs and the groups attached to their governments. It was not a case of rulers being “carried along by public opinion” or adapting themselves to “the mentality of the masses.”

As for religious leaders, both the historical evidence and social analysis usually place them on the side toward which they were drawn by those in power. From that position, they in turn helped lead “public opinion” and “the mentality of the masses” in the same direction—not the other way around.

That is the real historical logic of the problem. It is very different from the picture presented by contemporary researchers who represent bourgeois thought.

Taha Hussein may have been trying to answer this common view of the persecution of free thought in Arab-Islamic history when he denied that Islam itself was the source of this persecution or the cause of hostility toward new ideas and freedom of opinion.168 He did so while defending freedom of thought, calling for renewal, and urging contemporary Arab thinkers to reject the old habits of intellectual stagnation.

Yet Taha Hussein began, in On Pre-Islamic Poetry, as a pioneer in studying the heritage through a historical method freed from traditionalism,169 only to end up a prisoner of traditionalism in much of what he wrote later.

□

Despite the dominance of the “ahistorical” method and subjective interpretation in modern studies of our philosophical heritage, we can still find, here and there, signs of a genuinely scientific approach to history. A few examples are worth mentioning.

1 — Jamil Saliba argues that Ibn Sīnā’s “God” is “far removed from life and movement, mercy, love, and the other qualities we find in religions.”170

Saliba explains this partly through the influence of the political life of Ibn Sīnā’s time. In his view, the image of “God” in Ibn Sīnā’s metaphysics reflects the position of the Abbasid caliph after the central authority of the caliphate had broken down into principalities and smaller states with a wide degree of independence:

“The caliph remained in Baghdad without knowing what the sultans were doing in their different kingdoms. The caliph was therefore the One who does not move, the absolute Good that cannot be reached, and the First Principle toward which the intellects turn. The princes and sultans were intellects independent of him yet connected to him, because they shared in what he brought into being and received goodness from him.

“In Ibn Sīnā’s metaphysics, every planet is a king moving through the heavens in praise of God, just as the sultans and princes move in the service of the caliph who remains in Baghdad. Heaven became a state in which the directing power was separated from the power that sets things in motion, while political life was organized in the image of the celestial spheres and their movements.

“Ibn Sīnā’s ideas, then, are not visions sent down from heaven. They are confused dreams filled with the vapors of the earth.”

This is a genuinely historical insight. It connects Ibn Sīnā’s intellectual work closely and precisely with the social and political world in which he lived.

Yet the same researcher falls back into the “ahistorical” method in some of his other analyses.

Take his comparison between al-Fārābī’s “city” and Plato’s Republic.171 Saliba rightly notices the many differences between them. One of the most important is the difference between al-Fārābī’s idea of society, which embraces all the peoples of the earth and which he considers the highest form of human society, with the great universal state as the best state through which happiness can be achieved, and Plato’s idea of society, which is confined to a small city such as Athens or Sparta.

Saliba sees this difference. From the standpoint of a scientific approach to history, it is extremely important. Yet instead of asking about its historical roots, he explains it only through “the influence of religious belief”:

“Had he—al-Fārābī—not learned that ‘man is the brother of man, whether he likes it or not’? Had he not learned that ‘an Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab except through piety,’ and that piety brings all nations together within a single fold...?”172

We are not denying that religion can shape philosophical ideas, especially in a historical period when religion has enormous influence. But even under those conditions, religion cannot be the decisive factor. It is one factor among others, and all those other factors together still do not have the same decisive weight as the social relations that dominate a particular society at a particular stage of its history.

This applies directly to the difference between al-Fārābī’s vision of a large and far-reaching society and Plato’s much narrower vision.

The historical conditions surrounding Plato’s philosophy were those of a slave society. The Greek cities were divided from one another. They formed separate societies that were neither integrated nor closely connected, and they were often at war. They were therefore closed societies.

Intellectual work was largely confined to the class of “masters,” while manual work—the actual process of material production—was confined to the class of “slaves.” Philosophy therefore expressed the outlook of the master class alone.

This helps explain why Plato gave philosophers alone the right to lead the “republic,” and why he reserved philosophy for one section of the “people,” which he regarded as uniquely qualified to govern it.173

Although Plato lived under a form of slave-owning democracy, he was an enemy of that democracy. He saw many weaknesses in it and even regarded it as one form of the decline of the state. His Republic and Laws were both a rejection of this form of democracy.

But even the idea of democracy in Plato’s time had an aristocratic, slave-owning character. Democracy was understood as government elected by the class that made up the majority of the recognized political community. The Greek word democracy does indeed mean “rule of the people,” but “the people” meant the free citizens—the class that held political power—not the slaves.

In Plato’s teaching, the state, or republic, does not change or develop. It resembles his eternal Forms: fixed and incapable of change.

His division of society into classes was also based not on production, but on consumption.

In short, Plato lived at a time when the Athenian city-state—the state of slave-owning democracy—was in decline. When he condemned “democracy,” understood as rule by those seeking power and wealth, and condemned oligarchy—the rule of a minority over the majority—as well as democratic and despotic forms of rule, his thinking reflected the real political condition of the city-state. Slave-owning democracy had lost its earlier substance and much of its political, economic, and military strength.

For all these reasons, Plato’s thought remained within the limits of this particular reality. It revolved around problems confined to the Greek city-state and to the internal struggle among the political and ideological forces that represented its social order.

The historical conditions in which al-Fārābī lived were completely different.

His world was a medieval Arab-Islamic society in which feudal social relations had become firmly established. Its territory stretched across enormous parts of Asia and Africa, as well as parts of Europe. It contained many peoples, regions, and cultures. Political authority was divided among many centers, including rival forms of caliphal authority itself. Across this vast territory ran busy networks of trade and communication.

At the same time, the productive forces were developing in most regions of the state, although at different rates. This encouraged the development of the sciences. Scientific advances helped improve irrigation in agriculture and contributed to the growth of trade and urban crafts.

The interaction between science and material production was accompanied by another kind of interaction: human and cultural contact between the Arabs and their culture on one side, and the other peoples and cultures of the caliphate on the other.

Arabic played a major role in deepening this exchange because it was both the language of the state and the language of Islam. It became a shared means of expressing the results of material and intellectual contact among peoples with very different historical backgrounds. With both its existing strengths and the new capacities it developed, Arabic became something like a main channel into which many different streams of social consciousness flowed.

These historical conditions—in their economic, social, scientific, linguistic, and demographic dimensions—combined with Islam’s rejection of narrow ethnic loyalties to open before al-Fārābī the broad intellectual horizon reflected in his idea of the most complete society: a society embracing all nations within a single state.

2 — Muhammad Uthman Najati examines Ibn Sīnā’s ideas on psychology.

He points out that Ibn Sīnā drew heavily on Aristotle, but also benefited from sources that Aristotle himself could never have used, especially the medical and anatomical studies produced in the centuries after Aristotle.

This helps explain why Ibn Sīnā’s psychology surpasses Aristotle’s in many areas. European historians of philosophy have often treated Aristotle’s psychology—wrongly or at least too loosely—as the only complete model of ancient psychology. In reality, Najati argues, Ibn Sīnā’s psychology is the only genuinely complete model of ancient psychology as a whole.174

Najati also notes, however, that Ibn Sīnā’s psychology has important weaknesses. He connects these weaknesses to the limited tools available for research and experiment at the time.

Researchers in Ibn Sīnā’s age had to rely on observation with the naked eye. They did not know the microscope, let alone the many instruments available to scientists today. Their knowledge of the nervous system was therefore incomplete in many respects. For the same reason, they knew very little about the structure of the brain and the sense organs, or about the nature of nervous activity.175

This way of looking at the relationship between the development of philosophical thought—psychology was then part of philosophy—and the development of scientific knowledge is another important feature of a scientific approach to history.

Philosophy is relatively independent of the specialized sciences that examine particular parts of the universe. It differs from those sciences because it deals with questions that arise from its own task: the search for the broadest and most general laws.

But this relative independence does not mean that philosophy can develop apart from physics, chemistry, mathematics, the natural sciences, or the human sciences. Philosophy must draw on them, and especially on their latest discoveries, whenever these discoveries help it reach more general conclusions or confirm the validity of those conclusions.

From this point of view, Najati is right to connect both the advances and the weaknesses of Ibn Sīnā’s psychology with the level of scientific and technical knowledge in Ibn Sīnā’s age, just as they were also connected with the social relations of that age.

His study of “Sensory Perception in Ibn Sīnā” is mainly analytical, but it is also a careful specialist study. It is precise, covers its subject thoroughly, and follows the methods of specialized science—in other words, it preserves the kind of objectivity that such sciences can maintain independently of the philosophical commitments of different schools of thought.

This valuable study is far removed from the traditionalist method. Its analysis includes useful comparisons between Ibn Sīnā’s views and judgments on psychological questions and the discoveries of modern science, which have shown some of those older views to be wrong.

One example is Ibn Sīnā’s theory of psychic powers, to which he attributes biological functions such as nutrition, growth, and reproduction. Najati writes:

“Modern science rejects the idea of psychic powers as found in Ibn Sīnā and other ancient psychologists, because such powers cannot be subjected to observation and experiment. A scientific explanation of psychological phenomena requires us to observe them carefully, discover the relationships between them, and derive the laws that connect them, without reducing them to powers that cannot themselves be observed.”176

Najati then adds that Ibn Sīnā “did not fail to observe psychological phenomena carefully, but his investigations in this area are often mixed with metaphysical theories.”177

Observations of this kind are not unusual in Muhammad Uthman Najati’s presentation of Ibn Sīnā’s psychology. They clearly begin from scientific thinking. They are far removed from the assumptions of positivist philosophy and much closer to a dialectical view of psychological phenomena.

This is therefore one of the contemporary studies that tries to produce modern scientific knowledge about one part of our philosophical heritage without turning the supernatural ideas found in that heritage into doctrines to be preached in the present.

□

In recent years, however, another change has taken place.

The Arab liberation movement has developed to the point where ideological differences are turning into open ideological conflict. As a result, studies of the intellectual heritage have increasingly begun to state their own starting points openly and to present themselves as weapons in this struggle, on one side or the other.

On the traditionalist side, for example, an Arab journal concerned with studies of this kind devoted one of its issues to important aspects of our intellectual heritage.178 It explained that it was examining the heritage of “Islamic thought” at this particular moment because this was “one of the most dangerous stages in the history of its development”—meaning the development of the “Islamic world.”

The journal explains this “danger” by saying that the Islamic world is being exposed to many imported Western intellectual trends and ideologies whose novelty and apparent attraction are drawing in many minds.

Speaking in the name of the editors, it declares that “the age in which we live is an age of fierce ideological struggle unlike anything humanity has ever seen before.”

We can see here an ideological position expressed in three main ways.

First, the ideological struggle of our time is redirected away from its actual social basis and given a different meaning.

Second, as a result of this, the heritage is presented as purely religious. Its social and historical content is emptied out, while its national character is obscured.

Third, the journal adopts an increasingly right-wing tone toward progressive ideological movements by describing them as “imported Western” ideologies.

What matters most for us here, however, is the change taking place within the traditionalist camp itself. This change also appears in three ways.

First, traditionalists now state openly and directly that they begin their study of the heritage from an ideological position. In the past, they hid this position behind claims that they simply wanted to “revive the heritage” for its own sake. They would even object to any suggestion that the study of the heritage had anything to do with ideology.

Second, the traditionalist camp now accepts not only that ideological struggle exists, but that in our own time it has reached a level of intensity supposedly unmatched in human history.

Third, its attitude toward “imported Western ideological trends” has changed in a noticeable way.

The same editorial now speaks of the need to:

“probe deeply into these new ideologies and schools of thought, determine Islam’s position toward them, discover what can be accepted and what must be rejected, and find a way to adapt some of these modern trends and intellectual positions and bring them into conformity with Islamic life and institutions, so that they may ultimately—where possible—be absorbed into the framework of authentic Islamic thought. It is also necessary to identify the aspects of the traditional systems and ways of life prevailing in Islamic society itself that can be modified so that they can keep pace and fit with the conditions prevailing in the rest of the world.”

The journal is now speaking of “accepting” some of these “imported Western trends,” where it believes acceptance is possible. It speaks of adapting and subordinating some of them. It even speaks of modifying “the traditional systems and ways of life now prevailing” and making them compatible with conditions in the rest of the world.

This amounts, first, to accepting the need for some positive engagement with progressive intellectual trends, whereas the right-wing traditionalist camp had previously treated them mainly in negative terms.

Second, it amounts to admitting that “the traditional systems and ways of life now prevailing” can no longer remain exactly as they are. They too must undergo change if they are to adjust to the transformations of the modern world.

We describe this as a real change because these statements appeared in an Arab journal issued by an official institution in an Arab state that no one would yet place firmly among the progressive Arab regimes.

We therefore cannot treat them as the isolated personal opinion of a single writer. They should be understood as the expression of an intellectual current created by the conditions of this historical period—objective conditions connected across both the Arab world and the wider world.

□

On the other, progressive side, studies of different parts of the heritage have increasingly entered the ideological struggle directly.

Some of these studies focus on currents within the heritage that historically represented positions with relatively progressive social and political dimensions for their own time. Muʿtazilite thought, in general, is one of the leading examples.

One such study approaches the Muʿtazila from a contemporary progressive ideological position. It argues that Muʿtazilite thought took up “the question of human freedom and the human standpoint,” and that this question “concerns human beings and their relationship with society and the universe. Because these relationships continue and remain complex—and indeed because their complexity continues to increase—the question itself has remained alive, continuing to generate research and debate down to the present.”179

The study argues that examining the Muʿtazilite question today is important for reasons that go far beyond “doing justice to these predecessors and presenting their discussions of the subject.” It is also directly relevant to “the problems of our own age and to the Arab-Muslim human being living in the second half of the twentieth century (...) from an angle of great importance and seriousness for the Arab world in general and for us in Egypt in particular.”180

What is that angle?

The author describes it as:

“the need to clarify the thought of this Arab-Islamic school on the question of human freedom; the importance of shedding more light on this subject; and the need to stimulate intellectual debate about the place of this thought in the mind of our nation, in its conduct today, and in the future we seek for it. In short, we must ask what place this thought can have in the intellectual and cultural revolution that is needed if we are to change the intellectual position of our broad masses.”181

That is the starting point on which this new study of Muʿtazilite thought is built.

Its method is consistent with that starting point. It follows a scientific historical approach by identifying the political and social dimensions of the issue under study in light of the historical conditions in which that issue originally appeared.182

The study also does a good job of explaining the relationship between this inherited material and the ideological reason for studying it in the present.

One of the most important points concerns terminology.

The author notices that the problem of freedom, along with the political and social questions connected with it, was not discussed in the past under the terms “freedom” and “despotism.” It was discussed instead through the concepts of “compulsion” (jabr) and “choice” (ikhtiyār).

In other words, the terminology of the debate changed and developed, just as the scope and content of the debate itself changed and developed.183

The author also notes that some researchers—naturally, supporters of traditionalist ideology—have used the difference between past and present terminology to play down the importance of Arab-Muslim discussions of these questions. They have even tried to deny that the Arab-Islamic heritage deserves any credit for examining human freedom at all.

According to this claim:

“At no point in Islam was a connection ever established between ‘choice,’ as a theological problem, and ‘freedom’ in general. Nor was choice regarded as one aspect of freedom. It remained a narrow term, stripped of its potential force because of the direction Muslim theologians took in discussing the problem of free will. Human freedom of will was generally reduced to choice in individual situations.”184

The author answers that “a difference in the terms used to discuss a question is not a valid reason for concluding that the meanings placed under those terms were also different.”185

He supports his answer with many passages from recognized primary and secondary sources, along with examples from Arabic poetry dating back to the age of the Muʿtazila.186 Together, they show that the meanings carried by the older terms are consistent with the meanings into which those terms later developed in our own age.

□

Among the writings that follow this new direction and have appeared in recent years, we can also mention a study of Ibn Rushd whose title describes him as “the most controversial figure” and as “a man of thought and action.”187

The study succeeds in explaining both descriptions historically.

It begins with the long debate over how Ibn Rushd’s philosophical position should be understood, both in the Arab-Islamic world and in Europe.

Was his philosophy materialist and atheistic, as some philosophers and historians of philosophy have argued?

Was it idealist and rooted in Islamic faith, as another group has claimed?

Or was it a philosophy of compromise, attempting a “reconciliation” between religion and philosophy, as many traditionalist and bourgeois Arab and Muslim researchers have maintained?

The author of this new study does not try to enter the debate openly as one of its direct participants. In practice, however, he does take a side. He does so by uncovering the materialist and progressive elements in the philosophy of the thinker from Córdoba.

These elements place Ibn Rushd in what the author sees as his true historical position: a philosopher for whom

“discussion has an exceptional importance because his thought was joined to the practice of that thought. This involved firm positions against many enemies of the enlightened rational thinking that Ibn Rushd defended, and for which he suffered persecution, rejection, and attacks on his reputation.”

Ibn Rushd’s true historical place, the writer rightly explains, is one in which we see him as

“a mirror reflecting many aspects of the intellectual, political, and cultural structures of his society, including the forces that connected them and those that set them against one another.”

For that reason, the writer first had to sketch the main social, political, and cultural features of the society to which Ibn Rushd belonged.

The resulting picture is one of intense contradictions. These contradictions placed Ibn Rushd, as a philosopher, on the side that rejected—among other things—the following:

First, a relationship between political power, its military apparatus, and the people it governed based on repression and despotic control.

Second, the views of religious scholars, theologians, and some philosophers on such questions as the creation of the world, the sending of prophets, divine decree and human freedom, justice and injustice, and resurrection.

Disagreement over these questions took on “such a violent character because it concerned the material structure of the world from a particular point of view, from which (...) many conclusions and opinions followed that threatened the political structure of the state—of which the jurists formed an important part. Questions such as divine decree, justice, and injustice also directly affected people’s lives, their attitudes, and their relationship with political power.”

Third, the denial that human beings have a real presence and an active role in the world, or that they can act freely.

Fourth, the idea that men and women differ by nature.

Ibn Rushd instead saw the difference between them as one of degree. That degree, he argued, “is determined by the type of work a woman performs, and the measure is her ability to endure its difficulties. When that ability is present, a woman may surpass a man.”

This study of Ibn Rushd by Salah Hazin, summarized here in a way that does not alter its essential argument, represents the new direction that has emerged in recent years for studying the heritage through a scientific historical method.

It also contributes to dismantling the myth that Arab-Islamic philosophy was essentially a philosophy of “reconciliation.” The traditionalist method imposed this idea on Arab-Islamic philosophy without any real basis beyond ideological motives—motives that often remained hidden beneath the heritage studies of traditionalists and other representatives of contemporary bourgeois thought.

□

When discussing modern studies of the heritage that represent this new direction, we should not overlook the serious attempt made by Ahmad Abbas Salih in a series of articles published in the Egyptian magazine al-Kātib between 1964 and 1965, and later collected in a separate book under the title The Struggle Between the Right and the Left in Islam.

The importance of this attempt comes, first, from the conditions in which it appeared.
