From all this he concludes that approaching mysticism, whether Christian or Indian, allows us to see that the similarities in mystical practice and in the basic truth of these teachings support the idea that God is present everywhere and “opens every door that leads people to Him.”

Finally, he arrives confidently at this conclusion:

“With this understanding, it is easy to see that whether we approach the bridge from its Western side or its Eastern side, we will meet, just as the common light and truth will meet.”

Is it really a contradiction that Orientalism contains these two apparently opposite tendencies?

In rational thought, we are told, East and West cannot meet. Yet in mystical and supernatural thought, they can meet and become one world.

From the standpoint of imperialist and bourgeois ideology, this is a contradiction only on the surface. At a deeper level, the two tendencies fit both ideologies perfectly well.

Ideologically, it is useful to unite East and West around supernatural thought, around the glorification of illiteracy, and around the idea of learning from a “book of life” that is not the real life of human beings.

And it is just as useful, ideologically, to insist on an absolute separation between East and West whenever thought is rooted in social reality.

Otherwise, why draw such a sharp line between rational and irrational thought?

Both have a history. Neither arose or lived outside history—the history of human beings, which means the history of human social activity.

The basic purpose of all these positions is to hide anything in intellectual life that points toward a relationship with the reality of class struggle as a force shaping the direction of human history.

Fourth — The positive trend in Orientalist studies of the Eastern heritage.

Although the three trends discussed above have dominated Orientalist studies, their dominance has never been complete.

Important Orientalist works have departed from them and approached the Eastern heritage from positions closer to objective study than to the partisan outlook shaped by imperialist ideology.

Some of these more positive studies have even been based on a sound historical outlook or a scientific method. This trend includes both bourgeois Orientalists and Marxist Orientalists and researchers.

□ Among the first group, one scholar especially worth mentioning is the French scholar Paul Masson-Oursel and his scientific historical study of ancient Eastern philosophy.

His study stands out for its systematic method. The facts he presents challenge the very foundation on which the theory of philosophical centrality was built. His work begins from a sound theoretical understanding of the basic unity of human thought.

At the beginning of his introduction, Masson-Oursel writes:

“No one today can believe that the Greeks, the Romans, and the peoples of medieval and modern Europe were the only masters of philosophical thought. In other parts of humanity, several centres of abstract thought also appeared. Their light shone clearly and spread across the world. And since these centres were not isolated from one another, as people once thought, we must recognize that Western thought cannot be understood by itself. Its historical explanation requires us to place it again within the wider human setting, because true history is the unity of world history.”231

He applies this method throughout his study.

For this reason, he rejects the colonial claim that Africa has no history of civilization. He writes:

“In this field of research, which is so valuable for the study of thought itself, we are now beginning to discover that most of Africa was not savage, as people once believed. Even while isolated in desert or forest, it exerted influence in different directions, and influences travelled from the Nile through Libya, Nubia, and Ethiopia.”232

Throughout the book, we also find a sound understanding of the objective relationship between myth, religion, and philosophy—different forms of social consciousness—and the reality of humanity’s material activity.233

Masson-Oursel also firmly rejects the “theory” that divides human beings into separate racial groups, arguing that “pure groups exist only in a few narrowly defined cases.”234

□ Richard Walzer followed a similar method in an extensive study of Islamic philosophy.235

He carefully identified both its external sources and its internal ones. He rejected two equally unhistorical positions: the claim that Islamic philosophy was a purely Arab creation, and the opposite claim that it was produced solely from Greek philosophical sources.

Walzer openly acknowledged:

“The time has not yet come to write a definitive history of Islamic philosophy. Our knowledge of this philosophy has not yet reached the maturity and completeness needed for such a vast undertaking. Many facts remain unknown, and many works have been neglected for centuries...”236

He was also right to say that understanding the character of the main cultural sources of Islamic philosophy “is essential if we are to understand the original and individual solutions that Arab philosophers gave to the philosophical problems they addressed.”237

His mistake, however, was that he concentrated mainly on the external sources. He mentioned the internal sources only briefly and indirectly.

For example, he writes that “al-Fārābī’s interest in Plato arose from specifically Islamic problems that existed in his own time, and this interest helped him reach an original and influential solution.”238

He also says that when Islamic philosophers absorbed Greek thought in a productive way, “their work was a serious attempt to transform this foreign body of thought, so different from the Islamic heritage, and make it a living part of Islamic culture.”239

But the actual nature of those problems, and of this “Islamic heritage,” remains unclear.

Another sound feature of Walzer’s method appears when he says:

“The more we learn about human history, the more we realize that nothing in history creates itself from nothing. History gives new forms to materials that already existed. Islamic philosophy is one workshop in this process through which human civilization continues.”240

It is important to add, however, that Walzer’s study as a whole still begins from idealist and bourgeois positions. Because of this, it contains a number of weaknesses in method.

For example, he was right to reject the idea that foreign works were translated simply because the caliphs had a personal “thirst for knowledge.” But he failed to identify what we regard as the real cause: the needs of social development itself required scientific knowledge to develop. Instead, Walzer merely says that the cause “is not clear.”241

He also explains the differences between the “Arab philosophers”—whether a particular thinker leaned more toward Neoplatonism or toward Aristotelianism—as a matter of “personal temperament.”242

In doing so, he fails to take account of the wider conditions that made those differences necessary.

□ Maurice De Wulf, despite his own commitment to neo-Thomism, took a positive view of Arab-Islamic philosophy on several points. He rejected the claim that it was simply a copy of Peripatetic philosophy, arguing that Arab philosophers developed an independent approach to the problem of existence.243 Nor did he overlook the implication of the theory of emanation in the philosophy of al-Fārābī and Ibn Sīnā: that matter is eternal, rather than something newly created through emanation from the highest intellect.244 De Wulf also recognized that al-Ghazālī rejected rational knowledge in favour of theology bound by religious doctrine. Yet al-Ghazālī still remained committed to philosophical ways of thinking, even as he made them serve the doctrines of faith.245

□ The great Orientalist Hamilton A. Gibb was burdened by metaphysical prejudices about Western thought and the Arab mind. Even so, he sometimes approached Islamic history in more realistic terms. He observed, for example, that Islam took different forms in different times and places under the influence of local geographical, social and political conditions.246 He was right to apply this idea when examining the distinctive features of the different regions where Islam existed as a social order, a culture and a religion.

When discussing Sufism, Gibb also tried to trace its links with ordinary people, especially rural communities and urban craftsmen. He was unable to see the class roots of this relationship, and so he could not recognize the revolutionary side of the Islamic Sufi movement. But his explanation at least pointed in that direction from a distance. He described Sufism as an attempt “to preserve the ideal unity of all Muslims.”247

When he discussed the development of subversive Sufi tendencies within organized Sufism, and their continuation in two philosophical forms—Illuminationism in al-Suhrawardī and a philosophy of unity in Ibn ʿArabī—he wrote:

“The consequences of these two philosophies were extremely serious. Instead of renewing the substance of teaching in the schools, the Sufis redirected intellectual energies toward inward contemplation opposed to rational inquiry, without replacing it with a rigorous system...”248

These historical observations deserve attention even though we disagree with the intellectual and methodological assumptions behind them.

□ When we turn to the more positive current within Orientalist scholarship and its attitude toward our philosophical heritage, the French scholar A. M. Goichon stands out. She was not only a scholar of philosophy in the Orientalist tradition, but also a highly capable philosophical researcher with a strong command of her subject. She read Arab-Islamic philosophical texts with great care and had an especially precise understanding of their terminology.

She also avoided the position shared by the three earlier trends, all of which were in harmony with the ideological outlook of imperialism.

These strengths appear clearly in her valuable lectures on Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy249 and in one of her studies of Ibn Sīnā’s Definitions.250 We can acknowledge these qualities in Goichon’s work without reservation.

In her lecture on “The Great Themes of Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy,” she rejects a claim that became widespread among Orientalists and was later repeated by most modern Arab researchers.251 According to this claim, the Ibn Sīnā of Remarks and Admonitions contradicts the Ibn Sīnā of The Healing. He supposedly began as a Peripatetic philosopher in The Healing, then ended his career as a mystical Illuminationist in Remarks and Admonitions and in his symbolic stories: The Treatise of the Bird, Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān, Salāmān and Absāl, and the Treatise on Love.

The purpose of this claim is to bring Ibn Sīnā’s idealist side to the foreground while obscuring his materialist side.

Goichon rejects the idea that Ibn Sīnā contains this kind of contradiction. She argues that Remarks and Admonitions, although written late in his life and very different in appearance from The Healing, does not contradict the main lines of thought found in that earlier work.252

She also points out that although Ibn Sīnā says in the introduction to The Logic of the Easterners that The Healing was no longer sufficient to express his own thought, he also says in that same work that The Healing contains everything the general body of philosophers needs.253

Goichon takes this to mean that Ibn Sīnā remained committed to a rationalist line of thought in The Logic of the Easterners, just as he had been in The Healing.

She supports this by pointing out that the surviving pages of this incomplete work, only recently discovered, clearly follow the same general intellectual direction as Ibn Sīnā’s other writings. She goes further and argues that his shorter treatises, occasional writings and smaller works, taken together, provide important evidence for the same conclusion.

She also rejects the claim254 that Ibn Sīnā deliberately chose an “esoteric mode of presentation.” In her view, the differences among his works are more limited. Some are written as works of philosophy in the strict sense. In others, Ibn Sīnā allows his thought to move beyond the normal boundaries of philosophy in a mystical direction—but one so strongly rational in form that it would still be wrong to call him a mystic. It is possible, she suggests, that Ibn Sīnā did not wish to explain his position openly, or that he never had the freedom to write a precise work devoted to it.254

Goichon keeps the same position in her detailed treatment of Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy of existence.

Even when she discusses his theory of the soul, she does not regard his belief that the soul is a separate substance which survives the death of the body and lives a life close to that of the pure intellects as evidence of mysticism. Her reason is that Ibn Sīnā bases the soul’s eternal happiness on knowledge. The soul earns that happiness through the proper use of reason in the material world.

So, in her words, “the idea of happiness in heaven, and of misery in hell where intellects are deprived of knowledge of intelligible things, is entirely rational. In that case, it is impossible to identify a specifically Avicennian mysticism or determine its nature in the way people often claim.”255

Goichon finally concludes that, for Ibn Sīnā, there is no reality apart from existence. Essences that have not yet received existence have no reality in themselves.256

After following Ibn Sīnā’s texts closely on the question of existence and essence, she concludes that his philosophy is internally consistent. “Ibn Sīnā’s great mind,” she writes, “placed itself at a point from which his work appears as a single coherent whole,” and that work is “very far from being merely a translation of Aristotelian theories into Arabic.”257

□ Finally, it is fair to say that supporters of this positive trend are not a rare exception among Orientalists. But it would be difficult to review all of their positions here.

- 15 -

E — Marxist Orientalist Studies

Marxist Orientalists occupy a distinct place in the history of Orientalist scholarship because they approached our intellectual heritage in its different forms from an explicitly Marxist point of view. Their method was based on historical materialism, and their ideological outlook on scientific socialism.

For that reason, we do not find in their studies the same fundamental weaknesses that we found among other Western Orientalists and researchers, or among modern Arab researchers whose methods are idealist and ahistorical and whose ideological positions are imperialist or bourgeois.

This does not mean that Marxist studies contain no weaknesses at all.

As Marxists—or precisely because we are Marxists—we are, or should be, very far from making such an absolute claim.

Marxist researchers possess a method and an ideology that help them avoid the fundamental errors we have already discussed and illustrated. But the issue is not simply one of possessing the correct method as a theory or the correct ideology as a set of ideas. What matters after that is how the method is applied in practice.

Marxists proceed from a scientific conviction that historical materialism is valid, and that it is the only method capable of giving us scientific knowledge of our intellectual heritage. They also believe that such scientific knowledge alone is consistent with the ideology of the revolutionary proletariat, and that it can arm the mass base of the Arab liberation movement with an informed and constantly renewed political awareness. This is especially important in confronting the ideological struggle, which is becoming one of the central battlegrounds of our age.

They believe all this. But the real question remains the question of application.

This is where the individual researcher enters the picture.

Personal abilities are put to the test. The result may be success to varying degrees, or it may be failure.

The measure of success or failure is the distance between theory and application, between the method itself and the creative use of that method. The smaller this distance becomes, the greater the success. When the distance grows, failure begins.

This is where weaknesses appear in Marxist studies of the heritage. But compared with the fundamental weaknesses discussed earlier, these remain secondary. They do not arise from the method or ideology themselves. They come instead from a mechanical understanding of the method, from an incomplete view of the relationship between theory and concrete reality, or sometimes from a mismatch between a person’s intellectual commitments and their social position.

These secondary weaknesses may also arise for other reasons.

They may come from individual judgments about how general laws should be applied to a particular case. Such judgments may suffer from a lack of historical evidence about the specific case being studied. Or the case itself may be surrounded by distortions produced by outside forces.

This is exactly what has happened with the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage. Misleading studies separated this heritage from its indirect material and social foundations, leaving those foundations in the dark. As a result, modern generations—and even scientific researchers—have found it difficult to see the connection between the two.

Let us now move from the general point to a specific example.

A few pages ago we referred to the Marxist thesis that human society has developed, and continues to develop, through a series of historical stages. Each stage is defined by a particular form of social relations connected with material production. These forms follow, overlap with and grow out of one another along an upward but uneven historical path.

This view rests on the idea that relations of material production are the decisive factor shaping the movement of history.

When Marxism formulated this thesis, it drew on historical experience and on what it regarded as an objective agreement between that experience and the general laws of dialectical and historical materialism.

With the help of these laws, historical experience seemed to reveal a general pattern in human development. In broad terms, the sequence was:

primitive communism, then slave relations, then feudal relations, then capitalism, followed by socialism and finally the higher stage of scientific communism.

But does Marxism regard this pattern as a final and absolute truth?

Does it impose this sequence rigidly on every human society, as though the different social formations were ready-made moulds that every society must pass through in exactly the same way? Does it treat them as unavoidable stages that cannot vary, be skipped, overlap with other forms, or take on forms that are similar, different or even contrary to the familiar model?

We have already answered both questions.

First, we said that Marxism is not a rigid doctrine but a guide to action.

Second, when discussing this same theory of social formations, we said that the theory itself remains open to development whenever scientific research uncovers new features in historical experiences whose real character has not yet been fully understood.

We can add another point.

Marxism says that absolute objective truth exists, but it also says that our knowledge of it is relative. In other words, our knowledge develops in stages. We gain it piece by piece as human awareness and science develop.

In this sense, absolute truth is made up of the accumulated results of relative truths, as Lenin put it.258

So even in Marxist scientific thought itself, the familiar Marxist account of the social formations through which human society has developed is not a final formula expressing absolute objective truth in its entirety.

It still belongs to the realm of relative truths. It reflects the parts of historical reality that have become known so far. Other parts remain unknown.

We are not saying this as a digression. We are saying it because it leads directly to an example of the weaknesses that can appear in Marxist studies of medieval Arab-Islamic thought.

A Marxist researcher looking for the material foundations of this heritage may sometimes apply the familiar Marxist model of historical social formations too literally or mechanically.

The researcher may even invent a particular mode of production for which there is no historical basis, or whose features are unclear, or which had not yet fully developed, or which was actually a complex mixture of elements belonging to several different modes of production.

A mistake of this kind may come from an excessive desire to apply the Marxist model at any cost, even when the result is a “dogmatic” application259 that is foreign to Marxism’s own understanding of historical development.

One of the areas where Marxist researchers are most likely to fall into error or confusion is the answer to this question:

Which of the historical forms of social relations identified in the Marxist model best describes the social and economic relations of the Arabian Peninsula shortly before the rise of Islam, during the final period of the Jāhiliyya?

A similar problem appears when we ask about the true historical form of the mode of production under the Arab-Islamic state during the Umayyad and Abbasid periods.

Was it feudalism in the same form known in medieval Europe?

Was it a different form of feudalism?

Was it a distinctive mixture of slave, feudal and commercial relations?

Or was it something else entirely, with no direct equivalent among the traditional social formations familiar to Marxists?

Modern Marxist researchers—Arab scholars and Orientalists alike—often disagree on these questions.

That is because these are relatively new problems in Marxist studies of medieval Arab-Islamic society and of its intellectual movements. They are newer still in Marxist studies of Arab-Islamic philosophy, because Marxist work in this field began even later.

The very existence of these disagreements provides practical evidence that Marxist researchers do not treat the theory of social and economic formations as a final and absolute truth that can be applied in every detail, in exactly the same form, to every concrete situation in every historical period.

Nor do they treat it as a rigid ready-made formula to which every form of production and every kind of social relation in history must be mechanically forced to conform.

In fact, even the founders of Marxism, Marx and Engels, considered the possibility that other historical experiences—some only partly known in their own time, and others perhaps still to be discovered—might require changes in the way this theory was formulated.

Marx himself described one such historical form of property, which he said history showed us clearly. He called it “communal property” and described it as an “original form.”

Marx argued that property is “a condition of production,” and that “there can be no production, and therefore no society, without some form of property.” At the same time, however, he ridiculed the idea that this objective fact meant we had to “leap directly to one particular form of property, such as private property.”

Instead, he pointed to a form of “communal property” and to a particular mode associated with it, connected in some way with communal ownership.

Marx located this historical form “among the Indians, the Slavs, the ancient Celts, and so on.”260

This example, together with similar remarks Marx made on several occasions, later became widely associated with what was called the Asiatic mode of production.

□ The letters exchanged between Marx and Engels about forms of property in Eastern societies cast further light on this question.

In one of these letters, Marx wrote to Engels261 that he agreed with Bernier’s view that the key to understanding the phenomena of the East was the absence of private ownership of land.

“This,” Marx wrote, “is the real key even to the Eastern paradise.”

Engels replied262 that the absence of private ownership of land was indeed, in a deeper sense, the key to the whole East and the basis of its political and religious history.

But why, he asked, did Eastern peoples not develop private ownership of land, even in a feudal form?

Engels answered that the main reason lay in the natural climate and character of the land, especially the vast desert regions stretching from the Sahara in North Africa through Arabia, Persia and India and into the highlands of Asia and Tartary—what is now Soviet Central Asia and part of Turkestan.

Artificial irrigation, he argued, was the first condition of agriculture in these regions. Irrigation had to be organized either by the communal group, by the region, or by the central government.

Governments in the East, Engels wrote, traditionally had three main functions: finance, meaning the extraction of wealth from their own country; war, meaning the plunder of their own country and neighbouring countries; and public works (Travaux Publics), which were necessary to increase production.

The British government, he said, organized the first two functions and gave them an even more cunning form, while completely abolishing the third. The result was the destruction of agriculture in India.

Free competition was useless under these conditions.

The fertility of the land depended on artificial irrigation, and disappeared as soon as the irrigation system collapsed.

This, Engels argued, explains something that would otherwise be difficult to understand: whole regions that had once been magnificently cultivated later became abandoned deserts. He mentioned Palmyra, Petra, the ruins of Yemen, and many areas of Egypt, Persia and India.

It also explains, he said, how a single destructive war could empty a country of its population and destroy its civilization for centuries.

Engels then added:

“In my view, the collapse of trade in southern Arabia in the period before Muḥammad—which you rightly regard as one of the most important factors behind the Islamic revolution—belongs to exactly this kind of phenomenon.”263

Texts like these show that the founders of Marxism did not close the door of scientific inquiry to any historical experience. They were prepared to take new evidence into account when applying Marxist theories, based on the general objective laws of social development, to concrete historical conditions.

□ Among later and contemporary Marxists—and especially Soviet Orientalists and researchers—there was no single agreed picture of social relations in the Arabian Peninsula during the fifth and sixth centuries CE and at the time Islam first appeared.

We believe the main reason is that the historical evidence for this period of Arab history is not rich enough to allow modern researchers to reconstruct a complete and realistic picture of its actual economic and social relations.

This shortage of evidence comes above all from the methods used by the Arab historians who lived closest to the period. They often devoted great attention to secondary details that tell us very little about the underlying social reality.

Modern researchers, especially those who do not read Arabic sources directly, have therefore often had to rely on works written long after the earliest Islamic centuries, such as al-Shahrastānī’s famous Religions and Sects, or on the writings of modern travellers and later researchers.

These works look back at the older reality from a distance of more than fourteen centuries.264 They can therefore reconstruct it only indirectly, from the surviving remains of the distant past and from earlier written sources that are themselves incomplete.

The Russian-Soviet Orientalist Ignatius Krachkovsky, who had an exceptionally broad knowledge of Arabic studies, relied more heavily on pre-Islamic poetry.

He treated it as “the oldest surviving monument of the Arabic language,” and therefore, for the history of that period, as “not only the oldest source but in truth the only surviving source we have for the events it describes.”265

Krachkovsky therefore believed that pre-Islamic poetry gives us a faithful picture of Arab tribal life as a whole.266

He rejected the various theories questioning whether this poetry genuinely belonged to the pre-Islamic period, because he did not believe there was decisive evidence for doubting its value as a historical source for the study of pre-Islamic Arabia.267

□ Soviet historical studies contain several different views about the particular character of economic and social relations in the late pre-Islamic period.

The Soviet Orientalist Yevgeny Belyaev, author of The Arabs, Islam and the Arab Caliphate, discusses several of these theories.

One is what he calls the “commercial-capitalist” theory, which he attributes to Reisnev. Belyaev says that this theory was widespread in the 1920s and 1930s and that it “differs sharply from Marxist-Leninist theory.”268

He also discusses a “stage theory” and an “agrarian theory.”

The first argues that the rise of Islam “reflected and embodied the interests and ideals of the Bedouin tribes of Arabia.”

The second argues that Islam first arose as “an expression of the aspirations of the landless class.”269

Belyaev rejects both theories because, in his view, “neither has any scientific basis.”

He then refers to a study by S. P. Tolstov on the origins of Islam. Tolstov paid particular attention to slavery in the Arabian Peninsula during the fifth and sixth centuries CE. Belyaev describes his work as a deep historical study supported by evidence and argument.270

Another theory argues that “Islam first arose as the ideology of early feudal society.”271

The Russian Orientalists A. Yu. Yakubovsky and I. P. Petrushevsky reject this feudal interpretation, however, and instead stress slavery in Arabia, its origins and its development.272

Belyaev also praises the scientific value of what he calls the “deep study supported by convincing arguments” found in the third volume of the large Soviet work History of the World, published in Moscow in 1957. He says that it presents “the essential historical events and developments taking place in Arabia during the fifth and sixth centuries, including those connected with the first emergence of Islam.”273

Belyaev’s own position can be summarized as follows:

  • The population of the Arabian Peninsula was a mixture of nomadic Bedouins and settled communities living mainly from agriculture. Marx’s observation applies here: “From the beginning of recorded history, we find in the East a connection between settled urban life among one part of the population and nomadic life among another.”274

    During the fifth and sixth centuries CE, most of the population of Arabia—with the exception of the settled population of Yemen—still lived within a primitive form of social organization. Society had not yet divided into clearly defined social classes, and there was no state or developed system of government.

    The dominant structure was that of tribe and clan, based primarily on blood ties and descent, but also on forms of “brotherhood” that allowed outsiders to join a clan through political alliance.275

    At the same time, however, differences in wealth were becoming greater. Private ownership of livestock already existed, developing earlier than private ownership of land, and slaves were used both in herding and in agriculture.

    As inequality in the distribution of wealth grew, it created the material basis for the first signs of breakdown in the tribal economic and social order that had existed before the rise of classes.

    The power of clans and their leaders rested increasingly on wealth and economic position rather than simply on custom or social prestige.276

    Belyaev also argues that the level of development reached by Arabian society during this period—again excluding Yemen—corresponded to what Engels described as the stage before the full emergence of class society, when “human beings begin to use iron for their tools and implements, then move toward civilization with the invention of alphabetic writing.”277

    The Arabs of the Jāhiliyya had, in his view, reached this stage. Society had developed groups of craftsmen and farmers. Pottery was made, textiles were woven, smelted metals were used, swords and iron ploughs were produced, and gold and silver were worked.278

  • By the time Islam appeared, trade and lending at interest were helping to break down tribal relations and weaken the old order, because a tribal system could not easily coexist with an economy increasingly based on money.279

    The wealth of the Quraysh leaders included money, trade, farms, slaves and livestock.

    In Mecca, Medina and Ṭāʾif there were workers involved in obtaining and handling goods, as well as workers outside the traditional crafts who performed many other kinds of labour, including veterinary work, herding livestock and watering camels used in trade caravans.280

    The breakdown of the old communal tribal system, which happened earlier in Mecca than elsewhere, brought the clans of Quraysh into a new form of organization. A group of leading notables now dominated political life through simple formal institutions used to manage clan affairs, including the malaʾ, or council of notables, and Dār al-Nadwa, the assembly house.281

    By the end of the Jāhiliyya, paganism was also reaching the end of its historical life. New class relations were entering the old tribal communal order, helping produce a shift away from polytheism and toward monotheism.

    Alliances between tribes reflected a growing desire to unite Arabia and create a central authority. Such unity, in Belyaev’s view, required a monotheistic belief that people would respect and hold sacred.

    It was in this setting that Ḥanīfiyya, a form of Arab monotheism, appeared.282

    Yet Ḥanīfiyya did not spread widely in Mecca. This was not only because the Quraysh opposed it, but also because of the social conditions inside the city: the conflicts between merchants and moneylenders on one side and those harmed by usury on the other, and between slave owners and slaves who wanted freedom.

    Ḥanīfiyya did not originally express the aspirations of these oppressed groups. At first, its preaching went little beyond the idea that worldly life is temporary.

    But as Meccan society developed, Ḥanīfiyya developed with it and eventually entered a stage in which it helped prepare the ground for Islam.283

    Belyaev’s final conclusion is that Islam arose in Arabia as a new ideology reflecting the major changes taking place in Arab society: growing inequality in the distribution of wealth, slavery and expanding commercial exchange.

    With Islam came a new form of organization: the “community of believers.”

    This new community directly contradicted the old tribal system. It became the basic social foundation on which the Islamic state was built.

    Belyaev sees this as confirming the theory that “the first attempt to establish a state must involve destroying the tribal organization and breaking apart its structure.”284

□ When we turn to the historical form of the mode of production and social relations under the medieval Arab-Islamic caliphate, the general tendency among Marxist researchers is to regard feudal relations as dominant.

They disagree, however, about the specific historical form that this feudalism took.

The reason for this disagreement lies in the complex overlap between two sets of features.

The first were feudal features inherited from the social systems that existed in the conquered regions before the Arab-Islamic conquests, especially the Persian and Byzantine systems.

The second were new forms of production relations created by the Islamic system of landholding. This system itself changed repeatedly through new interpretations and practical measures, beginning with the land policy of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb during the early conquests and continuing into the ninth century CE.

These newer relations were marked, first, by several different forms of landownership and, second, by the use of both slave labour and free peasant labour on the land.

The complicated interaction of all these historical features made it difficult for researchers to identify the true character of the dominant economic and social system.

It also made possible conclusions such as the claim that Arab-Islamic society developed directly from a patriarchal tribal society285—the society of the Jāhiliyya—into a feudal society, without first passing through slavery as a complete, developed and dominant social system.

According to this view, “slavery also existed in tribal, pre-Islamic society, but only as a phenomenon contained within the broader social and economic structure of that society.”286

Some Soviet thinkers speak of both European feudal society and Arab feudal society, while stressing that feudalism in Europe differed from feudalism in the East.

They describe the difference in roughly the following way.

After the collapse of the centralized Roman Empire, Europe broke up into competing principalities. These fought one another as smaller political units were gradually brought together around larger feudal powers.

Out of these conflicts came the process through which larger national communities were formed. This process continued throughout the Middle Ages and did not reach its final stage until the nineteenth century.

The Vatican served as a major centre of authority in Europe and eventually became a state exercising power over the different European feudal forces, while retaining its specifically Christian religious character.

In the East, by contrast—as in Russia—there was no dominant church organized as a religious state existing alongside a separate civil state.

Instead, there was a vast Arab state controlling enormous parts of the East and holding them together under a single political authority. This made it possible for the economy and the sciences to develop.

While the Church in the West sought to maintain its authority over the feudal lords, everything in the East was subject to the caliph. The head of state often held absolute power.

Yet the caliph’s authority was not primarily theological. It was civil and political.

Unlike Western feudal lords, who were bound by religious authority and by their relationship with the pope, the caliph was rarely subject to religion in an absolute sense. More often, religion itself was made subject to his political authority and to the interests of the state.287

This account helps clarify some of the main political differences between Arab-Islamic society and European society.

But it does not explain the basic features of the mode of production in either one.

So the real difference remains unclear.

To identify it properly, we first need to know what kind of production relations existed before the Arab-Islamic conquest in the countries that later became part of the caliphate.

Then we need to understand how those relations changed after the caliphate was established and a new society emerged under its rule.

Most of the conquered countries had previously belonged either to the Byzantine social and economic system or to the Persian Sasanian system.

We therefore need to know the particular features of each.

Recent Soviet historical literature contains several attempts to answer this question.

One appears in the large Soviet encyclopedic work History of the World, which presents two theories about the Byzantine system.

According to the first, Byzantium had already become a feudal society beginning in the fifth century. By the seventh century, this system had become firmly established and the slave economy was approaching its end.

According to the second theory, the slave economy was still declining during the fifth to seventh centuries, while the feudal economy was only slowly taking shape.288

The Soviet Orientalist Belyaev, for his part, argues that modern research into the use of slaves in agriculture, irrigation and different crafts shows that slave ownership was also a feature of feudal society in the Byzantine Empire and the Middle East.289

He therefore takes feudalism to have been the dominant system in the territories ruled by Byzantium.

When discussing the social and economic relations and property laws of the countries conquered by the Arabs more generally, he likewise speaks of “the feudal system that was widespread there.”290

This includes both the regions previously ruled by the Sasanians and those previously ruled by Byzantium.

Elsewhere in his book, when speaking specifically about former Sasanian societies, Belyaev likewise treats their feudal character as an established fact rather than something requiring further argument.291

The Arab-Islamic society that emerged during the early conquests, however, was far from uniform.

As Belyaev describes it, the social and economic relations and property laws of the conquered countries were new and unfamiliar to the Arab conquerors.

The feudal system widespread in those regions did not interest them. Nor were they initially interested in owning the land, which they regarded as the common property of the Muslims.

As a result, “the land remained in the hands of the local feudal lords, chiefs, religious authorities and other owners. The landowners kept their full rights and privileges and continued to exploit the peasants as they had before...”292

At the same time, “the tribal and clan organization retained by the Arabs in the conquered countries prevented them from mixing with the conquered peoples...”293

Belyaev nevertheless regards the Umayyad period as “a distinctive period in Arab history.”

One of the main reasons, in his view, was “the social and economic changes that took place in the caliphate under the Umayyads and led to the victory of feudal relations among the peoples of the Arab state, including the Arabs themselves.”294

Even then, however, Belyaev believes that the final victory of these relations came only in the ninth century CE, when “the caliphate in Baghdad became a feudal state” and “the role of slaves in production declined.”295

□ We also find another contemporary Marxist thinker who dealt with the Arab-Islamic philosophical heritage in a work on medieval philosophy. He argues that when Islam emerged, feudal relations of production finally replaced slave-based relations of production. At the same time, he says that the particular nature of this feudal system still needs detailed study from a Marxist point of view.296

□ The first Marxist Orientalist studies of Arab-Islamic philosophy focused on the progressive role played by Islamic thinkers and philosophers in developing a culture that reflected the material and intellectual rise of the progressive class forces within Arab-Islamic society under the Abbasid Caliphate.

Among the leading scholars in this field were Yakubovsky; Sadriddin Ayni, the former president of the Academy of Sciences of Soviet Tajikistan; Ghafurov, director of the Institute of Oriental Studies in Moscow, formerly the Institute of Asia and Africa; Krachkovsky; Bartold;297 Krymsky; and Grigoryev.

Another feature of these studies is that they approached the intellectual heritage through scientific interpretation. On the hundredth anniversary of the birth of the Russian Orientalist Gordlevsky, an important study of his in this field appeared in Moscow as part of his collected works.

In 1939, the Soviet Union published a History of Philosophy containing a study of Arab-Islamic philosophy written from a materialist standpoint. Another work with the same title, History of Philosophy, was published in six volumes by the Soviet Academy of Philosophical Sciences and included a study of the historical development of Arab-Islamic philosophy.

In more recent years, Soviet Oriental studies began to examine particular questions within this philosophy in a more specialized way. There were also university dissertations in philosophy, such as A. S. Ivanov’s study, “Al-Fārābī’s Teaching on the Human Capacity for Knowledge.”298

Other specialized studies included a commentary on al-Fārābī’s treatise What Must Precede the Study of Philosophy, published in The Philosophical Treatises of al-Fārābī in Alma-Ata, Kazakhstan, in 1970; “The Problem of Sensory Knowledge in the Treatises of al-Fārābī,” based on papers from the scientific conference of young researchers at the Academy of Sciences of Soviet Kazakhstan, also published in Alma-Ata in 1970; “Al-Fārābī’s Theory of Knowledge,” published by the Social Sciences Division of the Kazakh Academy of Sciences in 1971; Al-Fārābī in Historical Scholarship, published in Alma-Ata in 1971; and “Some Questions Concerning al-Fārābī’s Philosophical Heritage,” included in the book Al-Fārābī: A Great Scholar of Encyclopedic Knowledge.

Several studies on different aspects of Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy were also published in Tashkent, the capital of Soviet Uzbekistan. A Russian-language book entitled Monuments of Arab Thought appeared with philosophical texts and commentaries. And in Moscow, during the past two years, the academic philosopher L. Sagadeev published two works, one on Ibn Sīnā and the other on Ibn Rushd.

Some earlier Soviet works also took a clear stand against Eurocentrism in philosophy. They supported, on the one hand, the idea that world philosophy forms a single whole and, on the other, the idea that different local philosophies have their own distinctive features, shaped by their particular national and historical conditions.299

□ We can see the main direction of these Soviet studies in the following examples.

1

The Soviet historian Bukhonsky writes that, for Ibn Sīnā, knowledge is based on our perception of things that exist outside us and independently of us. He says that Ibn Sīnā does not doubt the objectivity of knowledge or the importance of rational thought. In this sense, Ibn Sīnā is an opponent of irrationalism.

Bukhonsky also argues that Ibn Sīnā changed Aristotle’s concept of “form” in a way that brought a material principle into the explanation of the individual, particular thing. Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy also accepts the eternity of the world. This, Bukhonsky argues, reduces the weight of the theological and idealist elements found in Ibn Sīnā’s teaching on the soul.

Finally, Bukhonsky stresses that Ibn Sīnā dealt with questions of logic independently of Aristotle.300

2

The Soviet historian of philosophy Trachtenberg wrote a book entitled A Sketch of the History of Western Europe in the Middle Ages. A very large part of it is devoted to Arab-Islamic philosophy. Among the conclusions he reaches are the following.

On the Muʿtazila, he argues that their central concept was reason. Their belief that God creates the world continuously, through an endlessly renewed act of creation, leads in his view to the eternity of the material world. If creation is continuous, the argument goes, then if the world came to an end, God too would come to an end. The world must therefore be eternal for God to remain eternal. Trachtenberg sees a similarity here with Neoplatonism, which also sees God as continuously active in the universe in order to preserve the unity of the world.

On Ibn Rushd, Trachtenberg argues that Ibn Rushd understands God as the first mover. In this respect, he compares him with Descartes, who also regarded God as the source of motion.

But Ibn Rushd, he says, makes God the source of matter in terms of its end rather than its beginning. In other words, God is matter’s goal. This follows Aristotle’s distinction between an efficient cause, which produces something, and a final cause, which is the end or purpose toward which it moves. For Aristotle, God is a final cause: the ultimate goal of matter’s existence.

Trachtenberg argues that Ibn Rushd tries to explain matter in physical terms. Matter gives form to itself, and living beings arise through heat. When the heat disappears, those living beings disappear as well.

This idea of Ibn Rushd later passed to the Italian philosopher Pietro Pomponazzi (1464–1524), who was executed on the charge of being an Averroist, and to the Italian philosopher Bernardino Telesio (1508–1588), who adopted Ibn Rushd’s view that heat causes non-living matter to become living matter.

For Ibn Rushd, Trachtenberg says, the intellect of the world is a law—a law of necessity. He therefore asks: is the intellect of the world an essence, or is it not?

His answer is that, for Ibn Rushd, it is not an essence but a necessity. Ibn Rushd separates the idea of intellect from the idea of spirit or soul. He says that intellect is present in every existing thing.

The world is therefore intelligible because it follows laws. God does not intervene in its affairs, because the world is intelligible in itself—that is, it is governed by necessity and causation.

In Trachtenberg’s reading, this means that Ibn Rushd rejects al-Ghazālī’s theoretical position. Al-Ghazālī held that when one thing regularly appears together with another, this does not prove that one causes the other. The connection may simply be circumstantial or coincidental, and through repetition it comes to seem habitual. People repeatedly see burning occur when fire comes into contact with matter, for example, and so they come to regard fire as the cause of the burning.

Trachtenberg also sees Ibn Rushd as a materialist in his theory of knowledge. Ibn Rushd, he says, believes that knowledge is acquired when material things act upon our senses. If we add this to his belief in the eternity of matter and his recognition that the material world exists objectively, Trachtenberg argues that there can be no doubt about his materialism.

The world develops on the basis of reason. This too, in Trachtenberg’s view, is a materialist position. But Ibn Rushd’s materialism belongs specifically to the Middle Ages.

As the German historian Lange puts it, medieval materialists became extremely skilled at hiding what they really thought. They could therefore develop materialist ideas while outwardly presenting them in forms that defended religion and theology.

Trachtenberg also sees a similarity between Ibn Rushd and Hegel in the way both reduce God to a “general idea.” The similarity, as he sees it, lies in the fact that for both thinkers reason is a law of necessity. This amounts to recognizing necessity in the world: the world is intelligible because it operates according to rational laws.

Here again, Ibn Rushd recognizes that matter—the world—exists independently of consciousness. In other words, he recognizes the objective existence of the world.

3

Professor T. Skovsky, in the lectures on the history of philosophy that we mentioned earlier, says that Marxism rejects the claim that Ibn Sīnā, Ibn Rushd, and the other Arab philosophers were simply Peripatetics—followers of Aristotle.

The facts themselves, he argues, support this rejection. The Arab philosophers did not stop with Aristotle’s teaching as they received it. They developed it. Aristotelianism was indeed the basis of their philosophy, but they pushed Aristotle’s teaching in a materialist direction.

Discussing Ibn Sīnā’s logic, Skovsky says that his study of the nature of judgments and logical categories is especially valuable. The strength of Ibn Sīnā’s logic lies in the fact that he examines the actual content of logical categories, one of the most difficult problems in philosophy.

In his logical writings, for example, Ibn Sīnā distinguishes between explaining a certain judgment and explaining an essence. He also defines such categories as affirmation and negation, universal and particular, possibility and actuality. The last two—possibility and actuality—are closely connected with Ibn Sīnā’s metaphysics.

In medieval European philosophy, Skovsky says, one theory dominated: the doctrine that the world had been created out of nothing. Arab philosophers, by contrast, examined every kind of question concerning the world and nature.

Europe did not begin to discuss the problems of nature, or even to ask what nature is, until it became familiar with Ibn Sīnā’s works. From then on, European thinkers began asking questions about living and non-living things, and so on.

Skovsky also argues that Marxist analysis always relates the level reached by science and philosophy to the level of economic development. If we apply this approach to medieval Arab philosophy, he says, we must look at the economy of the Arab countries, which during the period of the conquests had reached a higher level than the economy of Europe.

At that time, many branches of science flourished among the Arabs alongside philosophy. This is only natural, he says: where science flourishes, philosophy flourishes too.

The much greater economic development of the Arab world compared with Europe may therefore have provided the basis for the appearance of materialist tendencies in Arab philosophy.

4

The German Marxist thinker Hermann Ley, in his Brief History of Materialism in the Middle Ages, which we mentioned earlier, argues that the central idea in Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy is that matter has laws of its own.

In Ley’s view, Ibn Sīnā opposes Platonic idealism, especially the changes that Plotinus introduced into Plato’s teaching. Through this same idea, Ibn Sīnā also moves beyond those parts of Aristotle’s teaching on matter and form that remained close to Plato.

Aristotle believed that the problems of coming into being, change, and passing away in nature could be solved by separating in thought the “form” of a thing from its “matter” and from its external existence. This separation creates a material realm and an intellectual realm, with an idealist division between the two.

Even so, when Aristotle is compared with Plato, Aristotle’s philosophy represents a development in the direction of materialist thought. Aristotle’s criticism of Plato helped open the way toward connecting recognition of the material nature of the world with recognition, at least to some extent, of the material character of the laws of nature.

From this point of view, Ley argues, Ibn Sīnā defended the real meaning of Aristotle more successfully than the European Scholastic thinkers of the feudal period did. Ibn Sīnā brought out the materialist side of Aristotle’s teaching on matter and form.

Medieval Scholasticism, especially Thomas Aquinas, treated Aristotle as an idealist dualist because he separated form from matter. Yet in the Metaphysics, or First Philosophy, Aristotle had criticized Plato’s “Ideas,” or Forms, and he developed this opposition to Plato in many of his other works as well.

Ibn Sīnā drew a further conclusion. If Aristotle accepted that matter and form are united in the things human beings produce, then this unity must also exist in nature.

Ley argues that this conclusion makes Ibn Sīnā a materialist. The same tendency can also be seen in the way Ibn Sīnā deals with questions on which Aristotle himself moves toward idealism.

□ These examples show the main direction taken by Marxist studies of Arab-Islamic philosophy. We find many similar examples among Marxist scholars and Orientalists elsewhere in Eastern Europe, as well as in Western Europe and other countries.

Naturally, these scholars differ in their interpretations, perspectives, and methods. They also differ in how familiar they are with the original sources of Arab-Islamic philosophy, how well they understand the texts, and how deeply they can penetrate the traditional forms of expression used in them.

Sometimes these differences may also come from something we discussed earlier: scholars differ in their ability to bring theory and practice together creatively when applying a method to a specific historical case.

What matters most to us here, however, is that the various Marxist studies of the heritage broadly agree with the progressive and democratic direction of the Arab liberation movement at its present stage of development, and with the ideology of the leading forces within that movement.

This comes after a period in which Western Orientalist studies had almost complete control over the study of the heritage. Most of those studies either conflict directly with this progressive line or stand opposed to it, while fitting instead with a current of Arab bourgeois thought that resists and obstructs the development of the Arab movement for liberation and progress.

- 16 -

From what we have seen so far, two different realities emerge in the study of the intellectual heritage of Arab history.

The first is negative: studies that distorted this heritage and either failed to recognize or deliberately ignored its progressive content.

The second is positive: studies that begin from materialist positions, along with studies shaped by movements of liberation.

Both kinds of positive study have helped correct unscientific attitudes toward our intellectual heritage in general and our philosophical heritage in particular.

But one problem remains. We still do not have a study that deals comprehensively with this heritage as a whole and follows it through its historical movement: its origins, growth, and development. Such a study would connect each stage with the development of economic and social relations and with the corresponding material and intellectual development of Arab-Islamic society, all within a world dominated by religious thought and Islamic institutions.

Because existing studies have not done this, they have not been able to bring out all the progressive content and materialist tendencies contained within the heritage across the full course of its development. Nor have they been able to define its different stages in their historical and logical sequence, or to show their complex relationship with the different stages through which religious thought itself developed.

We therefore need a comprehensive study—or several studies—built on this basis. Such work must try to understand the heritage as a connected whole, follow the links and sequence between its stages, and examine its basic problems. Only then can we bring out the other, concrete side of what this heritage contains.

The author of this book has no illusion that he can provide the study we need in anything like its complete form, or even meet all its most important requirements.

Such a task would be extremely difficult for one person even if that person had all the necessary resources. It is harder still when an individual effort lacks many of them.

The truth, then, is that this book is little more than an attempt—almost an adventure.

An undertaking of this importance, on a road that has barely been opened, will inevitably stumble over its own weaknesses and mistakes, perhaps even more often than it encounters the difficulties and challenges of the road itself.

This book is one attempt to respond to the present need for a fully historical study of the heritage. It is also an extended experiment in applying the materialist conception of history to this field.

Its main tasks can be set out as follows:

1

To study Arab-Islamic philosophy as the product of a historical process within the development of Arab thought itself,301 and as something connected with the development of Arab-Islamic society during the Middle Ages.

In other words, this philosophy did not arise simply from a single outside influence, as has sometimes been claimed—namely, the borrowing of the philosophies of the East and of the Greek West.

2

To uncover what some studies have neglected or hidden, and what others have revealed only partly: the progressive values and materialist tendencies contained within the philosophical heritage, such as those discussed earlier in this introduction.302

At the same time, we must remember that these values and tendencies appeared in forms shaped by their own historical period. They therefore differ from the forms taken by progressive values and materialist tendencies in our own age, as we explained earlier in some detail.303

This is an objective question, not a subjective one.

A qualitative change in social relations, from an earlier form to a higher one, objectively required the appearance of forms of social consciousness that were themselves more advanced than what had come before.

Our understanding of these needs is therefore based on material conditions.304

In practical terms, the new and developing relations of production created a need for new knowledge of nature—knowledge capable of meeting the needs created by the development of material social activity.

That knowledge, in turn, developed dialectically as it became more closely connected in practice with those needs.

The development of the natural sciences necessarily leads to a deeper understanding of the laws of nature and to a more materialist understanding of the world as a whole.

This explains why materialist tendencies appeared more clearly and at a higher level in Arab-Islamic philosophy than they had in Greek philosophy during its first life in antiquity.

This is precisely what we meant when we said that Greek philosophy, through its interaction with Arab-Islamic philosophy, acquired a new life—that is, a new stage of development.

8

To identify the distinctive features of Arab thought in its broadest sense.

Our method here begins from two principles.

The first is that we are talking about characteristics acquired through history.

Our approach does not allow us to speak of innate racial characteristics that make the thought of one people fundamentally different from that of another people or another human “race.” To do so would lead us into racism or racial chauvinism.

When we say that Arab thought has distinctive characteristics, we mean that it acquired certain features during its historical development, from the closing period of the Jāhiliyya and the beginnings of Islam down to the end of the Middle Ages.

These features were the historical result of a long series of changes in the kinds of questions that the development of Arab-Islamic society placed before Arab thought. Thought had to deal with those questions and search for answers to them. The methods it used, and the level it reached, developed alongside the growth of scientific knowledge about nature and the world as a whole.

The objective forces that produced these characteristics worked through the internal mechanisms305 of Arab thought itself. But those mechanisms could not have operated in isolation from the general laws governing the development of human thought, which are themselves objectively connected with the general laws governing the development of human society.

The internal laws governing the thought of a particular people are one concrete way in which those general laws take effect.

This is the basis on which, throughout this book, we identify the characteristics of Arab thought as they emerged and developed from simpler forms into more complex ones.

The second principle concerns the development of Arab-Islamic philosophy in particular, and the relationship between the features specific to its development and the general features found in the development of philosophical thought as a whole, regardless of place and time.

We accept without argument the historical fact that Arab-Islamic philosophy followed a particular path of development. This gave it a distinctive character.

On the one hand, its development was tied to the development of Islamic religious thought. On the other, it absorbed elements of both the Greek and Eastern philosophical traditions.

But this does not mean that we can accept Hegel’s claim that Eastern philosophy as a whole existed within a separate and self-contained framework, cut off from the general history of philosophy outside that framework and from the common features of philosophical development.

A comprehensive and realistic view shows that this claim is wrong.

Every philosophy develops under its own particular conditions, but no philosophy falls outside the historical forces that shape the general development of philosophical thought across different times and places.

By these historical forces, we mean the following:

  1. Every philosophy develops through a struggle between materialism and idealism.

  2. It also develops through a struggle between dialectical thought and metaphysics understood as a static way of thinking.

  3. The character and level of a philosophy are connected with the character and historical level reached by scientific knowledge of nature.

  4. Major qualitative changes in philosophy often come before social and political upheavals. At a particular historical moment, those philosophical changes become a theoretical basis for such upheavals.

  5. Philosophy can appear only through categories and concepts. Philosophy is the most abstract of the forms of social consciousness, and philosophical abstraction can only be expressed through the language of categories and concepts, whereas art expresses itself through images.306

If we look at Arab-Islamic philosophy both through its own particular history and through these general features shared by philosophy as a whole, we can understand the relationship between the two as a dialectical relationship between the particular and the general.

Something does not stop sharing common features with other things simply because it has its own distinctive character. Those common features appear within its particular form and are realized through it.

The same is true of Arab-Islamic philosophy. The distinctive path of its own development does not separate it from the common features found in the development of philosophy more generally.

We do not say this simply as an abstract theoretical claim.

We say it because this is what we see when we follow Arab-Islamic philosophy through its actual historical movement and through the conflicts it was forced to undergo: conflicts within itself, and conflicts with opponents who defended the ideology of the dominant social order.

Modern idealist and bourgeois researchers have used Hegel’s idea of a separate and self-contained Eastern philosophy and applied it to Arab-Islamic philosophy. They have used this idea of “particularity” to remove Arab-Islamic philosophy from the wider history of the philosophical struggle between materialism and idealism.

The disagreement over the relationship between the “particular character” of our philosophical heritage and the general features shared by the development of philosophy throughout the world is therefore not simply a methodological or academic disagreement.

At its core, it is an ideological disagreement.

- 17 -

What, then, is the identity of the philosophical heritage we are proposing to study?

There is no doubt that it has its own historical “particularity,” although, as we have seen, there is disagreement over how far that particularity goes.

Does it form a closed world, cut off from the general course of philosophical history? Or does it stand in relation to philosophy as the particular stands to the general—forming part of that wider history and sharing the common features found in philosophy everywhere and in every age?

But to whom, or to what, does this “particularity” actually belong, in real historical and objective terms?

Is this philosophy an Arab product, so that we should call it Arab philosophy? Or is it an Islamic product created by people from many different peoples, so that we should call it Islamic philosophy?

And what exactly does it mean to say that it is Arab or Islamic?

Does it mean that its creators were Arabs of pure blood and descent? Does it mean that Muslims from many different peoples took part in producing it? Or does the question go beyond national or ethnic origin altogether and concern an intellectual and linguistic identity instead?

In other words, should the identity of this philosophy be determined by the content of its thought and by the language through which that thought was expressed?

In its general form, this question has been debated since modern scholars first began to study the heritage.

Earlier Arab writers, however, do not seem to have regarded it as a problem at all. We do not find them giving any particular name to the philosophy of the heritage itself.

This suggests that they saw no barrier separating it from the general history of philosophy as they knew it.

That view seems to have remained dominant down to the time of Ibn Khaldūn. He expressed it very clearly when he wrote that the rational sciences are natural to human beings because human beings are thinking creatures. They belong to no particular religion. People of every religion can study them and are equal in their ability to understand and investigate them. They have existed among humanity since civilization first appeared, and they are known as the sciences of philosophy and wisdom.307

What we do find among earlier writers are certain names for the philosophers themselves.

They sometimes call them the “philosophers of Islam.”308 Al-Ghazālī calls them “those who philosophize within Islam.”309 Ibn Khaldūn calls them “the speculative thinkers among the people of Islam.”310

But these names do not tell us the identity of their philosophy. They tell us only that these individuals belonged to the society that had formed under the banner of Islam.

They do not mean that their philosophy represented the Islamic faith.

If they did, Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq could not have understood the phrase “philosophers of Islam” to mean that “those who practiced philosophy under Islam, Muslims and non-Muslims alike, are called the philosophers of Islam.” Nor would he have had to admit that their philosophy is called Islamic philosophy only “in the conventional sense,”311 rather than in a religious sense—even though he himself was keen to use the phrase in support of calling it Islamic philosophy in that latter sense.

We find the same thing when earlier historians call al-Kindī at one moment “the philosopher of the Arabs” and at another “the philosopher of Islam.”

They did not mean that al-Kindī had created an “Arab philosophy” or an “Islamic philosophy” in the sense of racial or religious identity.

What they meant is captured by the judge Ṣāʿid when he wrote that “there was no one in Islam”—by which he meant the Islamic lands—“who became famous for the sciences of philosophy and was called a philosopher other than Yaʿqūb,” meaning al-Kindī.312

So the works of the earlier writers do not give us a defined “identity” for the philosophical heritage.

Modern Orientalists and Arab scholars, by contrast, have debated the question at length, and the disagreement remains unresolved.

But their debate has focused on only one side of the problem: the “nationality” of this philosophy, if we may call it that.

They have tried to decide whether it belongs to the Arab “race” or to several different human “races” within the state of the Caliphate.

They have not tried to establish its identity through the intellectual content of the philosophy itself and through the relationship between that content and social reality.

Two positions have therefore emerged, and both are one-sided.

One calls it “Arab philosophy” because it was written in Arabic.

The other calls it “Islamic philosophy” because most of its leading figures were not of Arab origin.313

Each position takes one of these two facts and ignores the other, almost as though the second fact did not exist or had no importance.

The disagreement also makes the problem look superficial. On one side, it becomes a formal question about language. On the other, it becomes a question about whether the philosophers belonged to one ethnic origin or another.

But the issue goes much deeper than that.

The important point is not simply that this philosophy was written in Arabic, considered only as the outward language or vocabulary in which it appeared. Nor is the important point simply whether most of its leading figures were Arabs or non-Arabs, understood in this narrow and superficial ethnic sense.

We need to look at two deeper facts together.

First, the philosophy of this heritage was written in Arabic and no other language.

Second, the people who produced and represented it came from several different peoples, with several different languages. During the Middle Ages, these peoples became part of a shared state—or a succession of shared states—connected with Islam not only as a religion but, above all, as a historical reality: Islam had become the name of a particular historical social order.

A scientific approach therefore requires us, first, to take both facts seriously and, second, to search for the deeper reality that lies not in either fact by itself but in the unity of the two.

What is that deeper reality?

We must begin by looking at the place of the Arabic language within our intellectual heritage as a whole. From there, we can understand its particular place within the philosophical heritage.

Language, as such, is a means through which social consciousness is expressed within a particular historical society.

In this sense, language is a social instrument.

It is true that a language takes shape, grows, and develops through internal mechanisms and laws of its own. These have a greater degree of independence than the actual content of the thought the language expresses.

But this does not mean that the internal laws of language operate in isolation from the movement of thought or from the movement of society, both of which language serves to express.

The opposite is true.

Language is historical. It does not arise, grow, and develop outside the history of a particular form of social consciousness. And that social consciousness, in turn, does not arise, grow, or develop outside the history of the society to which it belongs.

Arabic is a clear example.

From the rise of Islam to the point when the social and political order of the Caliphate had taken a settled form, Arabic-speaking society was absorbing enormous economic, social, and demographic changes.

Arabic itself necessarily had to absorb those changes—in its vocabulary and in its philological structure314—through its own internal processes, which also had a history of their own.

Seen from this angle, Arabic was using all its resources of word formation and expression to create a new vocabulary capable of carrying the ideas produced by the structure of Arab-Islamic social relations during the Middle Ages.

Its own internal processes—derivation, the formation of new words, Arabization, and so on—proved flexible enough to absorb the different forms of social consciousness that belonged to this new structure.

We can therefore say that the Arabic vocabulary and grammatical system315 inherited from the Jāhiliyya were not the same Arabic that later carried the intellectual and philosophical heritage down to us.

The earlier language had a simpler structure, closely connected with the simpler history of Arab tribal society.

The later language had a much more complex structure, just as Arab-Islamic society itself had acquired a much more complex history.

That complexity existed on several levels at once. Economic and social forces, politics, culture, and demographic change all became intertwined and interacted with one another.316

We stress the demographic element because this human mixture played an enormously important historical role in the development of relations of production, with the distinctive forms they took in that period. It also played a major role in shaping the intellectual heritage that expressed the social structure created by those relations.

The Arab-Islamic world brought together the human energies of many peoples in one historical experience. They interacted through social activity and through the production of knowledge.

This gave new features to their shared material and intellectual activity—to the work of both material and intellectual productive forces.

Those features appeared both in social relations and in individual work. And within this particular historical setting, they were also expressed through a shared language that absorbed the results of the entire experience with an almost extraordinary power.

That shared language was Arabic.

Its vocabulary, its word structures, its grammar, and its forms of expression came to embody a whole network of relationships produced by this turbulent historical interaction, with all its varied and complex contradictions.

At the intellectual level, philosophical thought in particular provided a framework in which those contradictions could come together.

This was because philosophy, more than any other form of social consciousness, directly confronts the great problems of the universe, society, and thought. And it does so from positions that cannot remain neutral toward the contradictions and struggles taking place in the world outside the mind.

What we call Arab-Islamic philosophical thought became an intellectual framework in which the contradictions of Arab-Islamic society were brought together and expressed through this shared language—a language that itself carried the accumulated results of that society’s long history of conflicting interactions.

The inner relationships within this thought first developed through its understanding of Islam’s ideas about the universe and society.

They developed further as Arab-Islamic thought absorbed the struggle between these concepts when treated as abstract, absolute, and fixed principles, on the one hand, and the changing realities of economic and social life on the other.

In the course of this struggle, those inner relationships within Arab-Islamic thought took on ideological forms. They became the mature intellectual expression of the struggle itself.

We can trace the first signs of this transformation to the movement known as the Qadariyya and to the reactions it produced among intellectual and social groups that opposed Umayyad rule and its ideology of predestination.

These tendencies then became clearer from one stage to the next.

They first took a developed form in Muʿtazilite thought.

Later, they reached their highest forms in two parallel fields: philosophy and philosophical Sufism.

At the same time, they appeared in another form among the Brethren of Purity, where philosophy and philosophical Sufism overlap without ever forming a completely harmonious whole.

The conclusion we want to draw from all this is clear.

Arabic was not an external tool used by these intellectual and ideological processes. It was an active part of their inner development.

As Arabic was used to deal with all the material and intellectual phenomena created by the historical movement of the Arabs, in the name of Islam, across the Asian and African world around the Mediterranean, the language itself changed.

Its new and developing structure absorbed the intellectual dimensions of that entire experience.

Arabic therefore became a living mark of the shared history of the different peoples who were objectively drawn into this historical movement and who helped create both that history and its intellectual heritage, including its philosophical heritage.

So far, we have found no more accurate short description of this shared history than Arab-Islamic history.

The word Arab here does not mean belonging through pure blood or descent. That kind of pure descent has ceased to have any meaningful place in history.
