Instead, the word refers to the historical features associated with the forms of civilization produced by the Arab historical movement and by the interaction between the Arabs and the many peoples who took part with them in creating those forms and their history.

The word Islamic, in turn, points precisely to this wider participation and to those peoples themselves.

Its meaning here is therefore civilizational, not religious.

This shared history was created by a complex and interconnected social structure. Its political, legal, and legislative order was tied to the system of the Islamic Caliphate and to the material and economic foundations on which that system rested.

This did not mean that everyone living within the society of the Caliphate was necessarily Muslim by belief.

History tells us that many followed other religions and systems of belief: Christianity, Judaism, Sabianism, Mazdakism, and others.

So when we use the word Islamic here, we are referring only to a social and historical meaning.

If the best description we have for this shared history is Arab-Islamic, in the sense just explained, then its intellectual heritage in all its different forms must also be Arab-Islamic.

According to the analysis we have just given, even the language of that heritage is Arab-Islamic in this historical sense.

Here, then, the philosophy of the heritage reveals its real historical identity.

It is not purely Arab.

It is not Islamic in a purely religious sense.

Nor is it purely Islamic in a historical sense.

It is Arab-Islamic philosophy, in the meaning we have developed above.

That is the meaning of the term we have adopted throughout this book.

Chapter One

Pre-Islamic Arabia

A — The Pre-Islamic Period Between Two Stages

1 — The Historical Framework

We begin our study with the pre-Islamic period, or Jāhiliyya,317 because we want to trace the earliest historical roots of the ways people in the Arabian Peninsula understood the universe and nature, as well as their social relationships and conditions of life. These were the first forms of what we might call Arab thought or Arab culture before Islam.

Starting here will help us follow the history of this thought from its beginnings. Later, this will give us a basis for understanding the larger course of its development after Islam, through the many breaks, leaps, and transformations that took place in Arab history.

But there is another, less direct reason for beginning with the pre-Islamic period. In fact, this second starting point is essential if we want to understand its intellectual and cultural life. We must look at the structure of tribal society in the Arabian Peninsula, the material foundations on which that structure rested, and the forms it took during this period.

Here, however, our discussion is limited to the particular historical stage with which this chapter begins: the final stage of the pre-Islamic period.

Arab history before Islam can be divided into two main stages. Historians and researchers broadly agree that the later stage—the one that concerns us here—does not extend much further back than the fifth and sixth centuries CE. Historical works, whether written by Orientalists or others, generally discuss the period directly preceding the rise of Islam within these two centuries.

There are solid reasons for drawing the line here. Two facts in particular help explain it.

The first is pre-Islamic poetry, which is still regarded as our most reliable source for studying this period. Historians of Arabic literature have found no surviving poetry that can confidently be dated to more than about 150 years before Islam.318

This is an important historical fact. The images, attitudes, relationships, descriptions, and views of the world found in this poetry correspond closely to what we know about Arab tribal life in the final part of the pre-Islamic period. We do not find in it reflections of the much older forms of life revealed by archaeology or by classical Greek and Roman historians, especially those that existed before the fifth century CE.

At the same time, the highly developed form of the pre-Islamic poetry that has reached us clearly suggests a much longer history behind it. It could not have appeared suddenly in the form we know.

But the fact that no earlier poetry has survived also suggests that the poetry available to us belongs historically to the same period of pre-Islamic Arab history that later Muslim writers were especially concerned with. So it is reasonable to use the age of this poetry as a rough measure for the period we are studying.

The second fact comes from comparing the economic and social conditions of the Arabian Peninsula in the fifth and sixth centuries with those of earlier periods. Modern historical discoveries show a clear difference between the two stages.

We can describe that difference as follows:

  • In the fifth and sixth centuries, the societies of the Arabian Peninsula were mainly organized through tribal bonds. The population was divided into separate tribal groups, usually connected by descent and sometimes by alliances. These tribes remained independent of one another. There were no political institutions uniting them, and no tribe accepted an authority from outside itself.

    For most tribes, camel herding was a main source of livelihood and production. Some also depended on agriculture where natural conditions made it possible, as in Yemen, Hadramawt, the coasts of Oman, some towns of the Hijaz such as Taif and Yathrib and their surrounding areas, as well as Yamama and the oases.

    Nomadic life therefore remained more common than settled life based on agriculture. Later, we will see new forces begin to change this picture and partially weaken the old tribal system. But those changes did not alter the basic character of the historical stage as a whole.

  • Before the fifth and sixth centuries, the evidence available to modern researchers, archaeologists, and historians319 leaves little room for doubt that parts of the Arabian Peninsula—especially the south—had reached relatively advanced levels of agriculture, artificial irrigation, architecture, political organization in the form of states, and division of labor. The population included farmers, livestock herders, and craftsmen.

    Some traces of these conditions survived into the fifth century, though by then they were already in decline.320

    Engels appears to have come across some of this evidence as early as the middle of the nineteenth century. In a letter to Marx dated 24 May 1853, he wrote: “It seems that the Arabs, when they had a civilized existence in the southwest, were a civilized people much like the Egyptians, Assyrians, etc. Their architectural works show this.”321

2 — A Historical Break

The difference between these two stages shows that Arab history before Islam went through a historical break in its development. Similar breaks may also have happened at earlier times.

Such breaks probably occurred either at turning points between the different states that existed in ancient Arabia—some of which disappeared completely, while others left material remains behind—or through struggles between these states and between them and outside powers.

Among these states were the Minaeans (1300–630 BCE), the Sabaeans (800–115 BCE), the Qatabanians,322 and the Himyarites (115 BCE–525 CE).323

The Soviet Orientalist historian Belyaev says that we cannot know with certainty all the material and intellectual causes behind the decline and disappearance of Yemeni civilization during the Himyarite period between 300 and 525 CE.324

Even so, Belyaev himself gives us an important clue, alongside the evidence found in other sources.325 Taken together, this evidence allows us to identify the main causes of the partial break in development.

Foreign invasions and internal conflicts weakened Himyarite control over the major trade routes. They also weakened the system that maintained the Ma'rib Dam,326 which had been the backbone of year-round artificial irrigation and intensive agriculture in southern Arabia.

As this system broke down, the dam collapsed and agricultural lands were ruined. Development in the region was interrupted, and many of its people migrated to other parts of the Arabian Peninsula.

The Azd, including the Ghassanids, moved toward Syria. The Tanukhids migrated to Bahrain. The Mundhirids moved to Iraq, settling in the region between al-Hira and al-Anbar.327

This break marks the main difference between the final stage of the pre-Islamic period and the earlier stages. Those earlier societies contained elements that could have supported wider and deeper development and eventually spread it to other parts of the Arabian Peninsula.

3 — Break and Continuity

When we speak of a break, however, we do not mean a complete stop in development, followed by a completely new beginning from zero. That would be a static, or metaphysical, way of understanding historical change.

We mean a break in the dialectical sense: a break that forms part of continuity itself.

This dialectical relationship between break and continuity in the development of human society is based on a broader scientific understanding of motion in nature, society, and thought. Motion itself contains an internal contradiction.

Zeno of Elea (489 BCE–?) noticed this contradiction when he denied the existence of motion. He correctly recognized that thinking about motion involves a contradiction,328 but he could not solve the problem in the way dialectical thought later would.

From a dialectical point of view, we do not have to choose between seeing motion as something made only of separate breaks or as something completely continuous. There is a third possibility: motion is the unity of both discontinuity and continuity.

Take Zeno’s famous arrow. From this point of view, the arrow both is and is not at a particular point at a particular moment. The same is true at every point and every moment along the arrow’s path through time.329

The same applies to Zeno’s example of Achilles and the tortoise.330 If motion consisted only of separate moments, as Zeno imagined, then it would indeed be impossible for Achilles ever to catch the tortoise. But once we understand motion as a unity of both discontinuity and continuity, there is no such impossibility.

This dialectical idea of motion applies to historical development in society and thought just as it applies to motion in nature.

The history of society and the history of thought both contain quantitative and qualitative changes. In other words, their development combines continuity with breaks.

This is what we mean when we say that a break took place in Arab history before Islam between the final stage of the pre-Islamic period and the stages that came before it.

It was not an absolute break. The continuing development of Arab society did not stop completely. What happened was one part of a larger dialectical process in which continuity and interruption existed together.

The historical evidence confirms this. We can see it in several features of Arab society during the final pre-Islamic period. We will briefly list them here, then return to them later when we examine the structure of tribal society in greater detail:

  1. Signs of the breakdown of the earlier primitive system began to appear as society moved from a largely self-sufficient economy toward an economy based on goods for exchange, eventually including the use of money. One of the clearest signs was the decline of primitive communal ownership and the appearance of private ownership of the means of production.

  2. The authority of the tribal chief also began to change. In the older system, his authority rested mainly on tribal custom. Now his economic position began to matter alongside his traditional tribal standing.

  3. The earlier matriarchal, or totemic, pattern of family relations disappeared,331332 and patriarchal relations became dominant.333

From the viewpoint of historical materialism, none of these developments could appear in a society without a long history behind them.

A society must pass through earlier stages before conditions like these can emerge. Their presence in late pre-Islamic Arab society is therefore material and historical evidence that this period did not begin from zero after a complete break with everything before it.

On the contrary, it was the result of a continuing historical development. That development followed a single overall course, or dialectical unity, while also passing through several different forms of interruption.

Nor was this something unusual that happened only in Arab history before Islam. It followed a general pattern in the history of human societies.

History does not develop through absolute continuity, and it does not develop through absolute breaks. It develops through both together.

4 — What Language and Pre-Islamic Poetry Tell Us

Alongside these economic and social developments, we must also consider another important fact: by the final pre-Islamic period, Arabic language and poetry had already reached a highly developed level.

In some respects, they almost seem to have advanced beyond the tribal social order of the time, even though both language and poetry also reflect the tensions and crises within that order.

Later, we will see that the structure of the language, its linguistic features, and the style of pre-Islamic poetry and prose in the fifth and sixth centuries could not reasonably have appeared from nothing during those two centuries.

When Islam emerged in the Arabian Peninsula, it found a language already capable of expressing its message: its principles, its explanations of the world, and its laws.

Arabic could do this through meanings it already possessed, but it also proved remarkably flexible in taking on new meanings. It adapted to the new ideas introduced by Islam—to its principles, beliefs, and laws—with extraordinary ease.

Islam therefore found a mature language and a mature system of expression already available to it.

That language was capable not only of expressing the historical conditions that had made the rise of Islam possible. It was also capable of expressing the new historical possibilities that opened after Islam appeared.

The language of the Qur'an, which reaches the highest levels of Arabic expression, is therefore one of the most important signs of historical continuity in the development of Arab society before Islam, even as that continuity also contained dialectical breaks.

This mature language was not simply a linguistic phenomenon. At its core, it was a social phenomenon.

The advanced form in which Arabic appears in the Qur'an was one expression of the culture that had developed during the pre-Islamic period.

Could such a language, together with the artistic power it displays in both poetry and prose, really have been produced in only a century and a half before Islam?

Scientific reasoning completely rejects such an ahistorical idea.

One Western thinker expresses surprise at how quickly Arabic became a shared language of scholarship among the different peoples who belonged to Islamic civilization. He also notes how Arabic “shaped, through its own structure, some of the most significant features of Islamic thought; even Greek concepts underwent deep changes as they passed through this structure.”334

A historical materialist view of this important development assumes that a long history lay behind it—a history stretching back several centuries before the period immediately preceding Islam.

Repeated breaks in that long history may have caused later generations to lose knowledge of important stages in the development of Arabic and of pre-Islamic poetry before the fifth century CE.

But that does not change the objective reality itself.

Not knowing that something existed does not mean that it did not exist.

Later, we will return to the historical development of pre-Islamic poetry and other cultural features.

B — Features of Pre-Islamic Society

1 — Natural Conditions and Population

Here we are concerned with geography, geology, and climate, and with the effect these conditions had on the ancient distribution of the population across the Arabian Peninsula.

We do not mean that these natural conditions directly determined the economic and social relationships that appeared during different stages of Arab history before Islam.

At the same time, however, we should not ignore the part they played in shaping the early division of labor in some parts of the peninsula and in influencing the first directions taken by pre-Islamic society.

When we look at the geography of the Arabian Peninsula, one issue immediately stands out. Early Arab geographers disagreed about where its northern boundaries had lain before Islam, as we can see from Yaqut.335

Al-Hamdani, who wrote in the fourth Islamic century and therefore lived before Yaqut, places the lower Euphrates at the peninsula’s northeastern boundary and the Mediterranean coast of Palestine at its northwestern boundary.336

Belyaev, writing in modern times, doubts that al-Hamdani’s exact boundaries were correct. But he does not doubt that the Syrian Desert was considered part of Arabia before Islam. He also argues that in the fifth and sixth centuries, the political boundary between the Persian and Byzantine empires left the Syrian Desert in the hands of its native population: the Arabs.337

Ibn Hawqal gives us evidence supporting the same view,338 and we may find further support in Ibn Khaldun. He writes:

“... Between the Persian Sea and the Qulzum lies the Arabian Peninsula, as though it were a piece of land projecting into the sea. It is surrounded by the Abyssinian Sea to the south, the Sea of Qulzum to the west, and the Persian Sea to the east, extending toward Iraq between Syria and Basra, with a distance of fifteen hundred miles between them.”339

There is, of course, no real disagreement over the peninsula’s other boundaries. They are naturally marked by three seas: the Indian Ocean or Arabian Sea to the south, the Arabian-Persian Gulf to the east, and the Red Sea—known in earlier times as the Sea of Qulzum—to the west.

Ancient Greek and Roman geographers divided the Arabian Peninsula differently from Arab geographers of the medieval period.

The Greeks and Romans, working from the political situation of Arabia in the first century CE, divided it into three parts:

a. The desert region in the north, southwest of the Syrian Desert, where the Nabataean kingdom was located.

b. Arabia Felix, or Yemen.

c. The desert region where nomadic tribes were dominant.340

Arab geographers, by contrast, seem to have based their divisions mainly on natural geography and geology, and perhaps partly on economic conditions as well.

They divided the peninsula into five regions: Tihama, the Hijaz, Najd, al-Arud, and Yemen.

This division appears in al-Hamdani341 and Yaqut.342 Ibn Hawqal seems to have followed it too, judging from Ibn al-Faqih’s account of the boundaries assigned to each of these five regions.343

Ibn Hawqal also adds the Iraqi Desert, the Jazira Desert between the Tigris and Euphrates, and the Syrian Desert.344

The climate of the Arabian Peninsula follows from its geography and differs from one region to another.

Because most of the peninsula is desert, dryness is the dominant condition. Rainfall is irregular, and rainwater generally does not collect into regular, permanent waterways.

There are, however, regions with fertile soil and milder climates. These include Yemen and Hadramawt in the south, the mountains around Taif near Mecca, the city of Yathrib—later Medina—in the north, and Yamama in the southeast.

These differences shaped both the way people lived and the early division of labor.

In dry regions, unsettled nomadic life became dominant. People depended on livestock and moved in search of seasonal pasture and temporary sources of water.

In regions suited to agriculture, settled and more urban forms of life appeared. People farmed as well as raising livestock, and small craft industries developed to meet the needs of settled agricultural communities.

Other areas, especially the oases, produced a way of life that was partly settled and partly nomadic.

People there stayed in the oases during parts of the year to grow dates, some grains, and vegetables, especially toward the end of winter. During the rest of the year they moved with their animals, mainly camels, in search of pasture.

When they left, they would often leave some members of their families behind to protect the crops until they returned for the harvest.

The life of these oasis communities was part of a very long historical process through which nomadic groups gradually became settled communities tied to work on the land.

Looking at the picture in broad terms, we can divide the population of the Arabian Peninsula in the final pre-Islamic period into three groups according to how they produced the means of life.

The first was settled and worked mainly in agriculture.

The second was unsettled and depended on herding and migration.

The third lived between settlement and migration and represented a transitional stage from the second, lower condition to the first, higher one.

Each of these groups therefore represented a different early stage in the long human struggle to gain greater control over nature and produce the means of life.

From the earliest stages of this struggle, human beings advanced by developing the relationship between physical labor and intellectual labor.

The differences between these three groups still reflected a stage at which the production of basic necessities depended heavily on natural conditions, especially geography and climate.

This dependence marked human labor before people became able to free themselves from the absolute control of such conditions.

2 — Early Economic Factors

The people of the Arabian Peninsula did not, however, remain completely trapped by this dependence on nature.

Toward the end of the final pre-Islamic period, we begin to see ways in which they slowly and partially learned to make use of the possibilities offered by their geographical position, climate, and natural resources.

We can see this in several developments:

  1. They took advantage of the Arabian Peninsula’s location on major trade routes connecting different parts of the inhabited world.

  2. This position created income from services provided along caravan routes and led to growing trade, through which the use of money began to spread.

  3. These conditions allowed productive activity to grow and private ownership of the means of production to appear in forms specific to that historical stage.

  4. Where water and suitable soil were available, people used them for artificial irrigation and for growing a wider range of crops, including fruit, grain, and legumes. In this way they increased the productivity of the land.345

  5. Small craft industries producing everyday goods also appeared. People worked with metals, clay, and leather to make weapons, iron farming tools, pottery, and tanned leather. These crafts began to separate from agriculture.

These material developments were the main forces shaping the direction in which pre-Islamic tribal society changed.

This does not mean that society became completely independent of natural conditions. Such independence is neither assumed nor possible, because human society does not exist outside nature.

What is possible—and historically necessary—is for human beings to gain increasing control over these natural conditions and make the fullest possible use of them.346

This growing human control gives the development of each society its particular historical character, while the general laws governing the development of human societies continue to operate across all of them, however different their local conditions may be.

3 — The Direction of Change in the Economic Structure

We can trace this direction by following the historical development of the same features discussed above. As we do so, one thing becomes especially clear: by the end of the sixth century CE, these different parts of the economy were interacting with one another in a noticeable way.

The clearest example was the growing connection between agriculture and trade. Each helped the other develop. The use of iron tools in farming—including iron ploughs—together with artificial irrigation increased the production of grain and vegetables. This created a relative surplus beyond immediate local needs. At the same time, that surplus made it possible for trade to expand. Agricultural produce now became part of commercial exchange. In other words, it was increasingly being produced for exchange rather than simply for local consumption. It was becoming commodity production.347

We can therefore see agriculture and trade influencing each other. To make this picture clearer, we need to look at some of the historical evidence.

□ Trade: Accounts of periods before the Jāhiliyya tell us about the flourishing trade route once known in Arabia as the “Perfume Route” or “Incense Route.” Perfumes, incense, and similar goods travelled along it between India, Yemen, and the Mediterranean lands.348

This route had already flourished under the Minaeans and Sabaeans during the first millennium BCE. The two peoples competed for control over it, including the oases through which it passed in the north-west of the peninsula.349

Later, however, the route lost its commercial importance. After the Minaeans, the Sabaeans also lost control of the Red Sea and the coast of East Africa as maritime trade passed into Greek and Roman hands. During the first Himyarite state, in 24 BCE, the Romans even tried to seize Yemen itself so that they could control the region’s overland trade routes as well.

That attempt failed, but Roman control of the Red Sea was enough to destroy the commercial importance of the Perfume Route. It badly damaged both the trading and agricultural economy of Yemen, adding to the damage caused by the collapse of the Maʾrib Dam at around the same time.350

Following Jawād ʿAlī, we can even say that the collapse of the dam itself may have been one result of Roman control of Red Sea trade. The Himyarites lost so much of their commercial wealth that they no longer had the resources to maintain and repair the dam properly. Eventually, it collapsed.351

The Perfume Route later recovered its importance. This happened after the Byzantine Empire formed an alliance with Abyssinia and helped the Abyssinians conquer Yemen. Abyssinian influence then spread over the Red Sea trade routes and the old overland route running from the south of the peninsula to the north. This helped secure Byzantine trade with India.352

From the second third of the sixth century CE onward, the Perfume Route once again became an important part of international trade. Goods travelled along it between India, Yemen, Palestine, Egypt, Greece, and other parts of the Byzantine Empire.

Alongside it ran another route carrying goods that had crossed the Red Sea from East Africa—especially Somalia and Eritrea—through al-Yamāma and on to Iraq.353

Arabia had therefore become a meeting point for some of the most important trade routes connecting the populated worlds of East and West. This was true of the south and north of the peninsula, as well as its east and west. Both major routes connected south with north: one from the eastern side, the other from the western side.

The Ḥijāz in particular occupied an unusually important position. It lay between trade routes coming from the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea across the Arabian Peninsula, and routes coming from Persia, Iraq, Syria, and the wider Mediterranean world. It stood, in effect, at the centre of a network connecting the two great empires of that age: the Sasanian Persian Empire and the Byzantine Empire.

This location played a major part in the growth of trading towns in the Ḥijāz. These towns became commercial stations along the Red Sea route. Trading ports also developed where Roman ships could take on goods and products from India.354 Among them were al-Shuʿayba, the old port of Mecca before Jeddah became its main port, and Yanbuʿ, the port of Yathrib.355

The commercial importance of the Ḥijāz grew further after Abyssinian rule in Yemen came to an end and was replaced by Persian rule. Byzantine influence then withdrew from southern Arabia and from the Red Sea route. The two overland routes to India regained their earlier importance: one through the Euphrates and Tigris region, and the other through Yemen and Syria by way of Mecca. As a result, “al-Ḥīra under the Lakhmids and Mecca under Banū al-Naḍr made enormous gains.”356

By the end of the sixth century CE, the gains made by Mecca were increasingly concentrated in the hands of Quraysh’s leading families.357 Other tribal chiefs also profited when important trade routes passed through their territories.

The leaders of Quraysh themselves had by then become the main middlemen in international trade between India and China on one side, and the Mediterranean lands and East Africa on the other.358

Their commercial and financial power became so great, on top of their traditional tribal authority, that they imposed dues359 and taxes on smaller Arab merchants who were not allied with them, as well as on foreign merchants.360

Foreign traders also had a noticeable presence in Mecca, according to the Arabic sources. They included Romans and Persians who had commercial ties with the great Qurayshi merchants.

We should also remember that Mecca’s religious position as the home of the Kaʿba gave the leaders of Quraysh another source of wealth and helped strengthen the city’s commercial importance.

□ Agriculture: It is generally accepted that during the two centuries before the rise of Islam, Bedouins made up a larger share of Arabia’s population than settled people tied to the land.

But this is only a broad impression. The historical sources from the period give us no statistical figures, even approximate ones. We therefore cannot use this general fact as a firm basis for a strict analysis of the social and economic structure of pre-Islamic society.

The usual impression is that Bedouins greatly outnumbered settled people. Many analyses of the economic and social structure have therefore been built on this vague overall assumption.

Yet we also have a great deal of historical evidence pointing in another direction. Many places across the peninsula had people who irrigated and cultivated the land and who had considerable farming knowledge. In many areas, production sometimes exceeded local consumption needs and the surplus entered local markets for exchange.

This was not limited to one part of Arabia. Agriculture was certainly more widespread in some regions, especially the south, than in others. Yemen, for example, had lost some of the relative agricultural prosperity it had enjoyed when the Maʾrib Dam was still intact.

Even so, Yemen did not lose its distinct character as an agricultural country. Centuries of farming had given its people rich practical experience in reducing their complete dependence on natural conditions.

When we look at agricultural activity elsewhere in Arabia during the same period, we find similar practices and accumulated experience. Agriculture existed not only in Yemen, but also in Ḥaḍramawt, Oman in the south-east, al-Yamāma in the east, the Ḥijāz in the north, Tihāma in the west—both its northern and southern parts—and the many oases along desert routes and inside the desert itself, even in the volcanic regions known as the ḥarrāt.361

Across all these regions, groups of Arabs worked the land. Some were permanently settled, while others were only partly settled. They used underground water and seasonal surface water through methods that were relatively advanced for their time.

They farmed not only to meet their own immediate needs but also to produce goods for exchange. These products reached not only small local markets but also the larger markets that served the peninsula as a whole, as the historical sources mentioned earlier tell us.

Those sources sometimes give details about the range of agricultural products brought to these markets. Some of them had even been processed in ways that involved a degree of manufacturing.362

Faced with this evidence, the modern researcher can only regret that medieval Arab-Islamic historians who wrote about the pre-Islamic period give us no figures, even rough ones, for the amount of land under cultivation in the different parts of Arabia.363 Nor do they give us enough information to estimate how many people worked this land compared with the total population of the peninsula.

This makes it very difficult to reach a firm scientific conclusion about how much agriculture shaped the economic structure and the direction in which it was developing.

More importantly, it makes it difficult to know how strongly agriculture affected the social structure of Arabia as a whole, or of western Arabia—where the Ḥijāz lies—in particular.

When it comes to trade, however, we have more historical evidence to work with. Early historians give us enough information about commercial activity to form a clearer picture: its economic and social effects on the population, the reach of its foreign connections, and the scale of the profits made by the leaders of Mecca, especially the leaders of Quraysh.364

By the end of the sixth century CE, these men had come to dominate trade between the Arabian Peninsula and the outside world. In doing so, they became an important force in pushing the relationship between productive work and commerce toward a growing contradiction, as we shall see.

□ Craft production: Before drawing conclusions from what we have seen so far, we also need to ask what place handicrafts held in the economic structure of pre-Islamic society.

Where had crafts reached in the development of the economy—or, more precisely, in the development of the division of labour? And what was their relationship to commodity production during this period?

The answer helps us identify the historical stage that Arab society had reached in the late Jāhiliyya.

The simple existence of handicrafts is not enough. What matters is their relationship to agriculture.

Were crafts still carried out as part of agricultural life, or had they separated from farming and become independent occupations in their own right?

These two situations belong to two different stages of development.

When handicrafts are still part of the work done by farming communities, society is at an earlier stage in the division of labour. The later stage begins when some people become full-time craftsmen while others remain farmers.

This second stage is more advanced because such a division means that society has reached a point where people can produce more than they need for their own immediate daily survival. Production is becoming social production for exchange—in other words, commodity production. Its products can now enter trade.

At this stage, trade becomes a social activity that interacts positively with productive work.

The separation of handicrafts from agriculture is therefore an important sign of development. It marks a new stage in the history of ancient societies. It is a form of specialization in productive work. This usually brings greater productivity, gives human labour greater power to transform nature, creates new craft skills, and encourages improvements in technique.

This separation of handicrafts from agriculture—and their development into production for exchange—had in fact already taken place by the end of the Jāhiliyya.

Whenever the Arabic sources mention these crafts, they speak of their products as things that were exchanged, bought, and sold.365 They also speak of markets for them, and even of markets specializing in particular crafts, such as the goldsmiths’ market in Yathrib, later Medina.366

It is particularly significant for our argument that weapons were among the goods manufactured in Mecca at this time. Other Meccan crafts included pottery and the making of beds and couches.367

Some of the people who worked in these crafts—especially metalworking—were also well-known figures in the history of Islam’s beginnings.

Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra and al-ʿĀṣ ibn Hishām, the brother of Abū Jahl, were both blacksmiths.368 Umayya ibn Khalaf al-Jumaḥī worked in pottery,369 while ʿUtba ibn Abī Waqqāṣ was a carpenter.370 All of these men fought against Islam at Badr or Uḥud.371

Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ made and sharpened arrows,372 while Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt was a swordsmith.373 Both supported Islam.374

There were also the well-known crafts of al-Ṭāʾif, each with its own markets. These included tanning, charcoal-making, extracting tar, and distilling wine, among others.375

Yemen was famous for the quality of its crafts, especially weapons and textiles.376 Yathrib also produced metal goods such as jewellery and ornaments, as well as weapons.377

As we said, the existence of weapons production in Mecca itself is especially significant.

Why?

First, because of the particular nature of Mecca’s economy. Mecca was not an agricultural town. It lay in what the Qurʾān calls “a valley without cultivation.”378

Craft production in Mecca therefore could not have existed as a branch of farming. It had to stand on its own. This means it had already moved beyond household craft work intended simply to meet immediate personal needs and had entered the stage of production for exchange.

Second, the particular presence of blacksmithing in Mecca deserves our attention.

The relatively advanced use of iron at this time379 is itself a historical development with a specific meaning in Marxist social analysis.380

As we have just seen, blacksmithing was a common occupation. Even men of high standing within Quraysh, such as al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra and al-ʿĀṣ ibn Hishām, were associated with it.

Are we really to suppose that blacksmiths produced weapons but no agricultural tools, at a time when rising agricultural productivity was already attracting wealthy Qurayshi merchants from Mecca to invest part of their money in agricultural land at al-Ṭāʾif?381

That would make little sense.

We also know for a fact that iron ploughs existed during this period of Arab history, both before Islam and around the time Islam emerged.382

There is another point as well. Some modern Arab writers have argued that Quraysh became so absorbed in trade, and grew so wealthy from it, that they lost interest in warfare. Some other Arabs even mocked them for this and came to look down on them.383

There may be some exaggeration in this view, but its basic point is sound. Trade was the main concern of Quraysh in Mecca because it formed the foundation of the city’s economy and the chief source of wealth for its leaders.

This fact shaped the other forms of productive work in Mecca, especially handicrafts. Their main purpose became production for exchange. This applied even to weapons production,384 as well as to the other branches of blacksmithing, metalworking, goldsmithing, and related crafts.

Belyaev was therefore right to conclude that the Arabs of the Jāhiliyya had already moved beyond a division of labour between cultivators and livestock herders and had reached a later stage in which society was divided between craftsmen and farmers.

He writes that, at this later stage,

Arab crafts were not limited to pottery and weaving—fields in which they had reached a high level. They also worked with smelted metals. Iron was available in the territory of the Sulaym tribe, east of Medina, which became so well known for ironworking that its neighbours called it the tribe of the qayns, or blacksmiths. They were also known for smelting and refining iron (...) Farmers used a variety of iron tools, including iron ploughshares.385

□ Forms of slavery: The surviving accounts of the Jāhiliyya agree that slavery was not foreign to this part of the ancient world.

The forms of slavery we can see in the late Jāhiliyya suggest that the institution already had a long history in Arabia. But we do not have documents that tell us when it began or what forms it had taken in earlier periods.

For the period we are studying, however, the historical evidence clearly shows that slavery had a place in the social and economic structure.

Slaves were used as a productive force, not merely as objects of consumption.

We know that slaves were used for domestic work by the leaders of Quraysh in Mecca,386 by wealthy people in other towns, and in the households of tribal and clan chiefs. Slaves were also themselves a common and widely traded “commodity.”387

But their role went beyond domestic service and trade. Slaves—especially Abyssinians—were also used in productive work such as agriculture, including irrigation, as well as in crafts and livestock raising.388 Some were also employed in commercial work.389

Even so, the use of slaves as a productive force is not enough to conclude that slave relations of production were the dominant form of production in pre-Islamic society.

There are several reasons for this.

First, slave labour was not the main element within the productive forces. This was true in the urban and semi-urban economy as well as in the Bedouin economy based on herding and livestock raising. Free people made up a substantial part of the productive population, at least as large as the enslaved part.

Second, more slaves were used as household servants, guards, or goods traded between local and foreign markets than were used directly as productive labour. Their role as producers was therefore neither their main role nor the dominant one.

Third, most slaves were foreigners.

Many were Abyssinians of Ethiopian or Sudanese origin.390 Some were white Persians or Romans391 who had originally been taken prisoner during wars between the Persian and Byzantine empires and were later brought into Arabia for sale.

Foreign slaves in Arab society were therefore usually acquired through trade rather than directly through war.

Arab captives who became slaves after intertribal wars were much fewer in number than foreign slaves. The reason was that Arab prisoners taken in tribal wars were usually freed in one of two ways.

Either their tribe launched a counterattack against the tribe holding them,392 or a ransom was paid for their release.393

There was another factor as well. In pre-Islamic custom, being taken prisoner could bring shame on both the captive and the captive’s tribe. Some people were even said to prefer killing themselves rather than being captured.394

For all these reasons, Arab captives generally became slaves only when no one could pay their ransom and they could not ransom themselves. In that case, they could be bought and sold or put to work in productive or non-productive activities.

But, as we have already noted, these forms of work were not carried out by slaves alone.

In short, slavery in Arabia had its own particular form. Within each tribe, slaves were mostly foreigners, followed by people from other Arab tribes, while the members of the tribe itself remained free despite the differences in wealth and living conditions among them.395

□ The Bedouin economy: We do not have enough precise historical evidence to measure the role of the Bedouin economy against the settled economy of agriculture, trade, and craft production. We have already noted this problem.

Even so, the evidence that survives allows us to form a general picture.

The first point to make is that the importance of either type of economy cannot be judged simply by its size. What matters most is how strongly it affected the direction in which the whole economy of the late Jāhiliyya was developing.

There is no doubt that Bedouin Arabs outnumbered the people of towns and settled communities. Nor is there any doubt that their main means of living was livestock raising, especially camels. The economic return from this way of life may in itself have been considerable.

But its defining feature was its almost complete dependence on natural conditions: the climate, the timing of rainfall, the location of pasture, and so on.

Human beings had little control over these conditions apart from the ability to move from one place to another. Even that movement was not really a matter of choice. It was forced on them by the search for suitable weather and pasture, and whatever suitability they found was temporary.

This dependence on nature was both a weakness and a constraint. It helped keep the Bedouin economy relatively underdeveloped.

The tribal social system created further pressures that drained and reduced its resources. These included tribal wars, such as blood feuds, armed struggles over pasture or its protection, and the economic burden of maintaining armed nomadic groups.

The settled economy was moving in the opposite direction.

The forces driving agriculture, trade, and craft production were not only helping the settled economy grow. They were also beginning to influence the Bedouin economy itself.

Over time, the Bedouin economy could lose its earlier historical role and become drawn into the new process of development. In other words, it would increasingly come under the same forces shaping the settled economy, to the extent required by the wider laws of social development under the particular conditions of pre-Islamic Arabia.

The continuing interaction among the three main parts of the settled economy—agriculture, trade, and handicrafts that had become independent of agriculture—was gradually becoming stronger.

This gave the settled economy the decisive role in the new historical development of the economic structure of pre-Islamic society as a whole.

The old structure had been based mainly on a natural economy and primitive communal ownership. It was now moving toward a structure based on commodity production and private ownership of the means of production.

This transformation was already taking place objectively during the period we are studying, though at a relatively slow pace.

It meant that the settled economy, through its own forms of growth and development, was beginning to create the material and productive basis for a society divided into classes rather than one divided into scattered tribal units.

4 — The Direction of Change in the Social Structure

The direction of economic development described above appeared in a number of visible social changes. These allow us to see more clearly where that development was historically leading.

At the same time, these changes contained the beginnings of a contradiction between the developing economy and the social structure of the old, primitive tribal system.

In an earlier period, the level and forms of social life in Arabia had broadly matched the level of economic life.

That balance began to change when activity returned to the land and sea trade routes connecting Arabia—especially its western regions—with countries that were economically more advanced than the Arabian interior, including China, India, Persia, Syria, and the coast of East Africa.

This renewed contact with the outside world gave Arabia an important role as an international commercial middleman.

That role, in turn, pushed tribal leaders—especially the leaders of Quraysh—to move beyond simply providing a route for trade. They began taking a direct part in trade themselves.

This had an important economic effect. It began to separate the leaders of the clans of Mecca, especially those of Quraysh, from the leaders of tribes living away from the major trade routes.

Here we can see the beginnings of an economic divide that was bound to create a social divide as well.

The first difference was between regions that gained little or nothing from international trade and commercial brokerage and those that profited from both.

The second arose within the prosperous regions themselves: between their wealthy leaders on one side, and the poorer members of their own clans and the smaller tribes tied to them through loyalty and alliance on the other.

These early forms of economic and social inequality created a contradiction between an economic structure moving toward a new stage of development and a social structure that was lagging behind it.

We can therefore see two closely connected meanings in the changes taking place at this time.

First, they show that the old primitive tribal structure was beginning to break down.

Second, they show the first signs, emerging from within the tribal system itself, of the new social order toward which economic development was moving.

These two processes were internally connected. We can see them in the following developments.

First — The Emergence of Economic Exchange

As Arabia first took on the role of commercial middleman and then became directly involved in trade, the exchange of useful goods naturally began to take on a more developed economic form.

A measure of exchange value appeared: something against which the value of every item being exchanged could be compared.

Among the people of Arabia during the period we are studying, this measure took two parallel forms.

The first was barter based on one major commodity that effectively served as money.

The second was the more advanced and final form produced by exchange itself: money proper, which Engels called the “commodity of commodities.”396

Camels were the main commodity that performed the function of money.

This was because camels occupied such a central place in Bedouin life. Raising them was therefore one of the main forms of productive work in the desert economy.

In Mecca, however, and in the Arab markets drawn into the trading network of Quraysh, exchange was based mainly on metal currency.

Two main coins circulated: the Byzantine gold dinar397 and the Sasanian silver dirham.398

The use of both currencies reflected the different sources of the trade controlled above all by the leaders of Quraysh. They were operating between the two empires that dominated the eastern and western worlds of the time: the Sasanian Persian Empire and the Byzantine Empire.

It seems that Yemeni, or Himyarite, money was also used. This was not minted coinage but pieces of raw gold, either imported from Africa or collected from riverbeds in Yemen. Pieces of raw silver were also used.399

These unminted forms of money were exchanged according to their weight.400

Whatever form the currency took, the very fact that exchange was increasingly based on money was itself a sign that the tribal system was beginning to break down. Monetary exchange was fundamentally at odds with the communal values of tribal society.

The rise of economic exchange in this form also made trade an important force in the historical transformation we are trying to trace in Arabia.

This does not contradict the scientific principle that the exchange of commodities cannot by itself cause a social system to collapse. At most, exchange can speed up a process of breakdown that has deeper causes.

In other words, exchange cannot be the decisive factor.

The decisive factor is social production itself: the production of the material goods society needs.

Exchange comes after production. If nothing is produced, there is nothing to exchange.

But this does not mean that trade has no effect on development.

We have already seen the two-way relationship between agricultural production and trade in Arabia. Once farming produced more than people needed for their own immediate use, commodity exchange naturally developed and became more active.

Then exchange, in turn, encouraged further growth in productivity, including in handicraft production that had already separated from agriculture.

Second — The Decline of Primitive Communal Ownership

Primitive communal ownership had been the foundation of tribal society. But the history of pre-Islamic Arabia shows that this foundation was already close to collapse as the sixth century drew to an end and the seventh century began.

By this stage, communal ownership seems to have survived in little more than one form: shared ownership of grazing land and water sources such as wells and springs. Some pastures, wells and springs still appear to have belonged jointly to particular tribes. Reports about pre-Islamic Arabia often describe a place as “the pasture of the camels of such-and-such a tribe” or “the water of such-and-such a tribe.” In other words, they name an entire tribal group as the owner of the place.

But we do not find similar reports describing a particular piece of farmland as the property of a whole tribe or clan. We sometimes hear of herds of camels or other livestock being associated with the name of a tribe or clan. But this does not prove that the herds were collectively owned, because other reports from pre-Islamic Arabia point in the opposite direction. References to camels, horses and sheep owned by individuals are far more common. In the language of legal scholars, these reports therefore qualify the broader wording of the others, where whole herds are simply attached to the names of tribes.401

The reports about the many oases scattered across the Arabian Peninsula do not clearly tell us what form agricultural ownership took there. Arab chroniclers do tell us, however, that the people living in these oases were settled rather than nomadic, and that by the late pre-Islamic period they were living in villages and thriving towns with markets for trade. Yathrib, later known as Medina, and al-Ṭāʾif were among these towns.

From the settled way of life in these places, and especially from what we know about Medina and al-Ṭāʾif, we can reasonably conclude that private ownership of land was the dominant form in these oases. We know that communal ownership had no real place in towns such as Medina and al-Ṭāʾif.

As for the other oases, where farming was carried out by partly settled tribal populations, the reports do not tell us clearly whether fields and orchards were owned collectively or privately. The fact that whole groups migrated seasonally away from these oases is not enough, by itself, to prove communal ownership.

But we have already said that we are dealing here with a stage in which handicrafts had separated from agriculture. In other words, production for exchange had begun to develop. The logical conclusion is therefore that society had already moved beyond the stage in which people produced only for their own immediate needs—the stage that went together with primitive communal ownership.

Let us return, then, to the one surviving form of this primitive communal system: shared ownership of grazing land, together with the wells and springs connected to it.

Even this last form was now shrinking and moving toward disappearance. Tribal chiefs had begun to own large numbers of camels privately, and they increasingly reserved these communal resources for the use of their own herds. We also have reports showing that some irrigation waters had already become private property.402

Third — The Growth of Inequality in the Distribution of Wealth

This inequality was no longer limited to towns and settled communities. It had become a widespread feature even among the tribes of the desert.

Upper groups were beginning to form around tribal chiefs and their families. They owned large numbers of livestock,403 especially camels, far more than ordinary members of the tribe. At the same time, some members of the tribe owned nothing at all. The same kind of inequality could also be seen at times in the ownership of slaves.

This difference in wealth allowed tribal chiefs to take control of grazing lands and water sources for their own private benefit. They then created a kind of “legal” justification for this control by claiming a right of priority for themselves as a privileged group.404

At this point, inequality was no longer simply a matter of one person owning more personal property than another. The very nature of ownership had changed. What had developed was inequality in the private ownership of the means of production.

Large herds of livestock had become productive assets. Camels, in particular, had acquired the value of commodities. They were used in barter as a standard for measuring the value of other goods and therefore began to perform one of the functions of money.

So when a tribal chief and his close relatives owned large herds, those animals were no longer simply possessions for their own use. Raising them had become a productive activity aimed at exchange. The purpose was to increase income, and as money began to enter local trade, that income increasingly took the form of monetary wealth.

We know that chiefs and their relatives sold livestock beyond what they needed for their own consumption. They sold this surplus in local markets across the Arabian Peninsula, in markets outside Arabia, and along the commercial caravan routes through the desert.

This inequality in private ownership produced unequal standards of living and growing social differences within the tribe itself. The tribe began to divide into rich and poor among its free members, on top of the older division between free people and slaves.

Economic inequality and social division of this kind did not fit the normal workings of the old tribal system. They were therefore clear signs that this system had begun to break down.

The growing distance between the upper and lower groups within the tribe could be seen in many everyday details. Chiefs set up their tents on higher ground overlooking the tents of the rest of the tribe. Their tents were better and more valuable. Their household possessions included expensive rugs and costly metal and glass vessels. They had better weapons and finer saddles for their horses and camels.

A degree of material luxury had entered the lives of the chiefs, while the poor members of the tribe were living in hardship.

The well-known phenomenon of the ṣaʿālīk in this period was a direct result of this economic and social inequality. The ṣaʿālīk were poor men from different tribes who broke away from their tribal communities and lived independently in the desert, supporting themselves through raiding and plunder.

Their break with the tribe expressed two realities that pointed in the same direction.

First, they were rejecting a form of belonging that demanded complete attachment to tribal life and obedience to its rules and customs, however much poverty or oppression they suffered.

Second, their departure reflected a material need that had become unbearable within the tribe itself.

The significance is clear. Social inequality had begun to affect the weaker sections of the tribe so deeply that some of them were driven to break their tribal ties altogether. This was itself another sign that the tribal system was beginning to come apart from within.405

Fourth — Tribal Alliances

The way people made a living was changing. It was moving away from the old primitive communal form and toward a more individual form, because ownership of the means of subsistence and production was also changing.

These economic changes, in turn, changed the social structure of tribal society in pre-Islamic Arabia.

One of the clearest changes appeared in the bonds that held tribal unions together. During the late pre-Islamic period, blood and descent were no longer the only basis for forming these larger groups. Two new kinds of relationship were added: walāʾ, or affiliation, and formal alliance.

Walāʾ meant that “an individual, clan, subclan, or tribe attached itself to another tribe. They became its clients and broke their ties with their former tribe. This was not the same as the walāʾ of slavery or servitude (...) These clients had all the rights enjoyed by members of the tribe.”406

The second kind of relationship was alliance. Two or more tribes could form an alliance because they shared interests, whether immediate or long-term.

One example was the alliance that al-Muṭṭalib arranged between Quraysh and al-Aḥābīsh.407 Another was the alliance between the tribes of ʿĀmila, Judhām and Lakhm. Jawād ʿAlī rightly concludes that this alliance arose “from common interests and similar circumstances that brought them together, as we have seen with other tribes, until with the passing of time it came to be treated as a relationship of descent.”408

There was also a form of alliance in which weaker tribes became attached to stronger ones, until the whole alliance came to be known by the name of its strongest member. Arab chroniclers called this iṭfāʾ. They say, for example, that Ḍabba was “absorbed” when it allied with al-Ribāb, that al-Ḥārith was absorbed when it allied with Madhḥij, and that ʿAbs was also absorbed when it moved to Banū ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa on the day of Jabala.409

Perhaps the description that comes closest to the actual nature of these alliances, and to their historical and social meaning, is the one Herodotus, the Greek historian, gave to the idea of the tribe in the fifth century AD. He said that a tribe was not simply an alliance based on descent or kinship. It was also a political union.410

That is the main point we should draw from the spread of tribal alliances in late pre-Islamic Arabia.

The pure bond of blood and descent was beginning to weaken. The reason was that the old system of primitive communal ownership was breaking down, while private ownership of the means of production in the desert was emerging. This produced growing differences in living standards among members of the same tribe and created new forms of social inequality.

Herodotus, however, could not uncover the economic and social causes behind this kind of “political union.” He therefore treated it as part of the original meaning of the tribe itself. But the tribe had originally been based on blood and descent. Only later did that begin to change.

Fifth — Individual Exchange Rather Than Collective Exchange

The rise of private ownership of livestock among the tribes of late pre-Islamic Arabia also changed the form of exchange in the desert economy.

Exchange was no longer mainly carried out between one tribe and another as two collective units. It increasingly took place between individuals, both within the tribe and outside it.

This new form of exchange clearly shows that the unity of the tribe was beginning to break down. The tribal system had lost its old material foundation: communal ownership.

We do not lack evidence that individual exchange had become the common form during this period. Quite the opposite. What we would now have to search for is evidence that the older form—collective exchange—still survived. Such evidence is absent from the reports we have about this period.

And if this was true of the desert economy, it was even more true of agricultural and craft products. Exchange in these goods belonged to the settled or partly settled economy, which had moved even further away than the nomadic economy from the old communal relations of exchange.

It is true that markets throughout the Arabian Peninsula were supervised by tribal chiefs, especially those who called themselves “kings” in imitation of the Arab kings of al-Ḥīra and the Ghassānids.

The chief of Dūmat al-Jandal, for example, called himself a king. So did the chiefs of Taymāʾ from Banū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zayd. These chiefs began to act like kings by imposing a ten-percent tax411 on merchants using the markets under their control.

But their supervision of these markets did not mean that they conducted trade on behalf of their tribes as a whole. They were not collectively selling the tribe’s production in exchange for goods that would belong to the whole tribe.

This kind of collective exchange no longer existed.

First, there was no longer collective ownership of the tribe’s production.

Second, the chiefs did not supervise the markets in order to organize communal exchange. Their purpose was to create the administrative conditions that allowed them to increase their own private wealth. They collected the ten-percent tax from market traders. They collected tribute from tribes under their control and treated it as part of their personal income. They also charged merchants for allowing caravans to pass through their territories and for providing those caravans with protection.412

Third, these chiefs were themselves merchants. They sent their own goods to markets elsewhere, just as the kings of al-Ḥīra and the wealthy merchants of Mecca did.413

Sixth — The Material Basis of the Tribal Chief’s Authority

During the period we are studying, the authority of a tribal or clan chief414 no longer drew its strength from tribal custom alone.

Increasingly, the chief’s authority depended on his economic position. A man who possessed enough wealth could defeat his rivals and gain influence over members of the tribe by providing material benefits and services that affected their daily lives.

This is why tribal chiefs became increasingly concerned with accumulating wealth by every means available to them.

They expanded their private ownership of the means of production, both in the desert and in settled areas. They increased their commercial activity in markets inside Arabia and beyond it. They collected tribute and taxes imposed by force on tribes, merchants and caravans.

They even used the famous pre-Islamic ideal of generosity to strengthen their authority.

Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī, whose generosity became proverbial, expressed this clearly when he said:

They tell me, “You have squandered your wealth, so show restraint.” But had I not spent as they say, I would never have been a chief.

Nothing shows more clearly how important wealth had become in pre-Islamic society—sometimes more important than traditional tribal considerations—than two historical incidents mentioned by chroniclers and transmitters of reports.

The first concerns Abū Ṭālib, the Prophet’s uncle. Despite his high standing within Quraysh, he lost the offices of rifāda and siqāya—providing food and water to pilgrims—because of his financial weakness.415

The second concerns the conversion to Islam of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī, as related by al-Dhahabī through Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī, Ibn Sīrīn and Abū ʿUbayda ibn Ḥudhayfa.

According to this report, the Prophet said:

“ʿAdī, accept Islam and you will be safe. I know what prevents you from accepting Islam: the poverty you see among those around me, and the fact that you see all the people united against us.”416

He then asked him:

“Have you been to al-Ḥīra?”

ʿAdī replied:

“I have not been there, but I know where it is.”

The Prophet said:

“A woman will soon travel from al-Ḥīra without protection until she circles the House. And the treasures of Kisrā will be opened to us.”

ʿAdī asked:

“Kisrā ibn Hurmuz?”

The Prophet replied:

“Kisrā ibn Hurmuz. And wealth will become so abundant that a man will worry about finding someone willing to accept his money as charity.”417

Earlier in this conversation, the Prophet had already confronted ʿAdī with two other points, but neither had moved him to accept Islam. When the subject of wealth came up in this way, however, ʿAdī later said:

“I have already seen two of these things, and by God, the third will certainly come.”

The text itself explains that by “the third” he meant the abundance of wealth.418

The fact that wealth had acquired this level of importance in pre-Islamic society—an importance that could outweigh Bedouin customs and the respect traditionally given to those customs—could only become a broad social phenomenon in a society where purely Bedouin relations had already begun to lose their dominance.

At the same time, however, we should not look only at the signs of change. There were still many features of the older tribal system.

Nomadic migration remained common. Blood and descent still carried great weight. The whole tribe remained responsible for taking revenge on another tribe for one of its members who had been killed, even if the killing itself had been an individual act carried out for personal reasons.

The same applied to blood money. If a member of one tribe killed a member of another, the first tribe as a whole was still required to pay compensation to the other tribe as a whole, even when both the killing and its cause had been purely personal.

Migration also remained collective. The tribal chief decided when the tribe would move and where it would next settle.

The chief continued to lead the tribe in many matters of peace and in all matters of war, along with many other aspects of Bedouin life.

But these older forms now survived largely through the force of habit and continuity. Little by little, they were losing their economic foundations, and their place within the wider social structure was changing.

C — Western Arabia

1 — The Hijaz... Mecca

So far, we have looked broadly at the Arabian Peninsula during its final pre-Islamic period. But our subject now requires us to turn to the region that had a special historical importance at the time: the region where Arabia’s new historical development was taking shape.

This was what we call Western Arabia, where the Hijaz was located, and within the Hijaz, Mecca itself.

It was here, in particular, that the new history of Arabia was beginning to move.

It was also through this region that Arabia came into contact with the two great centers of the civilized world of the time: the Persian civilization to the east and the Byzantine civilization to the west.

The Hijaz, with Mecca at its center, stood at the meeting point of major international trade routes. These routes carried with them more than goods. They also brought other achievements of human history up to that time, at the beginning of the Middle Ages.

Together with these achievements,419 influences also entered the region from the countries ruled by, or dependent on, the two great empires. Persia and Byzantium were locked in a struggle over control of some of the most important parts of Asia and Africa surrounding the main sea routes, especially the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.

At that time, both empires represented, in their social systems, a historical mixture of two forms of society: slave society and feudal society.

The influences arriving from abroad through the trade routes—together with social, political, cultural and religious influences—interacted actively with the forces of change already developing inside Arab society during the final pre-Islamic period.

It was through this interaction that the new history of Arabia began to take shape.

In this region, at this particular time, we can see a historical process unfolding. Its signs appeared one after another, often overlapping, across economic, social, political, cultural and religious life.

The features we have already examined as signs of the breakdown of primitive tribal society represented only one side of this process: the side of destruction.

We must now look at the other side as well—the side of formation and birth.

A study of the historical conditions of this period allows us to identify the forces driving Arabia in a new historical direction.

We will begin that study with Mecca.

2 — Mecca in Its History

One of the more curious explanations given by Arab chroniclers for the name Mecca is that it comes from the verb imtakka, used of a young camel when it sucks all the milk from its mother’s udder and leaves nothing behind.

From this supposed origin, they explained the name by saying that Mecca “draws people in” or “sucks them toward itself” because it is a sacred city.420

Classical lexicographers adopted similar explanations. They said that makka or imtakka could mean to suck something completely dry, or to diminish it, and that the sacred city was called Mecca because “it diminishes sins, removes them, or destroys anyone who commits injustice there.”421

This kind of explanation is subjective and has no real historical value. Even so, it reflects the special place Mecca held in Arab history before Islam.

Its past was considered ancient, and the chroniclers told many stories about its earliest period. As one scholar puts it, “the chroniclers undoubtedly created stories of this kind because they believed such stories would make the sacred city appear more ancient and would present it as the sanctuary of all the Arabs before Islam.”422

Several centuries before the Arab chroniclers, Ptolemy referred in his Geography to a place called Mocaraba, which has been identified with Mecca.423 He may have been expressing something similar.424

Jawād ʿAlī interprets the word Mocaraba as something like muqarraba, from the idea of drawing near, because Mecca was “a sacred city in which people drew near to the idols with offerings.”425

The name used by Ptolemy does not appear in the works of other classical geographers and historians, apart from later Arab chroniclers.

Even so, this reference by an ancient geographer—one whose work was later relied on by Arab geographers of the Middle Ages—is extremely useful. It gives us evidence that Mecca was known in Ptolemy’s time, in the second century AD.

Before that period, however, we lack reliable evidence that can shed much light on its history.426

All these attempts to explain the name “Mecca” point to one thing: even in its earlier history, the city held a distinctive position in Arabia.

Whether that position originally came from religious importance or from other historical causes, Mecca clearly occupied a central place in the history of the pre-Islamic period that concerns us here.

Our subject is the beginning of a major historical shift: the transformation of the structures on which the old pre-Islamic order rested.

The period that matters most to us is therefore the period in which the signs of this change become visible. It is also the period that is least obscure to the historian, compared with earlier times for which reliable evidence remains scarce.

According to the Arab chroniclers, Quraysh first gained leadership over Mecca under Quṣayy ibn Kilāb. Before him, leadership had belonged to Khuzāʿa. Quṣayy took it from them during the time of ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith, known as Abū Ghubshān al-Khuzāʿī.427

The accounts differ over exactly how Quṣayy gained control, but they agree that it did not happen without conflict. Fighting took place, and Quṣayy eventually defeated Khuzāʿa, either directly in war or after the dispute was referred for judgment to Yaʿmur ibn ʿAwf ibn Kaʿb of Kināna.428

We do not know the exact date of these events.

The chroniclers give us little help except for one clue in a report claiming that Quṣayy bought control of the Kaʿba from Abū Ghubshān al-Khuzāʿī in exchange for a wineskin and a camel. This transaction was said to have given rise to the proverb:

“A worse bargain than the bargain of Abū Ghubshān.”429

The same report says that this happened during the reign of al-Mundhir ibn al-Nuʿmān, king of al-Ḥīra.430

Even though this detail appears within the legendary story of the “bargain,” it gives us an indirect clue about when Quraysh, represented by Quṣayy, first gained leadership over Mecca.

The al-Mundhir ibn al-Nuʿmān mentioned here must be the son of al-Nuʿmān I ibn Imruʾ al-Qays II.

It cannot be the later al-Mundhir ibn al-Nuʿmān of 631–632, “whom the Arabs called al-Gharūr and who was killed in Bahrain on the day of Jawāthā,”431 and who ruled al-Ḥīra for only eight months, “until Khālid ibn al-Walīd arrived in al-Ḥīra.”432 That ruler belonged to the period when Islam had already appeared.

The earlier al-Mundhir succeeded his father al-Nuʿmān I as ruler of al-Ḥīra in AD 418.433

From this indirect evidence, we can conclude that Quraysh gained leadership over Mecca during the first half of the fifth century.

In our view, this conclusion is probably correct. It also gives the events and developments of late pre-Islamic Western Arabia a normal historical logic.

The changes associated with the period of Quraysh’s rule in Mecca could hardly have arisen during the very short period immediately before the appearance of Islam, as the reports of the chroniclers might sometimes suggest.

Historical development requires more time than that.

For the same reason, the role played by Quṣayy himself at the beginning of Quraysh’s leadership in Mecca should not really be seen as the beginning of the process. It was more likely the result of a much longer historical development in which Mecca had already played an important role.

The developments that appeared once Quraysh’s leadership was firmly established under Quṣayy represented a qualitative leap—a major change produced by many smaller changes that had already been building over time.

These earlier changes grew out of an increasingly close relationship between two developments.

On one side was the new division of labor taking shape both in settled communities and in the desert.

On the other was the expansion of commercial middlemen and the growing use of money in exchange across the markets of the Arabian Peninsula.

3 — Developments... and Their Signs

The chroniclers agree that once Quṣayy had secured leadership over Mecca, a number of major changes followed.434

They give us many complicated and sometimes inconsistent details. But beneath those details lies historical material that helps us understand both the changes themselves and the direction in which they were moving.

Once we separate the useful evidence from the surrounding details, several main points emerge.

First — The Social Division of Meccan Society

The chroniclers say that when Quṣayy took control of Quraysh in Mecca, he divided Mecca into residential quarters among his people and assigned each group of Quraysh its place.435

We do not need to accept the chroniclers’ suggestion that Quṣayy simply decided, by his own personal will, to reorganize the city in this way.

What matters to us is the historical meaning of the event.

We see it as the result of objective historical conditions rather than the decision of one individual. A particular process of development had matured to the point where this change became possible at the right time and in the right place.

To understand its historical meaning, however, we first have to understand what the change actually involved.

In practice, it amounted to a social classification of the inhabitants of Mecca from among the clans of Quraysh and their allies.

One group occupied the central parts of Mecca around the Kaʿba. Because they lived in the biṭāḥ, the low-lying central area, they became known as Quraysh al-Biṭāḥ.

A second, lower-ranking group lived on the outskirts of Mecca and became known as Quraysh al-Ẓawāhir.436

But what was this classification based on?

We know that Quraysh al-Ẓawāhir were poor or only partly settled, and that their financial position was weak.437 Quraysh al-Biṭāḥ, by contrast, included “the merchants and the wealthy.”438

So the division was based on financial, economic and social position rather than on tribal custom.

Both groups belonged either to Quraysh itself or to groups allied with Quraysh. One was Quraysh al-Biṭāḥ and the other Quraysh al-Ẓawāhir. Both, in that sense, were part of Quraysh.

If tribal belonging alone had determined the division, all the clans of Quraysh would have occupied the preferred central area, while the allied clans from outside Quraysh would have been placed on the outskirts.

But that was no longer how things worked.

The old tribal values had already begun to weaken, together with the tribal system itself.
