Something had changed.

A new situation was producing new values. Commercial and social development was placing financial and trading position above older tribal considerations.

This is why Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Banū ʿAbd al-Dār came to stand at the front of Quraysh al-Biṭāḥ: they had become wealthier and more powerful in trade.

The same standard continued to operate afterward. The Umayyads eventually took the leading position within pre-Islamic Quraysh because they became its richest merchants and extended their financial influence over many tribes of the Hijaz outside Mecca.

If we go back to the beginning of Quraysh’s leadership—that is, to the period of Quṣayy, which the chroniclers treat as its starting point—we find that Ibn al-Kalbī and Ibn Isḥāq give essentially the same explanation for the transfer of power in Mecca from Khuzāʿa to Quraysh.

They say that when Ḥulayl ibn Ḥubshiyya, chief of Khuzāʿa and father of Ḥubbā, Quṣayy’s wife, died, Abū Ghubshān took over the guardianship of the Kaʿba.

By this time, however, “the descendants of Quṣayy had spread, his wealth had increased, and his standing had grown. Quṣayy therefore believed that he had a stronger claim than Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr to the Kaʿba and to authority over Mecca.”439

Here, even within the traditional account, we can see that the growth of wealth—and the higher social standing that came with it—was treated as a legitimate basis for Quṣayy’s claim to rule over the Kaʿba and Mecca.

The growing wealth of Quraysh increasingly changed the values of tribal society.

New values emerged in which material and economic position became the main point of reference, even though many tribal considerations still survived and continued to influence public life in a secondary way.

Through this process, Mecca moved to the center of the forces breaking down the old economic and social structure of tribal society.

Second — Usury

Engels describes money and usury in Athenian society as forces that brought oppression and loss of freedom to the population.440

He also says that no law threw the debtor at the feet of the moneylender more completely than the laws of the ancient Greeks and Romans.441

Broadly speaking, this description also applies to what was happening in Mecca and the rest of Western Arabia.

Wealth and money had become heavily concentrated in the hands of the leading men of Quraysh. These men were becoming an aristocracy not only within Mecca but within pre-Islamic society more generally.

As their wealth grew, the gap in wealth and social position between the inhabitants of Mecca widened. The difference was even greater when compared with the people of the desert.

The control of this Quraysh aristocracy over weaker groups also became harsher, including its control over small Meccan merchants.

These smaller traders could not compete with the great owners of commercial caravans. To take part in caravan journeys, they often had to borrow money at interest.

The interest charged could be extremely high—sometimes as much as one hundred percent.

The same kind of exploitation affected members of the desert tribes. They borrowed money at heavy rates of interest either to buy provisions before the seasonal markets or to earn a living through trade.

Moneylenders were also strict when demanding repayment of both the original loan and the interest. They gave debtors little time to recover financially.

A common saying of the period was that when a debt came due, the creditor would tell the debtor:

“Either pay, or increase the interest.”442

Usury brought large profits to the Quraysh aristocracy while bringing material hardship to weaker groups in towns, settled communities and the desert alike.

Their hardship was made worse by the taxes and charges imposed by the commercial aristocracy.

Small Arab traders who had no alliance with Quraysh had to pay them. Foreign merchants arriving in Mecca also had to pay them.443 So did caravans traveling from Syria to Yemen or from Yemen to Syria.444

Among these charges was the tithe imposed on Byzantine merchants entering Mecca.445

At the same time, the caravans belonging to this aristocracy had to make payments to the chiefs of the tribes whose territories they crossed, in return for protection along the route.

All these taxes, tolls and payments raised the cost of transported goods.

The burden eventually fell on consumers, agricultural producers, craftsmen and small traders. They had to pay higher prices for imported goods while receiving lower prices for the local products from which they earned their living.446

Meanwhile, the caravans of Mecca’s financial and commercial aristocracy grew until some contained thousands of camels,447 while financial and commercial power became increasingly concentrated in their hands.

Once again, then, we can see how the trade of Quraysh and the activities of its moneylenders accelerated the breakdown already taking place within the tribal society of late pre-Islamic Arabia.

We should add that usury was not limited to the Quraysh aristocracy of Mecca.

There were moneylenders in Yathrib, al-Ṭāʾif, Yemen and other parts of the Arabian Peninsula who lived comfortably from interest without having to work for it.448

Third — The Organization of Commercial Relations

The scale of the commercial activity carried out by the wealthy leaders of Quraysh required forms of trade organization that were highly developed by the standards of pre-Islamic Arabia.

Quraysh acted as commercial middlemen, traded with foreign countries, and operated in markets throughout Arabia.

These arrangements were clearly designed above all to benefit the upper group of Quraysh merchants and the people who dealt with them abroad, whether foreign governments or merchant groups.

Some of these arrangements concerned internal markets. Others concerned trade with foreign countries.

One important internal measure was the organization of seasonal markets, especially during the sacred months.

The timing of these markets was arranged so that trade could take place in peace and security during the months in which fighting was traditionally forbidden.449

The pilgrimage season was one of the greatest sources of profit for Quraysh.

Quraysh sold goods to the Bedouins arriving from the desert and to the inhabitants of villages far from Mecca. In return, they bought the goods and raw materials these visitors brought with them.

Quraysh’s caravans then carried the surplus of what they had bought to foreign markets in Syria and Iraq.

There they purchased the goods and materials needed by the people of the Hijaz and by the Bedouins of the desert.450

These internal arrangements also took other forms. Markets were protected through measures such as mukūs, fees collected from people selling goods there, and through taxes on sales profits. This kind of tax went back to the pre-Islamic period. The government of Qatabān originally collected one tenth of the profit made from buying or selling, but the tax was later extended until it was taken from profits of every kind. The same thing happened with other taxes: they went beyond what was needed for basic regulation and became a heavy burden on consumers, local producers, and small traders.

There were also rules governing many kinds of transactions, including leases, debts, pledges, and agricultural partnerships. Others dealt with property and housing, rights to use grazing land and the waters of rivers and springs, systems of weights, measures, and standards,451 and the handling of trusts, deposits, and written financial documents.452 Local alliances can also be included here, such as the alliance of Banū ʿAbd Manāf known as the Pact of the Perfumed Ones, and the alliances of Banū ʿAbd al-Dār.453

The arrangements governing trade with the outside world seem to have been more highly developed. Their methods were more advanced, and they also helped improve commercial services, expand Arab trade, and push the social changes already under way toward new practical possibilities.

These arrangements can be seen in the kinds of relationships through which the Quraysh aristocracy pursued its commercial and economic interests with countries beyond Arabia. The remarkable success of the Meccan aristocracy as commercial middlemen between Arabia and many different countries—even countries at war with one another, such as Persia and Byzantium—could not have happened by accident. It would have been impossible if trade had simply been left to informal contacts and improvised dealings. Some fairly advanced form of organization, by the standards of the time, must have stood behind it.

It seems clear that long experience and wide foreign contacts gave the Quraysh aristocracy two important advantages. They understood the political struggle between Persia and Byzantium in considerable detail, and they had a keen sense of exactly where they had to position themselves between the two rival powers if they wanted to preserve their commercial interests with both.

This is why modern researchers have generally concluded that the people of Mecca adopted a neutral position between the Sasanians and the Byzantines, and that this neutrality served their interests.454

Reports of their good relations with both the Romans and the Persians also suggest that these relationships were formally organized. It cannot have been a matter of chance, for example, that:

“The caravans travelling from Arabia to Syria would stop at particular markets assigned to them by the Roman government, so that it could collect the taxes imposed on ‘exports’ and keep watch over foreigners entering its territories. When these caravans first entered Roman territory, they stopped at Ayla, today known as Aqaba. From there they travelled to Gaza, where they came into contact with Mediterranean merchants. Some traders then continued from Gaza to Buṣrā.”455

Arrangements this specific must have resulted from “official” agreements between the owners of these caravans, or representatives of the Quraysh leadership acting on their behalf, and the Roman government or its representatives in Syria and Palestine.

The motive behind such agreements was probably not limited to the desire for mutual commercial benefit. As the passage just quoted suggests, the Roman, or Byzantine, government also wanted to monitor the movements of Arab merchants in the territories it controlled near the Arabian Peninsula. This concern may have come from Byzantine doubts about whether the Meccan leadership was truly neutral in the political struggle between Byzantium and the Sasanians.

O’Leary supports this possibility. He does not rule out the idea that some of the Roman merchants living in Mecca—and the traditional historians tell us that some Roman traders did live there456—may have spied on the Arabs for the Byzantines, reporting on Arab relations with Persia and on Persian contacts with the people of the peninsula.457

In any case, there is little doubt that commercial relations between the Quraysh aristocracy and the Byzantines were governed by agreements with certain conditions and limits. The same was true of its relations with Persia458 and Abyssinia.

One well-known report says that Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf concluded a treaty with the Roman Empire, that ʿAbd Shams ibn ʿAbd Manāf concluded a commercial treaty with the Negus of Abyssinia, and that Nawfal and al-Muṭṭalib, the sons of ʿAbd Manāf, made an alliance with Persia.459

The traditional historians also preserve a number of accounts of the Quraysh īlāf mentioned in the Qurʾān.460 Their most common explanation is that Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf established the īlāf and was the first to introduce it:

“He obtained guarantees of protection (ʿiṣam)461 from the kings of Syria, and so they traded in safety. Then his brother ʿAbd Shams obtained guarantees for them—that is, for Quraysh—from the ruler of Abyssinia, where he himself traded. Al-Muṭṭalib ibn ʿAbd Manāf obtained guarantees for them from the kings of Yemen. And Nawfal ibn ʿAbd Manāf obtained guarantees for them from the kings of Iraq. They thus established the two journeys: in winter to Yemen, Abyssinia, and Iraq, and in summer to Syria.”462

Almost all historians accept this explanation.

It clearly shows that the ʿiṣam obtained by Banū ʿAbd Manāf from governments in and around the Hijaz took the form of treaties. The figurative meaning of the word ʿiṣam itself supports this, since it can mean a covenant or pledge.

The same explanation, and the fact that historians generally accept it, also shows how far the Quraysh aristocracy—represented by Banū ʿAbd Manāf—had come to dominate trade in western Arabia during the second half of the fifth century CE.

Hāshim’s assumption of responsibility for providing water and food to pilgrims is associated with the year 464 CE.463 By then, Banū ʿAbd Manāf had enough power to conclude treaties and organize the region’s relations with foreign powers at the level of kings and rulers, according to what best served their commercial interests and social privileges.

Pre-Islamic poetry also gives us evidence for two points. First, it supports the interpretation of ʿiṣam as a covenant or treaty. Second, it confirms the economic and social dominance of Banū ʿAbd Manāf within Quraysh and Meccan society.

One example is the following poem by Maṭrūd ibn Kaʿb al-Khuzāʿī:464

O man who is moving on with all his baggage, why did you not stay with the house of ʿAbd Manāf?

May your mother lose you! Had you stayed with them, they would have protected you from hunger and hardship.465

They are the ones who secure covenants from distant lands, and who set out on the journeys of the īlāf.

Al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥanash al-Sulamī, Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf’s maternal brother, says:466

My brother Hāshim is no ordinary brother. By God, Hāshim is neither lacking nor idle.

Goodness is wrapped around him, and the grave-digger digs for him; he secures the pact and travels on behalf of those who stay behind.

The advanced way in which the Meccan aristocracy organized its commercial relations with the outside world had major economic and social effects on the lives of the people of the Hijaz, in both towns and desert communities.

First, it created stable arrangements for these commercial relations instead of leaving them to chance or to shifts in political conditions.

Second, it opened wide new areas for imports, exports, and the role of Arab traders as middlemen between eastern and western trade.

Third, it was a major factor in spreading the use of money throughout tribal society. Meccan merchants dealt in the different currencies used in the foreign countries with which they traded. As we said earlier, this brought into tribal society one of the most important forces speeding up its breakdown and dissolution.

Fourth, it drew large numbers of people from both towns and the desert into commercial activity. Some helped finance caravans at different levels. Many others worked as caravan guides or guards, or provided essential services at stopping points along overland routes and at seaports. Others traded consumer goods with the caravans and developed small-scale trade between tribes.

Tribal chiefs also received tolls, taxes, and valuable gifts in exchange for protecting caravans. They then invested their earnings in large commercial ventures. This widened the economic and social gap between the chiefs and ordinary members of their tribes, and made social inequality an increasingly powerful force in breaking down the tribal system.

Fourth — Organization of “Political” Authority

The economic and social changes described above made another development necessary. They created the material basis for a form of political organization suited to those changes—an organization capable of containing them and protecting the gains they had produced.

That material basis was private ownership of the means of production, together with the use of money to exploit others by controlling the labour of people who owned no property.

As we saw earlier in our discussion of pre-Islamic society, this basis appeared in several forms: ownership of slaves as a means of production, ownership of agricultural land, and ownership of money invested in trade and in lending at interest.

We also saw that economic development on this basis had already begun to break down the structure of the old tribal system. It created inequalities among members of society in living standards, in the distribution of wealth and products, and also in individual rights and social position—even among members of the same tribe or clan. In doing so, it began to move beyond the traditional rules of tribal life.

Put another way, pre-Islamic society was beginning to divide into groups whose economic interests came into conflict with those of other groups. In other words, it was moving toward the beginnings of class division.

These economic and social inequalities had already begun to produce early forms of social breakdown and rebellion, visible in groups such as the outlaws and expelled men.467 This was a sign that inequality was beginning to turn into genuine social conflict, laying the foundation for a division of society into classes, even if that division was still only at an early stage.

It was natural for the first signs of this process to appear in Mecca before they appeared in the desert.

Before this change, Quraysh had not been fundamentally different from the people of the desert in the structure of their tribal life. They were a clan like other Arab clans of the pre-Islamic period. Kinship and descent governed both their internal relations and their relations with other clans and tribes.468

But the economic forces we discussed earlier developed in Mecca’s commercial society before they developed in the desert. It was therefore natural that the old Bedouin system of tribal relations should begin to break down in Mecca first.

The breakdown of that system in Mecca also helped prepare the conditions for its later breakdown in the desert. This followed from Mecca’s commercial, economic, and religious importance, not only in western Arabia but throughout the peninsula, and from the influence that this position gave it over tribal relations across the region.

This influence was closely tied to the control exercised by the Quraysh leadership over economic activity in many parts of the peninsula.

As the old system of primitive communal relations broke down, some new form of social relationship had to take its place.

We have already seen the main economic and social foundations of this new form. Commercial and financial wealth was becoming concentrated in the hands of a section of Quraysh in Mecca and of tribal chiefs in the desert. The same was true of ownership of the means of production: slaves, livestock, rights to use irrigation water and grazing land, and the richest productive land around Ṭāʾif.

The economic dominance of the Quraysh aristocracy therefore had to produce its own “political” institution. Such an institution was needed to organize the relationship of power between this ruling group and the other social groups it exploited economically. It also had to give that relationship a legal form suited to the historical conditions of the time, and to impose its “legitimacy” on those same groups. They were now expected to submit politically to the “ruling” Quraysh aristocracy just as they already submitted to it economically.

The Meccan malaʾ, or council of notables,469 was the first expression of Quraysh dominance in a form that we could describe, in modern language, as “political.”

At that stage, the malaʾ represented the earliest embryo of a state: the political institution of the class that dominates economic activity in a class society.

At the same time, it represented the birth of that class itself within pre-Islamic society.

Historically, the Meccan malaʾ was made up of the city’s leading merchants, moneylenders, and slave owners. It concentrated all forms of authority in a single body—the malaʾ itself.

This body strengthened its authority with a force of repression, as reports about the Aḥābīsh of Mecca suggest.470 From these reports, we understand that the malaʾ used the Aḥābīsh as armed police. They guarded the Kaaba and also the homes of members of the malaʾ.

This use of guards is important for our argument.

Establishing armed guards around the Kaaba did not simply mean protecting its religious sanctity. It also meant protecting the wealth of Quraysh, who had taken advantage of that sanctity by using the Kaaba as a place to store their money.471

Likewise, guards posted around their homes were meant to protect them from “the anger of the discontented groups in the city of Mecca and the resentment of poor pilgrims.”472

The rise of the malaʾ as a form of “political” authority representing the group that controlled wealth and exploited others appears to have been historically connected with the rise of the Quraysh commercial aristocracy.

We have no sources or documents showing that a body with this economic and social character existed before the Quraysh aristocracy took control of Mecca and assumed responsibility for the Kaaba.

Everything we know about the leadership of Mecca and the custodianship of the Kaaba before Quraysh suggests that these roles were limited to supervising the pilgrimage and leading pilgrims as they performed the pre-Islamic rituals during the pilgrimage season.

Leadership rested on a purely tribal basis. A tribe or clan might gain precedence because it possessed some form of tribal honour recognized by pre-Islamic custom, or because it had defeated another group in intertribal warfare.

The traditional accounts of Mecca before Islam tell us that the custodianship of the Kaaba and the leadership of Mecca passed successively through the South Arabian tribe of Jurhum, then the tribes of Quḍāʿa, and finally Quraysh.

Jurhum established itself in Mecca by the second method—that is, through military victory.473 Even during the period of Khuzāʿa, Jurhum retained some part in the administration of pilgrimage. A group called Ṣūfa, belonging to Jurhum, had the authority to give pilgrims permission to leave ʿArafāt for Minā and to begin the stoning of the pillars.474

This lasted until the rule of Khuzāʿa ended and control of Mecca passed fully to Quraysh.

Before the rise of Quraysh, then, the custodianship of the Kaaba and the leadership of Mecca rested on traditional tribal foundations.

But things changed greatly when Quraysh came to power.

It is true that the traditional accounts describe fighting between Quṣayy, his people, and his allies on one side, and first the Jurhumite elite and then Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr on the other. In that sense, Quraysh under Quṣayy reached power by the same route as those before them: through fighting.

But the important question is not the fighting itself.

What matters is Quṣayy’s claim that he had a greater right to rule, and the way the traditional historians explain that claim.

The Arabic sources usually rely on Ibn al-Kalbī when telling the story of this historical change, while some use the account of Ibn Isḥāq. There is no real contradiction between the two versions. They differ mainly in one respect.

The first explains the basis on which Quṣayy claimed a greater right to control the Kaaba and rule Mecca. The second concentrates more on the details of the story and its outcome.

If we put the explanation together with the outcome, along with the details common to both accounts, the real meaning of this historical change becomes much clearer.

We have already referred to the explanation. The reports say of Quṣayy:

“…when Ḥulayl ibn Ḥubshiyya of Khuzāʿa died, and Quṣayy’s children had become numerous, his wealth had grown, and his honour had become great, he saw that he had a greater right to the House and to the affairs of Mecca…”475

The wording suggests that Quṣayy’s claim rested above all on the fact that he had become wealthy.

Having many children by itself was not enough to establish such a right. And the “great honour” mentioned in the report appears to have been something he acquired at a particular point in his life. The wording makes this clear. It was therefore not the inherited honour that had traditionally counted in tribal society. It was a new kind of honour gained through Quṣayy’s success in acquiring money and wealth.

The accounts of what Quṣayy did in old age support this interpretation.

They say that he transferred his authority to his eldest son, ʿAbd al-Dār:

“When Quṣayy became old and weak, ʿAbd al-Dār was his eldest son (888), while ʿAbd Manāf had gained greater honour during his brother’s lifetime (…) Quṣayy said to ʿAbd al-Dār: ‘By God, I will raise you to the level of the others, even though they have gained more honour than you…’”476

These texts make it clear that “honour” here means success in acquiring wealth.

As for the outcome, which interests Ibn Isḥāq more than the explanation, his account says after giving the details:

“…Quṣayy took charge of the House and the affairs of Mecca. He gathered his people from their settlements and brought them into Mecca. He became ruler over his people, the inhabitants of Mecca, and they accepted his rule. Quṣayy was therefore the first descendant of Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy to gain a kingship that his people obeyed. He held responsibility for the custodianship of the Kaaba, the provision of water and food to pilgrims, the assembly, and the war banner.477 In this way he gained all the honours of Mecca. He divided Mecca into quarters among his people and settled each group of Quraysh in the part of the city that later remained associated with them.”478

From all this, we can see that the transfer of Meccan leadership to Quraysh did not rest on an established tribal custom, nor was military victory the main principle used to justify it.

Its real basis was something new.

Economic and social development had given wealth a new kind of power. Money had begun to shape the logic of events, change the standards by which people were judged, and influence the direction of the new social reality that was taking form.

The earlier reports also describe a judgment issued by a man chosen to arbitrate between Quṣayy’s side and the opposing side of Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr, after heavy fighting had finally led them to seek peace.

The reports say that Yaʿmur ibn ʿAwf ibn Kaʿb gave the following judgment:

“Quṣayy has a greater right to the Kaaba and the affairs of Mecca than Khuzāʿa. Any blood shed by Quṣayy among Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr is cancelled,479 and he may cast it beneath his feet.480 But for any blood shed by Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr among Quraysh and Banū Kināna, the blood-money must be paid. And the way must be cleared for Quṣayy ibn Kilāb to take control of the Kaaba and Mecca.”

The reports add:

“From that day Yaʿmur ibn ʿAwf was called al-Sharrākh because of the blood claims he laid out and waived.”481

This is certainly a strange judgment. It immediately attracts attention.

But it also tells us that the new factor that objectively gave Quṣayy priority over those who had ruled the Kaaba and Mecca before him was also behind the striking form of Yaʿmur ibn ʿAwf’s decision.

Why did Quṣayy have a greater right to the Kaaba and the government of Mecca than Khuzāʿa?

Why was the blood Quṣayy had shed among Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr simply cancelled, with no punishment and no blood-money, while Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr were required to pay compensation for the blood they had shed among Quraysh and Kināna?

If such a harsh judgment had fitted comfortably within the tribal customs and traditions of pre-Islamic Arabia, it would not have attracted enough attention for people to give its author the name al-Sharrākh because of the blood claims his decision had swept aside and placed “beneath the feet” of Quṣayy without any apparent justification.

Does that mean the ruling was completely arbitrary?

We would say no.

Its outward form may look arbitrary, but its underlying content had a real historical logic that “justified” it.

The same economic development that gave Quṣayy “all the honour of Mecca” also provided the real historical logic behind a judgment of this kind.

And it was this same new logic that all the opposing sides accepted when they submitted to the judgment of al-Sharrākh without protest.

The Nadwa, or Assembly, and the malaʾ gave this same historical reality a concrete human and organizational form.

The Nadwa was the meeting place of the malaʾ in Quṣayy’s house. It served the newly born “class” created by the breakdown of the old primitive tribal order, and it served the embryonic “institution” emerging from the same conditions. The new class needed a new system of its own, and that system needed authority and institutions suited to its historical position.

The traditional historians have given us more than enough information about this Nadwa to form a clear picture of it.

They say that Quṣayy:

“Built the Assembly House and placed its door facing the House—that is, the Kaaba. All the affairs of Quraysh were conducted there: anything concerning marriage contracts, war, or consultation among themselves. Even when a girl reached the age when she began wearing a full garment, that garment was first cut for her there,482 and she was then taken back to her family.

“No war banner for Quraysh, or for any people allied with them, was raised anywhere except in the Assembly House. No boy was circumcised483 except there. No Quraysh caravan484 departed without setting out from there, and when they returned they stopped there first. (…) It was called the Nadwa because Quraysh used to gather there, for matters good and bad alike.”485

This account appears, with only small differences in wording, throughout the traditional sources.

As a representative example of the others, it shows that the Meccan malaʾ turned the Nadwa into a broad and almost absolute authority.

Even the private affairs of Mecca’s inhabitants came under its supervision, along with public affairs in both peace and war.

It dealt especially with contracts, transactions, and everything connected with economic and social life, as well as the affairs of religious festivals and pilgrimage seasons.

The Nadwa, acting in the name of the malaʾ, therefore exercised powers resembling legislative, executive, judicial, and administrative authority, all concentrated in a single body: the malaʾ, the upper stratum of Quraysh, or in other words the commercial aristocracy of Mecca.

As another sign that authority was restricted to this privileged group, the malaʾ limited admission to the Assembly House to members of Quraysh who had reached the age of forty.

The descendants of Quṣayy were the exception. All of them were allowed to enter, even before the age of forty. This was a privilege of those who held power.486

The traditional historians also say that when Quṣayy became old, he transferred responsibility for the Nadwa, the custodianship of the Kaaba, the provision of water and food to pilgrims, and the war banner to his eldest son ʿAbd al-Dār. This is the version given in al-Balādhurī’s Ansāb487 and Ibn Saʿd’s Ṭabaqāt.488

Al-Yaʿqūbī says that Quṣayy gave him the Nadwa alone,489 while al-Azraqī says that he gave him the Nadwa, the custodianship of the Kaaba, and the war banner.490

The accounts differ in detail, but all agree that the Nadwa was given to ʿAbd al-Dār.

What can we learn from this?

In our view, it points to two things.

First, the Nadwa had the character of a public institution. Responsibility for it was treated in the same way as responsibility for the formal duties connected with the Kaaba and the pilgrimage—the custodianship of the sanctuary, the provision of water and food—and with the war banner.

Second, every account agrees that Quṣayy specially favoured ʿAbd al-Dār by giving him control of the Nadwa. Quṣayy’s own stated aim was to raise him to the level of those who had gained greater honour than he had.

This suggests that the Nadwa had a special importance beyond the other public offices. Giving it to ʿAbd al-Dār was meant to raise his status and allow him to match the honour of his brother ʿAbd Manāf.

We have already seen that ʿAbd Manāf’s “honour” was his practical success in acquiring money and wealth.

This means that the Nadwa, precisely because it was a centre of Quraysh economic power, was important enough to offer ʿAbd al-Dār another path to an honour equal to that of ʿAbd Manāf.

The Nadwa and the malaʾ therefore appeared in Mecca together as an expression of Quraysh’s economic dominance in the form of political authority.

At this stage of pre-Islamic history, they showed that economic development in this part of Arabia now contained the beginnings of a “contradiction” between two sets of social forces.

On one side were the groups that controlled this economic development. On the other were the groups whose work objectively formed the internal mechanism that actually produced it.

The authority of the malaʾ and the Nadwa was the embryo of this contradiction.

It was the embryo of a state belonging to merchants, moneylenders, and those who exploited the other free producers: farmers, craftspeople, and livestock breeders.

The appearance of this embryonic form of the state also shows how historical breaks and historical continuity can form part of the same process.

Even in this early form, the state did not suddenly appear from nothing during the final stage of the pre-Islamic period. States had existed at earlier stages of Arabian history.

But the laws governing social change, like the laws governing change in nature, do not move along one unbroken line.

A break in that line does not come from outside the historical process. It is itself part of the way that process moves.

We discussed this point at the beginning of the chapter, so there is no need to repeat the argument here. It is enough to remove one possible misunderstanding.

When we speak here of the appearance of an early political authority representing an embryonic form of the state, we are not assuming that Arabia had never known other forms of the state before this period. In this same chapter, we have already referred to several Arab states that had existed earlier.

There is no contradiction between the two points once we understand the dialectical unity of historical breaks and historical continuity.

As for the historical causes behind the break that took place in the course of Arabian development, the documents and evidence available to us can help explain them, but they are still not sufficient for a complete explanation.

D — Arab Cultural Features in the Pre-Islamic Period

1 — Between Pre-Islamic Society and Its Culture

The relationship between social existence and social consciousness—that is, thought—is objective and universal.

It does not operate one way among some peoples or societies and another way among others.

What we mean is that material existence, in all its different forms, necessarily leaves its mark on human consciousness: on every human being, in every time and place.

The general laws that govern the history of social existence are the same in every society, just as the general laws governing the history of the natural world are the same everywhere.

What differs from one people or society to another is the concrete form these general laws take in a particular society and at a particular stage of history.

The forms of social relations are fundamental here.

The reflection of social existence in social consciousness is itself one of these general laws. There are no exceptions to it.

But the specific form this reflection takes is determined by the specific forms of social relations.

This general law therefore applies fully to the social consciousness of pre-Islamic Arabs.

Like the consciousness of every human society in every period, their consciousness necessarily reflected the reality of social activity as it existed in the different urban and Bedouin communities of the Arabian Peninsula during the historical periods we call the pre-Islamic age.

The way this objective process appeared in the consciousness of those societies is what we mean by the cultural features of pre-Islamic Arabia.

These features were forms of knowledge. They arose when the outside world—nature and society—was reflected in the consciousness of our ancestors and those reflections became forms of human understanding.

But this does not mean that their knowledge was complete or that it fully matched the realities of the world.

In fact, we should expect the opposite.

Knowledge is a complex process. Society and human consciousness must develop over a long historical period before human knowledge can come closer to the absolute truths of the world.

The cultural features of pre-Islamic Arabia were therefore made up of what the Arabs of that period knew about the world around them: the world that affected them and that they, in turn, affected; the world whose particular conditions shaped their lives and also existed within their consciousness in those same historical forms.

There is only one kind of correspondence that is always necessary here: the level reached by consciousness must correspond to the level reached by the social structure under the same historical conditions.

But in our case, we must take account of a historical fact that seems to challenge even this form of correspondence.

As we said earlier, the cultural forms we know from the last stage of the pre-Islamic period, immediately before Islam, had developed to a higher level than the social relations of that same period.

Does this mean that the law of reflection had somehow been broken?

To answer that question, we need to explain why the two levels had become so different.

The answer lies in the relative historical break between the older stages of pre-Islamic Arab history and its final stage.

That break created a gap between cultural forms and the social structure of the later period. The difference became so large that cultural forms could almost appear completely independent of the social structure on which their existence depended.

How, then, can we explain this?

How could a historical break affect the social structure in a way that it did not affect the cultural forms that this same structure had produced, even though the two remained objectively connected through the process of reflection?

A scientific explanation requires us to understand reflection dialectically, not mechanically.

Put another way, we must understand the changing relationship between the material and the spiritual, between the world and our knowledge of the world.

It is true that knowledge is a reflection of the world in human consciousness.

But that reflection does not happen as simply as an object or a person appears in a mirror.

Knowledge develops through a complex process with its own internal workings. It has a movement of its own that is relatively independent of the movement of the material world from which the original reflection comes.

That is the first point.

A second point follows from it.

Because knowledge is complex, internally structured, and relatively independent of the social structure on which its existence depends, it also tends to move more slowly.

It has a historical pace of its own. Its time does not simply match the external time of social reality itself.

For this reason, knowledge may not take shape in the cultural forms associated with a particular social structure until long after that social structure itself has developed.

This is why cultural forms generally show a certain degree of stability and continuity.

Fundamental changes in society—historical breaks or leaps from one social structure to another—do not immediately transform cultural forms.

Those forms can continue for some time to develop according to their older internal pattern even after the underlying social structure has changed.

Every major break in a particular historical process begins directly in the material and economic foundation of the social structure.

The continuing movement of history then takes a new form.

That may produce an upward qualitative leap, or it may produce a sharp downward turn that blocks the objective forces pushing development forward.

Such a blockage can itself result from objective forces that come from outside the internal conditions producing development.

One example is the Abyssinian invasion of Yemen.

This took place at a time when historical conditions were developing that could have produced a qualitative change in the basic structure of social relations, beginning in the south of the Arabian Peninsula and spreading its effects northward.

But the disruption caused by this foreign invasion interrupted those conditions.

It damaged the material foundations on which further development depended—the collapse of the Maʾrib Dam and the ruin of agriculture are examples—and it therefore blocked conditions that might otherwise have produced a very different kind of historical break: a positive qualitative leap in the continuing development of Arab history at a stage close to the rise of Islam.

This negative and restrictive break greatly widened the distance between two points on the same line of social development.

The first was the rising point reached during the periods of the Minaean, Sabaean, Qatabānian, and Himyarite states.

The second was the lower point represented by the final pre-Islamic period.

But we should stress again that the distance between these two points still belonged to the continuous course of Arab history across the different stages of the pre-Islamic age.

2 — Different in Form, Corresponding in Content

This, then, is our scientific explanation for the difference between two levels that would normally be expected to correspond objectively: the level of the social structure in the final pre-Islamic period, and the level of the cultural forms produced by that structure according to the dialectical law of reflection.

But there is a possible misunderstanding that we should clear up.

We are not saying that there was no correspondence at all between the culture of the final pre-Islamic period and the social structure of that period.

The difference we are describing concerns form only: the linguistic and expressive forms of pre-Islamic culture.

We are not saying that the content of that culture failed to correspond to the society that produced it.

Likewise, when we spoke a little earlier about stability and continuity, we meant cultural forms in particular. The same claim cannot simply be extended to their content.

The issue comes back to the general relationship between form and content.

However closely the form and content of a thing are connected, each still has characteristics of its own.

One of these differences is that form is the more conservative side of a thing, while content responds more quickly to forces of change.

The reason is that a genuine qualitative change affects the essence of the thing.

If content determines that essence, then the process of change naturally begins with the content.

The form, however, can continue to preserve its older shape until the conflict between the old form and the new content reaches a point where it can no longer continue.

At that stage the contradiction is resolved by bringing form and content back into correspondence, but now on the side of the new development—that is, on the side of the qualitative change that has taken place.

We can apply this principle directly to the historical reality we are discussing: the particular relationship between the forms and the content of pre-Islamic Arab culture.

Alongside the clear lack of correspondence between the forms of that culture and the social structure it expressed, there was a real correspondence between the content of the culture of the final pre-Islamic period and the social structure of that period.

The Russian Arabist Krachkovsky was right to identify this correspondence in the most important cultural form from the pre-Islamic period that continued into the age of Islam: poetry.

He wrote that pre-Islamic poetry gives a faithful and accurate picture of the main features of Arab tribal life and of the environment in which that poetry arose. For this reason, reliable specialists consider it the most trustworthy source for understanding the conditions, customs, and traditions of the Arabs during that period.491

3 — Defining the Cultural Features of the Pre-Islamic Period

This same “historical reality” will also guide us as we look in greater detail at Arab culture during one of the firmly established stages in the history of its earliest development.

To take a realistic approach here means seeing these cultural features in their historical movement—that is, seeing them in relation to the movement of Arab history during the final pre-Islamic period.

That period matters because important changes were building up within it.

A growing number of quantitative changes were pointing toward a qualitative break with the structure of the old primitive tribal system.

The cultural features we are about to examine reflected the character of this historical period with a striking simplicity and directness.

This is the basis on which we will now build our more detailed account.

First — The Linguistic Feature

When we describe language as a cultural feature, we do not mean that language, simply as language, is itself a complete cultural structure.

Language does not form an independent cultural entity in the way that poetry does on one side or philosophical thought does on another.

In that sense, language is more like the “raw material” needed to construct a building or manufacture a product.

But language differs from ordinary raw material in one very important respect.

Language has a life of its own because it is directly connected with human life—that is, with human social activity.

In this sense, language shares some characteristics with the living human beings who use it.

It has the capacity to grow and develop as the people who speak it grow and develop through the different forms of human activity in which they take part.

For this reason, reading the language of a particular people also gives us a way of measuring aspects of their life at different stages of development.

It shows us the images of the physical things they choose or create as tools in their daily shared activities, across every kind of human activity, productive or otherwise.

It is only in this sense that we can speak of language as a cultural feature.

Language is the living material needed to create any cultural structure or cultural entity.

But there is an important difference between language and those forms of human consciousness that themselves form cultural structures or forms of knowledge.

When such forms of consciousness reflect the social activity of a particular human community, they do so through a complex mental process with its own complicated movement.

Through this process, thought creates another kind of reality: an abstract mental reality.

There is a distance between this mental reality and material or social reality.

It is the distance between a thing as it exists and moves directly in the world, and that same thing after it has been transformed into knowledge through an indirect and complex movement of thought—one whose internal workings have a degree of independence of their own.

Language does not work in the same way.

There is no comparable distance between language and the things it refers to, except the simple distance between a thing and the direct symbol used to point to it, identify it, and distinguish it from other things.

The relationship between language and the things of the real world, and between language and human activity, is therefore simple and direct.

Language does not have the same independence of movement—not even the relative independence found in other forms of thought.

For this reason, language by itself carries no ideological meaning through its vocabulary or grammatical system.

It therefore carries no class meaning of its own either.

Within a given society, language is a natural tool available equally to every ideology and every class.

It is the common tool of all the people belonging to a particular society or people, both in matters they share and in matters on which they differ.

The reason is that language does not itself reflect the social relations in which class and group conflicts are contained.

Instead, it directly reflects people’s everyday activity in the broad areas of life they share—areas in which individuals from every class and every social group meet and communicate with one another through the same language.

This is also the source of the historical character of language.

It comes from this direct and simple relationship across the shared life of society, a relationship that continues throughout the society’s history even as one social structure gives way to another.

Language therefore carries the unity of that history through the continuing unity of the language itself, despite all the breaks, contradictions, and conflicts contained within the history.

For the same reason, when studying language in a subject such as ours, we must see it as organically connected with the history of the society to which it belongs.

And this same connection necessarily links language to the culture of that society.

Its culture is, first, a product of its history.

Its language is, second, the means through which that cultural product is expressed.

Given this view of language, a realistic picture of Arab culture in the late pre-Islamic period must also show the living relationship between language, culture, and the history of pre-Islamic society as a whole.

We will therefore proceed along two paths, the first serving as an introduction to the second.

First, we need a historical picture of the Arabic language as it existed in the late pre-Islamic period: the language people used to express their thoughts and feelings, and to give cultural form to their lives and activities. This was also the language in which the Qur’an was expressed, at the highest level of classical Arabic style.

Second, we need some idea of how closely the life of this language was connected to the life of the people who spoke it during the same period.

The road to a complete historical picture is a long one. It is full of unresolved problems and points that are still unclear. Following that road from the beginning all the way to the period we are studying would require a separate specialist study. So here we will take a shorter route and concentrate on the points most directly connected to our subject.

What matters to us first in the history of Arabic before Islam is the stage at which it emerged from a poorly documented earlier history. Historians and linguists have disagreed over how that earlier stage should be connected with the various “Semitic” languages, or with the languages spoken to the north and south of the Arabian Peninsula.

What concerns us is the point at which Arabic acquired an independent history of its own, both as a spoken language and as a written one. By the sixth century CE, we find it in the pre-Islamic poetry known to us and in other cultural forms attributed to that period. By the seventh century, we find it in the language of the Qur’an. And from the first Islamic century onward, we find it recorded in Islamic texts.

This is the important stage we want historical and linguistic research to help illuminate. Our present study does not need to go further back than this in the history of pre-Islamic Arabia.

We can begin by defining the language we are talking about. It is the language of the northern Arabs: the language they used to communicate with one another and, through its words and structures, to express their thoughts, feelings, and ways of life. This was the foundation of the language that later became the language of the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage, and it is the foundation of the Arabic we speak today.

Where did this language of the northern Arabs come from, both as a language of everyday communication and as a language of literature and culture? Where did its alphabet and its particular system of writing come from? And what form had it reached during the final period before the rise of Islam?

The accounts of the early Arab chroniclers cannot provide a scientific answer. First, they are full of confusion and contradiction.492 Second, many of them have a legendary or supernatural character.

For a sound judgment on a question like this, we need written documents or inscriptions that actually belong to the historical period under study.

Do we possess enough such evidence to reach a firm conclusion?

Archaeological and linguistic research agrees that inscriptions have been found in Syria and the surrounding region written in the Nabataean script, from which Arabic script developed. Specialists conclude from these inscriptions that the northern Arabs knew alphabetic writing by the fourth century CE.493

They also have little doubt that the language of the Nabataeans was a northern Arabic dialect. One piece of evidence is that many words found in Nabataean inscriptions are purely Arabic, such as qabr, “grave.” In some inscriptions, researchers have even noted that almost the entire wording is Arabic.494

Most of these Nabataean inscriptions have been found at al-Ḥijr, Petra, the Ḥawrān region, and Sinai.495

Some researchers strengthen this argument further.496 They maintain that the Arabs of the Hijaz used Nabataean writing in trade, and that between the end of the third century and the beginning of the fourth century CE they spread this form of writing through other parts of Arabia. As evidence, they point to two well-known texts: the Umm al-Jimāl inscription497 and the al-ʿUlā inscription,498 dated to 306 or 307.

According to this view, Nabataean writing then developed rapidly in the Hijaz because both trade and religious activity were developing rapidly there. Its use in these two areas gradually gave it a distinctly Arabic character, which had become clearly visible by the beginning of the fifth century CE.

The early Arab chroniclers gave a different account. They traced the origin of Arabic writing in the Hijaz to al-Ḥīra or al-Anbār, and they recorded many stories on the subject.499 But although these reports are common in their works, we have no historical evidence that proves them. At the same time, we have no historical evidence that decisively disproves them either.

Ibn Qutayba tried to combine the two views by saying that the people of Mecca learned writing from both the Nabataeans and the people of al-Ḥīra.500

But this does not really solve the problem. No one disputes that the people of Mecca had contact with both. The real question is different: which form of writing gave rise to the script used by the northern Arabs before Islam and to the Arabic script that later became dominant after Islam?

Because this is a historical question, it can be settled scientifically only through decisive historical evidence. In this case, that means pre-Islamic writings from al-Ḥīra, al-Anbār, or the Nabataean regions. Only evidence of this kind can establish the origin of both the script and the written language used by the northern Arabs before Islam.

Jawād ʿAlī followed this same path in his research on the subject. His investigation concludes that no pre-Islamic written text from al-Ḥīra or al-Anbār has yet been found. In fact, we do not possess a pre-Islamic written text belonging to any Arab from Iraq.

This is despite the many reports stating that writing was widespread among the Arabs of al-Ḥīra shortly before Islam, and that many people in the Hijaz knew this form of writing, learned it, and taught it to others.

By contrast, the investigation concludes that the only written material from the pre-Islamic period that has actually reached us comes originally from Syria and the surrounding region.

These writings alone, Jawād ʿAlī says, are in our possession. They allow us to say that their authors were Arabs, that their Arabic was close to the Arabic of the Qur’an, and that they wrote in a script different from the South Arabian musnad script.501

Their script, he argues, was derived from the script of the Aramaeans. Their culture was also strongly influenced by Nabataean culture because they lived close to the Nabataeans and had extensive contact and interaction with them.502

But even this surviving evidence consists of no more than five texts.

The earliest dates to 250 CE. It is the text mentioned earlier under the name “Umm al-Jimāl.” It was found on the tombstone of “Fihr ibn Shalī [or Salī], tutor of Jadhīma, king of Tanūkh,”503 together with a Greek translation.

The text is written in letters resembling early Kufic script and in a Nabataean dialect. Jawād ʿAlī thinks its writer was probably of Arab origin because of a mistake he made in applying the rules of Nabataean writing.504

Jawād ʿAlī also sees historical importance in this inscription, in addition to its linguistic importance, because it points to a connection between the Arabs of Iraq and the Arabs of Syria.

The second of these five texts is the Namāra inscription.505 It was written on the tomb of King Imruʾ al-Qays506 and dates to 328 CE.

The text is written in Nabataean script and in an Aramaic dialect, but its sentence structures are Arabic. It consists of five lines, arranged as follows:

1 — “This is the grave of Imruʾ al-Qays ibn ʿAmr, king of all the Arabs, who wore the crown.

2 — He subdued the tribes of Asad and Nizār and their kings, and defeated Madhḥij down to this day, and carried

3 — victory to the walls of Najrān, the city of Shammar. He subdued Maʿadd and appointed his sons

4 — over the tribes, making them his representatives before the Persians and the Romans. No king reached the level he reached

5 — down to this day. He died in the year 223, on the seventh day of September. May his sons be granted happiness.”507

Jawād ʿAlī concludes from the sound Arabic structures in the original text that its writer, or writers, were of Arab origin.508

This conclusion is strengthened by expressions in the text suggesting that the writer did not have complete command of the dialect in which he was writing and did not know it especially well.

Jawād ʿAlī also argues that the Arabic of the writer does not belong to the Arabic of the Liḥyānites, the Thamūdites, or the Ṣafaites.509

One piece of evidence is the repeated use of al- as the definite article.510 These three other forms of Arabic used h- for this purpose, while the Arabs of the south used an n at the end of the word. According to this argument, only the classical Arabic of the Qur’an used al- as the definite article.

The Namāra inscription also contains structures and expressions that, among Arabic dialects, belong only to the classical form of Arabic later used in the Qur’an.

This suggests that the writer of the inscription either spoke a dialect close to classical Arabic or was himself a speaker of that form of Arabic.511

The third of the five pre-Islamic inscriptions dates to 512 CE and is known as the Zabad inscription. It was written in Nabataean script, and its writing is close to the earliest Islamic Arabic script. But it contains little more than a number of names, some of them Arabic, including “Imr al-Qays” for Imruʾ al-Qays and “Saʿdū” for Saʿd.512 It begins with the words: “In the name of God.”513

The fourth inscription, in chronological order, is known among Orientalists as the Ḥarrān inscription. It dates to 568 CE.514

This text is especially important because it is written in an Arabic very close to the Arabic of the Qur’an. Its Nabataean script is also very close to early Islamic Arabic script.515

In both language and writing, then, it gives much clearer evidence of the point at which classical Arabic and its script were beginning to separate from Nabataean language and writing.

The fifth text is known as the “Second Umm al-Jimāl” inscription because it was the second inscription found at Umm al-Jimāl. It carries no date, but the Orientalists who examined it believe it was written in the sixth century CE. Its language is close to Qur’anic Arabic and is, to a large extent, free of Nabataean influence.516

These five texts are the only scientific evidence we have for this stage in the history of Arabic writing.

They suggest that the first Arabic script used by the people of the Hijaz before and after Islam developed from Nabataean script, which in turn developed from the script of the Aramaeans in Syria. This development took place against the background of close historical and commercial relations between these peoples.

The texts also suggest that the language in which they were written passed through a series of gradual stages. In chronological order, we move from a purely Nabataean language in the first Umm al-Jimāl inscription, to a mixed Nabataean-Arabic language in the Namāra inscription, and then to an Arabic largely freed from Nabataean influence in the Ḥarrān and Second Umm al-Jimāl inscriptions.

At the same time, we must take account of what historians and researchers, including many Orientalists, have said about the relationship between the Arabs and the Nabataeans.

Greek and Roman historians regarded the Nabataeans as Arabs. Orientalists, too, have argued that Nabataean civilization was Arab in its basic character, and that despite its close relationship with Rome, it preserved both its tribal features and its Arabic language.517

Littmann states that Nabataean is not far removed from classical Arabic and should be regarded as one of the Arabic dialects.518 He also notes that the personal names found in Nabataean inscriptions are usually Arabic in origin, which he takes as evidence that the Nabataeans were Arabs and that their dialect was Arabic.519

Jawād ʿAlī’s detailed comparative study in his encyclopedic work520 gives strong grounds for accepting these conclusions.

But scientific reasoning does not allow us to treat these five inscriptions as the final word on the origin of northern Arabic and its script.

Other possibilities remain, and future research may still uncover real evidence for them. We therefore have no good reason to reject such possibilities in advance.

What is needed is more research and excavation by Arab specialists, using the scientific and technical resources now available to them on a much greater scale than they were to the Orientalists who discovered these inscriptions in the past.

The second part of our inquiry—understanding the relationship between the life of the Arabic language and the life of the people who spoke it in the late pre-Islamic period—is also surrounded by uncertainty.

Some parts of this stage in the development of Arabic still need much more light. This is especially true of the language of pre-Islamic poetry and of the artistic prose that the early Arab chroniclers preserve in many forms, including speeches, sayings, proverbs, and stories.

Modern Arab researchers, and Orientalists before them, have long disagreed over the poetic and artistic prose texts attributed to the pre-Islamic period. The dispute concerns whether these texts really belong to that period at all.521

This dispute cannot be settled scientifically unless pre-Islamic writings are discovered that contain at least some of these kinds of texts. Only then could we form a clear picture of the language used by the northern Arabs shortly before and shortly after the rise of Islam for poetry, speeches, wise sayings, proverbs, and stories.

So another gap remains after the stage partly illuminated by the five inscriptions discovered so far.

What we need are written texts from the sixth or seventh century that show Arabic within its own independent historical setting: independent from Nabataean and other languages, both in its alphabet and in the language it expressed.

It is difficult to believe that the Arabic found in the Umm al-Jimāl, Namāra, Zabad, Ḥarrān, and Second Umm al-Jimāl inscriptions was exactly the form of Arabic used by the people of Mecca in the late sixth and early seventh centuries in their correspondence, poetry, speeches, proverbs, and stories of war, mythology, and religion.

It is equally difficult to believe that the means used to record those five inscriptions—especially the Ḥarrān inscription, with its Arabic language—were not also available during the same historical period for writing other Arabic texts that had fully separated from Nabataean script and from language influenced by Nabataean.

There must therefore have been pre-Islamic Arabic writings in the language of the poetry and prose that we later find recorded in Islamic sources and in the accounts of the early chroniclers.

As long as this missing link remains missing, we have only two main sources for understanding the linguistic dimension of late pre-Islamic culture.

The first is the language of the Qur’an.

The second is the body of texts attributed to the pre-Islamic Arabs and written down by Muslims from the middle of the first Islamic century onward.

We say that these texts were written “in their language” without hesitation. Whether or not every text really dates back to the pre-Islamic period, it is not reasonable to suppose that it was composed in a language completely unknown to the people of that period, or in a language that had not already passed through many stages of development.

In other words, classical Arabic cannot simply have been born with Islam or with the later age in which texts began to be systematically written down.

For any language to reach the level classical Arabic reached in the Qur’an and in the texts transmitted and recorded after Islam, it must already have lived for a very long time among the people who used it. It must have served hundreds of generations as a means of communication and as a way of expressing every part of life: their affairs, their relationships with one another, and their relationship with the universe and with nature.

The classical Arabic that appears in the Qur’an and in these other texts was therefore the product of hundreds of generations of Arabs before Islam.

And we can in fact read traces of all those generations in the language itself.

We find ancient words belonging to some of the oldest dialects of the Arabian Peninsula. We find other words belonging to later dialects developed by new generations of Arabs in the north of the peninsula and in the neighboring regions of Iraq and Syria.

We can also see a historical distance between the older meanings of these words and the newer meanings they acquired in the language of the Qur’an and in the poetry and literary prose attributed to the pre-Islamic period immediately before Islam.

We would be able to show the extent of this development, and some of its stages, much more clearly if we possessed writings from the time when Islam appeared and from the lifetime of the Prophet.

Here too, then, we face a missing link. We need written documents that belong to this precise historical setting.

Still, the material collected in the classical Arabic dictionaries, together with what we find in works on Qur’anic interpretation, hadith, Qur’anic readings, the Prophet’s campaigns, the “Battle Days of the Arabs,” Arab stories, collections of pre-Islamic poetry and their commentaries, and the poetic and linguistic examples preserved in works of grammar, gives us a rich and important body of evidence.

This material can support a scientific study capable of clearing away some of the uncertainty surrounding the life of Arabic during this stage in the development of Arab society.

From this large and varied body of material, we can begin with the following conclusions.

1 — The Unification of the Arabic Dialects

The first conclusion is that the classical Arabic preserved for us in the Qur’an, hadith, poetry attributed to the pre-Islamic period, and the various forms of artistic prose attributed to pre-Islamic Arabs and the earliest Muslims—including the Companions and the Rightly Guided Caliphs—was a common linguistic form in which the dialects of the northern Arabs, together with some southern dialects, had blended and come together.

We have plenty of evidence that the same historical conditions that gave Mecca its special and influential position in trade, economic life, society, and religion also made the dialect of Quraysh a center of attraction where other Arabic dialects, especially the northern ones, met and influenced one another.

During the sixth century CE, this interaction and blending must gradually have produced a shared form of Arabic distinct from the local dialects.

It became the language of artistic expression in poetry, public speaking, and short sayings of wisdom. It also became a shared language of communication among the different tribes when they came together at seasonal gatherings for trade, religion, and literature.

This kind of unification did not make the different dialects disappear.

Each Arab community continued to use its own dialect in ordinary everyday speech. At the same time, people could understand and use the common language when they met others at the great seasonal markets and gatherings.

Ibn Hishām522 may have been describing precisely this unity within diversity when he wrote:

“The Arabs would recite one another’s poetry, while each spoke according to the natural speech he had grown up with. This is why so many different versions of the same verses arose.”523

2 — An Objective Historical Process

This movement toward linguistic unity did not take place separately from the economic, social, cultural, and religious changes taking place in pre-Islamic society.

It was part of the wider development of that society toward new kinds of social relationships. Economic connections were beginning to bind its different parts together, gradually moving it away from tribal fragmentation and toward greater social unity.

This new unity was itself developing within a framework of growing social differences that would eventually provide the material basis for class divisions.

Language certainly has a degree of independence from a society’s economic foundations and from its wider social, political, and cultural structures. But that independence is never complete. Language does not exist outside the history of society, because it does not exist outside society itself.

Arabic therefore had to be affected by one of the most important changes taking place at the time: the movement away from tribal fragmentation and toward greater social unity.

This is why the dialect of Quraysh became the main basis of the developing common language.

The Qurayshi dialect did not become dominant because of some special quality contained in the dialect itself. Its influence came from the economic, commercial, social, and religious position of the Meccan Qurayshi aristocracy and from the influence that this position gave them over the wider course of social development.

The northern Arab communities increasingly had to deal with this aristocracy through its dialect rather than through their own separate dialects.

As a result, the dialect of Quraysh spread widely. This in turn allowed it to absorb useful features from other dialects. The process enriched its vocabulary and meanings and gave it a greater ability to bring different dialects together into a common language.

This was an objective historical process. It was not the result of deliberate personal choice or conscious selection.

Al-Farrāʾ524 imagined the matter differently when he wrote:

“The Arabs used to attend the seasonal gathering each year and make the pilgrimage to the House in the pre-Islamic period. Quraysh would hear the different ways the Arabs spoke. Whatever they liked in their speech, they adopted. In this way they became the most eloquent of the Arabs, and their language became free of ugly forms of speech and unpleasant words.”525

But the process was not a matter of deliberate “preference.”

It was the natural result of the wider conditions to which al-Farrāʾ himself refers in the first part of this passage.

We can see the result most clearly in the fact that a poet who did not belong to Quraysh would avoid the special features of his own dialect—its particular ways of forming words, pronouncing sounds, and building sentences—in order to address people in a language they already knew and accepted.

Many different forces had helped refine and polish this common language.526

3 — The Dialect of Quraysh in Early Islamic Scholarship

The two conclusions above make it much easier to explain why the dialect of Quraysh, rather than any other Arabic dialect, became both the material and the subject of the linguistic studies developed by Muslim scholars from the beginning of the age of systematic writing and authorship in Arabic.

It might be argued that Muslim scholars gave so much attention to the language of Quraysh simply because it was the language of the Qur’an.

From this point of view, their interest was religious rather than historical.

There is some truth in this, and it must be taken seriously. But it does not cancel out the other side of the question: the objective historical side. In fact, it confirms it.

The fact that the language of Quraysh became the language of the Qur’an was itself part of this historical process.

That remains true whatever religious motives guided scholars of Qur’anic interpretation and hadith, or scholars of language, grammar, literature, and rhetoric.

The same historical conditions that had already established the language of Quraysh as a common form of Arabic also explain why the Islamic message, in both Qur’an and hadith, addressed the Arabs in a language they already knew and shared.

There is no doubt that becoming the language of the Qur’an and hadith then strengthened the movement toward linguistic unity even further.

It also broadened the direct meanings of words, expanded the language’s figurative and expressive possibilities, and developed its ability to express the new ideas about the universe, society, and law that came with the changes of the Islamic period.

But we should also remember that linguistic studies did not remain entirely dependent on the study of the Qur’an and hadith.

Some branches gradually began to study questions of Arabic as subjects in their own right, becoming increasingly independent of their original religious purpose.

Arabic grammar is one example.

The earliest reasons for studying grammar were certainly connected with the need to establish rules for the grammatical forms of Qur’anic Arabic. Scholars did this partly by examining grammatical patterns in texts attributed to the pre-Islamic Arabs.

But despite these beginnings, the study of grammar gradually developed a life of its own. Its subject and purpose expanded, and specialist scholars emerged who wanted to study the Arabic language as a whole.

They began to study grammar for its own sake, not simply as part of the work of studying the Qur’an.527

Second — The Poetic Dimension

In this section, we look at pre-Islamic poetry—or rather, at the part of it that has reached us in written form—from a historical point of view.

Our concern here is with poetry as a historical, cultural, and social feature of late pre-Islamic Arab society.

We have no doubt that, in this respect, pre-Islamic poetry has a special value. Both its style and its content preserve vivid features of that society.

Its language, style, meter, subjects, descriptive images, and social images all contribute to this value.

The very existence of this poetry, with all these features, during such an important stage of Arab history before Islam makes it an important document. For scientific research, it is one of the richest, most varied, and most wide-ranging historical sources available to us.

But the scientific study of pre-Islamic poetry faces two problems that require a sound method of investigation.

Unless we find such a method, our use of this poetry as historical evidence will remain limited, and we will be able to draw only a small part of the scientific information and conclusions it may contain.

The first problem is authenticity.

A large amount of the poetry still classified as pre-Islamic has been questioned, both in earlier centuries and in modern times. There are even judgments close to certainty that much of this material was falsely attributed to the pre-Islamic period during later Islamic times and has no genuine basis for being dated that early.

The second problem is that all of this poetry has reached us in an apparently complete and finished form.

We cannot see the stages through which it developed.

To this day, we know almost nothing about the path by which it grew and changed before reaching the finished form known to us.

As Krachkovsky put it, we see only the static side of this poetry, not its dynamic side.528

This second problem casts a shadow over the first and makes the question of authenticity even harder to solve.

Because we do not know the history of how pre-Islamic poetry developed, we have lost an important tool for deciding what is genuine: comparison.

Ideally, we would compare the poems recorded during the Islamic period with earlier examples from the stages through which this poetry must have passed as it developed during the century and a half before the rise of Islam.

If the historical conditions for such a comparison existed, it could settle the argument over whether the surviving poems really belong to the pre-Islamic period.

If we had a clear picture of pre-Islamic poetry as it grew, changed, developed its techniques, and responded to changing historical conditions over what must have been a long history, the different stages of that development would give us a strict standard of comparison.

We could then distinguish much more precisely between poems that genuinely belong to the pre-Islamic period and poems that were later placed there falsely.

But because we still lack that historical picture, we also lack this reliable standard.

The problem is much the same as the one we faced when discussing the historical development of classical Arabic.

There too, we first encounter the language in an apparently complete and finished form, in the Qur’an and in pre-Islamic poetry as it was recorded during the Islamic centuries.

As we explained earlier when discussing the linguistic dimension, the final answer to that problem must await new discoveries of written evidence in Arabia—assuming Arab scientific institutions undertake the necessary archaeological work.

The same is true here.

For now, the question of pre-Islamic poetry can only be settled decisively by similar discoveries.

The few written remains found in Arabia so far, which we discussed earlier, cannot help us at all with the question of pre-Islamic poetry. They belong to historical conditions different from those in which pre-Islamic Arabic poetry must have arisen and developed.529

Still, waiting for new discoveries does not mean we have reached a dead end.

However uncertain the possibilities may be, we do not have to stop studying the problem until new evidence appears.

Other methods of investigation remain available to us.

One useful approach is to examine the foundations of the problem itself, together with the methods and investigations that have so far been used to deal with it.
