We will therefore turn to this alternative path and discuss it as far as our present purpose requires.

1 — The Historical Basis for Doubt

The historical basis for doubt begins with one firmly established fact.

The poetry composed during the pre-Islamic period continued to circulate only through memory and oral transmission until the age when it was systematically written down, in the third and fourth Islamic centuries.

In other words, for a long period it was not preserved in writing.

This meant, first, that a great deal of it was bound to disappear. Poems were scattered among different tribes and places, often far apart. The people who had memorized them also died out from one generation to the next.530

Second, the wording of the poems was bound to change as they passed from one person to another and from one place to another. Sometimes this happened deliberately, and sometimes unintentionally.

When systematic recording finally began, these two factors meant that the collectors could naturally recover only a small part of the original body of poetry.

What survived had already passed through roughly two centuries after the rise of Islam during which poems could be lost, altered, or distorted.

The disappearance of so much genuine pre-Islamic poetry also deprived us of a standard by which to distinguish authentic texts from invented ones.

This alone gives us reasonable grounds for questioning whether all the poems later written down and attributed to pre-Islamic poets really belong to them.

There is another factor as well.

During the Islamic centuries, both before and after poetry began to be systematically recorded, religious, political, and social interests sometimes encouraged different groups to invent poems and attribute them to the pre-Islamic period.

Linguists, scholars of Qur’anic interpretation and hadith, transmitters of poetry, supporters of rulers, and supporters of religious or political schools could all have reasons to produce such poetry.

A fabricated poem might be used to support a religious opinion or a sectarian position, defend a political cause, or strengthen the claims of a particular tribe.531

This is a historical reality that cannot simply be denied.

Once we take it into account, the historical basis for doubting the authenticity of some recorded pre-Islamic poetry becomes even stronger.

2 — Doubt Among Earlier Scholars

It seems that the question of whether all recorded pre-Islamic poetry was authentic was already present in the minds of early Arab and Muslim writers on literature and literary history.

Their books contain many references to different forms of poetic fabrication during the Islamic period and to poems that were falsely attributed to pre-Islamic times for the kinds of reasons just discussed.

One of the clearest examples is Ibn Sallām,532 who states that the poetry storytellers attributed to Tubbaʿ and Ḥimyar was fabricated.

He also says that Ibn Isḥāq and other transmitters of ancient stories like him invented this kind of poetry.

Abū al-Faraj, the author of al-Aghānī, also gives explicit accounts showing that these writers knew very well about the practice of fabricating poetry and attributing it to pre-Islamic figures.533

Even writers of the Prophet’s biography treated the problem in much the same way.

Ibn Hishām, for example, reproduces poetry that Ibn Isḥāq attributes to ancient pre-Islamic figures while telling stories about them. But Ibn Hishām himself notes that many learned authorities rejected Ibn Isḥāq’s attribution of these poems.534

Earlier scholars were also well aware of dishonest transmitters such as Ḥammād al-Rāwiya and Khalaf al-Aḥmar. They knew that such men sometimes attributed Islamic-period poetry to pre-Islamic poets, or even composed poems themselves and then presented them as pre-Islamic works.535

These many references in the works of early Muslim scholars show, as we have said, that they recognized the phenomenon of poetic fabrication.

What they could not do was explain it critically by uncovering its historical basis and tracing it back to the real conditions that produced it.

This was not because of any personal intellectual failing on their part.

It was because of the historical conditions in which they lived. Those conditions had not yet given them the scientific tools of knowledge needed for that kind of criticism.

3 — Doubts About Orientalist Methods

Among Orientalists, doubts about the authenticity of the surviving pre-Islamic poetry took a different form. They grew out of the modern development of methods for critically examining ancient texts and historical remains. The issue itself may first have been raised by Western Orientalists between 1850 and 1870.536

From the beginning of the twentieth century, new Orientalist studies began looking for the religious, political, and cultural roots of the problem. Its social roots, however, were either ignored or treated only formally and superficially.

In 1920, the English Orientalist Margoliouth argued that none of the poetry known as pre-Islamic was actually pre-Islamic in origin. In his view, it was entirely Islamic: it had been composed by Muslim poets.537

Other Orientalists, in studies dealing with particular aspects of Arab history before Islam, also questioned the authenticity of much of the surviving pre-Islamic poetry. Nöldeke, for example, argued that the Muslim transmitters who preserved this poetry had inserted the word “God” into it. According to him, they removed the names of pagan idols and replaced them with the name “God.” Where the original poem had mentioned al-Lāt, for example, “God” was later substituted in its place.538

But another group of Orientalists accepted that pre-Islamic poetry was broadly authentic, while acknowledging that some poems may have been altered and that some surviving texts may have been fabricated.

The English Orientalist Rom Landau belonged to this group. He argued that the very close resemblance between pre-Islamic Bedouin poetry and Umayyad poetry was what led some critics to suggest that the two might actually belong to the same period—that is, that both were Umayyad. On this view, pre-Islamic poetry would have been a kind of harmless forgery produced by the Umayyads, without any personal motive behind it.539

The French Orientalist Clément Huart, meanwhile, rejected the claim that the poetry of Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt was fabricated. He defended it as genuinely pre-Islamic.540

This position deals with only one pre-Islamic poet, but it still challenges the general principle behind doubts about pre-Islamic poetry. The same argument used to question pre-Islamic poetry as a whole had also been used against the poetry of Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt: namely, that it reached the Islamic period only through oral transmitters.

We find something similar in the work of the German Orientalist Wellhausen. He disagreed with Nöldeke’s claim that Muslim transmitters replaced the names of pagan idols in pre-Islamic poetry with the name “God.”

Wellhausen denied that Muslim transmitters had made this change. In his view, the appearance of the name “God” in pre-Islamic poetry, without the names of particular idols, did not result from later editing. It reflected a habit of the pre-Islamic Arabs themselves. Out of respect for the gods, they avoided excessive or casual use of the names of particular deities. They therefore sometimes used the word “God” in place of the name of an idol. At that time, he argued, the word did not necessarily mean one particular god. It could simply mean “lord” or “deity.”541

Again, this deals with only one specific issue. But it also challenges the blanket accusation that Muslim transmitters falsified pre-Islamic poetry. Instead, it points toward the need to study this poetry historically and to understand its relationship with pre-Islamic beliefs, ways of thinking, and customs.

There is, however, another approach among Orientalists that deserves particular attention when we consider the historical value of pre-Islamic poetry. This was the approach taken by the leading Russian Orientalist Krachkovsky.

After studying this poetry, Krachkovsky concluded that it gives us a truthful and faithful picture of Arab tribal life and of the environment in which the poetry arose. For that reason, he wrote, trustworthy specialists regarded pre-Islamic poetry as the most reliable source for learning about the conditions, customs, and traditions of the Arabs during the pre-Islamic period.542

Krachkovsky reached this conclusion through his detailed study of Arabic poetry, published in 1924.543 His method comes very close to what we would call a scientific method.

He did not rule out the possibility that ancient texts had undergone some correction while they were being written down. He did not even rule out the possibility that entire works had been fabricated.

But he saw an objective reason why the Arabs of that period were unable to establish the authenticity of everything they recorded. They did not yet possess a historical method or a comparative method. As a result, they were often unable even to formulate the kinds of questions that we can now help to analyze.

Yet we face a different limitation when we study pre-Islamic poetry today. We can see only its static side, not its dynamic side. In other words, we have the poetry only in its finished form. We cannot see the earlier stages through which it developed. Whichever way we look at it, we are always looking at the same final picture.544

Krachkovsky then raises another question: why is the language of pre-Islamic poetry so remarkably uniform?

Is this unity genuine?

Or was it created by later transmitters, or even by still later grammarians, who deliberately or unintentionally erased differences between dialects and turned the language into a single conventional form?

Or was the language itself an artificial literary language, developed before writing became widespread among certain tribes and adapted for poetry even though it differed from the everyday spoken language of most tribes?

Krachkovsky accepts the first possibility: he believes that the linguistic unity of pre-Islamic poetry was real.

The other two explanations—that the unity was created by transmitters or grammarians, or that the language of the poetry was an artificial literary language—do not, in his view, stand up to criticism. He states that most scholars had by then come to reject both.

On the first point, he accepts that two centuries of oral transmission after the rise of Islam must naturally have changed the language to some degree before the poems were finally written down. Linguists themselves may also have introduced changes unintentionally, especially since writing could not fully preserve pronunciation.

But Krachkovsky does not think these changes could have been either large or deliberate. Rhyme and meter, he argues, offered the strongest protection against major changes in the language of the poetry.

The evidence also shows, in his view, that grammarians did not erase differences between dialects. On the contrary, they made every effort to record and preserve them.

As for the second theory—that the language of the poetry was an artificial literary creation—Krachkovsky argues that this does not fit the actual lives of the poets, the simple content of their poetry, or its concern with camels, pasture, and similar features of everyday life. Under such conditions, an artificially manufactured poetic language would have been rather unusual.

He adds that the Arabian Peninsula preserved a broad linguistic unity until the ninth century. Grammarians believed that the Bedouins still spoke the pure language of ancient poetry in ordinary life. They turned to Bedouin speech not only to explain rare words found in poetry, but also to explain grammatical forms and sentence structures.

Krachkovsky therefore concludes that the language of this poetry shows a very high degree of mastery. That mastery itself points to a long period of development. Its maturity becomes especially clear, he says, when it is compared with the rhymed prose of the Qurʾān.545

Krachkovsky continues in this critical and historical way until he reaches his conclusion about the historical value of pre-Islamic poetry.

In this poetry, he says, we possess the earliest surviving record of the Arabic language. For the history of this period, it is not merely the earliest source. In truth, it is the only surviving source we possess for many of the events it describes.546

In his study of the traditions of the Arabic qaṣīda, Krachkovsky argues that the qaṣīda—the unified, stable, and structurally developed form of the Arabic ode—is what truly represents Arabic poetry.

The similarities between individual qaṣīdas, he argues, point to a long earlier history whose beginnings we cannot determine. Its roots must extend at least 150 years before the rise of Islam, which is the earliest period we can identify with any confidence.547

He then argues that the traditions of the Arabic qaṣīda eventually became an established expression of public opinion.

After the rise of Islam, however, the Arabian Peninsula naturally stopped being the only center where these poetic traditions, with their established social functions, came together. Arabia became only one province among others. The new centers of political life became the main centers of these traditions, especially Syria and Iraq. These regions produced the great wealth of poetry of the Umayyad period: al-Akhṭal, Jarīr, al-Farazdaq, and others.

If we judged the poetry of these poets purely by its form, Krachkovsky says, we would find it difficult to say that it had been written after the rise of Islam.548

We can therefore see that Krachkovsky approaches the problem of pre-Islamic poetry through a careful historical criticism. This leads him to the scholarly conclusion that the poetry is, in broad terms, authentic.

4 — Doubt Among Modern Arab Scholars

That, in general, is the position among Orientalists.

Among modern Arab scholars, pre-Islamic poetry has been approached in two sharply opposed ways.

The first was represented most clearly, openly, and boldly by Taha Hussein in his pioneering study, first published in 1926 under the title On Pre-Islamic Poetry, and then in a second edition in 1927 under the title On Pre-Islamic Literature.549

The second approach was strongly represented by traditionalists and Arabists among historians and teachers of Arabic literature in universities, as well as by many writers and literary figures across the Arab world.

The difference between these two approaches is striking.

The first begins with doubt so extreme that it leads to the claim that “the overwhelming majority of what we call pre-Islamic literature has nothing to do with the pre-Islamic period at all. It was fabricated after the rise of Islam. It is therefore Islamic literature, reflecting the life, tendencies, and passions of Muslims far more than the life of the pre-Islamic Arabs.”550

What remains of genuinely pre-Islamic literature, according to this view, is so small that it represents nothing and proves nothing. It cannot be relied upon to reconstruct a true literary picture of the pre-Islamic period.551

Supporters of this approach go so far as to say that the poetry attributed to Imruʾ al-Qays, Ṭarafa, Ibn Kulthūm, or ʿAntara has nothing to do with these men. Instead, it was invented by transmitters, produced through changes in grammatical form, manufactured by grammarians, embellished by storytellers, or created by Qurʾānic commentators, hadith scholars, and theologians.

To understand the pre-Islamic period, they argue, we should not rely on the poetry attributed to it, but rather “on the Qurʾān on the one hand, and history and legend on the other.”552

Nor, they say, should pre-Islamic poetry be used as evidence when interpreting the Qurʾān or hadith. Instead, the Qurʾān and hadith should be used to explain and interpret the poetry.553

The second approach takes the opposite position. It simply accepts the authenticity of all poetry attributed to the pre-Islamic period, without doubt, reservation, or any real impulse to reconsider these attributions by using the more advanced methods of analysis available in our own time.554

A third approach, however, has also appeared. It takes a middle position between these two extremes.

Perhaps its best representative—although those who follow this approach are still relatively few—is Jawād ʿAlī, author of an historical encyclopedia that can rightly be regarded as one of the most important modern additions to the Arabic library in its field: The History of the Arabs Before Islam.555

When dealing with the attribution of pre-Islamic poetry, Jawād ʿAlī uses historical criticism and comparison. His research is objective in the sense that it does not begin from a fixed and absolute position that has already decided the answer in advance.

Take, for example, the religious and moral poetry attributed to Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt. Some of this poetry agrees with, or closely resembles, Islamic beliefs and sometimes even Qurʾānic language.

Jawād ʿAlī considers several possible explanations for this similarity. He then examines each one critically and historically, in light of the available reports and the historical circumstances.

He eventually reaches the view that “this similarity and agreement probably resulted from fabrication and invention.”

His reasoning begins with the fact that Umayya was undoubtedly a poet, since the transmitters unanimously agreed on this.

It also rests on the fact that Umayya “was in revolt against his people and angry with them because they worshipped idols. He had some belief in one God and some knowledge of Judaism and Christianity.”

But even so, Jawād ʿAlī does not believe that Umayya “knew all the details found in the Qurʾān and hadith about the Throne and the Footstool, God and His angels, the Resurrection, Paradise and Hell, judgment, reward and punishment, and similar matters.”

All these details, he argues, “are purely Islamic. They are not found in this form among the Jews, Christians, or ḥanīfs. So when they appear in Umayya’s poetry in specifically Islamic words and expressions, this is the work of a group of people in the Islamic period. They put these ideas into his mouth, just as they—or others—put similar things into the mouths of other poets and orators.

“They did this because they believed it would serve Islam. It would show that some people in the pre-Islamic period had been learned, that Islam had therefore not appeared as something completely strange, and that some of these people had known the unseen and expected an Arab prophet to appear soon. They were then said to have wished that they might live again in his time, or that their lives might be prolonged until they could meet him and become Muslims.

“Stories of this kind became popular and widespread, just as similar stories have spread in every religion.”556

Jawād ʿAlī then supports this argument through a comparison of style.

He compares Umayya’s nonreligious poetry with the religious poetry attributed to him and uses the difference between them as a way of distinguishing genuine pre-Islamic poetry from later material falsely attributed to the pre-Islamic period.

On this basis, he argues that signs of fabrication in Umayya’s poetry can be seen “in its lack of consistency and in the differences in its style and spirit.

“When we look at the poetry attributed to him in praise, elegy, or other subjects not directly connected with religion, we find the style and texture of pre-Islamic poetry. But the religious and moralizing poems have a very different style. They are far removed from the known styles of pre-Islamic poets. Their language brings them closer to the poetry of strict jurists, Sufis, and Christian ascetics.

“It is therefore very far from the style of the pre-Islamic poets, even from the style of someone such as ʿAdī ibn Zayd al-ʿIbādī and the other pre-Islamic poets close to the rise of Islam who were said to have been Christians.”557

This example gives us an approach to pre-Islamic poetry that differs from both of the positions described above.

First, it differs from an approach that makes doubt the starting point and cause of research rather than something that may emerge as a result of research.

Second, it differs from an approach that begins with belief or certainty before any investigation has taken place, and then shapes the evidence so that the conclusion will fit the position already chosen in advance.

5 — Taha Hussein and Cartesian Doubt

Taha Hussein states openly that in studying pre-Islamic literature he intends to adopt “the philosophical method introduced by Descartes for investigating the truths of things.”

According to Taha Hussein:

“The basic rule of this method is that the researcher must free himself from everything he knew beforehand and begin his investigation with a mind completely empty of everything previously said about the subject. (...)

“Let us use this method when we study our ancient Arabic literature and its history. Let us approach this literature and its history after freeing ourselves from everything previously said about them, and after casting off all those heavy chains that bind our hands and feet, preventing free physical movement and preventing free intellectual movement as well.”558

It is worth noting that Taha Hussein adopts the formal side of Descartes’s method of doubt.

It seems to me that he takes it apart from its specifically Cartesian philosophical content, or empties it of that content.

Descartes’s method of doubt rested, first, on his own understanding of what philosophy studies and, second, on his rationalist theory of knowledge.

On the first point, Descartes believed that philosophy was concerned only with nature and the human being. In other words, when he developed his method of doubt, the idea of “God” did not, in his view, form part of the subject matter of philosophy.

This is why he argued that the human mind had to be cleared of every belief it had previously accepted. He called this process “doubt” and carried it to the point of saying that we must doubt all the knowledge that has accumulated in human consciousness over its long history.

On the second point—his rationalist theory of knowledge—Descartes also argued that the mind had to be cleared of knowledge that reached it through the senses.

In his view, no quality of things known through the senses could give us true knowledge.

This followed from his rationalist theory of knowledge, which rejected the idea that reliable knowledge could be built on sense experience. He denied that knowledge begins with the senses—that we move from sensory experience toward truth and finally arrive at basic principles, as Bacon had argued.

Descartes reversed this order.

For him, the movement toward truth, or knowledge, begins with reason itself, with what he saw as the natural light of the mind.

Knowledge therefore begins with intuition: the mind’s direct recognition of self-evident truths already present in the human soul.

Descartes regarded the soul as a substance existing in its own right, independent of the body. The body, in turn, was another substance existing in its own right.

Given this philosophical basis for Descartes’s method of doubt, we have to ask: did Taha Hussein adopt the method together with all these philosophical foundations?

Did he truly adopt it as a philosophical method?

Or did he understand it in a simpler way, seeing only its formal side while missing its deeper philosophical content?

In other words, did he take only the immediate, everyday meaning of the word “doubt,” separately from its Cartesian implications for the theory of knowledge?

To answer this question, we need to look at two sides of the issue.

The first is the scientific position toward Cartesian doubt itself.

The second is Taha Hussein’s own practical use of it.

□ On the first point, scientific analysis rejects the philosophical propositions on which Descartes’s method of doubt is based. It does so for the following reasons:

1 — At its foundation, the method rests on Descartes’s famous proposition: “I think, therefore I am.”

This proposition places Descartes directly in the idealist camp, because it establishes existence through thought. In other words, it denies the objective character of existence: the fact that existence is independent of consciousness, or thought, and comes before it.

2 — The method asks human consciousness to do something that it simply cannot do: eliminate the role of sensory knowledge from the process through which we arrive at truth.

The role of sensory experience is an objective fact. It cannot be abolished by an act of personal will, even when that act of will takes the form of a philosophical proposition or is supported by one.

3 — The method would require us to discard all the knowledge that human consciousness has gained over its enormously long history.

That is impossible.

This accumulated knowledge has become part of the historical formation of human consciousness itself. It has become an objective historical reality. It cannot simply be removed from consciousness, even by an act of consciousness itself.

4 — After “cleansing” human consciousness of everything it has learned through history, the method would return it to zero.

It would return consciousness to a childhood that humanity left behind thousands of years ago.

If such a thing were even possible, human consciousness would then have to spend thousands of new years passing once again through all the stages needed to reach the level it had already reached by the time of Descartes.

This completely “unhistorical” process is objectively impossible.

Rejecting these Cartesian propositions does not mean that everything human consciousness has learned throughout history is absolutely true.

Whether this inherited body of knowledge is correct or mistaken, wholly or partly, is a separate question that has to be studied on a different level.

Still, it is useful here to summarize the scientific position.

Historical materialist analysis sees the knowledge accumulated by human consciousness during its long development as a series of historical forms of consciousness. Each belongs to a particular stage in that development.

These forms of consciousness are direct or indirect reflections of the corresponding stages through which social reality itself has developed.

That does not mean, first, that these reflections must perfectly match the social reality that produced them.

Nor does it mean, second, that they must perfectly match the objective and absolute truths of the universe.

There can be many differences between the world as human consciousness understands it and the objective reality of nature and society.

But as human consciousness has developed—together with human societies and the natural sciences—each historical stage has revealed new relative truths and, in doing so, exposed errors in earlier forms of knowledge.

When we study that earlier knowledge and try to distinguish what was right from what was wrong, we therefore need a scientific method.

That method does not begin by “doubting” earlier knowledge in the Cartesian sense of removing it from consciousness or “cleansing” the mind of it.

It begins, first, by treating that knowledge as an objective reality with a history of its own—something with a real historical existence that cannot simply be erased.

Second, it studies that knowledge as something whose development was objectively connected with the development of the material and social reality from which it arose and through which it changed.

□ Now we come to the second side of the issue: Taha Hussein’s practical use of Cartesian “doubt” in his study of pre-Islamic literature.

Here it seems clear to us that he takes the idea of “doubt” only in its formal sense, without adopting the philosophical theory of knowledge on which Descartes built it.

It is true that Taha Hussein refers to the philosophical form of the method when he says:

“In literature, I want to adopt the philosophical method introduced by Descartes for investigating the truths of things at the beginning of the modern age.”

Immediately afterward, he adds:

“The basic rule of this method is that the researcher must free himself from everything he knew before and begin his investigation with a mind completely empty of everything previously said about the subject.”559

It is also true that, when defining how he intends to apply the method, he writes:

“When we begin to study Arabic literature and its history, we must forget our national feelings in all their particular forms. We must forget our religious feelings and everything connected with them. We must also forget whatever clashes with those national and religious feelings.

“We must bind ourselves to nothing and submit to nothing except the methods of sound scientific research.”560

But what, exactly, does all this mean?

From its tone, context, and indeed from the words themselves, we can understand it only in one way.

Taha Hussein wants to study Arabic literature and its history after freeing himself from the traditionalist view of this heritage: the view that simply accepts it as true.

He wants to free himself from automatically accepting the opinions, positions, and reports handed down by transmitters, chroniclers, storytellers, hadith scholars, Qurʾānic commentators, and the writers who recorded Arab-Islamic history.

This kind of freedom in studying the heritage is what Taha Hussein means when he says that “the researcher must free himself from everything he knew before and begin his investigation with a mind empty of everything previously said about the subject.”

It is also what he means when he says that “we must forget our national feelings in all their particular forms,” “forget our religious feelings and everything connected with them,” and “forget whatever clashes with those national and religious feelings.”

He is calling for freedom from inherited social influences and inherited restraints on the way we understand the heritage today.

Taha Hussein therefore wants to approach Arabic literature and its history by doubting these inherited influences and restraints, so that “we bind ourselves to nothing and submit to nothing except the methods of sound scientific research.”

Put differently, he wants us to study the heritage without prejudice either for it or against it.

He wants us to free ourselves from both traditional ways of approaching it.

Nothing Taha Hussein says about his method in On Pre-Islamic Literature points to anything substantially different from this.

What, then, should we conclude?

The answer seems clear.

Taha Hussein is very far from wanting to erase the Arabic literature and history preserved in our consciousness. He is not calling for the destruction of the sources that make up the actual historical body of this heritage. Nor is he asking us to “cleanse” our consciousness of these sources accumulated through history or to erase this objective historical reality from Arab consciousness altogether.

What he wants is something much more specific.

He wants to produce a new, contemporary understanding of this historical reality, free from the traditionalist understanding of it and subject only to “the methods of sound scientific research.”

□ Yet although Taha Hussein’s use of “doubt” in studying pre-Islamic literature has only a formal connection with the philosophical foundations of Cartesian doubt, we must still recognize the enormous positive role he played as a pioneer in the study of the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage.

His attempt to create a new, modern way of understanding this heritage was itself important.

So was his attempt to bring the modern “methods of scientific research” into that work.

In the 1920s, these two things together amounted to an intellectual breakthrough of great historical importance.

But once we move beyond this pioneering achievement, other aspects of Taha Hussein’s work appear as weaknesses in his method.

For one thing, he became so absorbed by doubt about the authenticity of pre-Islamic poetry that “doubt” almost became the reason for the investigation, rather than one possible conclusion produced by it.

For another, he often carried this method of doubt beyond what “sound scientific research” itself requires: a historical understanding of the reality being studied.

His commitment to doubting the attribution of pre-Islamic poetry became so strong that he stripped almost all this poetry of its historical value for the period before Islam.

Even the “very small amount” of literature that he accepted as genuinely pre-Islamic came to represent nothing and prove nothing. He said that it should not be relied upon to reconstruct a true literary picture of the pre-Islamic period.

He then made the categorical judgment that our knowledge of the pre-Islamic period should rest not on the poetry attributed to it, but “on the Qurʾān on the one hand, and history and legend on the other.”

He also argued that this poetry should not be used as evidence in interpreting the Qurʾān and hadith. Instead, the Qurʾān and hadith should be used to explain and interpret the poetry.

“Sound scientific research” rejects absolute judgments of this kind.

In principle, it rejects any absolute conclusion that is not supported by definite evidence from reality.

Yet On Pre-Islamic Literature was unable to provide evidence strong enough to justify conclusions this absolute.

That is the first problem.

The second is this.

We agree with Taha Hussein that much of the poetry attributed to the pre-Islamic period is of doubtful authenticity and that some of it was undoubtedly fabricated.

We also agree with most of the reasons he gives for doubting particular poems or judging them to be later inventions.

But we still cannot agree that poetry of doubtful authenticity, or even poetry known to have been fabricated, has no historical value for the pre-Islamic period immediately before the rise of Islam.

Indeed, we can say that the historical value of this later fabricated poetry does not differ in any fundamental way from the historical value of genuinely pre-Islamic poetry itself.

There are two reasons for this, and no scientific method can ignore them when studying literary phenomena of this kind.

The first is that the gap between genuinely pre-Islamic poetry and poetry fabricated shortly after the rise of Islam was not large enough to create a major difference in their historical relationship to Arab society.

Both kinds of poetry were connected with historical features shared by these two closely overlapping periods.

This applies both to the development of Arab society and to the development of Arabic poetry itself.

We can even appeal to Taha Hussein himself here. Whether he was right or wrong, he wrote that he knew of no nation that had held so firmly to literary conservatism, introducing change only gradually, as the Arabs had done.

“The life of the pre-Islamic Arabs,” he says, “is visible in the poetry of al-Farazdaq, Jarīr, Dhū al-Rumma, al-Akhṭal, al-Rāʿī, and others.”561

The second point follows from the very conditions under which Islamic-period poets and transmitters fabricated poetry and attributed it to the pre-Islamic period.

By definition, this fabricated poetry had to resemble genuine pre-Islamic poetry in both form and content. It had to fit the historical features of pre-Islamic Arab society.

Otherwise, the whole act of fabrication would have been pointless.

Yet Taha Hussein himself devotes fifty-five pages of his book562 to discussing the political, religious, and other reasons why Muslims fabricated large amounts of poetry and attributed it to pre-Islamic poets.

If this fabrication was to serve its intended purposes, then those producing it naturally had to imitate the pre-Islamic poets in the poetry or prose they attributed to them.

The fabricated poems therefore had to resemble genuine pre-Islamic poetry as closely as possible in language, style, subject matter, content, description, imagery, and other historical features.

That required the fabricators to possess a broad knowledge of all these features.

It also required considerable literary skill. They had to absorb those features well enough to produce poetry with a convincingly pre-Islamic form and identity, while hiding as far as possible every sign that the poem had actually been written during the Islamic period.

Most or all of these conditions existed among the Muslim transmitters, hadith scholars, Qurʾānic commentators, and theologians who fabricated such poetry.

Taha Hussein himself gives evidence of this.

He reports what the Kufan transmitter al-Mufaḍḍal al-Ḍabbī said about Ḥammād al-Rāwiya:

“He has corrupted poetry beyond repair.”

When al-Mufaḍḍal was asked why—whether Ḥammād made grammatical mistakes or other errors—he replied:

“If only that were the problem. Scholars can correct a man who makes mistakes. But Ḥammād knows the dialects of the Arabs, the styles of the poets, and their meanings. He keeps composing poetry in the style of one poet and inserting it into that man’s work. It is then transmitted from him far and wide, until the poetry of the ancient poets becomes mixed together and the genuine can be distinguished from the false only by a truly knowledgeable critic. And where is such a critic to be found?”563

The qualities described here—both Ḥammād’s method of fabrication and his deep knowledge of Arab dialects—were probably shared by many of those who fabricated poetry and attributed it to the pre-Islamic period during the age when oral traditions were being collected and books were being written.

If that is so, then poetry fabricated under these conditions must preserve many of the main features, qualities, and historical meanings of genuine pre-Islamic poetry.

Otherwise the fabrication would fail both as a literary exercise and in whatever religious, political, linguistic, or historical purpose it was meant to serve.

The claim about Ḥammād al-Rāwiya would otherwise make no sense: that he could continually compose poetry in the style of an earlier poet, insert it into that poet’s work, and spread it so widely that genuine and fabricated ancient poetry became almost impossible to distinguish except by an expert critic.

For this reason, a scientific researcher cannot follow Taha Hussein in his categorical judgments.

We cannot accept the claim that “the overwhelming majority of what we call pre-Islamic literature has nothing to do with the pre-Islamic period,” or that it is “Islamic, reflecting the life, tendencies, and passions of Muslims far more than the life of the pre-Islamic Arabs.”

Nor can we accept that the small amount of genuine pre-Islamic literature that remains “represents nothing and proves nothing,” or that it should not be used to reconstruct an accurate literary picture of the pre-Islamic period.

The same applies to his statement that the poems attributed “to Imruʾ al-Qays, al-Aʿshā, or other pre-Islamic poets (...) prove nothing and tell us nothing.”564

A scientific historical method requires a different approach.

We must treat pre-Islamic poetry—both the genuine poetry and the later fabrications—as living historical material with a real and objective connection to Arab social reality during two closely overlapping periods: the pre-Islamic period immediately before Islam and the early Islamic period immediately after it.

For our purposes here, this means looking closely at all the historical meanings found throughout the surviving body of poetry known to us as pre-Islamic poetry.

Those meanings are as varied as the social reality to which the poetry points.

The Historical Meaning of Pre-Islamic Poetry

The ancient Arabs themselves instinctively recognized that pre-Islamic poetry carried this kind of historical meaning when they said that poetry was the record of the Arabs.

They seem to have meant that poetry preserved Arab history itself, which is also suggested by the word dīwān, or record.565

When they spoke of “poetry” in this expression, they meant pre-Islamic poetry.

Among all Arabic poetry, this was the one body of poetry that did not need to be identified by the historical period in which it was produced. For them, it alone deserved to be called the record of the Arabs.

Likewise, the word “Arabs” in this expression naturally meant the Arabs of the pre-Islamic period, just as it did in traditional expressions such as “the battle-days of the Arabs,” “the markets of the Arabs,” and “the speech of the Arabs.”

By the historical meaning of pre-Islamic poetry, we mean everything in its content that expresses, through the poetic language of its time, the historical features that distinguish pre-Islamic Arab society from Arab society in the centuries after Islam.

These features concern both social reality and social consciousness.

The historical meanings that concern us here therefore have two main dimensions: a social dimension and a dimension of knowledge and thought.

A — The Social Dimension

The level reached by pre-Islamic poetry has to be judged according to its own historical period.

For that reason, it represents an earlier stage of development than Arabic poetry in the more advanced Arab-Islamic centuries—for example, the fourth Islamic century.

At this earlier stage, pre-Islamic poetry, like poetic art generally at a similar level of development, reflects social reality in direct, relatively flat, and highly detailed language.

It belongs to a stage at which poetry has not yet moved from being one particular way of recounting reality to becoming the artistic creation of a new reality of its own.

This is why the social world of the pre-Islamic period appears in such detail in the poetry of that period—or in poetry attributed to it.

A modern researcher can move quite easily from the poetic scene described in a verse to the social event or social reality behind it.

The distance between the two is short, simple, and direct.

This historical feature of pre-Islamic poetry may be the real basis for the old Arab saying that “poetry is the record of the Arabs.”

Another poetic feature goes with it.

Tribal social relations dominate the inner workings of pre-Islamic poetry almost completely.

The poet’s individual “self” appears only as one expression of this larger tribal relationship.

This is why the line between the poet speaking for himself and the tribe speaking through the poet becomes difficult to see.

The boundaries disappear, for example, between love poetry and war poetry:

I remembered you while spears drank deep of me, and Indian blades were dripping with my blood.

I longed to kiss the swords, because their flash was like the gleam of your smiling teeth.

— ʿAntara

The same happens between love poetry and poetry of pride, battle, praise, elegy, or any of the other traditional categories used to classify pre-Islamic verse.

Consider, for example, al-Munakhkhal ibn ʿĀmir al-Yashkurī and his poem beginning:

If you mean to reproach me, then go— go toward Iraq and do not turn back.

It is difficult to accept the traditional division of pre-Islamic poetry into separate categories.

It may make more sense to give the whole body of this poetry a single title:

the poetry of the Arab tribe before Islam.

But did the poetry of the ṣaʿālīk—the outlaw poets—possess some special feature that takes it outside this description?

In fact, it did.

The poetry of the outlaws contains a striking tension that may be one of the most important historical meanings found anywhere in pre-Islamic poetry.

On one side, it contains all the basic features of “the poetry of the Arab tribe before Islam.”

On the other, it contains all the elements of a rejection of that very world.

Yet these two sides do not reach the point of complete opposition or contradiction.

The outlaw poets did not write outside the linguistic and artistic forms of pre-Islamic tribal poetry.

Nor did they exist outside the economic and social relations of their age.

They wrote from a particular position within those relations—a position that expressed, in behavior, the beginning of their historical breakdown.

Their poetry therefore became an early and spontaneous form of awareness of this historical process.

It reflected the instability and loosening that had begun to affect the material foundations of tribal relations in Arabian society.

Within the tribe, social differences were developing between those who held positions of leadership and those who were subordinate.

These differences also produced growing material inequality, together with the oppression and suffering of one group at the hands of another.

This was the beginning of the breakdown we are describing.

It was also the first social source of the phenomenon of the ṣaʿālīk, the outlaws of pre-Islamic Arabia.

This social background produced the distinctive tension found in their poetry.

What makes their poetry unusual within the pre-Islamic tradition is its element of rejection: the rejection of tribal social relations at the point when those relations had reached maturity.

That rejection also involved resisting the tribe’s complete control over the poet’s individual self—the power of the tribal collective over the individual personality of the poet, a power that could almost completely surround and absorb that individuality.

ʿUrwa ibn al-Ward, one of these outlaw poets, put the issue with remarkable directness.

He compared two kinds of outlaw existing within the same social relations.

He expressed contempt for the first because this man submitted to the crushing conditions around him and accepted them.

He praised the second because he stood proud, rejected those conditions, and felt within himself the strength to overcome the obstacles holding back his ambitions.

1 — Of the first type, ʿUrwa says:

May God curse the outlaw who, when night falls, goes wandering among the paths, haunting every slaughtering place;566

who counts himself rich whenever, for a night, he gains the hospitality of some well-off friend;567

who rarely seeks wealth except for himself, until he stands like some weak, leaning shelter;568

who sleeps early, then sits there in the morning, brushing the pebbles from his dust-covered side;569

who helps the women of the camp whenever they ask, and ends the day exhausted like a worn-out camel.

2 — Of the second type, he says:

By God, what an outlaw—his face shines like the blaze of a newly kindled flame. (a)

He looks down upon his enemies as they drive him from their ground like a marked gaming arrow. (b)

And even when they are far away, they never feel safe from his return; they watch for him as a family watches for someone long absent. (c)

Such a man, if he meets death, meets it with honor; and if one day he becomes rich, he deserves it all the more. (d)570

Yet this distinctive feature of the pre-Islamic outlaw poets does not take their poetry outside the basic feature shared by pre-Islamic poetry as a whole.

That feature is the dominance of historical meaning—especially social meaning—over all the other elements that make up the poetry.

Even its artistic qualities become a burden on the poetry itself, and on later Arabic poetry as well, if we strip them of this historical meaning.

For this reason, scientific research cannot form a complete picture of the pre-Islamic period without also reading that period through pre-Islamic poetry itself, carefully and comprehensively, taking into account the full body of surviving texts.

B — The Knowledge Dimension

By the “knowledge dimension,” we mean the historical evidence in pre-Islamic poetry that can tell us something about how people at the time understood the universe and the world around them.

Pre-Islamic poetry was, simply by being poetry, one form of social awareness. As such, it also represented a particular stage in the development of that awareness through artistic expression. But poetry tells us more than this. Its texts also contain signs of other forms of awareness among the pre-Islamic Arabs. The clearest example is religious awareness, which at its core expresses a way of understanding the relationship between human beings and the world.

Pre-Islamic poetry contains many signs of this kind. We can use them to trace the forms religious awareness took, the directions in which it was developing, and the level it had reached in the period immediately before Islam.

Take, for example, this line by a pre-Islamic poet:

Yaghūth led us against Murād, and before dawn we had overcome them.571

Yaghūth was one of the well-known idols worshipped by the Arabs. The verse therefore tells us something about what its worshippers believed: they imagined that such idols had supernatural powers and could give them victory over their enemies in war.

Or take these lines by the poet al-Mutalammis:

Until she drank her fill there, as night drew near, after the stillness, when the church bells stirred her.572

Here we can see the presence of Christianity in the pre-Islamic Arab world. Pre-Islamic poetry contains many such references, and they are widely reported both by early historians and by modern historians of Arabic literature, especially poetry.573 The same is true of Judaism. Pre-Islamic poetry also gives us evidence of its presence in Arab society before Islam.574

If we look historically at the religious ideas found in pre-Islamic poetry—both polytheistic and monotheistic—we are led to an important conclusion. This poetry reflects a gradual movement in religious thought toward belief in one God.

That movement was itself an indirect expression of a broader change taking place in society. During the sixth century CE, at least in the northern part of the Arabian Peninsula, social life was beginning to move beyond a world made up of many separate tribal units. These tribes existed largely on their own and were constantly fighting one another for reasons rooted in older clan relations.

The direction of change was now beginning to weaken this fragmented tribal order. New economic and social forces were entering the old system and putting pressure on the narrow relationships of the closed tribe.

Trade and money exchange were expanding rapidly across the peninsula. More and more of this activity was being drawn toward one main center: the Quraysh leadership in Mecca, represented by the leading figures of the Dār al-Nadwa, the House of Assembly.

This economic and social movement toward greater unity had to find some form of expression in the awareness of the people living through it. And that is what happened. It appeared in poetry, with poetry’s own particular character, and it also appeared more broadly in religion.

In poetry, we can see it clearly in the work of the outlaw poets, whose poetry expressed a rebellion against tribal relations.

In religion, it began to appear in the movement of the ḥanīfs, who rejected idol worship and called for belief in one God. Their appearance marked the beginning of a revolt against polytheism, which was the religious expression of a society divided into many separate tribal groups.

Pre-Islamic poetry itself became one of the first means through which the monotheistic message of the ḥanīfs was expressed and spread. That message was an early sign that a new Arab social reality, a new social awareness, and a new Arab consciousness were beginning to emerge. In other words, it was one of the developments preparing the way for the rise of Islam.

Pre-Islamic poetry carried the message of the ḥanīfs in verses attributed to some of the leading figures in this monotheistic movement, including Quss ibn Sāʿida al-Iyādī, Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt, Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, Suwayd ibn ʿĀmir al-Muṣṭaliqī, and others.

In one passage attributed to Umayya, he says of the ḥanīf faith:

Every religion, on the Day of Judgment before God, except the faith of the ḥanīfs, is false.575

And Zayd ibn Nufayl is said to have written:

One Lord, or a thousand lords— which shall I worship when things are divided?

I have cast aside al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā together. That is what the firm and patient man does.576

Here we have a clear expression of monotheism through the rejection of religious plurality. This is the position that most clearly defines the meaning of the ḥanīf movement because it fits the historical reality most closely.

The rise of the ḥanīfs reflected a change already taking place in society. Social relations were moving toward a new form in which tribal division was no longer the main organizing principle. Social differences within society were becoming increasingly important instead.

This change in the material foundations of pre-Islamic society helped create the conditions for social awareness to develop toward the idea of one God. The later rise of Islam gave that idea its full historical expression on the social, intellectual, and ideological levels.

Third — Proverbs as a Cultural Marker

Proverbs can also reveal a great deal because they form another historical marker of pre-Islamic Arab culture.

At that stage, Arab culture was still mainly an oral culture. It grew directly out of everyday life and was passed on through speech rather than writing. In a culture of this kind, proverbs are among the simplest and most effective ways of expressing ideas and spreading them widely.

Under these historical conditions, a proverb combines two related qualities.

On the one hand, it can condense a particular event or situation into a short expression. On the other, it can turn that expression into a symbol, lifting the original event out of its individual setting and giving it a broader, more general meaning.

Because proverbs do both things, they can preserve historical evidence about many details of social life and about the different forms of social awareness.

The proverbs of the pre-Islamic Arabs in the period leading into Islam naturally contain this kind of evidence. They show how people viewed ordinary objects, everyday events, and practical situations. They also show how they thought about broader human questions and problems, within the historical limits of their time.

In these proverbs, we find the life of pre-Islamic Arabs and their reflections on relations between people in the different areas of human activity familiar to them. We find their moral standards, emotional states, alliances, loyalties, conflicts, and many different kinds of experience drawn from their actual conditions of life.

What concerns us most here, however, is the kind of knowledge these proverbs preserve about nature, society, and thought. This is what allows us to treat them, in some sense, as a cultural marker.

Pre-Islamic proverbs contain a great deal of such evidence, provided that we always read it within its historical setting. In other words, we must judge its value as knowledge according to the level of development reached by Arabian society at the time.

On this basis, we can learn something about their knowledge of the universe, society, and nature from sayings such as:

“More enduring than the two vultures.”577

“Beware the green growth on the dung heap.”578579

“The barren land has grown rich with pasture.”580

“Like the ostrich: neither bird nor camel.”581

“It is my house that is stingy, not I.”582

“Need leads to theft.”583

“Killing is the strongest deterrent to killing.”584

“The one who abandons you is the killer’s brother.”585

“Not everything white is fat, and not everything black is a date.”586

And so on.

Alongside proverbs of this relatively limited cultural kind, we should also consider another type that shows a higher level of cultural development. These are proverbs that express their meaning through artistic metaphor and therefore show a greater degree of aesthetic development.

Examples include:

“He rode on two wings,”

meaning that he moved very quickly;

“So-and-so is like a man riding two mounts,”

meaning that he cannot make up his mind;

“If only a woman wearing bracelets had slapped me,”587

meaning that the blow or insult came from someone of lower status;

“He came claiming that a cow was a donkey,”

meaning that he claimed something impossible and was therefore lying;

“My belly is where I need perfume; scatter the rest elsewhere,”

meaning that what he needed was food, not fragrance;

“The churning has brought out the butter,”

meaning that experience has separated what is true from what is false and revealed the truth;

and:

“His flood came before his rain,”

said of someone whose action comes before his threat.

There is also the saying that a flood drove a man to thirst, used for someone who falls into hardship because of abundance, or who receives harm from something that should have brought good.

There is, however, a problem here similar to the problem we encountered with pre-Islamic poetry: how sure can we be that these proverbs really date from the pre-Islamic period?

Arab proverbs from before and after Islam became mixed together, and many sayings were attributed to the pre-Islamic period only later, during the age when oral material was being written down. The same motives that are said to have led people in the Islamic period to compose poetry and attribute it to pre-Islamic poets may also have led them to invent proverbs and assign them to the same period.

We cannot avoid this problem.

Still, there are clues that can make the pre-Islamic origin of some sayings more likely, including some of the examples just quoted. Some clues come from the language of the proverb. Others come from its style. Others are connected to the historical event said to have produced it.

There is no need to examine this question in detail here.

Fourth — Literary Seasons as a Cultural Marker

We should also remember that Arabs in the pre-Islamic period did not live only inside the Arabian Peninsula.

They had communities and centers of activity in neighboring regions, where they came into contact with other peoples and ways of life. These included Mesopotamia, Syria, Palestine, and eastern Egypt.

Levels of social and economic development therefore varied across the Arab world, and levels of intellectual development naturally varied with them.

Differences could even be seen among the main centers within the Arabian Peninsula itself: Mecca, Medina—then known as Yathrib—and Ṭāʾif in the north, and Ṣanʿāʾ and the other towns and fertile centers of Yemen in the south.

It may even be fair to say that Mecca stood apart during this period. Its economic and social development showed features more advanced than those found in much of the rest of the peninsula.

One reason was that Mecca had drawn much of the higher tribal leadership into its orbit. This allowed its leading families to control the care of the Kaʿba, where the religious symbols of different tribes were gathered in the form of idols and other objects of worship. Many of these belonged to the strongest tribes and to those most closely connected with the commercial traffic moving along the great caravan routes between the north and south of the peninsula.

The leaders of Mecca used their religious responsibility for the Kaʿba and for pilgrimage during the sacred months as a means of holding commercial markets in Mecca. It also helped them dominate internal and external trade and strengthen the position of the Meccan aristocracy. They did this in the name of protecting the rituals associated with the Kaʿba and providing the many services required by visiting pilgrims.

Those services even included literature, which was the highest form of cultural expression in pre-Islamic society.

In practical terms, the religious pilgrimage seasons were also trading seasons. At the same time, they became occasions for the public recitation of poetry.

This was especially true of the market of ʿUkāẓ,588 where poets and orators took part in something close to a public contest. A poet whose poem won the approval and admiration of the assembled delegations could become the star of the season. If he had previously been unknown, his reputation might suddenly spread across the peninsula and then pass into history.

This literary tradition encouraged poets to spend more time refining their poems and bringing them to a level worthy of public competition and pride.

It also helped create and develop traditions and rules of literary criticism. In other words, it produced another, more advanced form of aesthetic and intellectual awareness within pre-Islamic society.

Poetry recitals were already accompanied by acts of criticism. According to established custom, someone among the assembled delegations would be recognized as having the ability to judge the artistic quality of poetry.589 The audience would listen to his judgment after the recitation. That judgment could then become the basis of the poet’s fame, the spread of his work, and what we might call critical debate about the poetry of the season—and even about the judge’s decision itself.

Fifth — Oratory and Soothsaying as Cultural Markers

Like poetry, public speaking in pre-Islamic Arabia was at once an intellectual, artistic, and religious phenomenon. It also carries much the same historical evidence as pre-Islamic poetry.

Like the poet, the orator served as a spokesman for his people—that is, for his tribe. He defended them, praised them, challenged their enemies, and upheld the tribe’s values, positions, and established relationships.

But in the final period before Islam, some orators began to move in a direction similar to that of the soothsayers. They used speeches as a form of preaching and as a way of encouraging reflection on questions about the universe, society, and morality.

Their speeches therefore often relied on short phrases designed to make an immediate impact. The language was tightly rhetorical, with balanced and rhyming endings. It was compressed and forceful, using every resource available to the speaker to strike the listener’s ear and mind at once.

Perhaps the best-known example is the famous speech attributed to Quss ibn Sāʿida al-Iyādī. Tradition says that the Prophet heard Quss deliver it at the market of ʿUkāẓ, before the rise of Islam, while standing on the back of a “red camel.”

He began:

“People, gather together. Listen, and understand. Whoever lives will die. Whoever dies will pass away. And everything that is coming will come.”

He then continued:

“Clear signs: rain and vegetation; fathers and mothers; those who depart and those who come. Stars that move, seas that do not disappear, a roof raised high and a bed spread below. A dark night and a sky filled with constellations.

“Why do I see people die and never return? Are they satisfied and therefore remain where they are? Or are they being held there, asleep?”

ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said:

“In the pre-Islamic period, the poet stood above the orator because people had a greater need for poetry. Poetry preserved their achievements, increased their standing, struck fear into their enemies, glorified their horsemen, magnified the numbers of their fighting men, and answered the attacks of poets from other tribes.

“But when poetry and poets became numerous, when poets began to make money from their poetry, travel to the markets, and rush to attack people’s honor, the orator came to stand above the poet...”590

This account by ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ does not describe the historical reality accurately when it presents poetry and oratory as having occupied different ranks at different times.

It is not true that pre-Islamic Arabs needed poetry at one stage in a way that differed from their need for oratory at the same stage. Poetry and oratory performed essentially the same social function during the earlier period he is describing.

Even when poetry was “preserving their achievements, increasing their standing,” and doing all the other things he lists, oratory was doing much the same.

In the earlier pre-Islamic period, well before the rise of Islam, the artistic boundary between poetry and oratory had not yet become clearly defined. Naturally, then, their social functions were not sharply separated either.

There was certainly a functional difference between poetry and public speaking. But when did that difference become clear?

Only at a stage when poetic speech had developed into an art with rules distinct from those of public speaking. The difference was not simply a matter of outward form. Each art had to develop its own internal laws.

That stage came relatively late compared with the earlier period of pre-Islamic Arab society.

In other words, a clear distinction between the rules governing poetry and those governing oratory could appear only after a certain level of social and intellectual development had been reached.

At that point, poetry could emerge as an art based more strongly on personal impulses, aesthetic feeling, and suggestive forms of expression, while oratory could emerge as another kind of art based more strongly on objective intellectual aims, logical organization, and forms of expression whose meaning was comparatively direct.

None of this means, however, that ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ’s account is completely without historical value.

If we look past the story he tells on the surface, we can find something else in it: an indirect reflection of a real process of change that was beginning to appear in the culture of the period just before Islam.

I mean the development of the economic and social structures of Arabian society and, more specifically, the movement toward social relationships that were beginning to weaken the purely tribal basis of social conflict, institutions, and divisions.

As this change developed, the relationship between poetry and oratory also began to shift.

This change is what ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ saw when he said that poetry and poets had become too numerous, that poets had begun to make a living from poetry, travel to the markets, and attack people’s reputations.

But his description does not explain the phenomenon itself. It is only the form in which the phenomenon appeared to earlier observers.

The deeper change was that, during the general weakening of old tribal relationships, pre-Islamic poetry was beginning to move toward the individual existence of the poet. It was beginning to express the conflict between the poet as an individual personality and the control that tribal relationships exercised over that personality.

The poetry of the pre-Islamic outlaws was one expression of the beginnings of this conflict.

At the same time, the weakening of the old order was also appearing in public speaking.

In speeches such as those attributed to Quss ibn Sāʿida, we find a style that moves away from the traditional role of pre-Islamic oratory as a tool serving the interests of a single closed tribe. These newer speeches began to deal with questions broader than tribal relations—relations that were themselves beginning to lose the conditions that had once allowed them to dominate pre-Islamic society.

The historical conclusion we should draw from what ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ tells us is therefore twofold.

First, the change affected oratory as well as poetry.

Second, it reflected a change in the social foundations that shaped the direction of both arts and connected them to the wider movement of social and intellectual development.

Sixth — Mythology as a Cultural Marker

Mythology is another cultural marker that cannot reasonably be excluded from the study of any people’s culture. In ancient societies, it was closely connected with all the other forms of cultural life.

Mythology includes mythical or legendary images, stories, epics, characters, and symbols, whether simple or complex. Historically, it represents one form of human awareness at an early stage of its development within the wider process of social development.

Mythology expresses a stage at which human beings relied heavily on direct sensory awareness in their first attempts to explain the natural and social world.

But we need to be careful about what this means.

The sensory character of awareness at that early stage was very different from the role of the senses in more developed societies.

Sensory experience is a natural part of human awareness and one of its permanent capacities. Human beings continue to use it in creative activity—in literature and art, and even in other forms of knowledge—no matter how advanced their society becomes.

But this creative capacity itself develops as human history develops.

What we might call sensibility is a way of discovering and seeing, even when it takes the form of an unconscious kind of vision. Its power to discover and see grows as human knowledge and experience grow. In other words, it develops as the conscious mind accumulates knowledge and experience through the material and cultural development of society.

For this reason, the sensibility of a poet today is fundamentally different from that of a medieval poet. The sensibility of a medieval poet was, in turn, different from that of a poet in ancient times, including a poet in pre-Islamic Arabia.

A modern poet draws, even at the level of sensibility, on the accumulated knowledge of many historical periods and on an entire system of modern achievements. The modern poet therefore has a capacity for discovery and insight that cannot be compared with that available to poets in ancient societies.

We say all this because, when discussing mythology as one feature of pre-Islamic Arab culture, we need to recognize something very simple: it was perfectly natural for the Arabs of that period to have this historical form of awareness.

Their mythology reflected the strongly sensory character of awareness at that stage.

The Arabs were no exception among the peoples of the world. Like other peoples, they had a mythology in their ancient history. Pre-Islamic Arab mythology had its own distinctive features, shaped by the particular history of Arab society at the time.

Even mythical material borrowed from peoples with whom the Arabs came into contact took on the characteristics of the society of the Arabian Peninsula.

Pre-Islamic Arab mythology expressed the attempts of this particular kind of tribal society to reach beyond what could immediately be perceived by the senses and to explain features of the universe that people at the time could not yet explain rationally in any other way.

They looked, for example, at natural phenomena that had a powerful and direct effect on their lives: the changing seasons, the alternation between fertile years and drought, the movement of the sun and moon between day and night, the changing positions of the stars, and the apparent permanence of some stars in the same place.

They also faced questions that could not be reduced to directly observable physical things: poetic “inspiration,” death, the passing away of life, and the continuation of existence.

They were equally struck by events in tribal warfare, such as unexpected victories and defeats that could not be explained by what they had materially expected to happen.

Because they did not yet possess a developed rational framework for understanding such things, they explained them mainly through this immediate, sensory form of awareness.

Myths and legends gave expression to that way of seeing the world.

These explanations took the form of unseen beings such as jinn and devils. They said, for example, that every poet had a devil who inspired his poetry. They even assigned particular devils to particular poets, giving each one a name and a set of characteristics.591

They also told stories about the miraculous deeds of famous warriors.

And they sometimes explained great natural events by giving extraordinary powers to weak animals. One story, for example, said that the collapse of the Maʾrib Dam was caused by:

“red rats digging into the dam and searching with their feet, pulling loose a rock that a hundred men could not lift, and then pushing it away with the claws of their feet...”592

One striking feature of pre-Islamic Arab mythology is the way it gives a sensory and physical form to abstract meanings.

To express the idea of poetic inspiration, for example, people imagined it as a particular being: a “devil.” They then gave this devil human physical qualities—things that could be seen, touched, and heard.

Likewise, to express meanings such as heroism, terror, beauty, ugliness, cruelty, and so on, they might imagine a jinn, a female jinn, a ghoul, a saʿlā,593 or some similar being.

These beings did not exist as visible creatures in the ordinary world, of course. But in the mythological imagination, they were still given human qualities.

The same was true of the supernatural forces people imagined behind natural phenomena. They pictured these forces as living beings with bodies, emotions, desires, attitudes, and actions like those of human beings.

We can see this in the way they imagined relations among the heavenly bodies and the influence of those bodies on human life, in their worship of natural phenomena themselves,594 and in the relationships they imagined between themselves and the idols and sacred objects—the gods they had made with their own hands.595

This feature of pre-Islamic Arab mythology had a real historical basis in the level of development reached by human awareness at the time.

The consciousness of a polytheistic tribal community had not yet developed to the point where it could easily understand questions about the universe in purely abstract terms. It could not yet separate ideas and meanings completely from their physical and sensory connections with the world.

But this feature also had a history of its own, connected with the history of polytheism in the Arabian Peninsula.

The strongly sensory forms we still find in Arab mythology during the final pre-Islamic period were therefore a continuation of a much older tradition.

At the same time, however, a new development was beginning to appear in the period just before Islam. It would eventually move beyond this deeply rooted polytheistic outlook.

New features were beginning to emerge within pre-Islamic Arab awareness itself. They were developing at a pace that is striking even from our point of view today.

The most important of these changes was a movement toward a view of the world that went beyond immediate sensory forms and entered a limited realm of abstraction.

Naturally, this new development still appeared through mythological forms and remained mixed with older mythological traditions.

Its clearest expression was the way some pre-Islamic Arabs began to think about God.

Their understanding was beginning to move beyond the physical and sensory forms of polytheistic worship toward something more abstract: the idea of divinity as one God existing beyond the world of visible objects.

This gave idols a new position in pre-Islamic religious awareness.

During the final pre-Islamic period, this change also found expression in stories with mythological features about Abraham and his ḥanīf religion of one God. This religion stood in basic opposition to the old polytheism, with its many gods and idols corresponding to the many tribal units that made up pre-Islamic “society.”

Historical study makes it clear that such stories began to circulate among the pre-Islamic Arabs at the same time that the group known as the ḥanīfs was emerging as a new voice.

The ḥanīfs opposed the religious face of pre-Islamic polytheism, including its rituals and forms of worship, and called instead for the religion of Abraham: belief in the one and only God.

This particular development in pre-Islamic awareness was limited and partial, and several factors contributed to it.

Among the most important was the spread of Jewish and Christian beliefs in the main population and economic centers of northwestern Arabia during the sixth century CE, followed by their spread in southern centers as well.

But we must also recognize what was, in reality, the decisive factor: the historical change taking place in the economic and social foundations of pre-Islamic society itself.

Both internal and external forces were creating the material and cultural conditions for this transformation.

The logical outcome was the breaking apart of a society made up of separate tribal units: scattered, closed in on themselves, and caught in destructive struggles for the bare minimum needed to survive—a form of survival that was barely survival at all.

The movement toward breaking apart these separate tribal structures was, in its real historical meaning, a dialectical process of destruction and construction at the same time.

Plurality was moving toward unity.

A new society would emerge within a single unifying framework. Across its vast territory, different peoples, cultures, experiences, capacities, and historical traditions would meet and interact.

The society toward which change was already pointing in the final pre-Islamic period would therefore be a society marked by diversity within unity, rather than by the old fragmentation into separate tribal worlds.

E — Signs of Rational Thought among the Pre-Islamic Arabs

1 — The Nature of Arab Thought

We would not normally raise the question in this form. Scientific thinking does not allow us to speak so absolutely about the fixed “nature” of a people’s thought.

But a number of Muslim and European researchers, both earlier and modern, studied certain features of Arab thought at one particular stage of history and then treated those features as permanent racial characteristics.

They took characteristics produced by one historical period and applied them to Arab thought throughout its entire history.

This is the problem.

The characteristics of thought among any people or nation reflect the conditions created by the real circumstances of that people’s life. And because the lives of peoples and nations move, change, and develop, the forms of thought that reflect those lives must also move, change, and develop.

They cannot remain fixed and unchanged through every stage of history.

To put the problem more precisely, some researchers looked at Arab thought during the pre-Islamic period and found characteristics that matched the historical conditions of that period. They then concluded that these characteristics defined the nature of Arab thought for all time.

They turned limited judgments into absolute ones and treated them as final truths.

Our objection is not really a defense of some supposed permanent “nature of Arab thought.”

The problem is the method itself.

For us, this is first of all a question of how historical research should be done.

The Andalusian judge Ṣāʿid al-Andalusī596 wrote in his Categories of Nations, after discussing “the knowledge of the Arabs in their pre-Islamic period”:

“As for the science of philosophy, God Almighty granted them nothing of it, nor did He make their natural character suited to taking an interest in it. I know of no one of pure Arab descent who became famous for it except Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī597 and Abū Muḥammad al-Ḥasan al-Hamdānī.”598

Quite apart from making God the sole source of knowledge, this passage shows us Ṣāʿid’s method.

He begins with the fact that pre-Islamic Arabs did not know philosophy and then turns this into a general judgment about the whole Arab people and their supposed inability to acquire philosophical knowledge.
