We know that he generalizes in this way because he carries the same judgment forward as far as the ninth century, in the case of al-Kindī, and the tenth century, in the case of al-Hamdānī.

Al-Shahrastānī writes in Religions and Sects when discussing philosophy among different nations:

“Among them are the sages of the Arabs, but they are few. Most of their wisdom consists of spontaneous flashes of natural insight and passing thoughts, and at times they spoke of prophecy.”

We do not agree with Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq’s view that al-Shahrastānī is speaking here only about the Arabs before Islam.599

The context makes it clear that al-Shahrastānī is discussing the position of philosophy, or “wisdom,” among Arabs in general, as one of the various nations mentioned in his discussion.

Indeed, elsewhere ʿAbd al-Rāziq himself interprets al-Shahrastānī’s words in the same general way that we do. He writes:

“He”—meaning al-Shahrastānī—“described Arab nature in a way that made it close to abstract reflection and universal questions of the kind associated with philosophy. He then said that Arab sages were few and that most of their wisdom came through intuition and spontaneous expression, but he did not explain why their sages were so few despite this natural aptitude.”600

Aḥmad Amīn understood al-Shahrastānī’s remarks in the same way we do. Commenting on the passage quoted above, he writes: “Some Orientalists have observed that the Arab mind does not look at things in a general, comprehensive way, and is incapable of doing so. Some earlier Muslim authors had already noticed the same point. In al-Shahrastānī’s Religions and Sects, in the discussion of the sages...” Aḥmad Amīn then quotes the passage from al-Shahrastānī that we cited above, along with another passage making the same point.601

So even al-Shahrastānī, despite his major place among the great historians of philosophy, approached the question of Arab intellectual nature in this absolute and methodologically unsound way.

Before Ṣāʿid and al-Shahrastānī, we find similar judgments among earlier Arab writers such as Abū ʿUthmān al-Jāḥiẓ.

Al-Jāḥiẓ writes:

“Everything said by the Persians, and every idea produced by non-Arabs, comes only after long thought, effort, solitude, consultation, cooperation, extended reflection, study of books, the second man passing on the knowledge of the first, and the third adding to the knowledge of the second, until the fruits of all that thought accumulate in the last of them.

“But everything among the Arabs comes through immediate intuition and spontaneous expression, almost as if it were inspiration. There is no struggle, no forcing of the mind, no turning an idea over and over, and no need for assistance...”602

It is true that al-Jāḥiẓ means this as praise rather than criticism.

In his view, the Arabs are more intelligent than Persians and other peoples because they can grasp immediately, through quick intuition, what others reach only after long reflection.

But our concern here, as we have said, is methodological.

Al-Jāḥiẓ draws an absolute and final boundary between Arab and Persian thought. In doing so, he starts from a static, metaphysical way of thinking rather than a historical one.

Western writers produced similar judgments.

The famous French philosopher Ernest Renan, who died in 1892, wrote:

“It is both mistaken and misleading to call the Greek philosophy translated into Arabic ‘Arab philosophy,’ since no beginnings or foundations of this philosophy can be seen in the Arabian Peninsula...”

Renan begins his judgment about Arab philosophy from a false premise: that no beginnings or foundations for philosophy had appeared anywhere in the earlier history of the Arabian Peninsula.

His claim therefore includes the pre-Islamic period that we are studying here.

But this starting point cannot justify an absolute judgment about the nature of Arab thought in every historical period. Such a conclusion is incompatible with sound scientific research.

Renan’s broader judgments about the history of philosophy in general, and Arab philosophy in particular, were also based on his well-known theory distinguishing “Semitic thought” from “Aryan thought”—in other words, a racial theory that has since been disproved by science, and especially by Marxist science.603

Other Western scholars approached Arab philosophy from a similar starting point. They included De Boer in his History of Philosophy in Islam, L. Gauthier, Baron Carra de Vaux, and others.

They argued that what is called “Arab philosophy” was not really Arab because many of its leading figures were not of Semitic origin.604

2 — Through Everyday Experience

When we discussed pre-Islamic proverbs, we noted that they preserve some of the knowledge Arabs had at the time about nature and thought.

In reality, they accumulated this knowledge through direct experience.

But it was naturally scattered and unorganized because it arose from ordinary daily experience rather than from deliberate investigation aimed at gaining knowledge for its own sake.

People learned these things while responding to immediate and recurring practical needs in the normal course of life.

Once acquired, some of this knowledge could serve as a basis for analogy. People began to treat what they had learned as standards or general rules that could be applied to similar situations.

But this still did not amount to what we today call scientific knowledge.

Pre-Islamic knowledge lacked systematic induction, the organized drawing of conclusions, and the linking of separate results into a coherent scientific system.

This limitation was completely natural in its historical setting.

But it does not mean that the basic elements needed for the growth of a distinct pre-Islamic culture were absent.

For this reason, we think Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq was right when he wrote:

“Whatever the condition of the Arabs at the appearance of the Muhammadan religion, intellectually they were not at the level of the earliest and most simple human communities, at least in the area that concerns us here”—meaning the beginnings of philosophical thought—“as can be seen from what we know of their religions and what has been transmitted of their literary remains.”605

He also wrote:

“Whatever may be true, imaginary, or exaggerated in the reports about the sages and judges of the pre-Islamic Arabs, these reports still tell us something about the kind of thinking that the Arabs called wisdom and about the people whom they called sages and judges.

“It was practical thought, connected with deciding disputes that arose among them, giving judgments on problems they faced, and treating illnesses that affected them...”606

There was indeed a group among the Arabs whose level of culture was somewhat higher than that of the population around them.

These were the sages. Alongside the knowledge gained from experience, they preserved many sound proverbs and memorable sayings that circulated among followers of the different religions that had contact with the Arabian Peninsula in more than one region.607

Early Arab historians also wrote about the knowledge of the pre-Islamic Arabs.

Ṣāʿid al-Andalusī, writing in the eleventh century, said that they possessed knowledge:

“of the times when the stars rise and set, and of the stellar signs and the rains associated with them. They acquired this through close attention and long experience because they needed such knowledge for their livelihood, not because they were trying to learn the underlying truths or train themselves in the sciences.”608

This final point in Ṣāʿid’s statement reflects a sound historical method.

He explains pre-Islamic knowledge as the result of spontaneous experience arising from practical needs, not from a conscious attempt to pursue knowledge for its own sake.

That matches what we said earlier.

Ibn Khaldūn offers a similar explanation.

He argues that the Arabs in their early period, around the rise of Islam, did not possess the sciences that later flourished under Islamic rule because their society was still simple and largely Bedouin, and because teaching, authorship, and the systematic recording of knowledge had not yet developed among them.609

It is clear that Ibn Khaldūn does not explain the absence of organized scientific knowledge among the early Arabs by appealing to some permanent Arab racial nature.

He explains it through the conditions of their life at that particular stage of history.

In this respect, Ibn Khaldūn is using a scientific method of research.

3 — Rational Reflection

We now come to the way pre-Islamic Arabs approached questions of knowledge.

Did their thinking contain any genuine rational reflection?

Or did they simply accumulate information from everyday experience in response to the practical needs of daily life?

The first thing that draws our attention is that the words “wisdom” and “sages” were widely used in pre-Islamic Arabia.

The word “wisdom” was used for a particular kind of speech found in the work of poets such as Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā, especially in his famous Muʿallaqa, and in the speeches of people such as Quss ibn Sāʿida al-Iyādī and the soothsayers.

The term was also applied to the behavior and judgments of people who were known at the time as “sages.”

Among them were al-Ḥārith ibn Kalada al-Thaqafī and his son al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith.

People turned to such figures when immediate problems arose in their lives.

They acted much like judges in settling disputes. They applied rules handed down through social custom to new situations. They also advised individuals and guided them toward what they regarded as good social behavior.

Aḥmad Amīn believed that the Arab “sages” represented the most intellectually advanced group among them.610

If we then look at how the meanings of “wisdom” and “sage” developed after Islam, and especially after the rise of philosophy, we find something suggestive.

“Wisdom” eventually came to mean philosophy itself, while “sage” came to mean philosopher.611

This gives us some reason to think that even in the pre-Islamic period, these words referred to an early and simple form of rational reflection.

It was still spontaneous and unsystematic, but it attempted to draw general judgments from individual cases and then apply those judgments to later situations by analogy.

This kind of thinking already involves the use of reason.

It takes something general from particular cases through a basic act of abstraction. Then it brings that general rule back to a new particular case and applies it there.

That too is a form of rational reflection.

Pre-Islamic thought, however, did not yet carry out this process with a conscious understanding of the separate steps involved.

If we return here to the dialectical relationship between language and human life, we can once again draw a clear conclusion. The words “wisdom” and “sages,” in the developed sense discussed above, could not have existed in the language of the pre-Islamic Arabs—or been used as they were—unless those Arabs had actually possessed some degree of what we have called rational thought.

Of course, we do not mean that this kind of rational thinking had developed beyond what the historical conditions of their society could support. Nor do we mean that rational thought in the pre-Islamic period had already reached the level of philosophy.

One example of this early form of rational thinking may be found in the following observation:

“The Arabs’ long experience of herding livestock drew them away from medicine based on divination and superstition and brought them closer to medicine based on practical experience. They observed pregnancy, birth, growth, and the various biological stages connected with them. They dissected bodies and gained some knowledge of the location of the organs and the functions those organs performed in the animal body. As a result, they came reasonably close to explaining the causes of illness and recovery.”612

What interests us here is the final point: their attempt to explain illness and recovery. This is in itself an act of reasoning. It uses the results of direct sensory experience to draw broader conclusions.

Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq noticed something even clearer and more specific. He wrote that, at the time Islam appeared, the Arabs were already engaging in “forms of rational inquiry that came close to philosophical investigation, since they dealt with questions beyond the physical world: the nature of God, whether the world was eternal or created, souls, angels, jinn, and similar matters.” He also says that when the Qur’an was being revealed, the Arabs were already “arguing and debating religious beliefs,” and that questions such as the sending of prophets, life after death, and the resurrection of the dead were especially disputed among the different religious groups.613

Al-Maqrīzī, Taqī al-Dīn Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī (d. 845 AH/1441 CE), also makes a revealing observation on this subject. He writes:

“The name ‘philosophers’ is applied to certain groups in India, including the naturalists and the Brahmins. They practice severe forms of spiritual discipline and deny prophecy altogether. The name is also applied to the Arabs, though in a lesser sense. Their wisdom comes from their own reflections and from observing nature. They accept prophecy, but they are weaker in the sciences. Among the philosophers are also the sages of the Greeks, who fall into several groups: the early pillars of wisdom, the Peripatetics, the Stoics, the followers of Aristotle, and the philosophers of Islam.”614

By “the Arabs, though in a lesser sense,” al-Maqrīzī means the Arabs before Islam. Two things make this clear. First, he says that “their wisdom comes from their own reflections and from observing nature,” a description that fits the pre-Islamic Arabs. Second, he separately mentions “the philosophers of Islam” at the end of the passage. So the word “Arabs” in the earlier sentence clearly does not include philosophers of the Islamic period.

Al-Maqrīzī therefore believed that the Arabs before Islam had their own “philosophers,” though in his view they deserved the name less fully than others. He also gave a sound and realistic explanation for why this was so.

We would not, of course, go as far as al-Maqrīzī and call the pre-Islamic Arabs “philosophers.” But his comments do support the conclusion that some degree of rational inquiry existed among them. What he called “philosophy” is what interests us here.

F — Religious Phenomena in Pre-Islamic Society

1 — Religion as a Social Phenomenon

Before discussing the religious phenomena of the pre-Islamic period, we need to establish an important fact.

Religion, whatever form its beliefs and teachings take in different periods, does not suddenly appear among people in isolation from their earthly lives. It is not cut off from the historical development of their society, economy, politics, or ideas. Nor does religion arise simply because individuals want it to.

Hegel made this point in his Lectures on the History of Philosophy when discussing the relationship between religion and philosophy. He was responding to those who claimed that religion arose from tyranny and anger, or from priests who deliberately deceived the people for selfish purposes.

Hegel was right to reject this view. Religion cannot be explained as the product of a private desire on the part of one group of people, whether priests or anyone else.

Religion has its own social roots. It also has roots in the development of human knowledge. The history of human thought and the history of religion show that religious belief and human knowledge have always influenced one another.615

For forces that oppose progress, however, it is very important to present religion as something separate from its social roots, and especially as something completely detached from class struggle.

Within this same ideological outlook, many historians of Islam, both old and modern, have worked hard to present Islam, first, as the beginning of a completely new history for the Arabs, entirely disconnected from their life before Islam. In this view, everything Islam brought—its teachings, beliefs, concepts, and laws—had no connection at all with the Arabs’ earlier past, whether recent or remote.

Second, these historians have tried to make the history of Arab thought begin with the rise of Islam, as though the Arabs had possessed no earlier intellectual or cultural heritage worth mentioning. Islam is made to look as though it created the Arabs from nothing.

This view of Islam, and of Arab history before Islam, is wrong in three ways. First, it contradicts historical reality. Second, it is opposed to scientific knowledge. Third, it conflicts with Islam’s own texts, teachings, and laws.

It contradicts reality because a large body of historically and scientifically reliable evidence shows that Arab history before and after Islam forms one continuous history. Everything that appeared openly or beneath the surface of Arab society after the rise of Islam was part of the further development616 of conditions that already existed during the pre-Islamic period, especially in its final stage during the sixth and early seventh centuries.

This view is also opposed to science because everything we know from the study of social and cultural development rules out the idea that religion can suddenly appear in a society, at a particular moment, from outside that society’s history and outside the wider course of human development.

Social science, when it studies the objective and dialectical patterns of human history, shows that every religion arose as an incomplete reflection, in people’s ideas and beliefs, of the social relationships that existed at a particular stage of history.

It is therefore wrong to explain the appearance of any religion as an event cut off from the concrete course of human life on earth. No religion in human history has appeared at a level beyond the concrete social relations of the society in which it arose.

So we return to our earlier point: every religion that has appeared in history has had social roots in the part of the world where it emerged. It has also had roots in the development of human knowledge and experience.

Finally, the view of Islam described above also conflicts with Islam’s own texts and teachings. Those texts preserve many features of pre-Islamic Arab history, customs, traditions, and laws. Islam kept some of them, changed others, and rejected those that could no longer survive alongside the new social relations already beginning to emerge within pre-Islamic society itself, as we explained earlier in this chapter.

2 — Paganism

Of all the religious phenomena found in Arab society shortly before the rise of Islam, paganism was the most widespread and had the deepest historical roots.

As the earliest form of religion in human history, and as the most basic expression of religious belief, paganism can be traced far back into Arab history.

We still lack scientifically accepted evidence that would allow us to date its beginnings precisely. But we can go back at least to the period of the Sabaean state in Yemen, which dates to around the eighth century BCE.

Modern excavations uncovered the remains of a theatre connected to a large temple, together with an impressive set of terraces. Archaeologists were able to identify this great structure as the “Temple of the Sun” and to establish that it belonged to the Sabaean state. This means that the people of Yemen under that state worshipped the sun.617

Paganism continued after that in different forms throughout the Arabian Peninsula, down to the sixth century and the period immediately before Islam.

At some point, however, the historical development of the people of the peninsula suffered a break for reasons that remain unclear. Historians mention among the possible causes the collapse of the Maʾrib Dam in Yemen, which had been built by the Ḥimyarite state. Its collapse caused a great flood that drowned farmland, displaced the population, and forced many people to migrate beyond the peninsula to Syria, Palestine, and elsewhere. This is the flood known as the “Flood of al-ʿArim,”618 which is also mentioned in the Qur’an,619 as the historical accounts tell us.

This break in history interrupted the earlier course of development in the peninsula.

As a result, from the first centuries CE until the sixth century, we see a kind of cultural regression. The development achieved under the Sabaean, Minaean, and Ḥimyarite states did not continue along the same upward path. A primitive communal system and a largely nomadic way of life came to dominate, until the later pre-Islamic period, when the first signs of class division began to appear.

This helps explain why very early forms of pagan religion were still present so late in Arab history—for example, the placing of idols in the Kaaba as symbols of gods and objects of worship.

We have already seen that idol worship around the Kaaba eventually acquired a class character. The Quraysh leadership used it as a means of maintaining control, exploiting others, and making profits.

Alongside these forms of paganism, however, there were others resembling the religions of the more developed ancient Arabs of Yemen. As we have seen, these included the worship of heavenly bodies such as the sun, moon, and Venus, as well as other cosmic and natural phenomena.

There was also some fire worship among certain tribes. This may have reached them through contact with the Zoroastrians of Persia, given their geographical proximity and commercial relations.

The Qur’an620 also refers to tendencies within pre-Islamic pagan belief that departed from the dominant religious outlook. One of these is the tendency Islamic writers call the Dahriyya. The Qur’anic passages suggest that these people either denied creation and a Creator, denied only life after death, or denied prophecy alone.

In pre-Islamic usage, dahr means time. Their use of this term, together with other expressions carrying a similar meaning, seems to have reflected their belief in fate.621

3 — Judaism and Christianity

Although paganism was the most visible form of religion in the Arabian Peninsula during the sixth century, Judaism and Christianity also had a strong presence in some areas.

It appears that both religions first entered among tribes living in the northwestern regions bordering Syria and Palestine, where Arab populations also lived.

The first major centre of Judaism inside the peninsula was Yathrib and the surrounding areas of the Hijaz.622 From there it spread into Yemen,623 where it became so firmly established that by the beginning of the sixth century it had become the religion of the state.624

Judaism then played a visible role in the conflict between the Ḥimyarites and the Abyssinians.

Most historians describe this conflict as though it were purely religious—a struggle between Judaism and Christianity. But although it took a religious form, it was in essence a political conflict between the rulers of Abyssinia and the Ḥimyarites.625

After the sea route across the Indian Ocean between India and Africa had been discovered, the Ḥimyarites began using it for maritime trade from some time after the first century CE. This trade grew under their control, and they eventually built towns along the Red Sea coast in response to its expansion.

These Yemeni coastal towns became transit points for valuable goods bound for Byzantium.

At the same time, Byzantine influence was spreading in Abyssinia alongside Christianity. The Byzantines began to seek control of Yemen’s strategic commercial position.

As so often happens when religion is used in the service of political ambition, the Abyssinians began attacking Ḥimyarite positions in Yemen in the name of Christianity, while in reality serving Byzantine political aims. Religion was also used to win the Christians of Yemen over as allies of Abyssinia.

The Ḥimyarites responded by encouraging the spread of Judaism in their own country.626 Judaism therefore also became a political weapon, used against Christianity because Christianity had become an instrument of Abyssinian policy.

The struggle for control of Yemen continued in the name of Christianity and Judaism into the sixth century.

At that point, Dhū Nuwās, king of Ḥimyar, began persecuting Christians and seizing their property and wealth. The Abyssinians used this as a reason for military intervention in Yemen in 525 CE. They defeated Dhū Nuwās’s army, and he killed himself by riding his horse into the sea and drowning.627

This brought the last Jewish political authority in Yemen to an end, although Judaism itself remained deeply rooted there.

The Jews of Yemen are known to have been Arabs by origin who adopted Judaism as a result of this earlier political history. This is why they spoke Arabic rather than Hebrew.628

With their victory, the Abyssinians achieved one of their main goals: the occupation of Yemen and control of the great trade route known since ancient times as the “Incense Route.”

But their ambitions did not end there.

Toward the end of the sixth century, under Abraha al-Ashram, their governor in Yemen, they sought to occupy Mecca, which had by then become the most important commercial centre in the region.

Abraha personally led a military expedition against Mecca and used elephants for transport. For this reason, the Arabs called the year of the Abyssinian attack the “Year of the Elephant.”

But as Abraha’s army reached the approaches to Mecca, it was suddenly struck by an outbreak of smallpox that caused terrible losses. Abraha returned to Sanaa defeated.

Islamic historians generally hold that the Year of the Elephant was also the year in which Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the future prophet of Islam, was born.629

The Abyssinian campaign against Mecca was therefore one more episode in the struggle for political control, rooted above all in economic interests.

Yet Muslim chroniclers usually explain it in purely religious terms.

The Abyssinians’ defeat led the conflict to enter a new stage involving new powers.

Khosrow Anūshirwān (531–578 CE), the Persian king at the time, took advantage of the weakness that the Abyssinians suffered in Yemen after this defeat. He moved to seize the opportunity and establish Persian control over this strategic part of the peninsula.

His aim was helped by the fact that the Arabs of Yemen had already rebelled against Abyssinian rule under the leadership of Sayf ibn Dhī Yazan. The Yemeni leader appealed to Khosrow Anūshirwān for help.

Khosrow immediately took advantage of the situation. He assembled an army and sent it across the “Persian” Gulf to Yemen.630

The result was that the Abyssinian occupiers were driven out, only to be replaced by Persian occupiers. Persian rule continued until the rise of Islam, when the Muslims expelled the Persians and Yemen once again became an Arab-Islamic territory.631

4 — The Ḥunafāʾ

Christianity and Judaism therefore competed in this part of the Arabian Peninsula in the service of political ambitions expressed in religious terms.

But this describes only one side of the Jewish-Christian presence in pre-Islamic Arabia. There was another side as well, connected with the development of religious thought.

The presence of these two religions helped change religious awareness in the peninsula by encouraging a more abstract way of thinking about existence, one that moved beyond the simple, sensory outlook of pagan religion.

Pagan ideas and Jewish and Christian ideas about the existence of the world had lived side by side for a long time. It was therefore natural for them to influence one another and for debates to spread about creation, God, the nature of God, resurrection, the Last Judgment, and prophecy.

Over time, this long interaction left its mark on people’s thinking.

Eventually, a group appeared within pre-Islamic society whose position on these great questions of existence differed from all three established religious positions. They were neither pagan nor Jewish nor Christian. Instead, they developed a distinct and reflective outlook.

This was a sign that something new was beginning to emerge from within the old order itself.

Such a group did in fact appear during the final period before Islam. It emerged from among those whom pre-Islamic society knew as “sages.” Its members rejected idol worship and the belief in many gods and called instead for belief in one God, but without adopting the specifically Jewish or Christian approach to religion.632

These were the people known as the Ḥunafāʾ, or Aḥnāf.

We have already referred several times in this chapter to what we called the phenomenon of the Ḥunafāʾ shortly before Islam.

Who were these people? Why were they called Ḥunafāʾ? What exactly did they believe? Did they add a new religion to those already found among the pre-Islamic Arabs?

Arab chroniclers and Muslim commentators give the following names as members of this group:

Quss ibn Sāʿida al-Iyādī, Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt, Arbāb ibn Riʾāb, Suwayd ibn ʿĀmir al-Muṣṭaliqī, Asʿad Abū Karib al-Ḥimyarī, Wakīʿ ibn Salama ibn Zuhayr al-Iyādī, ʿUmayr ibn Jundab al-Juhanī, ʿAdī ibn Zayd al-ʿIbādī, Abū Qays Ṣirma ibn Abī Anas, Sayf ibn Dhī Yazan, Waraqa ibn Nawfal633 al-Qurashī, ʿĀmir ibn al-Ẓarib al-ʿAdwānī, ʿAbd al-Ṭābikha ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Wabara ibn Quḍāʿa, ʿAllāf ibn Shihāb al-Tamīmī, al-Mutalammis ibn Umayya al-Kinānī, Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā, Khālid ibn Sinān ibn Ghayth al-ʿAbsī, ʿAbd Allāh al-Quḍāʿī, ʿUbayd ibn al-Abraṣ al-Asadī, and Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib.634

According to the Arab chroniclers, most of these people lived during the final years before Islam, while some also lived into the first years of the Islamic period.

Yet those same chroniclers say that some of them became Christians, including ʿAdī ibn Zayd al-ʿIbādī and Arāb ibn Riʾāb. They also claim that others lived centuries before the final pre-Islamic period.635

Their accounts of the beliefs of these individuals also show that they did not all hold exactly the same opinions. Nor were they linked together or in regular contact. In other words, they did not form an organized group united by a common movement or shared activity.636

This means that the only thing clearly shared by all these “Ḥunafāʾ” was one broad principle. Independently of one another, and often without even knowing one another, they rejected idol worship and belief in many gods and accepted the existence of one God.

Beyond that, the chroniclers give us no clear picture of what they believed, either collectively or individually.

There is, however, one other subject the sources discuss besides this general religious principle: their way of life and moral conduct.

The chroniclers tell us that these Ḥunafāʾ “kept away from other people; some wandered through the land searching for the ḥanīf religion of Abraham; some had read and understood the revealed scriptures; they reflected on the universe; they avoided wine and shameful acts; and they advised people to stay away from idols and draw closer to God.”637

But we do not know how they could have “kept away from other people” while at the same time wandering through the land in search of the religion of Abraham. Where would the religion of Abraham have been found if not among people and within human society?

What we can still take from these reports is that some of the “sages” of the pre-Islamic period were looking for a way of understanding the world that differed both from paganism and from Judaism and Christianity.

They reflected on the universe and tried to follow a moral way of life that matched their intellectual convictions.

As for the name Ḥunafāʾ, the writings of Arab chroniclers and the research of Orientalists638 suggest that the term was already known among the Arabs before Islam and was used for this particular group of sages.

The term appears, both in the singular and the plural, in many Qur’anic verses.639 These passages suggest that the existence of the Ḥunafāʾ before Islam was taken for granted. They also indicate that the basic meaning of the term, as applied to the group’s religious position, involved two things: first, a complete rejection of paganism; and second, a departure from established Jewish and Christian beliefs.640

A scientific historical approach to the question of the Ḥunafāʾ does not need to depend on the exact individuals named by the chroniclers, whose lists are often confused and inconsistent. Nor does it depend on which of those figures supposedly became Christian, or which are said to have lived long before the final pre-Islamic period.

The same applies to doubts about whether some of the people listed among the Ḥunafāʾ even existed as described. Quss ibn Sāʿida is one example. There are also doubts about poems and other sayings attributed to figures such as Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt.

The scientific question does not depend on resolving every one of these disputed details.

What matters is not whether this or that named person really belonged to the Ḥunafāʾ, or whether a particular saying was truly his.

It might even be proved that none of the specific people listed by the chroniclers actually belonged to this group. The larger historical question would still remain.

That question is the appearance, during this particular period shortly before Islam, of a distinct religious current known as the Ḥunafāʾ.

The chroniclers may have confused the names. They may wrongly have called some of these individuals Ḥunafāʾ. They may have attributed sayings to them that they never uttered.

But it is much harder to believe that the chroniclers simply invented, without any basis in historical reality, the existence of the group itself—a group that represented a current, or a phenomenon, of social change taking place within religious consciousness during the final pre-Islamic period.

The essential historical question is the appearance of this current at precisely that time.

There is little reason to think that Muslim storytellers and chroniclers simply invented it.

One indication is that later scholars, especially Orientalists, do not seem to have seriously entertained that possibility—even those who regularly doubted or challenged almost everything Muslim writers recorded about the history of the Arabs before Islam.

On the contrary, the Orientalists who studied the Ḥunafāʾ generally took their historical existence in the pre-Islamic period for granted.641

Some therefore concentrated on the origin of the word ḥanīf and tried to discover where the pre-Islamic Arabs had taken the term from when they used it for those who called for belief in one God shortly before Islam.

Others tried to prove that the pre-Islamic Ḥunafāʾ were actually a group of Arab Christian ascetics.642

The historical evidence, then, does not deny that this phenomenon existed. It supports it.

But even if we had no such written evidence, the logic of history itself would still require us to recognize the phenomenon.

The rise of the Ḥunafāʾ was a natural result of the changes taking place in sixth-century pre-Islamic society, especially in its economic and social relations.

There was also the factor mentioned earlier: the long interaction, within religious consciousness, between pagan views of the world and Jewish-Christian ones.

We should neither ignore this factor nor underestimate its role in producing a phenomenon such as the Ḥunafāʾ.

But even this religious interaction—how deeply it affected people, how quickly its influence spread, and the direction that influence took—was itself shaped, ultimately, by the decisive development of economic and social relations.

Those material changes helped determine the direction taken by changes in other areas of human consciousness, even when the connection worked through indirect and largely invisible mechanisms.

We have already seen that, toward the end of the pre-Islamic period, social development was beginning to break apart the fragmented tribal framework and move toward a broader form of unity capable of containing new and more developed social conflicts.

Signs of this movement could already be seen in many parts of pre-Islamic life and at different levels.

First, tribal relations were beginning to move toward large alliances643 between groups of tribes, instead of remaining divided into small isolated units, each tribe fragmented further into clans and sub-clans.

These larger alliances necessarily meant that something deeper was changing in the old idea of narrow, closed tribal independence.

Previously, every tribal unit, however small, had strongly defended its separate independence in order to preserve its internal cohesion and the purity of its own traditions.

Once those same units began entering wider alliances that brought together many tribes and clans, they were giving up part of the old meaning of “independence.”

That, in turn, was one sign of the rapid breakdown of the primitive tribal system.

Second, two major events occurred in the peninsula within a relatively short period before the rise of Islam.

The first was the political conflict in Yemen. After Abraha’s failed Abyssinian campaign against Mecca, this conflict acquired a new historical meaning. It became a struggle between local forces within Yemen and outside powers that either already occupied the country, as the Abyssinians did, or hoped to occupy it, as the Persians did.

The conflict, together with the events leading up to it and the results that followed, created an objective basis for a shared sense that the traditional system of tribal relations had to be reconsidered.

That old system rested on fragmentation: separate, closed, neighbouring tribal units, each existing largely on its own.

The need to rethink those relations began to appear in greater cooperation in the face of external dangers. Most of the peninsula’s inhabitants increasingly had reason to fear that those dangers could eventually reach them as well unless they found a new form of social organization capable of resisting them.

The struggle between the Persian and Roman empires for direct control over the peninsula’s strategically important areas grew more intense after Persia took Yemen from the Abyssinians. The danger that foreign conquest might spread into new parts of Arabia therefore became increasingly clear.

The second major event was the famous Battle of Dhū Qār in 609 CE.644

This battle was the clearest expression of that shared feeling that a new kind of relationship was needed among the different tribes of the peninsula, especially those living near the frontier zones of the two competing empires, Persia and Rome.

Some modern writers describe this shared feeling as a form of “national consciousness.”645

In the modern scientific sense of the term, this description is historically premature. Even so, it is not entirely removed from the reality of the period.646

The Battle of Dhū Qār expressed more than the shared feeling just described.

It also showed that the many different changes taking place throughout the peninsula before Islam were beginning to move in a common direction.

If the report is true that Muḥammad, the future prophet of Islam, witnessed the battle and later said of Dhū Qār, “This was the first day on which the Arabs gained redress against the non-Arabs, and through me they were victorious,”647 then his use of the terms “Arabs” and “non-Arabs” for the two sides gives the battle an almost decisive historical meaning.

That meaning came from the nature of the changes then taking place throughout the region.

The general movement of events was beginning to produce, in embryonic form, an Arab society in a qualitative sense, rather than simply the quantitative collection of separate tribal groups that had made up “pre-Islamic society.”

What, after all, had pre-Islamic “society” been if not the numerical sum of separate tribal units?

And even if we assume that Muḥammad himself never said, “This was the first day on which the Arabs gained redress against the non-Arabs,” and that the saying actually came from another Arab of the same period, the point would remain.

The statement itself, made around the time of the battle, would still show that the victorious side at Dhū Qār was beginning to be understood as “the Arabs,” rather than simply as a collection of tribes that had gathered together to confront the “non-Arabs.”

It would also suggest that when Islam later gave the peninsula a means of unification, it did so at a particular historical moment because the peninsula’s need for unity had itself become historically mature.

It was within this historical setting that the phenomenon of the Ḥunafāʾ appeared at the level of religious consciousness.

At that level, the Ḥunafāʾ represented another mature expression of the same wider transformation.

But to understand this properly, we should also look at several religious developments that came before the Ḥunafāʾ or appeared alongside them.

These developments took place within pagan religion itself. They can be seen as streams flowing into the broader historical movement toward unity during the final period before Islam.

We find them in a number of developments.

First, groups of tribes began sharing the worship of the same idol.

For example, the tribes of Khathʿam, Bajīla, Bāhila, Daws, Azd al-Sarāt, Hawāzin, al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb, Jurm, Zubayd, al-Ghawth ibn Murr ibn Udd, and Banū Hilāl ibn ʿĀmir all worshipped the idol known as Dhū al-Khalaṣa.648

Similarly, the tribes of Quḍāʿa, Lakhm, Judhām, ʿĀmila, and Ghaṭafān all worshipped the idol known as al-Uqayṣir.649

Second, a practical system had developed for organizing the pagan pilgrimage seasons in Mecca.

Different responsibilities were divided among the economically and religiously powerful Meccan leaders. These included feeding pilgrims, guarding the Kaaba, supplying water, and carrying out other practical duties connected with the pilgrimage.

The tribes of the region, especially those of the north, were also expected to observe certain common rules during the pilgrimage.

Among these was a voluntary ban on warfare during the religious seasons. This ban applied to three particular months, known under this arrangement as the sacred months—months that had to be respected and in which fighting was forbidden.

Economic, social, cultural, and religious relations all came together in these practices and influenced one another. The result was a growing degree of real integration within the wider movement toward the formation of a new state.

The seasonal markets held during the pilgrimage were among the most active and effective parts of this whole process.

Taken together, these developments within pagan religion were closely connected with changes in social life.

They were the result of a historical process then moving toward the breakdown of the old, fragmented tribal framework and toward the transformation of the loose numerical collection of pre-Islamic tribes into an Arab society in the fuller, qualitative sense.

The rise of the Ḥunafāʾ was a real historical product of this same process.

As far as we can reconstruct its main features, the Ḥanīf movement did more than simply move beyond the fragmented tribal framework. At the level of religious consciousness, it challenged that framework at its very roots.

Its call for the rejection of idols and belief in one God was also a rejection of the pagan religious basis of tribal fragmentation.

Paganism had originally reflected a divided tribal consciousness. Its many gods corresponded to a human world divided among separate communities.

The many gods of pagan religion make sense historically because ancient people themselves lived within many separate and closed human communities—nomadic, rural, or urban—during the earliest stages of social development.

Seen in this way, the Ḥunafāʾ’s rejection of idols and their call for belief in one God also implied a rejection of the social foundation on which the entire pagan view of the world had been built.

This is precisely why we give the Ḥunafāʾ such importance as a major link in the transition from the pre-Islamic period to the Islamic one.

Yet in some ways they resemble a “missing link” in the history of human development.

As one writer puts it:

“The picture drawn by the Qur’anic commentators and chroniclers of the beliefs of the Ḥunafāʾ is not clear. It is vague and blurred in many respects, and tells us more about their moral conduct than about their religion. It tells us nothing about what they believed concerning God, how they imagined Him, or how they worshipped Him...”650

Why is the picture of the Ḥunafāʾ’s beliefs so vague and incomplete?

The question becomes even more pressing when we consider reports that many of them could read and write, and that some had studied the “scrolls,” the “Book of Luqmān,” and the “revealed scriptures.”651

Reports like these seem to open a window for the researcher, only for the view beyond it to disappear once again into uncertainty.

What were these “scrolls”? What was the “Book of Luqmān”? And which “revealed scriptures” were these Ḥunafāʾ reading and, as the reports seem to imply, drawing their beliefs from?

The word “scrolls” was used by the pre-Islamic Arabs in several different senses and was not limited to religious writings.

The Qur’an itself uses the term without always specifying what writings are meant. In one place they are described as “purified,”652 and in another as “honoured.”653

The Qur’anic commentators say that the first description refers to the pages of the Qur’an,654 while the second refers more generally to the pages of revealed scriptures.655

Other Qur’anic verses identify them more specifically, as in: “Has he not been told what is in the Scrolls of Moses?”656

But the Qur’anic verses that mention the Ḥunafāʾ deny that they were Jews or Christians.657

So Jewish and Christian scriptures cannot have been the source of their beliefs.

Does that mean the reports are referring to the pages of the Qur’an?

That cannot be right either, since the Ḥunafāʾ belonged to the period before the Qur’an appeared.

As for the “Book of Luqmān,” we have no historical evidence that allows us to know what it contained or to learn anything new from it about the Ḥunafāʾ.

In fact, everything we know about Luqmān himself658 and about this supposed book only adds another layer of uncertainty.

There is, however, one small point that may offer some light. At first it seems unrelated to the Ḥunafāʾ, but we will try to show that it may not be so distant from them.

A report tells us that Suwayd ibn al-Ṣāmit came to Mecca for pilgrimage or ʿumra. Muḥammad approached him and invited him to Islam.

Suwayd replied, “Perhaps what you have is like what I have.”

Muḥammad asked, “What do you have?”

Suwayd replied, “The Book of Luqmān,” meaning the wisdom of Luqmān.

Muḥammad said, “Show it to me.”

Suwayd did so.

Muḥammad then said, “These are good words, but what I have is better: a Qur’an revealed to me by God. It is guidance and light.”

He then recited some of the Qur’an to Suwayd and invited him to Islam. Suwayd did not reject what he heard. He said, “This is good,” and then went on his way.659

There are several points of interest in this account.

First, Ibn al-Athīr explicitly tells us that the “Book of Luqmān” meant the wisdom of Luqmān. This “wisdom” was apparently not entirely distant from what Muḥammad himself was teaching after his public mission had begun.

Second, Suwayd ibn al-Ṣāmit, although the chroniclers do not list him among the Ḥunafāʾ, had clearly broken with pre-Islamic paganism in much the same way they had. Otherwise, how could Muḥammad have described the sayings Suwayd showed him from the “wisdom of Luqmān” as good?

Third, we can draw a broader conclusion from this.

What we have called the phenomenon of the Ḥunafāʾ was probably not limited to the small number of named individuals listed by the chroniclers.

If it really was a broad historical phenomenon, then its meaning and influence must have extended beyond those particular people.

It may have appeared under the name of the “Book of Luqmān” or the “wisdom of Luqmān,” just as it appeared under the names “Ḥunafāʾ” and “Aḥnāf.” It may also have appeared under other names that we have not yet discovered.

It may likewise have expressed itself in different forms: speeches, poetry, or sayings of wisdom that circulated like proverbs.

And beyond all of this, its meaning and historical direction found their fullest expression in Islam itself, as the report from Ibn al-Athīr suggests through the words attributed to the founder of Islam.

If this phenomenon had developed so widely and had become so historically important, how did it leave its own period behind in such a “vague and blurred” form?

Why did this happen?

The answer is difficult.

But the question demands continued investigation, just as scholars have continued to search for the answer to the problem of the “missing link” in the history of human evolution.

5 — Religious Phenomena in the Qur’an

What we have seen so far shows that the religious phenomena of Arab society shortly before Islam reflected the particular historical relationship between pre-Islamic social reality and pre-Islamic social consciousness.

But in the phenomenon of the Ḥunafāʾ they also reflected a sign of historical change within religious consciousness itself.

In its real historical meaning, this change in religious consciousness was an almost direct expression of the transformation taking place in the material foundations of the old tribal system.

That system had reached a point where social conflict was beginning to emerge from within it. Differences in wealth and social position were widening inside individual tribes and across pre-Islamic society as a whole.

Seen in this way, the appearance of Islam within this society was clearly not a sudden event that descended upon it without any previous connection to the historical conditions already developing there.

The opposite is true.

The Islamic mission appeared specifically in Meccan society, where social conflicts had become sharper than in any other part of the peninsula.

This itself shows that Islam did not arise in a vacuum.

It arose because the objective conditions of pre-Islamic society had developed in a way that called for something new. The economic, social, and intellectual development of Arab society had reached a point at which Islam could emerge from that existing reality in its new form.

The Qur’an, as the central phenomenon of Islam, supports this analysis.

Throughout its surahs, especially those from the Meccan period, we find concrete images of all the phenomena described in this chapter.

Some appear through symbols and suggestion. Some take the form of concentrated or more extended instruction. Others appear as warnings of punishment in the next life or promises of reward.

We can therefore say that the religious phenomena discussed above were reflected in the Qur’an just as the other features of pre-Islamic Arab society were reflected in it.

We will now read several Qur’anic passages that give a direct picture of the different religions, tendencies, and beliefs found among the people of pre-Islamic Arabia in different parts of the peninsula.

  • Verses that mention Jews, Christians, Sabians, and Zoroastrians on the one hand, and those who associated other beings with God in worship on the other:

Those who believe, those who are Jews, the Sabians, the Christians, the Zoroastrians, and those who associate others with God—God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. (Surat al-Ḥajj, 22:17)

  • Verses that speak about the Dahriyya, meaning those who denied divine creation of the universe and resurrection after death:

They say, “There is nothing but this worldly life of ours. We die and we live, and nothing destroys us except time.” But they have no knowledge of this. They are only guessing. (Surat al-Jāthiya, 45:24)

  • Verses about people who accepted a Creator and believed that the world had been brought into existence, but denied resurrection and the return of the body after death:

He gives Us an example and forgets his own creation. He says, “Who will bring these bones back to life after they have decayed?” Say, “The One who created them the first time will bring them back to life, and He has full knowledge of every creation.” (Surat Yā Sīn, 36:78–79)

  • Verses about people who accepted divine creation and resurrection but rejected prophecy and worshipped idols on the grounds that these idols would act as intermediaries between them and God. Some of these people made pilgrimage to the idols at the Kaaba:

True religion belongs to God alone. As for those who take protectors besides Him, saying, “We worship them only so that they may bring us closer to God,” God will judge between them concerning what they disagree about. (Surat al-Zumar, 39:3)

Through passages like these, Islam itself shows how closely connected it was to the historical transformation discussed throughout this chapter.

That transformation was the process by which pre-Islamic Arab society was undergoing changes in the material foundations of its tribal system. One result of those changes was a shift in the way people understood the world.

The first chapter ends here.

Can we now say that we have succeeded in outlining the main features of one stage in the history of Arab thought660—a stage that stands at the beginning of the history we are trying to trace?

We call it a “beginning,” but not in the literal historical sense.

It was certainly not the first stage in the actual development of Arab thought.

It is only the earliest stage available to us because the stages that came before it have so far disappeared completely from the written, archaeological, and epigraphic record of Arab history, for reasons that have not yet been discovered.

PreviousChapter OneNextConclusions of Chapter One

Conclusions of Chapter One

1 — Social Development

From this chapter, we can draw several main conclusions about the level of social development in pre-Islamic society.

First: We have seen that the Arabs of the Arabian Peninsula before Islam were not isolated from the outside world.

Their geographical position in the middle of the civilized world of antiquity and the Middle Ages helped prevent such isolation.

The peninsula became an international bridge for trade. Through it, the peoples of East and West, Asia and Africa, exchanged natural and manufactured goods. Social, political, and cultural influences also moved back and forth across it.

Second: The great trade routes running through the peninsula from south to north and north to south created both material and cultural contact between the Arabs and peoples, communities, and states outside Arabia.

By the end of the sixth century CE, these contacts helped create the objective conditions for the breakdown of the primitive tribal system and its distinctive social structure.

At the same time, the first signs appeared of a new and more developed social order that could eventually replace the old nomadic tribal structure.

That old structure had already begun to weaken under the pressure of growing economic and social differences.

These differences appeared in nomadic areas, in settled and semi-settled farming regions, and especially in towns.

They were beginning to prepare the way for a new form of social division that would later develop into class division: first between the rich and poor within the tribe, and then between those who owned the means of production and those who did not.

Third: This social development had not yet matured enough to produce a state among the pre-Islamic Arabs.

But it had already produced the first seed of a state in Meccan society, which at the time was more developed than Arab society elsewhere in the peninsula.

This was mainly because trade and commercial wealth had become concentrated in Mecca, where private ownership was also becoming more clearly defined.

These developments led the wealthy leaders of Quraysh to organize themselves in order to protect their interests and regulate their material relations with other groups in Mecca and with the inhabitants of the peninsula more generally.

From this emerged an early political organization known historically as Dār al-Nadwa.

Arab historians have compared it with the council of elders in Athens, who gathered in the assembly known as the Ekklesia to discuss public affairs.661

2 — Intellectual Development

This social development was clearly reflected in the different forms of culture that could arise in a society living under such historical conditions.

These forms of culture, however, did not all develop to the same degree, and they did not all reflect social reality in the same way.

The first chapter allows us to draw the following broad conclusions.

First: Poetry and language were more highly developed than the other forms of culture found in pre-Islamic society.

This suggests that both had deeper roots in the peninsula’s older history, when parts of Arabia had reached a relatively high level of development.

The clearest evidence comes from the south of the peninsula, especially Yemen, where historically known states such as Sabaʾ, Maʿīn, and Ḥimyar had developed advanced forms of civilization going back to the period before the Common Era.

For reasons that historians have still not been able to explain with confidence, a historical break occurred between that ancient past and the pre-Islamic society of the sixth century CE.

This break cast a long shadow over the economic and social conditions of the sixth century, which appeared in much less developed forms.

Yet poetry and language do not reflect that decline in the same way.

These two parts of pre-Islamic culture had developed far beyond the other areas of life around them.

Second: Pre-Islamic knowledge consisted mainly of scattered and unsystematic results drawn from direct sensory experience and simple forms of reasoning.

Such knowledge developed through everyday contact with nature and with the cosmic phenomena visible to people and directly affecting their lives.

It also developed through the particular social relations in which people lived.

Those relations produced specific customs, traditions, and customary legal practices that served among them much the same purpose that formal laws served in more developed societies.

Third: Of all the forms of consciousness found in pre-Islamic society, religion was the most strongly affected by changes in people’s material life.

As long as the primitive tribal system remained dominant, dividing society into tribal communities based on blood and kinship in their narrowest form, paganism remained the dominant religion.

This was because paganism reflected, in religious consciousness, the structure of the tribal world itself.

The human world was divided into many small and fragmented communities, and pagan religion reflected that same pattern.

It did so in two ways.

First, paganism gave a simple and early form to the relationship between human beings and the natural forces and phenomena that directly affected their daily lives.

It presented those forces as holding absolute, fixed, and unavoidable power over human beings.

Second, paganism rested on a multiplicity of gods that reflected the multiplicity of separate tribal communities.

But shortly before Islam, pre-Islamic society began to undergo changes in its social structure.

Its social relations were starting to move toward a new form of division, one that was preparing the ground for class division.

Religious life began to respond to this wider social transformation.

A movement toward belief in one God now became visible.

It appeared first in Jewish monotheism, which established a base for Judaism in certain regions.

It appeared second in the Christian form of monotheism, which established a base for Christianity in other regions.

Then, toward the end of the pre-Islamic period, a new religious form emerged.

It did not adopt the Jewish or Christian understanding of one God. Instead, it moved toward the understanding of monotheism that would later become Islamic.

This was the religion of the Ḥunafāʾ.

At the level of religious consciousness, it was the clearest expression of pre-Islamic Arab society’s growing conflict with its old, fragmented, and plural tribal system.

The Period of the Rise of Islam

(610–632 CE)

A — The “Class” Reaction

1 — Muhammad and Quraysh

Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh grew up poor and orphaned, despite belonging to Quraysh. He came from the Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the branch of the Hāshim clan descended from his paternal grandfather. The Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib were among the least wealthy branches of the Hāshim clan, especially the household of Muhammad’s uncle Abū Ṭālib, who took him in during his childhood after the death of his grandfather.

Muhammad began working at an early age, “herding the sheep of the people of Mecca.”662 He would later say: “Moses was sent as a prophet while he was a shepherd, David was sent while he was a shepherd, and I was sent while I was tending my family’s sheep at Ajyād.”663

He later worked for Khadīja bint Khuwaylid, who became his first wife, accompanying one of her trading caravans between Mecca and Syria.

The reports that Muhammad had contact with the ḥanīfs seem to have a real basis. He may even have been one of them. There is still a great deal of historical uncertainty surrounding the ḥanīfs as a group, but the historians do give us some clear indications of a close connection between the founder of Islam and this movement.664 The Qur’an itself also confirms this connection when it describes the ḥanīf faith as the religion of Abraham and presents it as the true religion:

Say: My Lord has guided me to a straight path, a true religion, the faith of Abraham, a ḥanīf, who was not one of the polytheists.665

And who is better in religion than one who submits himself to God, does good, and follows the faith of Abraham, a ḥanīf?666

This confirms a real connection between Islam and the ḥanīf movement. The movement had emerged in an agricultural region, al-Yamāma, and its preachers had spread into the settled parts of Arabia, especially Mecca. Some of these preachers were prominent figures in pre-Islamic society.

As we argued earlier, the rise of this movement was one expression of the changes taking place in the foundations of social life in pre-Islamic Arabia. The ḥanīf movement was itself one part of a larger set of connected developments. All of them grew out of the broader movement of that society toward change.

And this change could not remain limited to the material foundations of society. It also had to reach the way people understood their world. At that historical stage, this social consciousness took mainly a religious form.

Looking at the rise of Islam in this way, in relation to the conditions of Arab society at the time—and also to the conditions of nearby societies beyond Arabia—helps us see the social and intellectual roots of the major tasks Islam was about to take on.

Islam would play a historically progressive role in carrying out these tasks, changing both the social and intellectual landscape of more than one society, across more than one continent, throughout the Middle Ages.

From the beginning of Muhammad’s mission, it became clear that he stood on a different side from the leaders of Quraysh, at least in the immediate conflict taking shape around him.

Those leaders held material power. They were the great merchants and moneylenders of the Meccan elite, the leading figures associated with the Dār al-Nadwa.

Islam, by contrast, was taking a position that would help drive the movement of change in a progressive direction. In historical terms, this meant helping society move from its earlier and more primitive form of social relations toward a more developed one, in line with what Muruwwa sees as the general objective laws of historical development.

That is why the reaction against Muhammad came so quickly.

At its root, this reaction clearly had a “class” character, even though the conditions for a fully developed class division had not yet matured. The first signs of such a division were, however, becoming increasingly visible, especially in Meccan society. The reaction to the proclamation of Islam was one of the clearest and most revealing of these signs.

Once Muhammad began preaching publicly, the people of Mecca divided broadly into two camps.

On one side were the wealthy: the great merchants, moneylenders, landowners in al-Ṭāʾif, and those who enjoyed privileges connected with control over the pilgrimage and the seasonal markets.

On the other side were the poor: people with no property, hired workers on commercial ventures and caravan journeys, slaves, and oppressed clients of non-Arab origin.

The first group immediately rejected the new message with anger and contempt. At first, they tried temptation and bribery. When that failed, they turned to persecution in its harshest forms.

The second group found in the new message an expression of feelings they had previously been unable to express openly. It gave voice to their vague but real sense of injury caused by social and material inequality, harsh working conditions, and exploitation. The demands imposed by moneylenders and monopolists weighed especially heavily on them.

Some people from this group therefore joined the movement quickly, despite the severe suffering this brought upon them. Others feared the consequences of openly joining it and waited to see how the struggle would end.

From the beginning of his mission, Muhammad condemned those who piled up wealth, consumed the property of orphans and the poor, practiced usury, and monopolized basic necessities. He also condemned the worship of idols and the belief in many gods.

The leaders of Quraysh therefore saw in the new message the specter of a social and intellectual revolt.

If the movement succeeded, it would first destroy the pagan religious status of the Kaʿba, which was also a major center of trade attracting people from across Arabia and beyond. The religious importance of the Kaʿba was closely tied to its commercial importance.

Second, it would threaten the privileges of the Quraysh leadership, privileges that were fundamentally economic and political.

2 — Monotheism and Resurrection

The Qur’anic verses spoke for the new message. Their literary power reached the highest level of expression familiar to the people of the time, whose appreciation of poetry and eloquence was highly developed by the standards of that period.

It was therefore natural that the Qur’an’s style would appeal strongly to their aesthetic sense. They were struck by the force of its language, the beauty of its composition, and the precision of its references to the stories and laws of earlier peoples, as well as to the traditions, customs, and way of life of pre-Islamic Arabia.

At times they said Muhammad was a poet. At other times they called him a sorcerer. Some went even further in trying to discredit him and called him mad.

In its Meccan verses and surahs, the Qur’an centered its message on two main ideas:

monotheism and resurrection.

As for monotheism, what concerns us here is not its religious meaning as an article of faith. That belongs to another field of study.

What concerns us is what lies beneath that religious meaning: the social dimension of monotheism.

The ḥanīfs had already expressed something of this social meaning, but only in a broad and general way. They could not yet bring its specific form into full view because the ḥanīf movement appeared at a time when the forces breaking apart the tribal order were still only beginning to develop.

By the time Islam appeared, however, the breakdown of the tribal order had become a real historical necessity.

And the need was no longer simply to destroy the old order. The economic, social, political, and intellectual conditions had matured far enough that two tasks now stood side by side: the collapse of the tribal system and the creation of another system to replace it.

This new system would need political, legal, and intellectual structures capable of responding to the changes already taking place in the material foundations of society and in social relations.

At the center of those changes was a change in the division of labor.

That change, in turn, required society to be organized on a new basis. People could no longer be divided simply by tribal belonging, as though their place in the production of society’s material needs did not matter.

The division of Arabia into separate and largely independent tribal units had become a real obstacle to the next stage of historical development.

That obstacle therefore had to be broken through.

A unifying framework had to emerge, one capable of containing the new kinds of social conflict that were developing. It had to exist first as a real material force that could unite people, and second as a unifying idea at the level of consciousness.

Islam provided exactly this kind of presence on both levels: as an institution and material force, and as an idea, principle, and belief.

This, in Muruwwa’s view, was the social meaning of monotheism beneath its immediate religious meaning as an Islamic belief.

Many Qur’anic verses point in this direction:

He has laid down for you the same religion that He commanded Noah to follow, and that We have revealed to you, and that We commanded Abraham, Moses, and Jesus to follow: uphold the religion and do not divide over it. (Surat al-Shūrā, verse 14)

Obey God and His Messenger, and do not quarrel with one another, or you will lose heart and your strength will leave you. Be patient; God is with those who are patient. (Surat al-Anfāl, verse 46)

Do not be like those who divided and fell into disagreement after clear proofs had come to them. (Surat Āl ʿImrān, verse 105)

Hold firmly, all together, to the rope of God, and do not divide. Remember God’s favor to you: you were enemies, and He brought your hearts together, so that by His grace you became brothers. (Surat Āl ʿImrān, verse 103)

Muhammad gave this social dimension of monotheism a clear and direct expression in the first political document he issued after the migration to Medina.

The document set out the first principles for cooperation among the different groups living in the city, of whom the Muslims were now one part.

It took the form of a written agreement. Muhammad “wrote an agreement between the Emigrants and the Helpers in which he made peace with the Jews, entered into a covenant with them, confirmed them in their religion and property, and laid down mutual rights and obligations.”667

The document begins:

“This is a document from Muhammad the Prophet between the believers and Muslims of Quraysh and Yathrib, and those who follow them and fight alongside them: they are one community apart from all other people...”668

This is the first principle of the document.

And it points toward the historical direction society was taking: a movement away from the loose, quantitative gathering of separate tribal groups and toward the relations of a larger urban society.

As for the belief in resurrection, which formed the second main axis of the Islamic message, the Qur’an’s own use of the word can help us uncover the social meaning behind it.

The Qur’an repeatedly describes the “Day of Resurrection” as the “Day of Dīn.”

If we look at the meaning of the word dīn in the Arabic of the period when the Qur’an first appeared, we find that among its meanings were “reckoning,” “judgment,” and “recompense.”669

The Day of Resurrection, then, is the day when people will be called to account in the world to come for everything they did in this earthly world, the world of human life.

Behind the metaphysical meaning of the belief in resurrection, there is therefore a social meaning rooted in human life itself and in the real relationships people have with one another in the material world.

Yet during the early Meccan period, before the migration, this social meaning remained limited.

Those who accepted the new message were promised a good reward in the afterlife, while those who rejected and opposed it were threatened with severe punishment on the “Day of Resurrection.”670

At that stage, the message still remained mainly within a moral and otherworldly framework.

For the weak, the oppressed, and the exploited, it did not yet bring material change into their immediate earthly lives. And for those who were actually carrying out oppression and exploitation, it did not yet provide a material restraint on their actions.

The promises of reward and punishment had not yet been joined to the practical laws and institutions that began to appear after the migration to Medina and during the successive victories over Islam’s opponents in Mecca and then across the rest of Arabia.

3 — In Mecca Before the Migration

Why did the new message remain in Mecca for about thirteen years, facing the Quraysh aristocracy with exhausting persistence, while that aristocracy opposed and persecuted it with such fierce determination that the balance of power nearly turned against the movement altogether?

Why did this continue until the conditions for migration to Yathrib finally became possible?

One explanation lies in what we discussed in the previous section: at that stage, the new message did not yet offer an immediate material solution for the weak, the oppressed, and the exploited among the people of Mecca.

For that reason, these groups largely stood apart from Muhammad and his small number of followers. Their attitude was almost one of indifference as to whether the movement succeeded or failed.

This was despite Islam’s declared opposition to usury, monopoly, and the hoarding of gold and silver. Such principles directly challenged some of the main foundations of aristocratic Quraysh power in Meccan society.

A realistic explanation of this situation suggests that the main reason the oppressed people of Mecca, as social groups rather than as individuals, held back from supporting Islam before the migration was the way they understood the Qur’anic promises of reward and punishment.

They understood these promises as postponing the issue to the next world. Reward and punishment seemed to belong to a moral and otherworldly realm rather than to the immediate material conditions of life.

This explanation therefore rejects the view of some biographers of Muhammad,671 who argued that the Quraysh leadership frightened these oppressed groups into staying away from the new religion by persecuting Muhammad and his followers.

According to that view, fear prevented these groups from taking the role they might otherwise have played in securing the movement’s victory, even though some of its principles were close to their own interests as broad social groups—especially its opposition to usury, monopoly, and the hoarding of gold and silver.

But the reality, in Muruwwa’s view, is that these oppressed groups could not yet see in the movement a material gain that would rescue them from their present hardship.

In the verses promising reward and punishment, they could see only a reward postponed until the “Day of Resurrection.”

So we have to ask: if they had found in Islam, during the Meccan period, an immediate way out of their present material suffering, would they still have held back from supporting it?

Or would they have supported it enthusiastically, no matter how harsh Quraysh persecution became?

We can ask the same question in another way:

Could the promise of future reward and punishment in the afterlife, by itself, have attracted these deprived groups during the early Meccan period while also acting as a deterrent to the ruling Quraysh aristocracy?

At this point, the question is mainly about consciousness.

Were both sides of this social conflict intellectually prepared to understand reward and punishment in the afterlife as forces that could attract one side and restrain the other?

Let us allow one modern biographer of Muhammad to answer in his own way.

Discussing one of the reasons Quraysh refused to accept Muhammad’s message, this writer says that they were driven by “their fear of resurrection and of the punishment of Hell on the Day of Judgment.”

He continues:

“Here is Muhammad proclaiming to them, in terrifying verses that make hearts tremble with fear, that their Lord lies in wait for them, that they will be raised again on the Last Day in a new creation, and that their deeds alone will speak for them.”672

But after quoting these frightening verses, the writer adds:

“...They did not know resurrection, and they did not accept what they heard about it. None of them imagined that he would be rewarded or punished for the deeds of this life after leaving it. Their fear of the future concerned this life. They feared illness, loss of wealth and children, and loss of standing and prestige (...). As for reward after death, resurrection on the day when the trumpet is blown, Paradise prepared for the righteous, and Hell prepared for the unjust—none of this entered their minds...”673

Dr. Haykal clearly falls into a contradiction here.

On the one hand, he speaks of “their fear of resurrection and of the punishment of Hell on the Day of Judgment.” On the other, he says that they did not know resurrection and did not accept the idea.

Even so, he reaches the heart of the matter when he identifies what actually frightened the leaders of Quraysh.

As he says, their fear of the future concerned this life.

They feared illness, loss of wealth and children, and loss of status and prestige.

In other words, they feared for their material interests and for the privileges they had gained through a long history of commercial, political, and religious control over the central institutions of Mecca.

That is the real issue.

On the other side, the deprived groups of Mecca had fears of their own.

They feared that postponing reward and punishment until the Day of Judgment would also mean postponing the solution to their own problem: the material suffering they faced under the absolute power of usury and monopoly.

Their fear too was ultimately “of the future in this life.”

That, here as well, is the real issue.

If this is the heart of the matter—and Muruwwa argues that it is—then the main factor determining the position of the two sides in the central social conflict of Meccan society was not whether they knew about resurrection or did not know about it.

It is correct to discuss the matter at the level of consciousness.

But what kind of consciousness?

The negative reactions that shaped the attitude of the Quraysh merchant aristocracy toward Islam throughout the thirteen years before the great migration to Medina were an early and undeveloped form of class consciousness.

They resembled an instinctive reflex.

The initial Islamic call produced a shock. It demanded the complete rejection of idols and insisted that religious belief be directed entirely toward the one and only God. At the same time, it openly mocked the idols the Meccans worshipped and condemned their worship without compromise.

These teachings immediately made the great merchants of Quraysh feel that their material interests were under threat.
