We can see this in the philosophical ideas and logical methods that appeared among various religious and political groups, especially the Muʿtazilites.

We can also see it in the administrative, financial, political, and other institutions of the Umayyad state.

These are clear examples of cultural influence. There is nothing here that can reasonably be described as the rejection claimed by that researcher.

2 — Islamic Law During the Period of Conquest

Even during the early period when the Arabs still lived in relative isolation, the conquests opened new possibilities for the development of Islamic law.

They created wider scope for the use of reason and personal judgment—what Islamic legal thought calls ijtihād.

We discussed this subject earlier.

What matters here is that the new conditions created by the conquests produced a broad range of new needs and problems. This gave a powerful new impulse to the development of Islamic law through rational judgment—in other words, through ijtihād based on reasoned opinion.

As we saw in Chapter Two, ijtihād had already been used before the conquests.

But it had operated within a fairly narrow range because life in the Arabian Peninsula itself had been relatively limited in scope.

We can also put the matter another way.

The general legal principles found in the two main sources of Islamic law—the Qurʾān and the Sunna—often first appeared in connection with a particular event or case. From that particular case, the principle would then be extended and turned into a general rule.

In this sense, we can say that almost all of these general rules developed out of specific and recurring situations in Arab life within the peninsula.

Because the range of those situations was still relatively limited, it was often easy to apply an existing text to a new case by analogy.

But Arab life expanded as the Islamic movement developed.

Social relations also began to change.

Islamic law therefore had to respond to new needs and problems created by this development and apply its general principles in new ways.

This required more active use of reason.

The effort to apply Islamic law to new events and new problems therefore gave thought more room to move. It encouraged people to judge situations in ways that increasingly showed the influence of rational reflection.

Then came the Arab conquests.

In these completely new conditions, the caliphs and Companions faced situations unlike anything they had dealt with before.

They therefore had to think more deeply about both general and specific laws before applying them to these unfamiliar circumstances.

Among the Rightly Guided Caliphs, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was the boldest in using ijtihād based on personal judgment to deal with these new situations.

We have already seen him do this in many areas.

He set aside one rule that had existed during the Prophet’s lifetime, modified another, and approached still others in new ways.

In each case, he used a flexible understanding of the relationship between law and changing circumstances.

One example was his decision to end the share of charitable funds given to the muʾallafa qulūbuhum—those whose hearts were to be won over.

During the Prophet’s lifetime, such people had been given money from charitable funds in order to attract them to Islam. This might be because their faith was weak, because their hostility needed to be prevented, or because they held an important position among their people.

The practice was based on the Qurʾānic verse:

“Charitable funds are only for the poor, the needy, those employed to collect them, and those whose hearts are to be won over...”

—Sūrat al-Tawba, 9:60.

ʿUmar ended this practice because, in his view, the reason behind the rule no longer existed.

The rule had originally served the need to strengthen and support the Islamic movement during its early weakness. By ʿUmar’s time, Islam had become strong, so the original reason for the rule had disappeared.741

The reasoning behind ʿUmar’s decision is important.

It shows Arab thought beginning to extract general principles from legal texts and to adjust particular rulings when the reasons behind them changed along with new needs and new social conditions.

We can see the same development among the Companions who spread through the new garrison towns and took on responsibilities in the courts, administration, and military leadership.

Throughout the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, they increasingly used ijtihād based on reasoned opinion.

Eventually, disagreements appeared between the judgments reached by different Companions. These disagreements became serious enough that complaints were made to the caliphs about conflicting legal interpretations.

In general, recording this development in ijtihād gives us an early sign of movement within Arab thought.

It allows us to follow that development after the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, when this kind of reasoning moved beyond strictly legal questions and began to enter discussion of the beliefs of religion itself.

During the Prophet’s lifetime, the situation had been different. He spoke with the authority of revelation, and “a believer could find no way around his judgment.” Any disagreement among Muslims could be settled by referring the matter back to the Messenger of God.

Here we should return to the disagreements that appeared immediately after the Prophet’s death over the question of the caliphate.

Each side defended its position through its own form of ijtihād—either by reasoning about the office of the caliphate itself or by interpreting statements and actions attributed to the Prophet in ways that supported its own aims.

These disagreements continued throughout the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs whenever different interests, political positions, and opinions came into conflict over the organization of the conquests, the administration of the conquered lands, or the courts.

They also reappeared whenever one caliph died and another took his place.

But the disagreement did not develop into fully formed schools of thought in the theoretical sense until the end of the Rightly Guided period and the beginning of Umayyad rule.

More precisely, this development began during the caliphate of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and the armed conflicts between his supporters and the Umayyads.

Out of these conflicts emerged the Khārijite movement.

The Khārijites created theoretical principles of their own. They drew these principles not only from the rules of Islamic law but, more importantly, from basic religious concepts themselves.

They used ijtihād to derive new meanings from those concepts in ways shaped by the position they had taken during the Battle of Ṣiffīn between ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya.

We will return to this later.

For now, we can conclude that the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, especially because of the new conditions created by the conquests, saw Arab thought take noticeable steps toward dealing with new questions and problems through a somewhat freer use of reason.

This development was not limited to legal matters. It also began to touch some questions connected with religious belief itself.

We should now notice that these developments in law and rational reflection were among the first signs that social and cultural interaction between the Arabs and the peoples of their vast state had already begun.

E — The First Social Revolution in Islam

1 — Between Two Movements

We describe the uprising during the reign of the third caliph, ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, as the first social revolution in Islam.

In saying this, we have not forgotten the earlier movement of apostasy that led to the Ridda Wars.

But there is an important difference between the two “revolutions,” and this is why we describe the uprising against ʿUthmān as the first of its kind in Islam.

The apostasy movement, although it was produced by social forces that we discussed elsewhere in this chapter, had the character of a counter-revolution against Islam.

The uprising against ʿUthmān was different.

It remained within Islam. In fact, the rebels armed themselves with Islamic ideas themselves.

They acted out of a desire to see the rules and laws of Islam applied fairly and properly, according to what they understood and believed to be the true spirit of Islamic law.

For this reason, we see it as the first revolution of its kind within Islam itself.

2 — An Umayyad Aristocracy

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb died in 644 CE.

By then, he had left a strong personal mark on the institutions of the Islamic “state,” and he deserves much of the credit for laying its practical foundations.

Among the changes associated with him were reforms to taxation and new interpretations of the jizya and kharāj.

He exempted certain people from the jizya, especially those who converted to Islam from other religions.

During his rule, additional taxes and fees also began to be imposed on craft industries.

Another well-known feature of his rule was the policy of religious tolerance he followed in the conquered lands.

He also took great care to watch the behavior of the governors he appointed there. When he received reports that a governor had wronged the local population, he dealt with the matter firmly.

At times he removed governors from office and confiscated money or property they had unjustly taken from its owners.

This was the conduct of ʿUmar, who became known in both Islamic and non-Islamic historical writing as “ʿUmar the Just.”742

But once ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān became caliph after him, new patterns began to appear in the behavior of the provincial governors.

They suggested that ʿUmar’s policy and style of rule were being abandoned, with serious consequences.

People began to feel that the money collected from the jizya, the kharāj, and other taxes was no longer reaching the state treasury.

Instead, it was flowing to the governors appointed by the third caliph, ʿUthmān.

Most of these men belonged to his own family and clan, the Umayyads.

As a result, large fortunes began to accumulate in the hands of a particular group in Medina, the capital of the caliphate.

Gradually, a new class of extremely wealthy people emerged there. As this class grew, so did the different forms of luxury and material comfort that surrounded it.

This new change requires us to say something about ʿUthmān himself.

He came from the aristocratic upper class of Quraysh—the group that had held supreme power in Mecca before the rise of Islam.

He belonged to the Umayyads, one of the ten main branches of Quraysh and among the richest and most powerful in pre-Islamic Mecca.

They had played a leading role in organizing and controlling Meccan trade, especially the family of Abū Sufyān.

It was Abū Sufyān who had led the fierce campaign of persecution and opposition against Muḥammad from the time he first proclaimed Islam.

ʿUthmān himself came from this same Umayyad branch of Quraysh and had been one of its richest men before Islam.

Alongside this class background, there was another factor.

By the time ʿUthmān became caliph after ʿUmar, he was already an elderly man. He no longer had full control over the direction of government—even if he had wished to resist the course taken by the Umayyad governors he appointed from among his closest relatives.

At the same time, the Arab-Islamic state had expanded enormously.

How could such a state be governed by a caliph who had taken ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s place while possessing so many qualities that sharply distinguished him from his great predecessor?

It seems that many of the Companions already understood the harmful effect these qualities might have on state policy.

When those effects began to appear in practice, opposition to ʿUthmān’s policies spread through the different Muslim political groups in Medina, even before anger exploded among ordinary Muslims and working people throughout the provinces.

Naturally, the supporters of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib were among the strongest opponents.

They saw ʿUthmān’s rise to the caliphate—and ʿAlī’s exclusion from it for the third time—as yet another injustice.

In their view, the difference between the two men in both personal and Islamic qualifications was enormous.

They therefore saw the decision not only as an injustice against ʿAlī himself, but also as an injustice against what they believed to be a divine right that had belonged to ʿAlī from the very beginning of the caliphate.

3 — The Revolution of Ordinary People

The Umayyad governors appointed by ʿUthmān went further and further in building wealth for themselves.

They did not rely only on the income from taxes already established under earlier laws.

They also imposed new, harsh, and heavy taxes on the population and seized land and property from people in the conquered territories.

In this way, these governors gave the state an increasingly semi-feudal character.

They themselves became major owners of farms, land, and other property.

To the inhabitants of the provinces, the whole state increasingly appeared to have taken on this new semi-feudal character.

Popular anger therefore grew, spread, and became sharper.

It was strongest among ordinary people and workers, but it also spread among political groups in Medina, especially those who had lost positions at the beginning of ʿUthmān’s reign or whose ambitions for such positions had been frustrated.

In this way, the causes of the coming explosion gathered both beneath the surface and in open political life.

The result was what later Islamic history called the “Great Fitna,” or the “Fitna of ʿUthmān.”

But those who gave it this name were not concerned with understanding its historical and social meaning.

That is why they chose a term that, in our view, conceals its real nature.

The true meaning of this explosion lies in the fact that it arose from ordinary people, Arab and non-Arab alike.

They were all Muslims.

And, as we have said, they wanted Islam to survive and prevail in the same spirit that had originally drawn them to it: a spirit of social change aimed at improving their material conditions and reducing the growing gap between them and the upper groups that were becoming richer at their expense.

No historian of Islam accused those who came from Egypt and Iraq in 656, as believing pilgrims on their way to Mecca, of rebelling against Islam or preparing a counter-revolution against the Islamic state.

On the contrary, the historians confirm that these people came to perform the pilgrimage while carrying with them both their belief in Islam and their anger toward those who oppressed them, seized their livelihoods, and accumulated wealth in Islam’s name.

They came to complain to the caliph, ʿUthmān, about the behavior of his relatives who governed in his name.

They then asked him to step down from the caliphate.

They did not make this demand because they personally hated him.

They believed his resignation was the only solution to the problem facing the people of the provinces: the caliph was unable to control the actions of his relatives, who ruled those provinces in his name.

ʿUthmān refused.

The representatives of the provinces were then unable to restrain either their own anger or the anger of the ordinary people who had sent them with this demand.

They surrounded his house.

ʿUthmān’s supporters resisted the siege.

The conflict ended only with the killing of the caliph himself.

The rebels then waited for a new caliph who, they hoped, would remove the social causes that had produced this first social revolution in Islam.

Here we should add that ʿUthmān’s social background, which we discussed earlier, was in our view a major factor in his refusal to leave office.

It was also a major factor in the style of rule that created the causes of the uprising.

One sign of this was the material luxury of his private life.

It was even said that when his daughter married, he gave her 600,000 dirhams from the state treasury, all of it drawn from jizya and kharāj—that is, for the most part, from the labor of working people.

4 — The Rise of the Khārijites

... A number of the political groups opposed to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—including ʿĀʾisha bint Abī Bakr, Ṭalḥa, and al-Zubayr—had helped stir up opposition that led to the killing of Caliph ʿUthmān.

Their anger came partly from the fact that ʿUthmān had favored the Umayyads over them in appointments to the highest offices.

At the same time, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib had sent his two sons, al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, to ʿUthmān’s house to defend him.

ʿAlī understood what ʿUthmān’s death could mean for Islam. He knew that people driven by political interests and ambition could use such an event to provoke further conflict.

Yet despite all of this, the same people who had helped encourage the movement against ʿUthmān suddenly changed their position immediately after his death.

They began demanding revenge for his blood.

They even accused ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib himself of encouraging his killing.

They did this because they feared that their own leadership and interests might face an even greater danger under ʿAlī than they had under ʿUthmān and the Umayyads.

They used ʿĀʾisha’s special position among Muslims as the Prophet’s wife and the daughter of the first caliph, Abū Bakr.

They also made use of the old resentment she held toward ʿAlī and turned it against him.

They accused him of responsibility for killing the caliph in order to stir the emotions of Muslims, many of whom saw ʿUthmān’s death as a terrible and dangerous event.

ʿĀʾisha had personal reasons of her own for responding quickly to these pressures.

She carried ʿUthmān’s bloodstained shirt and used it to stir public anger.

With the support of ʿAlī’s other opponents, she was eventually able to launch the conflict known as the Battle of the Camel in Basra.

She rode at the head of the fighters on a camel, displaying ʿUthmān’s shirt.

The Battle of the Camel became the “fuse” that reignited all the political and social conflicts that had begun with Muḥammad’s death.

Although ʿAlī’s side won the battle, the fuse continued to burn and set off further explosions.

This time, however, the conflict moved onto another level: Who would become caliph after ʿUthmān?

Objectively, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib was the only obvious candidate for the position at that moment.

From the beginning of the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, his name had repeatedly appeared among the candidates, only for someone else to be chosen.

By the time ʿUthmān was killed, none of those earlier candidates remained except ʿAlī.

In the eyes of most Muslims, it therefore seemed natural that the office should now pass to him without serious competition.

But two things changed the situation in ways that few people had initially expected.

The first was the continuing effect of the Battle of the Camel.

The second was the presence in Syria of a powerful Umayyad governor who represented Umayyad leadership, aristocratic interests, and political ambition.

That governor was Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān.

Muʿāwiya was already governor of Syria when the uprising against ʿUthmān took place.

He had held the position since the reign of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

During his long period in power there, he built strong relations with the wealthy and influential groups of Syrian society by generally protecting their class interests.

He left the courts and police in the hands of large local landowners, wealthy townspeople, and major merchants from the local population.

He also kept customs barriers at Syria’s borders even though the country had now become part of the Arab empire.

At the same time, he imposed high customs duties on goods that competed with Syria’s more developed local products.

Muʿāwiya also exempted religious clergy of every faith from taxation.

Through this policy, he helped the dominant groups in Syria preserve full freedom to exploit the majority of the population.

In return, he secured their strong support.

He also won the sympathy of the religious leadership toward his rule.

There was another factor.

Throughout ʿUthmān’s reign, Muʿāwiya had effectively become the absolute ruler of Syria.

He used this almost independent—or in practice fully independent—position to build another base of power that could guarantee his survival in this important office: a military base.

He created a strong army in Syria.

It was clearly Muʿāwiya’s own army rather than simply one unit within the army of the state as a whole.

We do not know whether Muʿāwiya followed this policy simply to guarantee that he would remain governor of Syria under whichever caliph happened to rule, or whether he had already begun preparing to declare himself caliph of the Muslims when the right moment came.

But his earlier intentions are not the most important question.

What matters is that the broad policy he had followed in Syria before the latest explosion gave him, when the “right moment” arrived, a real and material basis for declaring himself a candidate for the caliphate.

He could now challenge the man whom most Muslims saw as the leading candidate for that office: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

The “right moment” itself gave Muʿāwiya another advantage.

By this we mean the fuse first lit by the Battle of the Camel against ʿAlī.

A section of the Muslim population in Medina, Basra, and Kufa had pledged allegiance to ʿAlī as caliph.

ʿAlī then removed Muʿāwiya from the governorship of Syria.

In doing so, he did not fully take account of all the conditions through which Muʿāwiya had so skillfully strengthened his position.

Muʿāwiya now saw in ʿAlī’s decision a reason to aim beyond the governorship of Syria.

All the favorable conditions had come together for him to pursue the caliphate itself.

This ambition was not simply personal.

It also expressed the ambitions of what we may call the old Umayyad aristocratic class.

This class had not been created from nothing under ʿUthmān.

Rather, during his reign it developed from a tribal aristocracy inherited from the pre-Islamic period into a class aristocracy with an increasingly semi-feudal character.

In Syria, it also became a political support and official instrument for the dominant local exploiting classes.

There is one more factor to add: the personal qualities of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib himself.

On one side, he came from the Hāshimite branch of Quraysh, historically opposed to the Umayyads both before and after Islam.

On the other, throughout the Muslim community he had a reputation for an uncompromising moral idealism.

He held firmly to ideas of truth, justice, and goodness in an absolute way and refused to compromise with those he believed had departed from them.

Once we add these features of ʿAlī to everything already described, we can understand Muʿāwiya’s position from several angles.

We can also understand the position of the class—or classes—and social groups that supported Muʿāwiya in his struggle with ʿAlī over the caliphate.

It was under all these conditions that the Battle of Ṣiffīn743 broke out between the army of Iraq, led by ʿAlī, and the army of Syria, led by Muʿāwiya.

The fuse first lit by the Battle of the Camel was still burning.

It now set off the Battle of Ṣiffīn in 657, one year after the killing of ʿUthmān—or, in our terms, one year after the social revolution against his rule.

The Khārijites emerged from the Battle of Ṣiffīn.

With them appeared a new Islamic school, and at the same time a new political party.

Behind the religious form of their doctrine and the political form of their party lay a social ideology with democratic content.

This stood against the aristocratic—or, if the term is appropriate, class-based—content of the caliphate as it had existed before the Khārijites appeared.

We will not spend much time here on the historical details of Ṣiffīn and the events that produced the movement later known as the Khārijites.

They received this name because their founders “went out”—that is, rebelled—against the authority of the man under whose banner they had been fighting, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

This happened after ʿAlī accepted a proposal from Muʿāwiya’s commanders that the Qurʾān itself be used as the judge between the two sides.

The arbitration ended in the well-known deception arranged by ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, which left ʿAlī at a disadvantage.

The irony is that the people who became the Khārijites had themselves strongly pressured ʿAlī to accept arbitration.

Yet when the arbitration ended badly for him, they turned against him.

They rejected both ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya and declared both men unbelievers.

They then developed a set of principles that became the basis of a political, intellectual, and military program.

Under the banner of an Islamic religious doctrine, they pursued this program through a series of fierce and bloody conflicts.

As an armed human group that used violence against its opponents, they eventually came to an end.

But their principles did not disappear.

Those principles rested on an ideology that reflected part of the social reality not only of their own period, but of later periods as well.

We will examine those principles and that ideology later in this volume.

5 — The Intellectual Forms of Party Conflict

The period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs did not last long after political and party conflict entered this new phase.

The struggle now formed two separate fronts.

On the surface, they appeared distinct. In reality, they were closely connected.

The first was the conflict between ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya.

The second was the conflict between ʿAlī and the Khārijites.

The person of ʿAlī represented two causes that might seem sharply opposed to one another.

The first was the idea that the caliphate rested on divine right, together with an idealistic vision of truth, justice, and goodness.744

The second was Hāshimite group solidarity in its political struggle against Umayyad solidarity.

This second cause became attached to ʿAlī through the dynamics of the conflict, even though it was not necessarily part of his own personal understanding of his position.

For him, it was an objective reality rather than a personal motive.

Many of his supporters, however, placed this issue above everything else.

Because ʿAlī came to represent these two conflicting causes—whether he wished to or not—he became the center of the struggle on both fronts: the Khārijite front and the Muʿāwiya front.

Muʿāwiya, in his struggle against ʿAlī, also represented two causes.

But in his case they were neither contradictory nor separate. Each strengthened the other.

The first was his personal ambition to become caliph.

The second was Umayyad group solidarity combined with class ambition.

The conflict centered on ʿAlī himself came to an end with his death in the first month of 661 CE.

He was killed in the mosque of Kufa by a Khārijite, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muljam.

With his death, the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs ended.

But the question of ʿAlī’s right to the caliphate, understood as a divine right, did not disappear.

It remained a basic issue at the center of an intellectual and historical conflict that continues even today.

It also became the basis of a long political struggle that played a major role in opposition movements throughout both the Umayyad and Abbasid periods.

States were founded on this basis, and states fell because of it.

What concerns us here is the intellectual side of the question.

We should remember that the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs ended with three major political groupings established in social, political, and intellectual life:

the supporters of ʿAlī, the Umayyad party, and the Khārijites.

Other smaller groups appeared and disappeared quickly without leaving any important intellectual or political legacy.

We should also remember that the intellectual side of each of these three major parties was not separate from its social and political side.

At the same time, however, there is an important point we should not overlook.

Thought is one distinct form of social and political consciousness, but it can also develop a certain degree of relative independence.

In other words, ideas always have social or political roots.

But thought can begin to follow a partly independent path of its own, especially when it turns toward broad questions and begins expressing them through abstract concepts.

As this happens, the social and political roots of those ideas can become hidden beneath the surface.

But even when intellectual questions appear to move beyond the immediate concerns of social life and develop independently of them, they remain connected to their real origins in the life of their own society and period.

The conditions of time and place remain the real source from which these questions arise, even when thought later develops them along its own relatively independent path.

Seen in this light, the intellectual forms taken by the party conflicts at the end of the Rightly Guided period had not yet reached the stage of relative independence we are describing.

In other words, the intellectual side of these political conflicts had not yet developed into theories built on rational inquiry and clearly formed concepts.

For example, most of the intellectual debate between the three main parties during the lifetime of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib still revolved around religious texts and their interpretation.

This was true of the debate over the caliphate, the meaning of faith as defined by Islamic law, the theory of ijtihād, and other questions.

But this kind of debate laid the foundation for a later development.

Thinking about these questions gradually moved from being closely tied to the wording of texts toward examining the questions themselves more deeply, and only then returning to the texts as support for rational argument and as evidence that the reasoning was sound.

In this way, debate moved from treating these issues mainly as questions of law to treating them as questions of religion itself.

It moved, in other words, from discussion of legal rules to discussion of the principles of belief.

Out of this development grew the intellectual schools that we will examine in Part Two.

To sum up this chapter: the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs came to an end before the intellectual forms of the social and political conflicts of that period had fully undergone this development.

PreviousChapter ThreeNextSummary of Chapter Three

Summary of Chapter Three

1 —

The chapter begins with the Prophet’s death in 632 CE, twenty-two years after he began preaching Islam. His death created two different kinds of confusion among Muslims, each touching on the social, political, and religious meaning of Islam.

One group of Muslims could not believe that the Prophet had died. They understood his prophethood in a way that placed him outside the ordinary conditions of human life, and so they imagined that he could not die. Abu Bakr brought this confusion to a decisive end. He reminded people of the Prophet’s humanity and supported his argument with Qurʾanic verses stating that Muhammad was human.

Another group of Muslims was shocked by the Prophet’s permanent disappearance from his position as leader of the Islamic community. They did not know what would happen to that position after his death.

2 —

The chapter then follows the conflicts that developed around this position of leadership and the different forms they took.

As soon as the Prophet’s death was announced, old tensions that had previously been held in check suddenly broke into the open. There were tensions between Mecca and Medina, then between the Emigrants and the Helpers, then among the Emigrants themselves between the Hāshimites and non-Hāshimites, and finally between the Aws and Khazraj among the Helpers. All of this erupted while the Prophet’s body was still in the home of his wife ʿĀʾisha, before he had even been buried.

The struggle for power now came openly to the surface among all these groups. Their motives became clear in the meeting they immediately held at the Saqīfa of Banū Sāʿida to decide who would succeed the Prophet.

Although one of the leaders of the Helpers, Abu ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ, settled the immediate dispute by pledging allegiance to Abu Bakr as the Prophet’s first caliph, the matter was not settled historically or religiously. From that moment, the first seeds appeared of political and sectarian factionalism within Islam. These divisions continued to grow as events unfolded, and they produced their first major results before the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs had even come to an end.

We describe this factionalism as both political and sectarian because the political struggle over the caliphate soon took on the form of a religious dispute over what the caliphate itself meant.

One side held that the caliphate was a divinely appointed office. God, through the Prophet, had designated the person who should hold it. These were the supporters of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

The other side held that the caliphate was an office whose holder should be chosen by Muslims because they considered him fit for it.

This second group wanted the caliph to be selected through what became known as the principle of shūrā, meaning consultation among Muslims in choosing a leader. In practice, however, the selection of the four Rightly Guided Caliphs involved little more than a narrow and largely formal version of this principle.

At one point, the choice rested with a single individual, as when Abu Bakr chose ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb to succeed him. At another, it was confined to only a handful of people, no more than four at most, as happened when the third caliph, ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, was appointed.

We therefore concluded that the principle of shūrā never acquired a clear legal or practical form in Islam, not even during what is usually regarded as the most “democratic” period of the caliphate: the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs.

3 —

Among the reactions that followed the Prophet’s death, the chapter also discusses the decision by many people in regions far from Mecca and Medina—including al-Yamāma, Yemen, Hadramawt, Oman, and elsewhere—to renounce their allegiance to Islam.

The new caliph, Abu Bakr, sent military forces against them in the conflicts known in Islamic history as the Ridda Wars, or Wars of Apostasy.

We discussed several reasons for these rebellions.

Some tribes had never fully accepted Islamic rule because their chiefs saw no advantage in accepting Islam’s attempt to break down the older framework of tribal unity.

Other tribes had outwardly submitted because Islam had become the strongest political center in Arabia after the conquest of Mecca.

The settled agricultural regions were in a different position. Their existing systems of production gave them reasons to preserve their established traditions and social arrangements rather than accept changes they did not need.

These regions also produced people who claimed prophethood for themselves. Such figures naturally opposed submission to Muhammad’s message and teachings. Among them were Musaylima of Banū Ḥanīfa in al-Yamāma and the woman Sajāḥ among Banū Taghlib.

When Muhammad died, all these groups saw an opportunity to rise against Islamic rule. The military campaigns sent against them by the caliphs succeeded, however, and the rebels were brought back under the authority of the caliphate.

4 —

The chapter also discusses the Islamic conquests beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

We saw that Arab expansion began only a year after the Prophet’s death. Its first direction was toward Syria and Palestine, which were then under Byzantine rule. The conquests continued for more than seventy years, until the Arab state stretched across vast areas of three continents.

The historical evidence led us to conclude that the main driving forces behind this movement were social rather than religious. For this reason, we rejected the view of some Orientalist scholars that religious fanaticism was what drove the Arab conquests.

Looking at the conditions in which the wars were fought and the victories won by the Arab armies, we concluded that success depended both on conditions within the conquered countries and on conditions among the conquerors themselves.

Among the conditions in the conquered lands was the weakness of the Byzantine and Persian states after their long wars against one another. The populations of Syria, Palestine, Egypt, and Iraq were also burdened by heavy taxation. In Syria, they faced religious persecution from the Byzantine Church as well.

On the Arab side, the conquerors did not initially rule the peoples of these countries through the feudal system used by their previous rulers, because the Arabs themselves had not practiced this kind of government before the conquests.

The Arab conquerors also followed a policy of religious tolerance. They did not plunder the cities they conquered, though they did confiscate the property of the wealthy and the nobility. Nor did they take land away from its existing owners until the reign of the third Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUthmān.

The policies followed by the Arab conquerors also allowed us to draw several further conclusions.

One was that their religious tolerance had a material basis. They had an interest in limiting the number of Christians who converted to Islam so that revenue from the jizya, the tax imposed on non-Muslims, would not fall.

Another was their favorable treatment of local Christian clergy. These clergy had opposed the Byzantine church authorities, and that religious opposition also carried a political meaning: resistance to the rule of a foreign occupying power, Byzantium.

We also concluded that the Arab conquerors did not change the existing division of labor among the local population.

5 —

We noted that the cultural and social interaction between the Arabs and the peoples of the conquered countries did not yet show its full effects during the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. Those effects became much clearer later.

We concluded that this interaction was delayed mainly because, during the early period of conquest, the conquerors lived separately from the local population. They were occupied with military defense and the organization of their armies, and they did not take part in material production.

For this reason, we rejected the claim made by some modern researchers that the Arabs rejected the cultures of these peoples.

The issue was not rejection. It was the particular conditions in which the conquerors were living. Those conditions delayed cultural interaction for a time. Once they changed, the process developed with tremendous force.

6 —

We also noted that the conditions created by the conquests opened the way for a new kind of intellectual activity in Islamic law: independent legal reasoning based on personal judgment, or ijtihād bi-l-raʾy.

This movement had a positive role in the development of Islamic law.

The second caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, practiced this kind of personal reasoning with both boldness and foresight.

We concluded that the appearance of this method shows Arab thought beginning to move in a new direction. After the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, it would enter a different intellectual climate, one closer to rational inquiry.

Thought would then begin to examine the doctrines of faith themselves, as we shall see.

7 —

The conclusions we have drawn about the Arab conquests and Arab policy in the conquered lands apply only to the earliest period of expansion.

Later, we saw major changes in the relationship between the Arabs and the local populations.

One development during the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs is especially striking. Under the third caliph, ʿUthmān, a semi-feudal aristocratic “class” began to form among the Umayyad governors whom he appointed from among his own relatives.

These governors pursued personal enrichment, accumulated land, and burdened the population with taxes. In doing so, they created the conditions for a social uprising in the conquered provinces.

That uprising eventually led to the killing of the caliph himself.

It also produced a new factional struggle that reached the point of armed conflict between the fourth caliph, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and Muʿāwiya, the governor of Syria and representative of the Umayyad party.

A new party also emerged from ʿAlī’s own ranks during the Battle of Ṣiffīn: the Kharijites.

This new form of political and factional conflict, with its new participants, would have a major effect on the rise of an intellectual and “ideological” movement. As we shall see, that movement became one of the main forces pushing Arab thought into new areas of rational inquiry, where the first seeds of Arab-Islamic philosophical thought would begin to grow.

PreviousThe Era of the Rightly Guided CaliphsNextGeneral Review

General Review

Now that we have finished the first part of this study, we should pause for a general review of its main themes. This will help us preserve the unity and sequence of the argument and keep sight of our main purpose.

Our aim is to follow the historical process through which Arab thought developed alongside Arab society itself: from the pre-Islamic period, through the rise of Islam, and eventually into the Abbasid age, when Arab philosophy flourished alongside the experimental sciences, the rational sciences, and major changes in social relations.

We use the phrase “historical process” because we believe that Arab philosophy, when it finally emerged, was the mature result of much earlier intellectual seeds.

Those seeds were connected to roots already growing in Arab and Islamic societies. They developed within a historical setting shaped by social, political, religious, and cultural forces, all of which came together within the continuous process we have been describing.

For that reason, we have tried to study the concrete features of this philosophy in a way that follows the logic of the historical reality from which we believe it emerged.

This does not mean, of course, that we ignore the outside influences that later flowed into this process and helped turn it into a great river that continued for centuries.

What we mean is that we want to follow this river from its earliest springs, however small and limited they may first have been, until other streams began flowing into it from many directions, carrying the cultures of different peoples and rich elements from many civilizations.

In fact, when we say that Arab-Islamic philosophy belongs to the environments of Arab life itself, this already includes recognition of those outside influences. Arab life had by then become deeply mixed with the lives of the other peoples with whom the Arabs had come into contact through the same historical process.

We have deliberately paused to make this point because we want to preserve the connection between all parts of this study, from beginning to end.

Following the logic of the historical reality we have adopted, we therefore had to begin with the pre-Islamic period immediately before Islam.

This allowed us to look for Arab thought at its earliest visible sources, or in its earliest seeds. In other words, we began where the visible part of the long historical process that eventually led to philosophy first comes into view.

We have left aside the still earlier and much less visible part of that history, which stretches back for centuries before the Common Era, to the period when the ancient Arab states that later disappeared were still in existence.

This is the point from which our general review of Part One now begins.

A — The Pre-Islamic Period

What mattered to us in studying the pre-Islamic period was to see how Arab life was changing at that stage, the direction in which it was moving, and the role played by thought in that movement.

As far as we were able to determine, Chapter One led us to the following conclusions.

First: The people of the Arabian Peninsula had long maintained trading relationships with peoples at either end of the commercial routes that carried goods through Arabia along two major international routes.

Over time, these relationships went beyond the exchange of material goods and became channels of cultural interaction as well.

The Arabs did not remain mere carriers of other people’s goods. By the period immediately before Islam, they had become owners both of merchandise and of the means used to transport it.

This led to the rise of merchant groups and to the growth of many towns. Older settlements that had once been little more than large villages also expanded. Mecca, after developing into an important commercial center, came to be called the “Mother of Cities.”

This development also made it possible for some Arabs to become owners of agricultural land.

Byzantine gold coins and Persian silver coins came into widespread circulation across different parts of the peninsula.

At the same time, distinct social groups emerged whose wealth set them apart from the rest of society. They could accumulate money, merchandise, and valuable property, and they could exploit those who lacked such resources.

They employed poorer people in commercial caravans, agriculture, domestic service, and small crafts. They also lent money at extremely high rates of interest, or usury, placing borrowers under severe pressure.

This new social differentiation began to weaken the older system that had dominated the peninsula: the primitive tribal order.

A clearer division of labor appeared, along with early signs of class division. The exact form differed between the desert and the towns, especially Mecca, which had become the most developed center of this new class structure.

Second: This new social order inevitably began to create a political form suited to it.

That form appeared most clearly in Mecca, where social tensions had become sharper than elsewhere.

The leaders of Quraysh gathered in the Dār al-Nadwa, the assembly house where they discussed the organization of civic, economic, and religious affairs.

We regarded this as an early, embryonic form of the state.

The Dār al-Nadwa combined legislative and executive powers. Those powers belonged exclusively to the wealthy leaders, who imposed their decisions on the weaker and poorer sections of society.

Third: Religious life in this pre-Islamic society reflected both its intellectual condition and its social structure.

Religious ideas expressed new ways of thinking about relations between human beings, on the one hand, and between humanity, the universe, and nature, on the other.

We saw the social side of these religious developments appear in two main forms.

The first was the way the wealthy leaders of Mecca concentrated religious authority in their own hands and in their own city.

The Kaaba stood there, containing the idols of many tribes, whose members came on pilgrimage at particular times each year. These religious seasons also became commercial markets.

Religious leadership therefore gave the wealthy of Mecca a material basis for protecting their economic interests. It became an important source of profit and wealth and strengthened their “class” power.

The second form appeared in various local movements calling for people to abandon idol worship and worship instead a single, universal, invisible God.

The wealthy of Mecca opposed these movements because, at least in the short term, they threatened both their leadership and their material interests.

The conflict between Judaism and Christianity was another example of the way social struggles could appear in religious form.

We are referring especially to the conflict that developed in Yemen toward the end of the sixth century. It was clearly less a religious struggle than a conflict between local rulers and the Abyssinians, who wanted to control Yemen in the name of Christianity and were backed by the Byzantine state.

Religious life also had an intellectual side that appeared, on the surface at least, to have a degree of independence from these social conditions.

The various religious movements, along with spiritual and religious reflections, appeared in the sayings of the “wise men,” a recognized group in pre-Islamic Arabia; in the speeches of soothsayers; in the ideas of some poets; in widely repeated proverbs; and in certain myths.

All of these expressed new intellectual tendencies. They were accompanied by a simple form of rational debate, still at a very early level.

We can see examples of this kind of debate in the Qurʾan, when it describes the objections raised by Muhammad’s pre-Islamic opponents against the beliefs he preached during the earliest phase of the Islamic mission.

These objections show that some people in pre-Islamic Arabia had already developed forms of reflective thought about the nature of existence.

Some of them even seem to have thought about existence in a way resembling the natural philosophers of ancient Greece.

Muslims later called such people Dahriyya, because the Qurʾan describes them as saying:

“There is nothing but our first life. We die and we live, and nothing destroys us except time.”

In their different forms, these religious developments were the clearest cultural and intellectual expressions of the changes taking place in pre-Islamic Arab life as society moved toward a new stage of social and intellectual development.

At the same time, another area had developed to a striking degree: artistic expression, especially poetic language.

Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry remained a model even during later Islamic periods that were far more socially and intellectually developed.

This allowed us to conclude that this form of artistic expression, together with the remarkable richness of its language, must have been connected to a much longer earlier history. That history was not completely broken by the historical rupture between the ancient civilization of Arabia and the pre-Islamic period we are discussing here.

B — The Rise of Islam

We devoted Chapter Two of Part One to the period in which Islam arose.

Our examination of the beliefs introduced by Islam, the laws it established, and the many questions raised by this major event in Arab society led us to the following conclusions.

First: The new religion, Islam, had a clearly historical character.

This was true not only of its social message and religious beliefs, but also of many of its religious forms and doctrines.

In other words, Islam developed out of social, religious, and intellectual tendencies already moving within pre-Islamic society and pushing it toward historical change.

Islam expressed forms of human consciousness that could develop at that particular stage of human history—and not only of Arab history.

We also saw this historical character in the artistic form of Islam’s great central text, the Qurʾan.

The Qurʾanic text appeared as a remarkable and powerful development of the Arabic art of expression, which, as we have already seen, had reached a high level during the pre-Islamic period immediately before the rise of Islam.

Muslims regarded the Qurʾan as divine revelation and believed that human beings were incapable of producing anything like it.

Yet even with this belief, Muslims did not deny that the Qurʾan used the forms of Arabic eloquence itself, though in a form they regarded as higher, purer, and more magnificent.

There is no doubt that this is true.

But it also supports our argument that the Qurʾanic text has a historical character, in the sense that it represents the continued development of a cultural form already present in pre-Islamic life.

Second: Many of the beliefs preached by Islam were also found in Judaism, Christianity, and the Ḥanīf tradition.

These included beliefs about the creation of the universe, the Creator, one God, the coming into existence of the world, the afterlife, and resurrection, together with a strong rejection of idol worship.

In presenting its religious beliefs, the Qurʾan also addressed many questions that were already being widely debated in pre-Islamic society.

All of this supports the conclusion we reached in Chapter Two: Islam emerged from its own society and its own historical period.

It did not arrive on earth cut off from its historical relationship with this world—or, at the very least, with the part of the world in which it first appeared.

Third: These same religious beliefs contained, beneath their religious form, an expression of the level that social consciousness had reached among the people of that society.

We explained this through the principles of monotheism and resurrection.

We saw monotheism as a metaphysical expression of a real social development.

The new class divisions emerging in pre-Islamic society were beginning to break apart the narrow framework of tribal organization and create the need for a broader social framework capable of bringing people together into larger and more unified communities.

We interpreted the principle of resurrection in a similar way.

It gave metaphysical expression to the hopes of the poor masses: on the one hand, for compensation for the hardship of their material lives, and on the other, for justice against the higher social groups whose wealth set them apart or who oppressed them through exploitation.

Fourth: Many of the social laws introduced by Islam directly reflected the objective social conditions of the time.

They attempted to reduce the material suffering of the poor by banning usury and monopoly and by imposing certain taxes on the wealthy.

Islam also introduced laws regulating social relations, including relations connected with production.

But these laws remained within the basic framework of private property and the class differences that arose from it.

Fifth: Islam established a “theory” of knowledge, including knowledge of the general principles and rules of religious law, in which divine revelation was treated as the only source of those principles.

Human beings, meanwhile, were limited to knowledge gained through the senses and to the direct, purely empirical knowledge that sensory experience could provide.

In this way, Islam created a reciprocal relationship between knowledge and faith.

Within this framework, rational knowledge available to human beings could go no further than using sensory knowledge to support religious belief.

It was therefore natural for us to conclude that Islam closed the way to intellectual debate over matters of faith and questions concerning the world beyond nature.

Islamic texts do not leave this conclusion unsupported.

The Qurʾan and sayings attributed to the Prophet contain passages that either forbid or discourage debate over such questions.

But when Arab thought found this route to further development blocked, it turned in another direction: toward independent legal reasoning based on personal judgment in applying the general rules and principles of Islamic law.

It followed this path until historical conditions made it possible to reopen the first path as well—the path of rational debate over questions of faith and over the metaphysical nature of the universe.

Those conditions did eventually appear.

After the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, political and sectarian struggles became more intense. From those struggles came the living seeds of philosophical thought.

Those seeds then developed naturally within Arab-Islamic life until, in the ninth century CE, they produced what became known as Arab philosophy.

C — The Age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

We devoted Chapter Three of Part One to the most important historical developments of this period.

These developments created the setting in which different forms of religious conflict and later political and sectarian conflict took shape.

This conflict matters to our study because, once the Umayyad period began, much of it developed into an intellectual and “ideological” struggle.

Other intellectual and ideological currents either became part of this struggle or developed alongside it. These included the Muʿtazila, the current represented by the ideas of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, the Qadariyya, and others.

Chapter Three also examined another major historical development of the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs: the Arab conquests, which began during the rule of the second caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

The importance of these conquests for our study lies in their major role in placing Arab thought on the path that would eventually lead toward scientific and philosophical thinking.

The conquests created the historical conditions for social and cultural interaction between the Arabs and the peoples of the conquered countries.

That interaction later played an enormous role in shaping the distinctive features of Arab culture and Arab thought.

It also brought together internal and external cultural elements, and Arab philosophy was one of the products of that combination.

Our discussion in this chapter took place within the framework of all these historical developments.

Within that same framework, we can now present the main conclusions reached during the chapter.

First: The struggle over the caliphate that broke out immediately after the Prophet’s death released a form of social conflict that had previously taken different forms during his lifetime.

At the beginning of Islam, the main conflict had been between two sides: the new religion and its followers on one side, and the wealthy leaders of Quraysh and their traditions on the other.

Later, after Islam spread and defeated its opponents in Mecca following the Hijra, the main conflict changed.

On one side stood the Helpers and the Emigrants. On the other stood tribes that continued to hold on to their pre-Islamic traditions and social arrangements.

After the Prophet’s death, however, the main contradiction shifted again.

This time, the opposing sides were Muslims themselves.

The caliphate, as a religious office, appeared to be the main issue around which the conflict revolved.

Behind it, however, lay social motives and the desire to control the political power that came with the office.

One striking fact is that the Ridda Wars, which occupied the Muslims immediately after the Prophet’s death, did not replace the caliphate as the central issue in this conflict.

Even the wars of conquest, which began moving beyond the Arabian Peninsula under the second caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, while the Ridda Wars had not yet fully ended, failed to shift the main conflict away from the question of the caliphate.

Another striking point is the remarkable success Muslims achieved in both the Ridda Wars and the wars of conquest even though the central conflict over the caliphate remained unresolved.

The reason was that the different Muslim groups shared certain social interests: suppressing the rebellion within Arabia and expanding Arab territory beyond the peninsula.

These shared interests helped push the dispute over the caliphate into the form of a religious disagreement over the nature of the office itself.

Was the caliphate a divine office, or was it a worldly political office whose holder should be chosen by Muslims themselves?

Behind this religious form, however, we saw a deeper social difference.

The idea of the caliphate as a divine office expressed, in our view, the hopes of ordinary people for social justice.

The idea of the caliphate as a worldly political office expressed the interests of the wealthy aristocracy.

This religious form of the conflict remained clearly visible on the surface of events only during the reigns of the first two caliphs, Abu Bakr and ʿUmar.

Second: Beginning with the reign of the third caliph, ʿUthmān, the religious form of the struggle over the caliphate increasingly revealed its social and political basis.

One important reason was the conduct of the governors who represented the caliph in the provinces under his rule.

Their main concern became personal enrichment, often through outright seizure.

They took possession of other people’s land and imposed heavy taxes on the population.

Discontent with these policies grew and accumulated in different regions until it developed into a social revolt.

Groups of ordinary people came in delegations from several provinces to Mecca and Medina to protest to Caliph ʿUthmān and demand that he give up the caliphate.

When he refused, the delegations surrounded him in his house, and he was eventually killed.

Some of the political factions struggling for power in Mecca and Medina had played a part in pushing the revolt toward this outcome.

After ʿUthmān’s death, some of these same political forces used his killing as a pretext to redirect the legitimate social revolt against unjust governors.

The political struggle was driven back toward its original center—the struggle over the caliphate itself—but now in a much sharper and more violent form.

This directly led to a series of “internal” wars among Muslim leaders.

These included the Battle of the Camel in Basra, fought between ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib on one side and Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr, led by the Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾisha, on the other.

They also included the Battle of Ṣiffīn between the armies of ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya.

Then came the wars of the Kharijites, who had broken away from ʿAlī’s ranks at Ṣiffīn and formed a new party that fought both ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya after declaring both of them unbelievers.

Third: The wars of conquest did not unfold separately from the “internal” events created by these political struggles among Muslim leaders.

The policies followed by the conquerors in the territories under their rule were strongly affected by the course of these conflicts.

Their effects spread through the conquered lands, and Muslims there divided between supporters of one side and supporters of another.

ʿAlī had a large following in Iraq and Iran, while Muʿāwiya’s supporters were dominant in Syria.

In Egypt, factional loyalties were less visible among the ordinary population.

They appeared more clearly, however, in the views of jurists and transmitters of the Prophet’s sayings among the Companions and their followers.

In other words, the division was strongest among educated circles and people known for forming and expressing considered opinions.

Fourth: For most of the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, Arab rule in the conquered countries remained mainly military in character.

The conquerors built cities that were originally intended as bases for their armies, and the way they lived in these cities kept them separated from the lives of the local population.

This military character delayed the process of cultural and social interaction.

Later, as we shall see, that interaction would have enormous consequences for the development of Arab thought and Arab culture.

    Two examples may be useful here. 1. Abd al-Rahman Badawi in his book Aristotle (Cairo, 1964, 4th ed.). 2. Tayyib Tizini in the work cited above. Badawi, as an idealist thinker, argues that for Aristotle true existence is the existence of essences, and that there is no difference between Plato and Aristotle in their view of the “status of existence” (p. 55). He also says that “the central idea in Aristotle, running through every part of his system, is the idea of matter and form” (p. 282). Tizini, by contrast, as a materialist thinker, argues that Aristotle’s basic principle is the objective, real existence of the material world, and that consciousness—thought or essence—derives from the existence of that material world. Tizini therefore believes that this basic principle in Aristotle must be brought clearly to the foreground, because it is here that Aristotle breaks decisively with Plato’s theory of abstract forms, with “Platonism” itself (p. 101). Tizini further argues that Aristotle’s concept of substance, insofar as it includes the eternity of matter in general, marked a major and fundamental step toward a precise dialectical-materialist concept of matter (p. 121).↩︎

    In Marxism, the Leninist theoretical principle for identifying stages in the history of philosophy rests on the idea that philosophical development results from a unity of quantitative and qualitative change—that is, from a unity between gradual development and breaks within that development. Engels explains this unity through the law of the negation of the negation. He writes: “Ancient philosophy was spontaneous materialism. For that reason it could not explain the relation between thought and matter. But the need to clarify this question led to teachings about a soul distinct from the body, then to the claim that the soul was immortal, and finally to spiritualism—that is, the unity of soul and body. In this way ancient materialism was negated by idealism. But idealism itself, in the later development of philosophy, also proved unable to sustain itself, and it too was negated by modern materialism. Modern materialism is therefore a negation of the negation. It is not simply a continuation of ancient materialism. Rather, it adds to the enduring foundations of ancient materialism the whole intellectual content produced by two thousand years of philosophical and natural-scientific development, as well as by the development of history itself over those two thousand years” (Engels). See Anti-Dühring, chapter 12, “Dialectics: Negation of the Negation”; Arabic translation by Fu’ad Ayyub, Dar Dimashq, 1st ed., 1965, pp. 165–166.↩︎

  22. 22

    Marxists explain the flourishing of classical German philosophy in the nineteenth century, despite Germany’s economic backwardness compared with other European countries at the time, in two ways. First, they see it as one expression of philosophy’s relative independence from the economic base. Second, they see it as the result of two sets of factors: external European factors and internal German ones. In Germany, quantitative changes were accumulating within a process of development. So although the country’s economic and political conditions were still relatively backward in qualitative terms, there was movement within them: a process of formation through accumulating quantitative changes. These accumulations could then turn into new qualitative forms—political, intellectual, or theoretical.↩︎

    Lenin exposed the partisanship of idealist philosophers through concrete examples, despite the many masks behind which their philosophical partisanship could hide. Lenin described neutrality in philosophy as “a disguised baseness, concealing idealism and fideism” (p. 354). In the conclusion to the book (p. 358), he wrote: “Modern philosophy is partisan, just as it was two thousand years ago, and the two parties struggling against each other are, in essence, materialism and idealism.”↩︎

    Thales (621–550 BCE) tried to develop a fairly integrated view of the world as a unified material whole. He believed that water was the original basis of everything that exists, and that the earth was a round cylinder resting in water.↩︎

    Anaximenes (588–524 BCE) believed that air was the basis of everything that exists, and that all things in the world arise through the condensation and rarefaction of air.↩︎

  33. 33

    Anaximander (611–547 BCE) approached the origin of the world differently. He argued that the world’s basis did not lie in a concrete material substance, but in an indeterminate substance he called the apeiron. Existing things arise through the interaction of cold and hot, two inseparable qualities of the infinite apeiron. The apeiron is an abstract category, comparable to the category of matter in Marxism.↩︎

  34. 34

    Heraclitus (520–470 BCE). Materialist historians of philosophy associate Heraclitus with the emergence of dialectics as an almost fully developed method for analyzing everything that exists. Lenin believed that Heraclitus expressed some essential points of dialectics very well (Philosophical Notebooks). Heraclitus held that the basis of everything must be material and that fire was the primary material basis. Fire is in constant motion and change, continually coming into being and passing away. He gave a material explanation of the soul. Everything turns into something else according to the law of necessity.↩︎

  35. 35

    Democritus (second half of the fifth century BCE), together with Leucippus and Anaxagoras, founded the atomist school. They assumed the existence of an infinite number of indivisible particles moving through empty space. These particles, absolutely dense and differing in shape and size, are atoms; atoms and the void are eternal. Against Zeno, Democritus defended the validity of sensory knowledge without setting it against rational knowledge. Nothing exists in the world except atoms and the void. He held that existence and time are eternal. Everything that exists does so for a cause and by necessity; even chance has a cause. He also explained the existence of the gods in material terms.↩︎

  36. 36

    Epicurus (341–270 BCE). His philosophy represents the highest stage in the development of ancient Greek atomism. In his theory of knowledge he takes a sensory approach and begins from materialist positions. Like Democritus, he holds that only atoms and the void exist, and that all things and natural phenomena are different combinations of atoms. Coming into being and passing away are simply processes of atoms joining together and separating. Nothing comes from nothing, and nothing turns into nothing. He went beyond Democritus on the question of the weight of atoms, affirming that atoms have weight. He looked for the source of atomic motion within the atoms themselves—that is, for an internal, self-generated source of material motion. His idea that atoms deviate from a straight path contributed to the development of ancient Greek materialism. He linked happiness to knowledge: there can be no happiness without understanding humanity’s place in the world and freeing people from fear—fear of the gods, death, and an unseen afterlife. He denied that the gods intervene in nature, human destiny, or the world. His school was the last major materialist school of ancient Greek philosophy.↩︎

  37. 37

    In the Christian Middle Ages, nominalism and realism were the two main currents within which the various schools of Scholastic philosophy developed. They were the historically distinctive form taken by the struggle between materialism and idealism within that philosophy: nominalism represented the materialist side, while realism represented the idealist side. The nominalists denied the real existence of universals—essences—and affirmed the real existence of individual things, arguing that the universal exists only as a name. The realists, by contrast, held that universals had real existence apart from individual things. Among the best-known representatives of Scholastic realism were John Scotus Eriugena (810–877), followed by the philosopher-theologian Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury. Among the best-known nominalists was the French philosopher Roscelin (1050–1120), whose view that the word “universal” is merely a verbal label with no reality of its own is considered one of the earliest expressions of materialist nominalism in medieval Scholasticism. He was followed by English representatives of nominalism, the best known being Duns Scotus (1274–1208), Roger Bacon (1214–1294), and William of Ockham (–1341).↩︎

    Lange was a major representative of bourgeois philosophy and a historian of philosophy. He became famous for a work described as the first major study in bourgeois materialist history. In 1866 he published History of Materialism and Critique of Its Importance in the Present Age. It was reissued in 1969, when bourgeois philosophers believed that the study had finally destroyed materialism.↩︎

    Calls to break with the Arab cultural heritage appeared in different forms and within different ideological currents. They first appeared in the first third of the twentieth century as calls to replace the Arabic alphabet with the Latin alphabet, gradually cutting people off from that heritage. This appeared in two currents. One was in Lebanon, represented by Father Marun Ghusn and later Sa‘id Aql, and was driven by a sectarian political aim: isolating Lebanon from its Arab surroundings as an expression of the ideology of the colonial Lebanese bourgeoisie. The second appeared in Egypt, represented by Abd al-Aziz Fahmi and Salama Musa. This current expressed the ideology of the emerging Egyptian bourgeoisie, based on an Egyptian nationalism separate from Arab nationalism. The slogan of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution was “Egypt for the Egyptians.” After the Arab-Israeli war of June 1967, the same call appeared in another form, under the claim that the Arab defeat resulted from “civilizational” factors rooted in the country’s “civilizational” backwardness and reflected in the literature of the Arab intellectual heritage itself. This newer form appeared in two ways: in literature and in theoretical thought. It appeared artistically, for example in the poetry of Unsi al-Hajj and Nizar Qabbani, and theoretically in the Kuwait symposium on “The Crisis of Arab Civilizational Development,” held in April 1974; see al-Adab, Beirut, no. 5, 1974. In the papers presented at this symposium, the idea of discarding the heritage appeared only indirectly, and perhaps unintentionally, but the logic of the arguments leads in that direction.↩︎

  43. 43

    When we speak of the originality of Arab thought—by which we mean all intellectual work originally written in Arabic, rather than translated into it—we mean that this thought is objectively connected to a particular historical and social reality, which it reflects in its own distinctive ways. We insist on this originality for two reasons. First, to affirm this connection as a methodological principle. Second, to affirm the dialectical unity between originality and contemporaneity, or modernity, and therefore to reject the colonial-bourgeois concept of “modernity” detached from originality. Colonialism spent a long period trying, in the cultural sphere, to implant this concept in the minds of the Arab intelligentsia. Its aim was to make it possible to cut modern Arab thought off from its own history—its originality—and redirect it toward ideological dependence on colonial Western thought.↩︎

    Here too, Ibn Khaldun is an exception. Speaking about the translation of Greek philosophy into Arabic, he writes: “Muslim thinkers devoted themselves to it and mastered its branches. Their investigations reached the furthest limits in these sciences. They agreed with many views of the First Teacher [Aristotle] and disagreed with many others, accepting or rejecting them because his fame had become the standard of reference. They wrote major works on these subjects and surpassed those who had come before them in these sciences. Among the greatest of them within the Muslim community were Abu Nasr al-Farabi and Abu Ali Ibn Sina in the East, and Qadi Abu al-Walid Ibn Rushd and the minister Abu Bakr Ibn al-Sa’igh in al-Andalus, along with others who reached the highest level in these sciences.” Muqaddima, book 6, chapter 13, p. 865, Beirut ed. This does not contradict Ibn Khaldun’s statement in chapter 15 of the same book, p. 971, that Muslim philosophers adopted the doctrines of earlier thinkers, led by Aristotle, following his view “step for step except in a few matters.” In that later passage, Ibn Khaldun is speaking specifically about the structure of the cosmos, not philosophy as a whole. He is discussing the philosophers’ denial concerning the world of the celestial spheres.↩︎

    In the terminology of early historians, classification into “classes” (tabaqat) was not based on social class in the modern sense. It usually meant chronological grouping. A “class” could therefore mean a generation of poets, hadith scholars, philosophers, and so on, with a generation usually spanning between ten and twenty years. Sometimes a geographical criterion was used, as Ibn Sa‘d did in his Great Book of Classes when he arranged biographies of the Companions according to the cities where they settled. See Ibn Sa‘d, Classes, Dar Sadir/Dar Beirut, 1957, Ihsan Abbas’s introduction, vol. 1, p. 12. Books of tabaqat, then, are specialized biographical works devoted to a particular group of historically important people. This form of writing among Arabs and Muslims goes back to the third century AH. Al-Waqidi may have been the first to write in this form, followed by his student Muhammad ibn Sa‘d; both wrote about hadith scholars. In the same century, many literary writers produced books on classes of poets, such as Ibn Sallam’s Classes, Ibn Qutayba’s Poetry and Poets, and Ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s Classes of Poets. Later came works on the “classes” of physicians, sages, Shi‘is, Shafi‘is, and so on.↩︎

  97. 97

    The history of Arabic literature gives us an example in which most of these personal, class, and ideological motives come together, along with a desire to flatter the ruling power. Abdallah ibn al-Mu‘tazz (247–296 AH), whose caliphate lasted no more than a day and part of another day, wrote a book called Classes of Poets, containing biographies of about 127 male and female poets from the Abbasid period. Three points about this book were noted by its editors, Abd al-Sattar Ahmad Farraj and Abbas Iqbal. First, Ibn al-Mu‘tazz ignores several of the greatest poets of his age, including Ibn al-Rumi (221–283 AH). He also ignores Ibn al-Rumi in his book al-Badi‘. Why, when Ibn al-Rumi was such an important poetic figure in the Arabic tradition? The editor and publisher Abd al-Sattar Farraj links this omission to two positions taken by Ibn al-Rumi. First, Ibn al-Rumi had satirized al-Mu‘tazz, the author’s father, after he was removed from the caliphate. Second, Ibn al-Rumi “was closely associated with al-Qasim ibn Ubayd Allah, one of Abdallah ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s enemies, who advised that he be arrested when al-Mu‘tadid died.” Here the motive is personal. Second, Ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s book gives biographies of poets who praised or had connections with the Abbasid caliphs (...) and gathers poetry stamped with the outlook of poets dependent on Abbasid caliphs, ministers, and leading officials. It also tries to reveal the relationship between each poet and the person he praised (Abbas Iqbal). Here the motive is class-based and ideological. Third, the editors observe that despite Ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s fame and the importance of his book, later biographers rarely mentioned it; “it was as though most of them did not know it.” Abd al-Sattar Farraj points to a convincing political reason: “al-Muqtadir returned to the caliphate and remained caliph for more than twenty years after Ibn al-Mu‘tazz was killed. There is no doubt that most transmitters do not favor someone from whom power has turned away and whom the events of time have brought down.” This is a case of flattering the ruling power. See Ibn al-Mu‘tazz, Classes of Poets, edited by Abd al-Sattar Ahmad Farraj, Dar al-Ma‘arif, Egypt, no date, pp. 10, 12, 583, 588.↩︎
